![numbered Display Equation](images/c02_M0024.gif)

*or equivalently the class-averaged inaccuracy,* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c02-disp-0025" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c02\_M0025.gif"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>C</mi></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2260;</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c02_M0025.gif)

*Show that the class-averaged inaccuracy of* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0115.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c02_ILM0115.gif)*is the risk* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0116.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c02_ILM0116.gif)*corresponding to the loss function* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c02-disp-0026" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c02\_M0026.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> if </mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>C</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> if </mi><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x2260;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c02_M0026.gif)

*Does it make sense for a loss function to depend on the number of classes? Does it make sense for a loss function to depend on the marginal distribution of the class labels?*

## 2.6 The Reality of the Unknown Function

A reasonable question to ask at this point is whether the unknown function *f*, or the joint probability distribution <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0117.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c02_ILM0117.gif), actually exists. One quick and easy answer is that this is a mathematical model which is rich enough to be broadly applicable and simple enough to analyze, and as such, it is defensible on purely utilitarian grounds.

A somewhat more nuanced answer is that we use the language of probability to express our imperfect state of knowledge about the world. The data which we observe were generated by a process which we do not fully understand: we introduce <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0118.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c02_ILM0118.gif)as a name for this process, and use the theory of probability both to derive names for various aspects of the unknown process (such as the conditional distribution <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0119.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c02_ILM0119.gif)and the marginal distribution <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0120.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c02_ILM0120.gif)) and also to enable us to quantify our uncertainty about the process. If we accept using probability in this way, and accept as our goal the development of a function <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0121.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c02_ILM0121.gif)which has low risk when used for prediction (recall that the idea of risk follows from <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0122.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c02_ILM0122.gif)but does *not* require that we accept the existence of an unknown function *f*), then the existence of an unknown function *f* to be learned is straightforward. Given the joint distribution <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0123.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c02_ILM0123.gif)and a point *X* = *x* at which to predict a response or class *Y*, compute the risk of predicting every possible value of *Y* at *X* = *x*, and predict a value of *Y* which corresponds to the minimal risk, breaking any ties, if there are multiple distinct values of *Y* which are minimal-risk predictions at *x*, in some deterministic but arbitrary way.^([18](#c02.xhtml#c02-note-0018)) Define *f* to be the function which makes these minimal-risk predictions. This will be revisited in the context of classification with the development of the Bayes classifier in [Section 4.1](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0002).

## 2.7 Training and Selection of Models, and Purposes of Learning

Given a practically computable optimality criterion (training risk, for example) for approximations of *f*, a major goal is to find an optimal approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0124.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c02_ILM0124.gif)in the set of all functions <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0125.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c02_ILM0125.gif). Generally, this set is too large to search effectively. The purpose of each regression or classification method is to specify a subset <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0126.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![](images/c02_ILM0126.gif)of the set functions mapping <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0127.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c02_ILM0127.gif)which is simultaneously small enough that an approximately optimal approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0128.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c02_ILM0128.gif)can be found and big enough that <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0129.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c02_ILM0129.gif)is close to *f*, the true function, in many applications.

Specification of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0130.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![](images/c02_ILM0130.gif)is called *model assumption* and, given <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0131.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![](images/c02_ILM0131.gif), computation of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0132.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c02_ILM0132.gif)from a dataset *S* is called *training a model*. Sometimes <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0133.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![](images/c02_ILM0133.gif)can be described by a finite number of scalar parameters, in which case the method which gave rise to it is called a *parametric method*. Otherwise, the method is called a *non-parametric method*.^([19](#c02.xhtml#c02-note-0019))

There are at least two reasons for solving the Problem of Learning. The first reason is that in the future, we will be presented with unmarked feature vectors, *X*[*n* + 1], …, and will be asked to make predictions <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0134.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c02_ILM0134.gif)of the unobserved responses or class labels. Solving the Problem of Learning in this case is *predictive learning* or *predictive modeling*.

The second reason for solving the Problem of Learning is to find relationships between observed features vectors *x*[1], …, *x[n]* and their corresponding observed response or class labels *y*[1], …, *y[n]*, in order to enhance human understanding of the process by which the data were generated. This enhanced understanding often serves an applied purpose, or it may be a goal in and of itself. The data of Problem 2 (“Ballot”), for example, might reveal relationships between demographic features and voting behavior which could be used by political parties in various ways. Solving the Problem of Learning in this case is *explanatory learning* or *explanatory modeling*.

In any given application, the two reasons for solving the Problem of Learning are not necessarily exclusive. One may wish both to predict and to explain.^([20](#c02.xhtml#c02-note-0020)) The relative emphasis on prediction or explanation may influence the choice of approximation method. An approximation method might not be used for explanatory modeling, even if it has low risk, if the structure of the approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0135.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c02_ILM0135.gif)it produces does not reveal easily interpreted relationships between *x*[1], …, *x[n]* and *y*[1], …, *y[n]*. Such an approximation method also might not be used for predictive modeling, as some clients are reluctant to trust an approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0136.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c02_ILM0136.gif)which has not been validated through interpretation by experts in the field of the application. This book focuses primarily on predictive modeling, because it has been called for more often than explanatory modeling in the author’s experience.

## 2.8 Notation

Throughout this book, unobserved feature vectors and responses (or classes), thought of as random variables on <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0137.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>![](images/c02_ILM0137.gif)and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0138.gif"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c02_ILM0138.gif), are denoted by upper-case letters *X* and *Y* respectively. Specific values of feature vectors and responses (or classes), thought of as fixed points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0139.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>![](images/c02_ILM0139.gif)and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0140.gif"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c02_ILM0140.gif), are denoted by lower-case letters *x* and *y* respectively (sometimes *y* is replaced by *c* or *d* in the case of classes). Context should prevent confusion in the rare exceptions. A list of notation is provided in Appendix A.

The letter <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0141.gif"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></math>![](images/c02_ILM0141.gif)denotes both the probability of an event *and* a probability density or mass function. In the latter case, the density or mass function may be multiplied by a positive, non-unit constant. Application and convenience determine whether <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0142.gif"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></math>![](images/c02_ILM0142.gif)integrates or sums to one or to some other positive number. By way of example, consider <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c02\_ILM0143.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace ![numbered Display Equation](images/c02_M0027.gif)

If we are asked to choose, from a set of approximations, an optimal one, then these density or mass functions can be multiplied by any positive constant without changing the result: in particular, normalizing constants of certain statistical models can be ignored for analytical or computational convenience. But if we are asked what is the risk of a particular approximation, these functions must integrate or sum to one.

## Notes

# 3  
Regression

> A statistical model involves the identification of those elements of our problem which are subject to uncontrolled variation and a specification of that variation in terms of probability distributions.
> 
> —David J. Bartholomew, *Unobserved Variables: Models and Misunderstandings*, 2013
> 
> Essentially, all models are wrong, but some are useful.
> 
> —George E. P. Box and Norman R. Draper, *Empirical Model Building and Response Surfaces*, 1987

This is the one chapter in this book which is dedicated to regression, and it presents regression mostly from the classical, statistical, least-squares point of view. We open the discussion of practical learning methods with least-squares regression for (at least) four reasons. First, it is *useful:* the underlying model assumptions are, in many applications, close enough to correct that this method has been widely used in the literature of many scientific domains.^([1](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0001)) Second, it is *relatively easy to treat analytically*, and a study of the analysis and the closed-form solutions it yields can provide insight into “what is going on” with this approach to regression. The author hopes this will lead to more informed application. The exercises of this chapter are an integral part of the analytic development (solutions, as always, can be found in Appendix B). Third, it enables *the transformation of classification problems into regression problems*, which is an approach taken by logistic regression and neural networks in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml). Finally, *the thorough understanding we have of least-squares regression sets the bar high for what is to follow in later chapters* where, generally speaking, our theoretical understanding is not as complete.^([2](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0002)) Perhaps the contrast will motivate some readers to improve the current state of the art.

For simplicity, in [Sections 3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0002) through [3.7](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0008), the domain of the function *f* which is to be learned is assumed to be the *m*\-dimensional real numbers, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0001.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c03_ILM0001.gif). Categorical features are addressed in [Section 3.8](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0009) and adding flexibility to a linear model by expanding and transforming the features or response is addressed in [Section 3.9](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0010). The range of *f* will always be <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0002.gif"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>![](images/c03_ILM0002.gif), except as briefly mentioned in [Section 3.10](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0011).

Linear regression is an old technique^([3](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0003)) and the subject of a large and excellent literature. The reader is directed to Rawlings et al. (2001) for a thorough introduction to the theory and practice of fitting linear regression models to data, and to Searle (1971) for more in-depth development of the theory.

## 3.2 Loss

Although choice of loss function is subjective, squared-error loss <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0005" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0005.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0005.gif)

is by far the most commonly used, with absolute-error loss <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0006" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0006.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>y</mi><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0006.gif)

a distant second. This is partly a matter of computational and analytic convenience, though Exercise 3.7 shows that squared-error loss also arises naturally from an additional model assumption and a widely used parameter estimation criterion. An advantage of absolute-error loss is that the fitted model is more robust to outliers in the data and so regression with absolute-error loss is sometimes called *robust regression*. This chapter addresses squared-error loss exclusively.

**Exercise 3.1** *Suppose that there are no observable features, and that the response *Y* is real-valued, so the linear model of [Section 3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0002) is Y* = *θ*[0] *plus mean-zero noise. The predicted value for future Y*’s is *θ*[0]. *Compute the risk of predicting any given value of θ*[0], *and find the risk-minimizing value or values of θ*[0], *under*

1.  squared-error loss, and
2.  absolute-error loss.

**Hint:** The answers will be in terms of the distribution of Y. For part (B), the fact that <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com"><msup><mo>&#x222b;</mo><msub><mo>&#x03b8;</mo><mn>0</mn></msub></msup></math>![](images/ex3_1.jpg)dt <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com"><msub><mrow><msup><mo>&#x222b;</mo><mo>&#x221e;</mo></msup></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>&#x03b8;</mo><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></msub></math> may be useful, and it may be assumed that the cumulative distribution function of *Y* is continuous on <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0005.gif"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>![](images/c03_ILM0005.gif)or, even more, that *Y* has a density function on <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0006.gif"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>![](images/c03_ILM0006.gif).

## 3.3 Estimating the Model Parameters

Given an (*m* + 1)-long (column) parameter vector *θ*, the linear model predicts that at point <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0007" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0007.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0007.gif)

in feature space, the response will be <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0008" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0008.gif"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0008.gif)

The difference between an actual response *y[i]* from observed datum (*x[i]*, *y[i]*) and the predicted response (1, *x[i]*)*θ* is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0009" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0009.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0009.gif)

Viewed this way, *e[i]* is what is left over from the observed response, after the effect of the model has been removed. For this reason, *e*[1], …, *e[n]* are called *residuals*.

Using training risk as an estimate of risk, searching for a minimum-risk approximation to *f*[*θ*] is equivalent to searching for a parameter vector *θ* which minimizes the training risk, close=")"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></mfenced><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msubsup><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi> RSS </mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0010.gif)

Note that the training risk is equal to the sum of the squares of the residuals: it is called the *residual sum of squares* and denoted RSS. Since minimizing training risk is equivalent to minimizing the residual sum of squares, fitting a linear model under squared-error loss is called *least-squares linear regression*.^([5](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0005)) Minimizing the quadratic form (**y** − **x***θ*)^T(**y** − **x***θ*) over <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0007.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0007.gif)is an exercise in multivariate calculus.

**Exercise 3.2** Show that the unique minimizer of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0008.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> train </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></mfenced><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0008.gif)is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0014" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0014.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0014.gif)

*when* **x** *is of full rank.*^([6](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0006))

With respect to squared-error loss, using training risk to estimate risk, the optimal linear approximation is <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0010.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0010.gif).

## 3.4 Properties of Fitted Values

Let <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0011.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c03_ILM0011.gif)denote the least-squares estimate for *θ* found in Exercise 3.2, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0012.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0012.gif). These are the *fitted model parameters*. Let **i** denote the *n* × *n* identity matrix and let **h** denote the *n* × *n* matrix **x**(**x**^T**x**)^(− 1)**x**^T. The *fitted response* and the *fitted residuals* are respectively <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0015" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0015.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mspace width="2.em"/><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="2.em"/><mspace width="1.em"/><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">i</mi><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0015.gif)

Given a new feature vector *x*[*n* + 1] which does not appear in the training data, the *predicted response* at *x*[*n* + 1] is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0016" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0016.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0016.gif)

**Exercise 3.3** *The symmetric n* × *n matrix* **h** = **x**(**x**^T**x**)^(− 1)**x**^T *is called the hat matrix because multiplication by* **h** *“puts the hat on* **y***” in the sense that* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0013.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0013.gif). *Prove three properties of the hat matrix:*

1.  **hh** = **h**, *that is*, **h** *is idempotent;*
2.  **hx** = **x**, *that is,* **h** *acts as the identity map on the column space of the design matrix **x**;*
3.  **h***z* = 0 *for any n-long vector z orthogonal to the column space of* **x**. **Hint:** *This will be useful in Exercises 3.4 and 3.5.*

Together, parts (A), (B), and (C) of Exercise 3.3 say that left multiplication by **h** is a linear projection of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0014.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![](images/c03_ILM0014.gif)into the column space of **x**. The column space of **x** is precisely the set of *n*\-long vectors of the form <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0017" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0017.gif"><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>11</mn></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>12</mn></msub></mtd><mtd><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>21</mn></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>22</mn></msub></mtd><mtd><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd/><mtd><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mspace width="4pt"/><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0017.gif)

that is, the column space of **x** is the space of *n*\-long vectors which can be realized as the response of some linear model applied to the inputs *x*[1], *x*[2], …, *x[n]* with no error.

The fundamental random thing in the linear model is the vector of residuals, **e**, with <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0018" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0018.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="2.em"/><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="2.em"/><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> Var </mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">i</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0018.gif)

From this, it follows that **y** is also random,^([7](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0007)) with <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0019" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0019.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mspace width="2.em"/><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="2.em"/><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> Var </mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">i</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0019.gif)

and therefore all of the fitted and predicted values, being linear functions of **y**, are also random.

accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![](images/c03_ILM0015.gif)*is the estimated response at x*[*n* + 1]: <displayedItem mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

*Note that σ*² *and θ are unknown, while* **y**, **x**, **h**, **i**, *and x*[*n* + 1] *are known.* **Hint:** *Recall that the variance of a real random variable *Z* satisfies* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0016.gif"><mrow><mi> Var </mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mi>Z</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msup><mi>Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mi>Z</mi></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0016.gif).

The exercise shows that the fitted and predicted values are unbiased estimates of the quantities they are estimating: the *bias* of an estimator <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0017.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c03_ILM0017.gif)of a fixed quantity *z* is <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0018.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mo>\[</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>\]</mo><mo>-</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0018.gif), and an estimator is *unbiased* if its bias is zero. In particular, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0019.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c03_ILM0019.gif)is an unbiased estimate of the model parameters, *θ*. Historically, unbiasedness has been considered a desirable property, and effort concentrated on finding optimal unbiased estimates, where *optimal* usually meant *minimal variance* under certain restrictions. Since the 1960’s, however, it has been appreciated that biased parameter estimates can lead to better predictive linear models, and that there is a *bias–variance trade-off* to be managed. [Chapter 5](#c05.xhtml) is devoted entirely to the bias–variance trade-off, beginning with the case of least-squares regression.

Two other sums of squares will be useful later: the *total sum of squares* is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0021" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0021.gif"><mrow><mi> TSS </mi><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0021.gif)

where <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0020.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0020.gif)is the mean response in the data. The TSS measures the overall variability of the observed response about its mean: it is (*n* − 1) or *n* times the sample variance of the response.^([8](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0008)) It is a property only of the data, not of the linear model.^([9](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0009)) The *model sum of squares* is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0022" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0022.gif"><mrow><mi> MSS </mi><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0022.gif)

The MSS measures the overall variability of the fitted values about the mean observed response. When MSS is large relative to TSS, the fitted values vary about the mean, and they can only do so through the presence of some estimated linear effect (that is, because some of the components of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0022.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c03_ILM0022.gif)are not zero). Conversely, when MSS is small relative to TSS, this suggests that the fitted linear model does not explain much of the variability in the data. In terms of fitted values, the residual sum of squares is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0023" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0023.gif"><mrow><mi> RSS </mi><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0023.gif)

and it measures the variability of the observed response around the fitted response: a way to interpret this is as the variability in the data *not* explained by the linear model.

**Exercise 3.5** *Show that* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0024" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0024.gif"><mrow><mi> TSS </mi><mo>=</mo><mi> MSS </mi><mo>+</mo><mi> RSS </mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0024.gif)

**Hint:** *TSS, MSS, and RSS are the squared lengths of certain vectors. Show that one of these vectors is the sum of the other two, and that the two summands are orthogonal to each other.*

A statistic for assessing the quality of a fitted model, denoted *R*², is defined in terms of RSS, MSS, and TSS: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0025" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0025.gif"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mi> RSS </mi><mi> TSS </mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi> MSS </mi><mi> TSS </mi></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0025.gif)

It is interpreted as the proportion of the variation in the observed response which is explained by the model. See [Section 7.9](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0015) for further discussion, including a modification of *R*², called *adjusted R*², which balances the proportion of variation explained against the number of non-zero parameters in the model.

## 3.5 Estimating the Variance

There is another parameter in the model to be addressed: σ², the variance of the residuals. It is not important for determining the least-squares estimate of the model parameters *θ*—we have seen that <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0029.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0029.gif)—but estimating σ² is essential for making statistical inferences about the response in terms of fitted or predicted values.

The last line of Exercise 3.4 (<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0031.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mo>\[</mo><mover accent="true"><mi xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0033.gif"><mrow><mi> RSS mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0033.gif)) can be applied to show that <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" tr </mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

Recalling a result from linear algebra, and assuming **x** is full rank,^([10](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0010)) <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0028" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0028.gif"><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> tr </mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi> tr </mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi> tr </mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi> tr </mi><mo>(</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mrow><mi> identity </mi><mi> matrix </mi></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0028.gif)

so <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0029" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0029.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mi> RSS </mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0029.gif)

Thus an unbiased estimate for the residual variance σ² is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0030" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0030.gif"><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi> RSS </mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0030.gif)

## 3.6 A Normality Assumption

We now add the assumption that the residuals are Gaussian-distributed, that is, that *e*[1], …, *e[n]* are independent, identically distributed <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0037.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0037.gif). It then follows that **y**, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0038.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c03_ILM0038.gif), <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0039.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c03_ILM0039.gif), <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0040.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![](images/c03_ILM0040.gif), and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0041.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c03_ILM0041.gif)are also Gaussian-distributed with the means and variances given in Exercise 3.4.

Furthermore, for *i* = 1, …, *m*, let <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0031" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0031.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mfrac><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><msqrt><msubsup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></msqrt></mfrac><msqrt><mfrac><mi> RSS </mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></msqrt></mfrac></mrow></math></displayedItem>

(3.1)![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0031.gif)

and let <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0032" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0032.gif"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mfrac><mi> MSS </mi><mi>m</mi></mfrac><mfrac><mi> RSS </mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mi> TSS </mi><mi> RSS </mi></mfrac><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

(3.2)![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0032.gif)

From the theory of quadratic forms of Gaussian random variables,^([11](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0011)) it can be shown that statistics *t[i]* have Student’s *t* distribution, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0033" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0033.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#x223c;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0033.gif)

and, if *θ*[1] = *θ*[2] = ⋅⋅⋅ = *θ*[*m*] = 0, statistic *F* has Snedecor’s *F* distribution, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0034" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0034.gif"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>&#x223c;</mo><mspace width="4pt"/><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0034.gif)

These two facts play a central role in testing hypotheses about the parameter vector of a linear model.

For any given value *ν*, both the hypothesis that *θ*[*i*] = *ν* and the hypothesis that *θ*[*i*] ≤ *ν* can be tested by computing the statistic *t[i]* of (3.1) with *θ*[*i*] = *ν*. The null hypothesis that *θ*[*i*] ≤ *ν* is rejected (in favor of the alternative hypothesis that *θ*[*i*] > *ν*) if the probability that a *t*[*n*−*m*−1]\-distributed random variable exceeds the observed value of *t[i]* is below a user-specified threshold, τ. The null hypothesis that *θ*[*i*] = *ν* is rejected (in favor of the alternative hypothesis that *θ*[*i*] ≠ *ν*) if the probability that the absolute value of a *t*[*n* − *m* − 1]\-distributed random variable exceeds the observed absolute value of *t[i]* is below a user-specified threshold, τ. The hypothesis that the *i*th feature plays no real role in the fitted linear model, and therefore should be excluded from the model, is equivalent to the hypothesis *θ*[*i*] = 0.

The hypothesis that *θ*[1] = *θ*[2] = ⋅⋅⋅ = *θ*[*m*] = 0 is tested by computing the statistic *F* of (3.2). This hypothesis is rejected (in favor of the alternative hypothesis that *θ*[*i*] ≠ 0 for some 1 ≤ *i* ≤ *m*) if the probability that an *F*[*m*, *n* − *m* − 1]\-distributed random variable exceeds the observed value of *F* is below a user-specified threshold, τ.

Under the assumption of independent <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0042.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0042.gif)\-distributed residuals, the likelihood of the data for a given parameter vector *θ* is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0035" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0035.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x220f;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mo>-</mo><mfrac><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mfenced></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1.em"/></mrow></math></displayedItem>

<a href="#c03-disp-0035-5">(3.3)</a>![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0035.gif)

or, equivalently, the log-likelihood is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0036" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0036.gif"><mrow><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0036.gif)

**Exercise 3.7** *Show that the parameter estimates* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0043.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0043.gif)*and* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0044.gif"><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi> RSS </mi><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0044.gif)*maximize the likelihood of the data in (3.3). Compare these estimates to the least-squares estimate of *θ* and the unbiased estimate of σ*².

Exercise 3.7 shows that under the normality assumption, the least-squares parameter estimate <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0045.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c03_ILM0045.gif)is the *maximum-likelihood estimate* for *θ*. Thus squared-error loss in the learning problem can arise implicitly in regression from a decision to use a maximum-likelihood estimate for a model with independent, Gaussian-distributed residuals. Maximum-likelihood estimates have many useful properties and are commonly used as estimates. Note that the maximum-likelihood estimate for σ² is not the unbiased estimate derived in [Section 3.5](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0006).

The assumption that errors are Gaussian-distributed should be checked. This can be done graphically with a quantile–quantile plot or by applying tests in D’Agostino and Stephens (1986), Mardia et al. (1979), or Thode (2002).

## 3.7 Computation

In practice, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0046.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0046.gif)is not found by computing a matrix inverse.^([12](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0012)) Instead, the QR-decomposition of **x**, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0047.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0047.gif), is computed and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0048.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c03_ILM0048.gif)is obtained as follows.^([13](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0013))

**Exercise 3.8** *Assuming that* **x** *is full rank, show that* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0051.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c03_ILM0051.gif), *the least-squares parameter estimate, is the solution of the* (*m* + 1) × (*m* + 1) *triangular system of equations* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0037" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0037.gif"><mrow><mi> first </mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi> coordinates </mi><mi> of </mi></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi> first </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi> coordinates </mi><mi> of </mi></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi></mrow><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0037.gif)

*where* **x** = **QR** *is the QR-decomposition of* **x**.

In light of Exercise 3.8, it is sufficient to compute the *n*\-long vector <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0052.gif"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi></mrow><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0052.gif)directly rather than computing the *n* × *n* orthogonal matrix <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0053.gif"><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi></math>![](images/c03_ILM0053.gif)and then multiplying it by **y**. This is what is done in practice (Gentle, 1998; Golub and Van Loan, 1996).

## 3.8 Categorical Features

A categorical feature taking values in an unordered set of size *K* can be encoded in a set of *K* or *K* − 1 binary (and hence real-valued) features by the use of indicator functions. For simplicity, say the model input consists of a single categorical feature, so the *i*th input is *x[i]* = (*x*[*i*1]), and identify the set in which *x[i]* takes values with the (unordered) set {1, …, *K*}. One way to encode the categorical feature is to define vectors *z*[1], …, *z[n]* by <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0038" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0038.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mtext>th</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>standard</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>basis</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>vector</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>of</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>K</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x23df;</mo></munder><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mtext>1</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>in</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>coordinate</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mtext>,</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><msup><mn>0</mn><mo>&#x0027;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi> elsewhere </mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></munder></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0038.gif)

and to use the real *K*\-dimensional feature vectors *z[i]* as input to a linear model. The binary indicator variables *z*[*i*1], …, *z[iK]* are called *dummy variables* for the categorical variable *x[i]* and the vector of dummy variables (*z*[*i*1], …, *z[iK]*) is called a *one-hot encoding* of the categorical variable *x[i]*.

For example, if feature *x*[1] is categorical and takes values in the set <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com"
