![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0039.gif)

In this encoding, the single categorical column of **x** has been expanded into three binary columns: the first binary column is the indicator for <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0058.gif"><mi> orange </mi></math>![](images/c03_ILM0058.gif), the second binary column is the indicator for <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0059.gif"><mi> blue </mi></math>![](images/c03_ILM0059.gif), and the third binary column is the indicator for <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0060.gif"><mi> purple </mi></math>![](images/c03_ILM0060.gif).

This leads to a complication, since the design matrix <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0040" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0040.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>11</mn></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>12</mn></msub></mtd><mtd><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>21</mn></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>22</mn></msub></mtd><mtd><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd/><mtd><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0040.gif)

is no longer full rank. The original categorical feature *x*[*i*1] takes exactly one value among the *K* categories, so *z*[*i*1] + ⋅⋅⋅ + *z[iK]* = 1 for all *i*, and therefore for all *i* = 1, …, *n*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0041" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0041.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>K</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0041.gif)

Thus the binary encoding of a categorical variable has resulted in a design matrix which has a column space of dimension *K* (instead of *K* + 1).

One way to address this complication is to omit the explicit intercept (represented by the column of 1’s in the design matrix and model parameter *θ*[0]). This only works when there is exactly one categorical variable.^([14](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0014)) Another way to address this complication is to expand a categorical feature with *K* categories into *K* − 1 binary features such that the corresponding *K* − 1 columns of the design matrix span a (*K* − 1)-dimensional subspace of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0061.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![](images/c03_ILM0061.gif)orthogonal to the *n*\-long vector of all 1’s. This could be done, for example, by truncating the last coordinate off the *z[i]*’s defined above. The choice of approach affects the interpretation of the model parameters. If the intercept is omitted, then model parameter *θ*[*j*] is the expected response, given that *x[i]* takes the value *j*. If the intercept is retained but the last coordinate of the *z[i]*’s is truncated, then value *K* becomes a default value of *x[i]*, and model parameter *θ*[*j*] is the effect, or *contrast*, due to *x[i]* taking the value *j* instead of *K*.

In the example above, if <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0042" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0042.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0042.gif)

then the model parameters would be denoted as (*θ*[1], *θ*[2], *θ*[3])—because *θ*[0] is usually reserved to denote an intercept term, and there is none in this model—and *θ*[*i*] would be interpreted as the mean response for data with a feature *x* belonging to category *i* (in the example, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0062.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#x2194;</mo><mrow><mi> mean </mi><mi> effect </mi><mi> for </mi><mi> being </mi><mi> orange </mi></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0062.gif), <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0063.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#x2194;</mo><mrow><mi> mean </mi><mi> effect </mi><mi> for </mi><mi> being </mi><mi> blue </mi></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0063.gif), and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0064.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#x2194;</mo><mrow><mi> mean </mi><mi> effect </mi><mi> for </mi><mi> being </mi><mi> purple </mi></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0064.gif)). If instead <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0043" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0043.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0043.gif)

then the model parameters would be denoted as (*θ*[0], *θ*[1], *θ*[2]), and *θ*[0] would be interpreted as the mean response for all data, which by default are in category 3 (purple). For *i* = 1, 2, *θ*[*i*] would be interpreted as the contrast in mean response due to the feature belonging to category *i* instead of category 3 (in the example, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0065.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#x2194;</mo><mrow><mi> difference </mi><mi> in </mi><mi> mean </mi><mi> effect </mi><mi> for </mi><mi> being </mi><mi> orange </mi><mi> instead </mi><mi> of </mi><mi> purple </mi></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0065.gif)and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0066.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#x2194;</mo><mrow><mi> difference </mi><mi> in </mi><mi> mean </mi><mi> effect </mi><mi> for </mi><mi> being </mi><mi> blue </mi><mi> instead </mi><mi> of </mi><mi> purple </mi></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0066.gif)).

## 3.9 Feature Transformations, Expansions, and Interactions

Linear regression can be made to capture non-linear relationships between the features and the response by transformations of variables and expansion of bases. For example, the model assumption could be that *f* is a quadratic function without cross terms, which in practice is written as a linear function in an expanded basis, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0044" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0044.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0044.gif)

or the model assumption could be that *f* is a quadratic function with cross terms (called *interactions*), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0045" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0045.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0045.gif)

A continuous feature can be made categorical if there is reason to believe that what is important is not so much the value of the feature as whether the feature exceeds one or more thresholds. Such discretization can be done following the outline in [Section 3.8](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0009).

**Exercise 3.9** Suppose feature vector *x* = (*x*[1], …, *x[m]*) measures the amount of each of *m* possible ingredients in a serving of food, and that a linear model *f*[*θ*](*x*) is used to approximate how much a person likes the item described by the ingredients *x* (large positive values of *f*[*θ*](*x*) are interpreted as “likes strongly” and large negative values are interpreted as “dislikes strongly”). In an item of food, let *x[a]* represent the amount of asparagus, let *x[b]* represent the amount of bacon, and let *x[c]* represent the amount of chocolate. Assume the linear model *f*[*θ*](*x*) includes quadratic terms and interactions, as above.

1.  Give values of *θ*[*a*] and *θ*[*c*] indicating that the person dislikes food containing asparagus but likes food containing chocolate.
2.  Give values of *θ*[*c*] and *θ*[2*c*] indicating that the person likes food containing chocolate up to a certain amount, but dislikes food containing too much chocolate.
3.  Give values of *θ*[*a*], *θ*[*c*], and *θ*[(*a*, *c*)] indicating that the person likes food containing asparagus and likes food containing chocolate, but dislikes food containing both asparagus and chocolate.
4.  Give values of *θ*[*a*], *θ*[*c*], and *θ*[(*a*, *c*)] indicating that the person likes food containing asparagus and likes food containing chocolate, and especially likes these two ingredients in combination.
5.  What is the meaning of *θ*[0] in this model?
6.  Suggest a discrete replacement of feature *x[b]* and a value of *θ*[*b*] to indicate that a person strongly dislikes food containing any amount of bacon, without regard to how much bacon is in the food.

## 3.10 Variations in Linear Regression

The brief treatment of linear regression given in this chapter concludes with an even briefer description of a few of the many variants which have been developed. Many more can be found in books such as Rawlings et al. (2001).

*Ridge regression* is a technique which explicitly seeks to optimize a *bias–variance trade-off,* about which much more will be said in [Chapter 5](#c05.xhtml). Given a value of a parameter λ ⩾ 0, the ridge regression estimate of the linear model parameters *θ* is the value <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0067.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03bb;</mi></msub></math>![](images/c03_ILM0067.gif)which minimizes <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0046" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0046.gif"><mrow><mi> RSS </mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0046.gif)

The *ridge parameter* λ is chosen to minimize some estimate of the risk of the fitted model. Note that when λ = 0, ridge regression is least-squares regression and when λ > 0, parameters *θ*[1], …, *θ*[*m*] will tend to be smaller than they would be for least-squares regression. Note also that the intercept coefficient *θ*[0] is not penalized. Ridge regression tends to produce lower-risk models than least-squares regression, particularly when the features are highly correlated. This will be revisited in [Section 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0018).

*Thus computing parameter estimates for ridge regression has approximately the same computational cost as computing parameter estimates for ordinary least-squares regression (provided m* ≪ *n).*

A technique related to ridge regression is the *lasso*,^([15](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0015)) which minimizes <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0049" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0049.gif"><mrow><mi> RSS </mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0049.gif)

Computing the lasso-fitted parameters is more expensive than the ridge or least-squares-fitted parameters. Lasso performs a useful sort of automatic feature selection: see [Section 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0018) and Hastie et al. (2001).

Cases where additive noise terms are uncorrelated but have different variances can be treated by a method called *weighted least squares*. Suppose that instead of <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0050" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0050.gif"><mrow><mi> Var </mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mtd><mtd/><mtd/><mtd/></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd columnalign="right"><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mtd><mtd/><mtd/></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22f1;</mo></mtd><mtd/></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd/><mtd><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0050.gif)

we have, for some *k*²[1], …, *k[n]*², <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0051" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0051.gif"><mrow><mi> Var </mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mtd><mtd/><mtd/><mtd/></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mtd><mtd/><mtd/></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22f1;</mo></mtd><mtd/></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd/><mtd><mrow><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0051.gif)

Define matrix <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0052" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0052.gif"><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mtd><mtd/><mtd/><mtd/></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd columnalign="right"><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mtd><mtd/><mtd/></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22f1;</mo></mtd><mtd/></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd/><mtd><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0052.gif)

The linear model <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0053" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0053.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0053.gif)

can be transformed to <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0054" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0054.gif"><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0054.gif)

where <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0068.gif"><mrow><mi> Var </mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>I</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0068.gif). The least-squares estimate of the parameters of the transformed model is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0055" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0055.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mfenced><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>W</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0055.gif)

**Exercise 3.11** *Show that* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0069.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c03_ILM0069.gif)*above minimizes the weighted sum of squares* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0056" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0056.gif"><mrow><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0056.gif)

Weighted least squares can be used to assign greater or lesser importance to certain observations. Cases where additive noise terms are correlated can be treated similarly, taking <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0070.gif"><msup><mi>W</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup></math>![](images/c03_ILM0070.gif)to be an inverse Cholesky factor^([16](#c03.xhtml#c03-note-0016)) of the covariance matrix: that is, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0071.gif"><msup><mi>W</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup></math>![](images/c03_ILM0071.gif)is a non-diagonal *n* × *n* matrix such that <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0057" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0057.gif"><mrow><msup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><msubsup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi> Cov </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mfenced><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mi>W</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0057.gif)

Linear regression can be expanded naturally to the case where *f* is vector-valued, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0072.gif"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#x2192;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c03_ILM0072.gif). The least-squares solution is found exactly as in the scalar-valued case.

*Logistic regression* is a technique for estimating probabilities, that is, continuous response vectors (*p*[1], …, *p[k]*) such that *p[i]* ⩾ 0 for all *i* and *p*[1] + ⋅⋅⋅ + *p[k]* = 1. It does this by mapping the range of *f* from the simplex of *k*\-long probability vectors <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0059" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0059.gif"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>:</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>}</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0059.gif)

into <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c03\_ILM0073.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![](images/c03_ILM0073.gif)by the map <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0060" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0060.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="4pt"/><mo>&#x21a6;</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfrac></mfenced></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0060.gif)

and fitting a linear model by maximum-likelihood estimation, using a different statistical framework than additive Gaussian-distributed noise—see [Section 4.6](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0017). Logistic regression is an example of a *generalized linear model*, in which the observed response is not itself a linear function of the features, but the result of applying some other function, called the *link function*, to the output of a linear function of the features.

Sometimes feature vectors in the data are themselves a random sample from a population, and inference about the whole population is desired. In this case, the features are known as *random effects*, as opposed to non-random features which are called *fixed effects*. In a *random effects model* there should be multiple observations of the response for each feature vector. A simple *analysis of variance* (ANOVA) example is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0061" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0061.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0061.gif)

where *y[ij]* is the *j*th observation of a response from the *i*th feature vector, *θ*[0] is an intercept, *θ*[*i*] is the effect for the *i*th feature vector (*θ*[*i*] is a random variable with with mean 0 and variance σ²[*θ*]) and *e[ij]* is the usual error in the response (*e[ij]* is a random variable with mean 0 and variance σ²[*e*]). Inference about *θ*[0] and σ²[*θ*] is inference about the population from which the features were drawn. A model with both random and fixed effects is a *mixed effects model*.

## 3.11 Nonparametric Regression

There are many regression techniques which do not rely on a linear model, or even on any statistical model at all. Many of the techniques for classification, presented in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml), have analogous regression techniques. Looking ahead to [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml), we conclude this section with two examples, *k-nearest-neighbor regression* and *regression trees*. The reader may wish to read [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml), at least up through [Section 4.8](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0023), and then return to this section.

A *k-nearest-neighbor regressor* is exactly like a *k*\-nearest-neighbor classifier in [Section 4.5](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0012), except that instead of predicting the minimum-risk class for a new point based on the class of *k* neighbors, the minimum-risk response is predicted based on the response of *k* neighbors. For squared-error loss, the mean response of the *k*\-nearest-neighbors is predicted.

A *regression tree* is trained and used exactly as a classification tree in [Section 4.8](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0023), except that instead of predicting the minimum-risk class for a new point entering a leaf node *t* of the tree based on the class of the data in *t*, the minimum-risk response is predicted based on the response of the data in *t*. For squared-error loss, the mean response of the data in *t* is predicted, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0062" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0062.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mi> training </mi><mi> data </mi><mi> entering </mi><mi> node </mi></mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>|</mo></mrow></mfrac><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><mi> training </mi><mi> data </mi></mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></munder><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0062.gif)

For squared-error loss, the impurity of a node is the sum over the data which enter it of the squared deviations of the response around its mean, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c03-disp-0063" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c03\_M0063.gif"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><mi> training </mi><mi> data </mi></mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></munder><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c03_M0063.gif)

that is, *I*(*t*) is the sample variance of the responses of the data in leaf node *t*.

Regression trees and *k*\-nearest-neighbor regression are *non-parametric regression methods*, because the number of parameters (the splitting criteria of non-leaf nodes and the estimated response returned by leaf nodes in the case of trees, the number of training data in the case of *k*\-nearest-neighbors) are not fixed prior to training.

## Notes

# 4  
Survey of Classification Techniques

> Understand the modeling premises implicit in the tools you use. And, if you don’t, understand that, too.
> 
> —Mark Jacobson, personal communication, 2006

> It’s a totally black-box, brainless approach. You don’t have to think—it just works.
> 
> —Jeremy Howard, referring to random forests in *Down with Experts*, 2012

> The statistician cannot evade the responsibility for understanding the process he applies or recommends.
> 
> —R. A. Fisher, *The Design of Experiments*, 1937

This chapter introduces the reader to a wide variety of approaches to the problem of *classification*, that is, to the problem of supervised learning when the range of the unknown function *f* is a discrete, unordered set of labels. It begins in [Section 4.1](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0002) by developing an optimal (minimum risk) classifier, the *Bayes classifier*, under the assumption that the joint probability distribution P(*X*, *Y*) from which data are drawn in known. This assumption is totally unrealistic, of course, but analyzing the Bayes classifier allows one to perceive and appreciate the role played by our subjectivity, encoded in the loss function <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0001.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0001.gif), and the roles played by various aspects of the joint probability distribution P(*X*, *Y*).

The practical part of the chapter begins in [Section 4.2](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0003), which contains a brief survey of many ways to approximate components of the Bayes classifier which are unknown in real applications, focusing in particular on the design principles behind practical classification methods. Viewing most methods as approximations of the Bayes classifier provides a common theme uniting the 14 or so practical classification algorithms described in [Sections 4.4](#c04.xhtml#c4_4) through [4.9](#c04.xhtml#c4_9), which at first glance may appear to be quite different from each other. Some of these methods (quadratic discriminant analysis, linear discriminant analysis, Gaussian mixture models, logistic regression) are based on relatively simple statistical models; some (*k*\-nearest neighbors, histograms, kernel density estimation, support vector machines) are based on geometric insight; and some are based on understanding of how humans solve problems, either at the behavioral level (*k*\-nearest neighbors, classification trees) or at the neurological level (neural networks).

Understanding the design principles behind applied machine learning algorithms can lead to tangible benefits. If one method works considerably better than another on an applied problem, and the practitioner understands how both methods work, then he or she has learned something about the data which should inform the next steps taken (more on this in [Section 4.10](#c04.xhtml#c4_10)). If domain knowledge about an applied problem suggests that useful structure relating feature vectors *X* to class labels *Y* exists and has a given form, and the practitioner understands which methods are (and are not) capable of efficiently approximating the structure believed to be present in the data, then he or she can select a method or a small set of methods to apply.^([1](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0001)) Finally, classification methods occasionally need to be modified in order to solve applied problems, and understanding the design principles behind the methods leads to better-informed modifications, which lead to a greater chance of applied success.

## 4.1 The Bayes Classifier

Suppose that one of the following two things is known about how data are generated: either class labels are drawn (independently) from a *known* conditional distribution on the set of class labels {1, …, *C*} given the features, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0001" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0001.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo><mspace width="2.em"/><mi> for </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0001.gif)

or class labels are drawn from a *known* marginal distribution on class labels^([2](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0002)) and features are drawn from a *known* conditional distribution of features given the class, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0002" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0002.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo><mspace width="2.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="2.em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo><mspace width="2.em"/><mi> for </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0002.gif)

Knowledge of either of these things (P(*Y* = *c* | *X*) or both P(*Y* = *c*) and P(*X* | *Y* = *c*), for all *c*) implies knowledge of the risk (expected loss) of predicting any class *c*, given a The *Bayes classifier* classifies a new datum *X* as the class with minimum risk, conditional on *X*. That is, at *X* = *x* the Bayes classifier predicts <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0005" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0005.gif"><mrow><mspace width="-22.0pt"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> Bayes </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi> argmin </mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi> argmin </mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>|</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

(4.1)![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0005.gif)

Any ties in the argument of the minimum are broken arbitrarily because they have no effect on risk. As indicated by Exercise 2.3, this results in minimum overall risk, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0006" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0006.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi> Bayes </mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> Bayes </mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">min</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></munder><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>|</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0006.gif)

The overall risk of the Bayes classifier, denoted R[Bayes] above, is called the *Bayes risk* or, for 0–1 loss, the *Bayes error rate*. The Bayes classifier is widely regarded as an optimal classifier, because minimization of risk is widely regarded as an optimal strategy for making decisions.^([4](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0004))

**Exercise 4.1** *Knowledge of the conditional distribution* P(*Y* | *X*) *enables construction of the Bayes classifier. Show that, in general, knowledge of the Bayes classifier does not enable reconstruction of the conditional distribution* P(*Y* | *X*). *In this sense,* P(*Y* | *X*) *contains stronger information than* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0003.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> Bayes </mi></msub></math>![](images/c04_ILM0003.gif). **Hint:** *Show that there are distributions* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0004.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0004.gif)*other than* P(*Y* | *X*) *which, when substituted for* P(*Y* | *X*) *in (4.1), do not change the classification decisions made.*

## 4.2 Introduction to Classifiers

The Bayes classifier classifies a new datum *X* to be the class *c* which minimizes the risk, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0011" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0011.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x221d;</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0011.gif)

In real life P(*Y* = *d* | *X*), P(*X* | *Y* = *d*), and P(*Y* = *d*) are unknown. Thus some kind of approximation is needed in order to follow the strategy of the Bayes classifier. The approximation may be of either the conditional distribution on class labels given the features, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0012" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0012.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0012.gif)

or both the marginal distribution of class labels^([5](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0005)) and the conditional distribution on features given the class label, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0013" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0013.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo><mspace width="2.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="2.em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0013.gif)

Description of what is approximated, and how it is approximated, provides an introduction to the practical algorithms described in [Sections 4.4](#c04.xhtml#c4_4) through [4.9](#c04.xhtml#c4_9).

A *likelihood method* approximates the likelihood function P(*X* | *Y* = *d*) separately for each class *d* either by positing a specific parametric form for this distribution and using training data to approximate the parameters of this form or by fitting a non-parametric statistical model to the training data of each class separately. Likelihood methods are among methods which require that the marginal distribution of class labels P(*Y* = *d*) be specified, or that it be learned from the training data.

A *prototype method* approximates P(*Y* = *d* | *X*) by assuming that this probability changes slowly with respect to some kind of distance^([6](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0006)) on <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0008.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>![](images/c04_ILM0008.gif), the set of feature vectors. Given a feature vector *X*, the distribution P(*Y* = *d* | *X*) is approximated by the distribution of the class labels among a set of *prototypical data points* near *X* (what “near” means may depend on the data). Depending on the specific method employed, prototypical data points may be observed data or may be synthetic points which correspond to no single, observed data point.

A *logistic regression* classifier approximates P(*Y* = *d* | *X*) by assuming that for classes *d* = 2, …, *C*, the log-odds in favor of class *d* over class 1, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0014" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0014.gif"><mrow><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0014.gif)

is a linear function of the features. Thus approximating P(*Y* = *d* | *X*) is akin to estimating the parameters of *C* − 1 linear functions <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0015" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0015.gif"><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0015.gif)

through regression, as described in [Chapter 3](#c03.xhtml).

A *neural network* approximates P(*Y* = *d* | *X*) in a way very much like a logistic regression classifier, except that it models the log-odds not as a linear function of the features, but as a linear function of the outputs of other functions called *neurons*. Approximating P(*Y* = *d* | *X*) with a neural network means simultaneously estimating the parameters of the linear function and the parameters of the neurons.

A *classification tree* approximates P(*X* | *Y* = *d*) by partitioning feature space <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0009.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>![](images/c04_ILM0009.gif)into regions and approximating, for each region *t*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0016" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0016.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0016.gif)

Classification trees are similar both to prototype methods (if feature vector *X* is in region *t*, the training data in *t* are “near” *X* and used to predict a class label for *X*) and to likelihood methods (within each region *t*, P(*X* | *Y* = *d*) is approximated by a constant, P(*X* ∈ *t* | *Y* = *d*)). The partitioning of feature space into regions also depends on the training data.

The author does not see how a *support vector machine* fits into this paradigm. Support vector machines use a type of loss function which depends not only on the true and predicted class labels, but also on the point *x* at which the prediction is made (a support vector machine can incur positive loss for predicting the correct class at <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0010.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0010.gif)). Support vector machines will be motivated geometrically in [Section 4.9](#c04.xhtml#c4_9).

## 4.3 A Running Example

A toy example is used throughout this chapter and [Chapters 5](#c05.xhtml) and [6](#c06.xhtml) to illustrate the behavior of classification methods: in particular, to show classification decisions made at points in feature space and method-specific details such as estimated likelihood functions for each class. In this example, there are three classes, *orange*, *blue*, and *purple*, and feature vectors are in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0011.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0011.gif).

The three classes are equally likely: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0017" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0017.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>orange</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>blue</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>purple</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0017.gif)

Within each class, features are distributed as an equal-weight mixture of three two-dimensional Gaussian distributions with unit covariance matrix and different means. The means of the nine Gaussians are shown in the left-hand cell of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1), colored according to class. In polar coordinates, the orange means are <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0012.gif"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow><mn>9</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow><mn>9</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow><mn>9</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0012.gif), the blue means are <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0013.gif"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>9</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow><mn>9</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>11</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow><mn>9</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>13</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow><mn>9</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0013.gif), and the purple means are <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0014.gif"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>15</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow><mn>9</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>17</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow><mn>9</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow><mn>9</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0014.gif). Thus, for example, the distribution of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0015.gif"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi> orange </mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0015.gif)has density function <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" <span class="equationNumber"><a href="#c04-disp-0018-4">(4.4)</a></span>![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0018.gif)![Figure 4.1 The left-hand cell shows a set of nine points which define the class densities of each of three classes, orange, blue, and purple. The points lie on circles of radius 1, 2, and 3 centered at the origin and angularly consecutive points are separated by an angle of . The distribution of the data in each class is a mixture of three equally weighted Gaussian distributions with means shown and unit covariance matrix. The right-hand cell shows a set of 150 points drawn randomly from this distribution: there are 48 orange, 49 blue, and 53 purple points. The points shown are used for training classifiers in the examples below.](images/c04f001.jpg)

[**Figure 4.1**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-1) The left-hand cell shows a set of nine points which define the class densities of each of three classes, orange, blue, and purple. The points lie on circles of radius 1, 2, and 3 centered at the origin and angularly consecutive points are separated by an angle of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0018.gif"><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow><mn>9</mn></mfrac></math>![](images/c04_ILM0018.gif). The distribution of the data in each class is a mixture of three equally weighted Gaussian distributions with means shown and unit covariance matrix. The right-hand cell shows a set of 150 points drawn randomly from this distribution: there are 48 orange, 49 blue, and 53 purple points. The points shown are used for training classifiers in the examples below.

Data are generated from this model independently, one at a time, as follows. First a class is chosen from P(*Y*), that is, uniformly at random from the set <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0016.gif"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi> orange </mi><mo>,</mo><mi> blue </mi><mo>,</mo><mi> purple </mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0016.gif). Then one of the three Gaussian distributions for the chosen class is selected uniformly at random. Then a point in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0017.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0017.gif)is drawn randomly from the selected Gaussian distribution.

A randomly drawn set of 150 points from the joint distribution P(*X*, *Y*) is shown in the right-hand cell of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1): there are 48 points from the orange class, 49 from the blue class and 53 from the purple class. Throughout this and later chapters, classifiers will be trained on this dataset using 0–1 loss. A test set of 50,000 points drawn from the same distribution is used to estimate the risk of trained classifiers.^([7](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0007)) The data illustrated in [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1) are given in Appendix D, along with fitted parameters of many of the methods described in this chapter.

The likelihood functions for the three classes, and the classification decisions made by the Bayes classifier, are shown in [Figure 4.2](#c04.xhtml#figure4-2). The Bayes risk, accurate to six decimal places,^([8](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0008)) is 0.191705.

![Figure 4.2 The left-hand cell shows the density function for the orange data in orange, the density function for the blue data in blue, and the density function for the purple data in purple. In this example, the prior distribution of the classes is uniform and 0–1 loss is used, so at any point, the Bayes classifier predicts whatever class has the highest density (Exercise 4.2). The regions of points classified by the Bayes classifier as orange, blue, and purple are shown in the right-hand cell, with the class boundaries highlighted in white. Shading in the right-hand cell is proportional to the marginal density of the data, P(X): mistakes in bright areas contribute more to the risk of a classifier than mistakes in dark areas. These plots are for comparison with the plots illustrating the behavior of methods described in this chapter and Chapters 5 and 6. The Bayes risk for this problem is 0.191705.](images/c04f002.jpg)

[**Figure 4.2**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-2) The left-hand cell shows the density function for the orange data in orange, the density function for the blue data in blue, and the density function for the purple data in purple. In this example, the prior distribution of the classes is uniform and 0–1 loss is used, so at any point, the Bayes classifier predicts whatever class has the highest density (Exercise 4.2). The regions of points classified by the Bayes classifier as orange, blue, and purple are shown in the right-hand cell, with the class boundaries highlighted in white. Shading in the right-hand cell is proportional to the marginal density of the data, P(*X*): mistakes in bright areas contribute more to the risk of a classifier than mistakes in dark areas. These plots are for comparison with the plots illustrating the behavior of methods described in this chapter and [Chapters 5](#c05.xhtml) and [6](#c06.xhtml). The Bayes risk for this problem is 0.191705.

## 4.4 Likelihood Methods

Suppose that the data from the *c*th class is randomly drawn from a distribution with likelihood^([9](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0009)) P(*X* | *Y* = *c*) on the sample space, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0021.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>![](images/c04_ILM0021.gif). A likelihood-based classifier uses training data to compute an estimate <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0022.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0022.gif)of the likelihood P(*X* | *Y* = *c*). Given the marginal or prior distribution of the classes P(*Y* = *c*) (estimated from the training data or obtained another way, as appropriate) the posterior distribution on the classes is estimated by <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0019" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0019.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0019.gif)

and a new data point *X* is classified to minimize estimated posterior risk.

The first three methods described in this section, quadratic discriminant analysis, linear discriminant analysis, and Gaussian mixture models, are *parametric methods,* because they specify a parametric form for the class densities. These have the advantage of being cheap to implement and the disadvantage that they can produce relatively high-risk approximations <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0023.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c04_ILM0023.gif)when the model assumptions on which they are based are far from the truth. The next two methods, kernel density estimation and histograms, are *non-parametric methods* and can be expensive to implement. The last method, the naive Bayes classifier, can be parametric, non-parametric, or a mixture of the two (in which case it is a *semi-parametric method*).

### 4.4.1 Quadratic Discriminant Analysis

Suppose that for each class *c*, the likelihood function P(*x* | *Y* = *c*) is a Gaussian density (all features must be real in order to use this method, so <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0024.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0024.gif)),^([10](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0010)) <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0020" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0020.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>|</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi><msub><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><msubsup><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0020.gif)

The name of this classifier comes from the fact that the estimated class boundaries (surfaces which partition feature space into regions of homogeneous predicted class) it produces are piecewise quadratic surfaces. [Figure 4.3](#c04.xhtml#figure4-3) illustrates the estimated densities <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0025.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0025.gif)and class predictions made by quadratic discriminant analysis trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1).

![Figure 4.3 Estimated class densities (left) and classification decisions (right) made by quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA) trained on the data of Figure 4.1. [**Figure 4.3**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-3) Estimated class densities (left) and classification decisions (right) made by quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA) trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). **Exercise 4.5** *Let* (*x*[1], *y*[1]), …, (*x[n]*, *y[n]*) *be n independent draws from the joint distribution* (*X*, *Y*), *where for each class c* = 1, …, *C*, *the feature vector* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0022" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0022.gif"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x223c;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0022.gif)

*Show that the parameters μ*[1], …, μ[*C*], Σ[1], …, Σ[*C*] *which maximize the likelihood of the feature vectors x*[1], …, *x[n] conditional on the class labels y*[1], …, *y[n] are given by* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0023" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0023.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math></displayedItem>

The total number of parameters for each class is *m* (for the *m*\-long vector <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0030.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub></math>![](images/c04_ILM0030.gif)) plus <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0031.gif"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0031.gif)(for the *m* × *m* symmetric matrix <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0032.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub></math>![](images/c04_ILM0032.gif)), which is quite a lot when *m* is large. If a class *c* is relatively rare, this can lead to an estimated covariance matrix <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0033.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub></math>![](images/c04_ILM0033.gif)which is singular. location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0034.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub></math>![](images/c04_ILM0034.gif)by a convex combination of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0035.gif"><msub><mover xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0036.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c04_ILM0036.gif)estimated under the assumption that all classes have the same covariance (see below for a definition of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0037.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c04_ILM0037.gif)) <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com"
