accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0025.gif)

for some parameter 0 *≤* α ≤ 1. This technique is called *regularized discriminant analysis*. Sometimes the number of parameters is reduced to 2*m* per class by assuming that the covariance matrix for each class is diagonal.

### 4.4.2 Linear Discriminant Analysis

Linear discriminant analysis is the same as quadratic discriminant analysis, except that the covariance matrices of the class densities are assumed to be equal (it is regularized discriminant analysis above with α = 0). The estimated class boundaries are piecewise linear, and the common covariance matrix Σ can be estimated from all of the data. [Figure 4.4](#c04.xhtml#figure4-4) illustrates the estimated densities <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0038.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0038.gif)and class predictions made by linear discriminant analysis trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1).

![Figure 4.4 Estimated class densities (left) and classification decisions (right) made by linear discriminant analysis (LDA) trained on the data of Figure 4.1. The estimated class boundaries are piecewise linear. Estimated class means are shown by black dots, and level curves of the estimated densities with 50% of the probability mass inside are shown by dashed lines (see Appendix C for how the level curves were obtained). Note that the level curves all have the same shape, differing only in location, unlike QDA (Figure 4.3). White curves show the Bayes class boundaries. LDA has estimated risk 0.229.](images/c04f004.jpg)

[**Figure 4.4**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-4) Estimated class densities (left) and classification decisions (right) made by linear discriminant analysis (LDA) trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). The estimated class boundaries are piecewise linear. Estimated class means are shown by black dots, and level curves of the estimated densities with 50% of the probability mass inside are shown by dashed lines (see Appendix C for how the level curves were obtained). Note that the level curves all have the same shape, differing only in location, unlike QDA ([Figure 4.3](#c04.xhtml#figure4-3)). White curves show the Bayes class boundaries. LDA has estimated risk 0.229.

### 4.4.3 Gaussian Mixture Models

Suppose that for each class *c*, the likelihood function P(*x* | *Y* = *c*) is a mixture of Gaussian densities, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0030" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0030.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0030.gif)

where *φ*(*x* | *μ*, Σ) denotes a Gaussian density function with mean μ and covariance matrix Σ, *w[jc]* are non-negative weights with <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0040.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0040.gif)for each *c*, and *J[c]* > 0 is the number of mixture components for the *c*th class. Gaussian mixtures are fit by the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm described in [Section 10.7](#c10.xhtml#c10_7).^([12](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0012)) The number of mixture components *J[c]* must be determined for each class using a model selection criterion, such as those discussed in [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml) (for example, a cross-validation estimate of risk, or Akaike’s information criterion). Setting *J[c]* = 1 for all *c* is equivalent to QDA.

Using a Gaussian mixture model for a likelihood-based classifier can result in an enormous number of parameters to estimate if *m* is large. Imposing structure on the covariance matrices (such as all being equal to each other, or diagonal, or a scaled identity matrix) can reduce the number of parameters.

[Figure 4.5](#c04.xhtml#figure4-5) shows two Gaussian mixture models fit to the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). The first model used two Gaussian components for each class (*J*[1] = *J*[2] = *J*[3] = 2), and the second model used three Gaussian components for each class (*J*[1] = *J*[2] = *J*[3] = 3). It is obvious to the eye that the fitted three-component Gaussian mixture model performs poorly (its risk, estimated from test data, is 0.228): *yet a three-component Gaussian mixture is the correct model, in the sense that the data were truly generated from a Gaussian mixture with three components per class.* As measured by likelihood (shown in [Table 4.1](#c04.xhtml#table4-1)), the fitted three-component model fits the training data better than the true model: on average, each data point is assigned approximately 50% higher likelihood under the fitted model than under the true model.

![Figure 4.5 Estimated class densities (left) and classification decisions (right) made using Gaussian mixture models trained on the data of Figure 4.1. The upper two cells correspond to Gaussian mixtures with two components for each class, and the bottom two cells correspond to Gaussian mixtures with three components for each class (graphing artifacts may cause a sawtooth appearance in densities which are truly smooth). Note that a three-component Gaussian mixture is the correct model, in the sense that the data were truly generated from a Gaussian mixture with three components per class. White curves show the Bayes class boundaries. The Gaussian mixture models have estimated risks 0.205 (two components per class) and 0.228 (three components per class).](images/c04f005.jpg)

[**Figure 4.5**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-5) Estimated class densities (left) and classification decisions (right) made using Gaussian mixture models trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). The upper two cells correspond to Gaussian mixtures with two components for each class, and the bottom two cells correspond to Gaussian mixtures with three components for each class (graphing artifacts may cause a sawtooth appearance in densities which are truly smooth). *Note that a three-component Gaussian mixture is the correct model, in the sense that the data were truly generated from a Gaussian mixture with three components per class.* White curves show the Bayes class boundaries. The Gaussian mixture models have estimated risks 0.205 (two components per class) and 0.228 (three components per class).

[**Table 4.1**](#c04.xhtml#tableanchor4-1) The log-likelihood of the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1), separated by class, under a three-component Gaussian mixture model fitted by approximate maximum likelihood (center column) and under the three-component Gaussian mixture model from which the data were drawn (right column). In each class, the fitted model assigns substantially higher likelihood to the data than the true model.

|  || Log-likelihood of class *c* data, fitted three-component model || Log-likelihood of class *c* data, true three-component model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Class *c* = 1 || − 136.41 || − 153.10 |
| Class *c* = 2 || − 145.45 || − 168.40 |
| Class *c* = 3 || − 158.60 || − 179.53 |

Some find it counter-intuitive that the “structurally correct” model could produce a trained classifier with quite high risk. The high risk of this fitted model is due to having too many parameters or too little data. In the language of [Chapter 5](#c05.xhtml), where this issue will be addressed at length, the Gaussian mixture model with three components for each class has low bias but high variance. Yet there is also merit in the intuition that knowledge of the parametric form of the correct model should be helpful: see [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml), in particular Theorem 8.5, and also the comment on rates of convergence in [Section 4.4.5](#c04.xhtml#c4_4_5).

Using mixtures of Student’s *t* distributions in place of mixtures of Gaussians may provide robustness against outliers. The density of Student’s *t* distribution with ν degrees of freedom is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0031" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0031.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x03bd;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#x0393;</mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#x03bd;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03c0;</mi><mi>&#x03bd;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mi>&#x0393;</mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mi>&#x03bd;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mo>|</mo><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>&#x03bd;</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><msup><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#x03bd;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0031.gif)

For small values of ν, Student’s *t* distribution has much heavier tails than the Gaussian distribution, while as ν → ∞, it approaches the Gaussian distribution. When ν = 1, Student’s *t* distribution is called the Cauchy distribution.

### 4.4.4 Kernel Density Estimation

A *kernel density estimate* estimates the density function which produces a sample of data by placing a probability mass at, and nearby, each observed datum. A kernel density estimate for the data of class *c*, for *c* = 1, …, *C*, has the form <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0032" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0032.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msubsup></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>K</mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mfrac></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0032.gif)

where *n[c]* is the number of training data of class *c*, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0041.gif"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x221e;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0041.gif)is a *kernel function*, and *h[c]* is a parameter known as *bandwidth*.^([13](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0013)) A kernel function in this context is any function which is relatively large near zero and relatively small away from zero: two commonly used kernel functions, the Gaussian and Epanechnikov kernels, are shown in [Figure 4.6](#c04.xhtml#figure4-6).

![Figure 4.6 Gaussian (left) and Epanechnikov (right) kernel functions. Both kernels are probability density functions of distributions on  with mean 0 and unit covariance matrix.](images/c04f006.jpg)

[**Figure 4.6**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-6) Gaussian (left) and Epanechnikov (right) kernel functions. Both kernels are probability density functions of distributions on <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0042.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0042.gif)with mean 0 and unit covariance matrix.

The kernel density estimate <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0043.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0043.gif)is large when the point *x* is near data of class *c* and gets smaller as *x* gets farther from data of class *c*. The bandwidth parameter *h[c]* controls how rapidly <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0044.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0044.gif)decreases as *x* gets farther from data of class *c*. Thus *h[c]* controls the smoothness^([14](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0014)) of the density estimate: if *h[c]* is small, then there is not much smoothing, while if *h[c]* is large, there is a lot of smoothing.

The effect of the bandwidth parameters *h[c]* is illustrated in [Figure 4.7](#c04.xhtml#figure4-7), where for simplicity the constraint *h*[1] = *h*[2] = *h*[3] was imposed. A value of the bandwidth parameter which is small (relative to the scale of the data) makes the density estimates “spiky” and highly concentrated about the observed data. A middling value of the bandwidth parameter produces density estimates which appear visually similar to the true densities illustrated in [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). A large value of the bandwidth parameter results in a density estimate which is almost constant in a large neighborhood around the data.

![Figure 4.7 Estimated class densities (left) and classification decisions (right) made using a Gaussian kernel density estimate with, from top to bottom, bandwidths h = 0.1, 0.5, and 5, trained on the data of Figure 4.1. White curves show the Bayes class boundaries. These kernel density estimates have estimated risks 0.246, 0.203, and 0.261, respectively. Bandwidth h = 0.5 was selected as approximately optimal using leave-one-out cross-validation, described in Section 7.3, to estimate risk from the training data.](images/c04f007.jpg)

[**Figure 4.7**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-7) Estimated class densities (left) and classification decisions (right) made using a Gaussian kernel density estimate with, from top to bottom, bandwidths *h* = 0.1, 0.5, and 5, trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). White curves show the Bayes class boundaries. These kernel density estimates have estimated risks 0.246, 0.203, and 0.261, respectively. Bandwidth *h* = 0.5 was selected as approximately optimal using leave-one-out cross-validation, described in [Section 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c7_3), to estimate risk from the training data.

Multivariate kernel functions are sometimes built up as products of univariate kernel functions. In that case <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0034" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0033.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><munderover><mo>&#x220f;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mfrac></mfenced></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0033.gif)

where *K*[1], …, *K[m]* are univariate kernel functions, *x[j]* and *x[ij]* denote the *j*th coordinate of *x* and *x[i]* respectively, and bandwidth parameters *h*[*c*, *j*] are allowed to depend on a class *c* as well as a coordinate *j* in feature space. This can be useful when features are measured on very different scales. The *m*\-dimensional Gaussian kernel is a product of *m* one-dimensional Gaussian kernels.

Common wisdom is that the choice of kernel function does not matter nearly as much as a good choice of bandwidth parameter, although theoretical comparisons of kernel functions have been made^([15](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0015)) (Epanechnikov, 1967; Scott, 1992). Rules of thumb have been developed for approximately optimal bandwidth selection, such as the *normal reference rule* (Scott, 1992), which for product kernels is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0035" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0034.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mfenced><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0034.gif)

where <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0046.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math>![](images/c04_ILM0046.gif)is the sample standard deviation of the *j*th feature coordinate among data of class *c*. Note, however, that such rules generally select bandwidths which minimize the risk of the kernel density estimate as an estimate of the true density with respect to squared-error loss, and that optimality with respect to that criterion does not imply optimality of a classifier based on the kernel density estimate. When using kernel density estimation in a classifier, bandwidths should be tuned to optimize the estimated risk of the classifier (though [Figure 4.8](#c04.xhtml#figure4-8) shows that the normal reference rule can do well).

![Figure 4.8 Estimated class densities (left) and classification decisions (right) made using a product Gaussian kernel density estimate, trained on the data of Figure 4.1 with bandwidths obtained from the normal reference rule, h1, 1 = 0.76, h1, 2 = 0.62, h2, 1 = 0.79, h2, 2 = 0.67, h3, 1 = 0.49, and h3, 2 = 0.98. White curves show the Bayes class boundaries. This kernel density estimate has estimated risk 0.199, although leave-one-out cross-validation prefers the bandwidth h = 0.5 classifier shown in the center cells of Figure 4.7.](images/c04f008.jpg)

[**Figure 4.8**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-8) Estimated class densities (left) and classification decisions (right) made using a product Gaussian kernel density estimate, trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1) with bandwidths obtained from the normal reference rule, *h*[1, 1] = 0.76, *h*[1, 2] = 0.62, *h*[2, 1] = 0.79, *h*[2, 2] = 0.67, *h*[3, 1] = 0.49, and *h*[3, 2] = 0.98. White curves show the Bayes class boundaries. This kernel density estimate has estimated risk 0.199, although leave-one-out cross-validation prefers the bandwidth *h* = 0.5 classifier shown in the center cells of [Figure 4.7](#c04.xhtml#figure4-7).

Although the number of bandwidth parameters *h*[1], …, *h[C]* is fixed in advance, note that each observed datum (*x[i]*, *y[i]*) adds a term <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0047.gif"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0047.gif)to one of the density estimates, and thus in effect the data are also parameters of the kernel density estimate, so the number of parameters increases without bound as *n* → ∞. In this sense, kernel density estimation is a non-parametric method. Since evaluation of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0048.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0048.gif)for each class *c* involves one evaluation of the kernel function for each data point, KDE can be expensive to implement when the number of data, *n*, is large.

### 4.4.5 Histograms

A histogram is a step-function approximation of a density function. As in kernel density estimates, histograms have a bandwidth parameter which must be chosen carefully. For each class *c*, a bandwidth-dependent tiling of feature space <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0049.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>![](images/c04_ILM0049.gif)into rectangular cells is given. When <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0050.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0050.gif), these cells are <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0036" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0035.gif"><mtable mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>&lt;</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>+</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>&lt;</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>}</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

<span class="equationNumber"><a href="#c04-disp-0036-6">(4.6)</a></span>![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0035.gif)

indexed by <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0051.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0051.gif), where *h*[*c*, *j*] is a bandwidth parameter for the *j*th feature and the *c*th class. Given any feature vector *x* and any class *c*, let <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0037" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0036.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0036.gif)

denote the rectangle *R[c]*(*i*[1], …, *i[m]*) which contains *x*: the index vector (*i*[1], …, *i[m]*) is found by setting <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0038" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0037.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="&#x230a;" close="&#x230b;"><mfrac><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mfrac></mfenced></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0037.gif)

for *j* = 1, …, *m*, where ⌊*r*⌋ represents the integer floor of a real number *r*. For any feature vector *x* and any class *c*, let *n*^(*R[c]*(*x*))[*c*] denote the number of training data of class *c* which fall in the rectangle *R[c]*(*x*). The histogram density estimate is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0039" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0038.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0038.gif)

This situation is illustrated in [Figure 4.9](#c04.xhtml#figure4-9).

![Figure 4.9 A partition of  into a grid of hc, 1 × hc, 2 rectangles Rc(i, j), shown with some of the purple data of Figure 4.1.](images/c04f009.gif)

[**Figure 4.9**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-9) A partition of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0052.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0052.gif)into a grid of *h*[*c*, 1] × *h*[*c*, 2] rectangles *R[c]*(*i*, *j*), shown with some of the purple data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1).

Note that unlike kernel density estimates, histogram density estimates depend on a choice of origin in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0053.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>![](images/c04_ILM0053.gif)in addition to bandwidth. The rectangular cells defined above can be translated by addition of any constant vector in \[0, *h*[*c*, 1]) × ⋅⋅⋅ × \[0, *h*[*c*, *m*]) to give additional flexibility to the classifier. As with product kernel density estimates, rectangular cells with different edge lengths *h*[*c*, 1], …, *h*[*c*, *m*] accommodate features measured on different scales.

The effect of the bandwidth parameters *h*[*c*, *i*] is illustrated in [Figure 4.10](#c04.xhtml#figure4-10), where for convenience the constraint *h*[1, 1] = *h*[1, 2] = *h*[2, 1] = *h*[2, 2] = *h*[3, 1] = *h*[3, 2] was imposed and the lower-left corner of cell *R*(0, 0) is located at the origin for each class. A value of the bandwidth parameter which is small (relative to the scale of the data) makes the density estimates “spiky” and highly concentrated about the observed data. It also causes many histogram cells to contain no data at all. In cells where *R*[1](*x*) = ⋅⋅⋅ = *R[C]*(*x*) = 0, the histogram classifier treats P(*X* = *x* | *Y* = *c*) as the same small, positive number for all classes *c*, and uses the estimate P(*Y* = *c* | *X* = *x*)∝P(*Y* = *c*) for *c* = 1, …, *C*. A middling value of the bandwidth parameter produces density estimates which appear visually similar to the true densities illustrated in [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). A large value of the bandwidth parameter results in a density estimate which is constant in large rectangular regions.

![Figure 4.10 Estimated class densities (left) and classification decisions (right) made using a histogram density estimate with, from top to bottom, bandwidths h = 0.5, 2, and 8, trained on the data of Figure 4.1. These histogram density estimates have estimated risks 0.444, 0.260, and 0.281, respectively. Bandwidth h = 2 was selected as approximately optimal using leave-one-out cross-validation, described in Section 7.3, to estimate risk from the training data. Points in empty histogram cells are predicted to be the most frequent class (purple), which is the minimum-risk prediction based on the estimated marginal distribution P(Y = c) = nc/n.](images/c04f010.jpg)

[**Figure 4.10**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-10) Estimated class densities (left) and classification decisions (right) made using a histogram density estimate with, from top to bottom, bandwidths *h* = 0.5, 2, and 8, trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). These histogram density estimates have estimated risks 0.444, 0.260, and 0.281, respectively. Bandwidth *h* = 2 was selected as approximately optimal using leave-one-out cross-validation, described in [Section 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c7_3), to estimate risk from the training data. Points in empty histogram cells are predicted to be the most frequent class (purple), which is the minimum-risk prediction based on the estimated marginal distribution P(*Y* = *c*) = *n[c]*/*n*.

Histograms are computationally more efficient than kernel density estimates, since histogram cells are typically far fewer than the number of training data (this is shown explicitly by the development of a histogram classifier using hash tables in [Section 14.9](#c14.xhtml#c14_9)). On the other hand, histograms use the training data less efficiently than kernel density estimates in the sense that, with bandwidths chosen appropriately (and in dimension *m* = 1), the mean squared error of a histogram density estimate is <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0054.gif"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0054.gif)while the mean squared error of a kernel density estimate is <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0055.gif"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0055.gif). For comparison, the mean squared error of a parametric density estimate is *O*(*n*^(− 1)) when the parametric model is correct. See Scott (1992) for details.

Histograms are particularly useful when knowledge about the data suggests that there is a natural way for it to be binned into rectangular cells. Categorical features, for example, have this property.

### 4.4.6 The Naive Bayes Classifier

The *naive Bayes classifier* is a likelihood method which is based on the assumption that the features (coordinates of *X*) are all independent, at least approximately. This means that the likelihood function P(*x* | *Y* = *c*) for each class can be expressed as a product of *m* marginal likelihoods: at the point *x* = (*x*[1], …, *x[m]*), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0043" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0042.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x220f;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0042.gif)

The naive Bayes classifier is trained by estimating the one-dimensional coordinate density P(*x[i]* | *Y* = *c*) for each class *c* and feature *i* in some way (any of the ways above, for example) and plugging the estimates into the product. [Figure 4.11](#c04.xhtml#figure4-11) illustrates kernel density estimates of marginal densities <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0056.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0056.gif)and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0057.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0057.gif), the resulting estimated joint densities <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0058.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0058.gif), and class predictions made by the naive Bayes classifier trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). This technique should not be neglected merely because of its pejorative name.^([16](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0016))

**Exercise 4.9** *Show that a naive Bayes classifier where all features are assumed to be Gaussian-distributed is equivalent to a quadratic discriminant classifier where all covariance matrices are assumed to be diagonal.*

## 4.5 Prototype Methods

The general idea behind prototype methods is to classify new data points by considering the classes of nearby training data points, where “nearby” is defined in terms of some kind of distance which makes sense for the application at hand. Training data are represented by *prototypes*, which are feature vectors in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0059.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>![](images/c04_ILM0059.gif). Prototypes may be observed data points or may be idealized data points.

### 4.5.1 *k*\-Nearest-Neighbor

Given training data (*x*[1], *y*[1]), …, (*x[n]*, *y[n]*) and a new point *x*, the *k*\-nearest-neighbor (KNN) algorithm classifies *x* to the most frequent class of the *k* nearest training data (ties, when possible, are usually decided randomly).^([17](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0017)) Small values of *k* result in wiggly class boundaries, while large values result in smooth ones. Taking *k* > 1 can provide robustness in the presence of mislabeled training data. *Every* data point is a prototype in the *k*\-nearest-neighbor classifier.

The effect of the number-of-neighbors parameter *k* is illustrated in the left-hand cells of [Figure 4.12](#c04.xhtml#figure4-12). A small value of *k* makes the behavior of the classifier sensitive to particular data points. Note how the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier predicts that a region in the top center of the upper-left cell is purple, due to the single out-lying purple data point visible in at the top center of the right-hand cell of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). Moderate values of *k* strike a balance between sensitivity to local variations in the class densities and smoothing away noise in the data. Large values of *k* result in classifiers which are relatively insensitive to local variations in the class densities.

![Figure 4.12 Classification decisions made using k-nearest-neighbors (left) and learning vector quantization (right), trained on the data of Figure 4.1. Numbers of nearest neighbors k = 1, 9, and 100 produce estimated risks 0.248, 0.202, and 0.247, respectively. Numbers of LVQ prototypes 60, 6, and 3 (20, 2, and 1 per class, shown in black) produce estimated risks 0.213, 0.195, and 0.245, respectively. The values k = 9 and 6 LVQ prototypes were selected as approximately optimal using leave-one-out cross-validation, described in Section 7.3, to estimate risk from the training data.](images/c04f012.jpg)

[**Figure 4.12**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-12) Classification decisions made using *k*\-nearest-neighbors (left) and learning vector quantization (right), trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). Numbers of nearest neighbors *k* = 1, 9, and 100 produce estimated risks 0.248, 0.202, and 0.247, respectively. Numbers of LVQ prototypes 60, 6, and 3 (20, 2, and 1 per class, shown in black) produce estimated risks 0.213, 0.195, and 0.245, respectively. The values *k* = 9 and 6 LVQ prototypes were selected as approximately optimal using leave-one-out cross-validation, described in [Section 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c7_3), to estimate risk from the training data.

Straightforward implementation of a *k*\-nearest-neighbor classifier requires computation of the distance between each new point <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0060.gif"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0060.gif)to be classified and every training data point: *O*(*n*) work per point to be classified. If the number of points to be classified is sufficiently large, a more efficient implementation of *k*\-nearest-neighbor can be achieved using a data structure called a *multidimensional binary search tree* or, more commonly, a *k-d tree* (Bentley, 1975). A *k*\-d tree requires *O*(*n*log *n*) work to construct, but using a *k*\-d tree requires only *O*(log *n*) work, on average, per point to be classified.

This is a very old classification method: 1-nearest-neighbor goes back to a 1951 technical report of the United States Air Force School of Aviation Medicine (Fix and Hodges, 1951). General *k*\-nearest-neighbor is due to Cover and Hart (1967).

### 4.5.2 Condensed *k*\-Nearest-Neighbor

Condensed *k*\-nearest-neighbor is an attempt to get the performance of *k*\-nearest-neighbor at lower cost (Hart, 1968). Given training data (*x*[1], *y*[1]), …, (*x[n]*, *y[n]*), a condensed set *S* is formed in the following way: initially, *S* = {(*x*[1], *y*[1])}. For *i* = 2, 3, …, *n*, if *x[i]* is misclassified by the *k*\-nearest-neighbor classifier trained on *S*, then (*x[i]*, *y[i]*) is added to *S* and otherwise is discarded. Once *S* has been constructed using all of the training data, the condensed *k*\-nearest-neighbor classifier is the *k*\-nearest-neighbor classifier trained on the subset *S*⊆{(*x*[1], *y*[1]), …, (*x[n]*, *y[n]*)}. The condensed set *S* is a set of prototypes which are actual data points. Of course, instead of training the *k*\-nearest neighbor classifier on *S*, one can use other classifiers—such as condensed *k*\-nearest-neighbor.

### 4.5.3 Nearest-Cluster

Nearest-cluster is another attempt to reduce the cost of *k*\-nearest-neighbor. The idea is simple: run a clustering algorithm on the training data from each class separately (see [Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml)). The centers of the resulting clusters are the prototypes for each class, and new data are classified by the *k*\-nearest-neighbor classifier trained on the set of prototypes (the class of a prototype is the class of the data from which it is constructed).

The class prototypes constructed by the nearest-cluster classifier need not be actual training data points, as they were in *k*\-nearest-neighbor and condensed *k*\-nearest-neighbor. For example, if <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0061.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0061.gif)and the *k*\-means^([18](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0018)) clustering algorithm (described in [Section 9.2](#c09.xhtml#c9_2)) were used, the prototypes typically would not be observed feature vectors. On the other hand, if the *k*\-medoids clustering algorithm (described in [Section 9.6](#c09.xhtml#c9_6)) were used, then the prototypes would be observed feature vectors.

### 4.5.4 Learning Vector Quantization

In the *k*\-nearest-neighbor and nearest-cluster classifiers, prototypes for a class are selected only based on the training data for that class, not based on all of the training data.^([19](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0019)) Learning vector quantization (LVQ), first described in Kohonen (1986), uses all of the training data to choose the class prototypes. For each class, some number of initial prototypes are chosen: this could be done by randomly sampling the training data for each class or by using a clustering algorithm as in the nearest-cluster classifier. Training the prototype set (which is the same as training the LVQ classifier) is done by moving the prototypes toward data points of their own class and away from data points of any other class. The trained LVQ classifier predicts the class at a point *x* to be the class of the nearest prototype to *x*. Application of LVQ requires that feature space <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0062.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>![](images/c04_ILM0062.gif)be such that a point <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0063.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0063.gif)can move a given distance in a given direction (for example, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0064.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0064.gif)).

The training algorithm starts with a step size ε < 1 and iterates the steps shown in [Figure 4.13](#c04.xhtml#figure4-13) until some convergence criterion or upper bound on iterations is reached. Some versions of LVQ decrease ε in step (7) of every iteration, for example, by using the update rule <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0044" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0043.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03f5;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#x03f5;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mi>i</mi><mi>I</mi></mfrac></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![Figure 4.13 The learning vector quantization algorithm.](images/c04f013.jpg)

[**Figure 4.13**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-13) The learning vector quantization algorithm.

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0043.gif)

where index *i* counts the iterations of the algorithm from 0 up to *I* − 1, and *I* is a user-specified number of iterations to perform. Another, more sophisticated version of LVQ^([20](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0020)) uses different values of ε for each class *c*, updating ε[*c*] in step (7) by the rule <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0045" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0044.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03f5;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03f5;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03f5;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>x</mi><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>p</mi><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>are</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>of</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>the</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>same</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>class</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">min</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi>&#x03f5;</mi><mo>,</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03f5;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03f5;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mfenced></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>x</mi><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>p</mi><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>are</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>of</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>different</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>classes</mtext><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0044.gif)

where *c* is the class of prototype *p* and ε < 1 is the initial value of ε[1], …, ε[*C*]. Thus the training algorithm shrinks ε[*c*] when it finds evidence that LVQ is performing well on class *c*, and increases ε[*c*] (up to a maximum of ε) when it finds evidence that LVQ is performing poorly on class *c*.

The effect of the number of prototypes *k* is illustrated in the right-hand cells of [Figure 4.12](#c04.xhtml#figure4-12). In these examples, the prototypes were initialized by selecting proportion P(*Y* = *c*) of the *k* points from feature vectors of class *c* uniformly at random without replacement, for each *c* = 1, …, *C*. The “more sophisticated” update rule was used with each ε[*c*] initialized to ε = 0.3, and 6000 iterations were performed. Larger values of *k* make the behavior of the LVQ classifier sensitive to particular data points, while smaller values of *k* make the behavior less sensitive to particular data points. In the extreme case of one prototype per class (*k* = *C*), the boundary between each pair of classes is linear.

## 4.6 Logistic Regression

Logistic regression solves the classification problem by turning it into a regression problem, explicitly estimating the vector of class probabilities <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0046" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0045.gif"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0045.gif)

Specifically, the model assumption made by logistic regression is that the (*C* − 1)-long vector of log-odds with respect to some specified class, which without loss of generality may as well be class 1, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0047" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0046.gif"><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0046.gif)

is a linear function of the feature vector *X*. That is, it is assumed that <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" where θ[*c*] denotes row *c* of θ.

Given a value of matrix θ, class-membership probabilities can be recovered from (4.2). For *c* = 1, …, *C*, define linear functions <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0050" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0049.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>+</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0049.gif)

and note that *T*[1] = *T*(*X*, θ[1]) = 0. Linear function *T*(*X*, θ[*c*]) is the logistic regression estimate of the log-odds in favor of class *c* over class 1, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0065.gif"><mrow><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0065.gif), for *c* = 1, …, *C*.

**Exercise 4.10** *Show that under the logistic regression model assumption (4.2), the probability that a feature vector *X* belongs to class c is*^([21](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0021)) <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0052" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0051.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></msubsup><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

(4.3)![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0051.gif)

Training a logistic regression classifier means finding an estimate <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0070.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c04_ILM0070.gif)of matrix θ. The training data are assumed to be independent, which means that the class label *Y[i]* is a single draw from the multinomial distribution with probability parameter P(*Y* | *X* = *x[i]*), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0053" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0052.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x223c;</mo><mi> Multinomial </mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0052.gif)

Thus the log-likelihood^([22](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0022)) of the data (*x*[1], *y*[1]), …, (*x[n]*, *y[n]*) is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0055" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0054.gif"><mrow><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0054.gif)

An estimate <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0071.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c04_ILM0071.gif)of θ is found by (approximately) maximizing this log-likelihood using a numerical optimization algorithm.^([23](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0023)) Details, including computation of the gradient of the log-likelihood (equivalently, by Exercise 4.11, the gradient of the training estimate of risk under cross-entropy loss) may be found in [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml). The trained classifier is then <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0056" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0055.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi> argmin </mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0055.gif)

where, for *c* = 1, …, *C*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0057" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0056.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></msubsup><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0056.gif)

**Exercise 4.11** *Show that estimating θ by maximizing the multinomial likelihood above is equivalent to estimating θ by minimizing training risk with respect to cross-entropy loss (defined in [Chapter 2](#c02.xhtml)).*

The lower-right cell shows the three estimated probabilities  for c = 1, 2, 3, plotted as functions of the features x. Logistic regression has estimated risk 0.220.](images/c04f014.jpg)

The class boundaries are piecewise linear. ## 4.7 Neural Networks

### 4.7.1 Activation Functions

A neural network classifier requires an *activation function*, which is often a “soft” (piecewise differentiable) version of an indicator function. Most commonly used is the *sigmoid*^([24](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0024)) function, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0058" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0057.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0057.gif)

which is a soft version of the indicator function^([25](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0025)) \[*v* ⩾ 0\]. This activation function is graphed in the upper-left cell of [Figure 4.15](#c04.xhtml#figure4-15).

![Figure 4.15 Activation functions used in neural networks.](images/c04f015.jpg)

[**Figure 4.15**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-15) Activation functions used in neural networks.

Other activation functions used sometimes in neural networks are the *symmetric sigmoid*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0059" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0058.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">tanh</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0058.gif)

which is a sigmoid shifted and scaled to take values in ( − 1, 1), the *rectified linear unit* (ReLU), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0060" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0059.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi>v</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0059.gif)

and the *radial basis function*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0061" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0060.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo>-</mo><msup><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0060.gif)

which is a soft version of the indicator function \[*v* = 0\]. These activation functions are graphed [Figure 4.15](#c04.xhtml#figure4-15). For specificity, we will use the sigmoid function <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0073.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0073.gif)in the rest of this section.

### 4.7.2 Neurons

The fundamental unit of a neural network is a *neuron*, which is the composition of an activation function σ and a linear map <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0074.gif"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0074.gif)specified by a (*k* + 1)-long parameter vector θ = (θ[0], θ[1], …, θ[*k*]). It will be convenient sometimes to think of the parameter vector as the concatenation of a scalar parameter^([26](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0026)) θ[0] and a *k*\-long vector θ[⋆] = (θ[1], …, θ[*k*]). A neuron, then, is the composition^([27](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0027)) <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0062" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0061.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>+</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>v</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>+</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></munderover><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0061.gif)

where vector *v* = (*v*[1], …, *v[k]*) is the input to the neuron. The geometric meaning of a neuron becomes more apparent when the length of vector θ[⋆] is separated from its direction, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0075.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0075.gif). The unit vector <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0076.gif"><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></math>![](images/c04_ILM0076.gif), length ‖θ[⋆]‖ and the scalar parameter θ[0] define a hyperplane H(θ[⋆], θ[0]) in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0077.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0077.gif), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0063" type="mathematics"><math display="block"
