columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="{" close="}"><mi>v</mi><mo>:</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mfenced></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="{" close="}"><mi>v</mi><mo>:</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>-</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

<span class="equationNumber"><a href="#c04-disp-0063-9">(4.9)</a></span>![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0062.gif)

The neuron specified above is a soft version of the indicator function <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0064" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0063.gif"><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>v</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>-</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0063.gif)

which is 1 when input *v* is in the direction of θ[⋆] from hyperplane H(θ[⋆], θ[0]) and is 0 when input *v* is in the direction of − θ[⋆] from hyperplane H(θ[⋆], θ[0]). The geometry of this situation is illustrated in [Figure 4.16](#c04.xhtml#figure4-16).

![Figure 4.16 For any scalar θ0 and k-long real vector θ⋆, the set of points  is a hyperplane in . The hyperplane lies at distance  from the origin, either in the direction of θ⋆ (if , that is, if θ0 < 0) or in the direction of − θ⋆ (if , that is, if θ0 > 0). The hyperplane H(θ⋆, θ0) cuts  into two half-spaces. The neuron σ(θ0 + θ⋆v) increases from  as v moves away from H(θ⋆, θ0) in the direction of θ⋆, eventually approaching the value 1. The neuron σ(θ0 + θ⋆v) decreases from  as v moves away from H(θ⋆, θ0) in the direction of − θ⋆, eventually approaching the value 0. This notation will be used again in Section 4.9.](images/c04f016.jpg)

[**Figure 4.16**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-16) For any scalar θ[0] and *k*\-long real vector θ[⋆], the set of points <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0078.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0078.gif)is a hyperplane in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0079.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0079.gif). The hyperplane lies at distance <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0080.gif"><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></math>![](images/c04_ILM0080.gif)from the origin, either in the direction of θ[⋆] (if <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0081.gif"><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0081.gif), that is, if θ[0] < 0) or in the direction of − θ[⋆] (if <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0082.gif"><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0082.gif), that is, if θ[0] > 0). The hyperplane H(θ[⋆], θ[0]) cuts <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0083.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0083.gif)into two half-spaces. The neuron σ(θ[0] + θ[⋆]*v*) increases from <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0084.gif"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>![](images/c04_ILM0084.gif)as *v* moves away from H(θ[⋆], θ[0]) in the direction of θ[⋆], eventually approaching the value 1. The neuron σ(θ[0] + θ[⋆]*v*) decreases from <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0085.gif"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>![](images/c04_ILM0085.gif)as *v* moves away from H(θ[⋆], θ[0]) in the direction of − θ[⋆], eventually approaching the value 0. This notation will be used again in [Section 4.9](#c04.xhtml#c4_9).

The length of the *k*\-long vector ‖θ[⋆]‖, is called the *activation rate* and affects how sensitive the neuron is to its input. If ‖θ[⋆]‖ is large, then the value of the neuron changes quickly from nearly 0 (or 1) to nearly 1 (or 0) as *v* crosses from one side of H(θ[⋆], θ[0]) to the other—so the neuron closely approximates an indicator function. If ‖θ[⋆]‖ is small, the value of the neuron changes slowly as *v* moves from one side of H(θ[⋆], θ[0]) to the other—so for a substantial set of *v*’s, the neuron is approximately a linear function of *v* with gradient θ[⋆].

### 4.7.3 Neural Networks

A *neural network* composes multiple neurons into a single function.^([28](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0028)) Some of the neurons in a neural network use the feature vector as input, some use the output of other neurons as input, and some may use a combination of the two.^([29](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0029)) The parameters of a neural network are the parameters of the neurons (including the way in which the neurons are connected together) and the parameters of an *output layer* of linear functions defined as in logistic regression, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0065" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0064.gif"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>+</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0064.gif)

but unlike logistic regression, none of the linear output functions are constrained to be zero. Neurons are typically arranged in layers according to what kind of input they receive. The *input layer* of neurons receives feature vectors as input, while any layer other than the input or output layers is called a *hidden layer* of neurons.

[Figure 4.17](#c04.xhtml#figure4-17) shows a neural network with an output layer of *C* linear functions, *T*[1], …, *T[C]*, and a single hidden layer of *N* neurons, *Z*[1], …, *Z[N]*. Each neuron in the hidden layer receives as input the entire feature vector, *X* = (*X*[1], …, *X[m]*). Each linear function in the output layer receives as input the entire vector of values of the hidden neurons, *Z* = (*Z*[1], …, *Z[N]*). The parameters of this neural network can be written as two matrices, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" or, in more compact notation, as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0073" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0072.gif"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

The vector of outputs *T* = (*T*[1], …, *T[C]*) is transformed into a vector of probabilities just as in logistic regression,^([30](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0030)) <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0074" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0073.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></msubsup><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0073.gif)

In a neural network context, the map <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0075" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0074.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x21a6;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></msubsup><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0074.gif)

is called the *softmax* function. As in logistic regression, a new data point is classified to minimize estimated risk.

Neural networks can have multiple hidden layers. A two-hidden-layer neural network could be made from the one shown in [Figure 4.17](#c04.xhtml#figure4-17) by using the vector *Z* as input to another layer of neurons (possibly a different number of them than in the first layer), the output of which is then used as input to the linear functions *T*[1], …, *T[C]*.

Training a neural network means estimating values of all of the parameters. Neural networks are trained by minimizing squared-error or cross-entropy loss^([31](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0031)) on training data using a numerical optimization method (for example, the fitted neural networks shown in [Figure 4.18](#c04.xhtml#figure4-18) were trained by applying the BFGS algorithm, described in Chapter 10, to 1000 randomly generated initial states and retaining the single fit with maximum likelihood). An important computational element of neural networks is *back-propagation*, which refers to an efficient method of computing the gradient of the training risk for use in a gradient descent algorithm. Details, including computation of the gradient of the training estimate of risk under cross-entropy loss, may be found in [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml). A technique which has been found useful in training deep networks (that is, networks with many layers) is described in [Section 11.3.11](#c11.xhtml#c11_3_11).

Geometrically, the *N* hyperplanes corresponding to the *N* hidden neurons in [Figure 4.17](#c04.xhtml#figure4-17) partition <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0087.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0087.gif)into <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0088.gif"><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></mfrac></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>+</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">min</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mfenced><mo>&#x2264;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0088.gif)polyhedra (except in degenerate cases, where there are even fewer polyhedra) (Buck, 1943), and the complete state of the hidden layer, *Z* = (*Z*[1], …, *Z[N]*), may be viewed as a soft version of a binary codeword which identifies the polyhedron containing input *X*. The linear functions of the output layer can, then, be viewed as linear functions of (approximate) binary codewords.

[**Figure 4.18**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-18) Part of a neural network considered in Exercise 4.12.

Classification decisions made by a single-hidden-layer neural network trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1) are shown in [Figure 4.19](#c04.xhtml#figure4-19). This figure illustrates the effect of the number *N* of hidden states in a single-hidden-layer neural network: in one extreme, the case *N* = 1 forces all class boundaries to be mutually parallel hyperplanes; as more neurons are added, the classifier becomes more sensitive to particular data points.

![Figure 4.19 Classification decisions made using a single-hidden-layer neural network trained on the data of Figure 4.1. Numbers of hidden-layer neurons 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 256 produce estimated risks 0.401, 0.201, 0.213, 0.224, 0.235, and 0.246 respectively. A range of two to five hidden-layer neurons was selected as approximately optimal using leave-one-out cross-validation, described in Section 7.3, to estimate risk from the training data. Dashed black lines show hyperplanes on which a fitted hidden neuron outputs the value  (omitted in the 256-neuron network).](images/c04f019.jpg)

[**Figure 4.19**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-19) Classification decisions made using a single-hidden-layer neural network trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). Numbers of hidden-layer neurons 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 256 produce estimated risks 0.401, 0.201, 0.213, 0.224, 0.235, and 0.246 respectively. A range of two to five hidden-layer neurons was selected as approximately optimal using leave-one-out cross-validation, described in [Section 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c7_3), to estimate risk from the training data. ### 4.7.4 Logistic Regression and Neural Networks

Consider a neural network with no hidden layer, shown in [Figure 4.21](#c04.xhtml#figure4-21). The output vector of class probabilities is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0082" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0081.gif"><mrow><msubsup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></msubsup><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mfenced><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></msubsup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0081.gif)![Figure 4.21 Logistic regression drawn as a no-hidden-layer neural network. The dashed arrows indicate that constant output node T1 = 0 may be regarded as a function of the feature vector (with fixed parameter vector θ(1)1 = 0) or may be omitted from the network.](images/c04f021.gif)

[**Figure 4.21**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-21) Logistic regression drawn as a no-hidden-layer neural network. The dashed arrows indicate that constant output node *T*[1] = 0 may be regarded as a function of the feature vector (with fixed parameter vector θ^((1))[1] = 0) or may be omitted from the network.

Without loss of generality, it can be assumed that any one of exp (*T*[1](*X*, θ^((1))[1])), …, exp (*T[C]*(*X*, θ^((1))[*C*])) has any given positive value by scaling them all (the scaling factor, which depends on *X* and θ^((1)), cancels out in normalization). In particular it can be assumed that exp (*T*[1](*X*, θ^((1))[1])) is identically one, which is equivalent to assuming that its parameter vector θ^((1))[1] is identically zero. This is exactly logistic regression.

This remark gives another interpretation of neural networks. A neural network with a single hidden layer is logistic regression performed on a basis of “soft” indicator functions of disjoint polyhedra, where the polyhedra are chosen adaptively when the neural network is trained. Neural networks with multiple hidden layers are logistic regression on more complex adaptive bases.

## 4.8 Classification Trees

A classification tree is a decision tree algorithm which assigns class labels to data. All data enter the root node of the tree, and each internal (non-leaf) node partitions the data in some way, based on the feature vectors. Each leaf (terminal node) assigns a particular class label to all data which enter it. [Figure 4.22](#c04.xhtml#figure4-22) shows a small classification tree.

![Figure 4.22 A classification tree which maps an input vector  to one of three classes. The root node is at the top. This tree was trained on the data of Figure 4.1, and pruned to have five leaf nodes.](images/c04f022.jpg)

[**Figure 4.22**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-22) A classification tree which maps an input vector <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0099.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0099.gif)to one of three classes. The root node is at the top. This tree was trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1), and pruned to have five leaf nodes.

### 4.8.1 Classification of Data by Leaves (Terminal Nodes)

Let a tree be given, and let *t* denote a leaf node of the tree. The event “datum (*X*, *Y*) enters node *t*” will be denoted *X* ∈ *t*: by construction, at least one training point enters each leaf node of the tree. Let *n[c]* denote the number of training data of class *c*, *n^t[c]* denote the number of training data of class *c* which enter node *t*, and *n^t* = ∑^(*C*)[*c* = 1]*n[c]*^(*t*) denote the total number of training data which enter node *t*.

The probability that a datum (*X*, *Y*) enters node *t*, given that its class is *c*, is estimated by the proportion of training data of class *c* which enter it,^([33](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0033)) <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0083" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0082.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0082.gif)

This estimate is then used to make predictions as a likelihood classifier. That is, the estimated posterior probability that a datum (*X*, *Y*) is class *c*, given that it enters node *t*, is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0084" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0083.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0083.gif)

where <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0085" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0084.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0084.gif)

Node *t* classifies all data which enter it as the class *c* which minimizes the estimated posterior risk, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0086" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0085.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x221d;</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfrac><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0085.gif)

**Exercise 4.13** *Show that if the prior distribution is estimated from the training data such that* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0101.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0101.gif), *then* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0087" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0086.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow></math></displayedItem>

*and* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0088" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0087.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><msup><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msup></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

*Show that with this prior, under 0–1 loss, a leaf node classifies all data which enter it to be the most common class among the training data which enter it.*

### 4.8.2 Impurity of Nodes and Trees

The *impurity of a leaf node t* is a function, *I*(*t*), of the estimated posterior distribution on the class of a datum (*X*, *Y*) given that *X* ∈ *t*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0089" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0088.gif"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0088.gif)

which measures how diffuse the distribution is on the set of values {1, …, *C*}. Commonly used measures of impurity are: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" ![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0089.gif)

^([34](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0034))Under each of these definitions, the impurity *I*(*t*) is non-negative, is uniquely maximized when the probability distribution <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0104.gif"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0104.gif)is the uniform distribution, and is minimal and equal to zero when this distribution assigns probability one to one class and probability zero to all other classes.

The *impurity of a tree* is the expected impurity of a leaf node with respect to probability distribution <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0105.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0105.gif)on leaf nodes, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0092" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0091.gif"><mrow><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mrow><mi> all </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> leaf </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> nodes </mi><mspace width="4pt"/></mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></munder><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0091.gif)

**Exercise 4.14** *Show that when the impurity of a leaf node is measured by the Gini index of diversity, the impurity of the whole tree can be expressed as:* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0093" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0092.gif"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>-</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mrow><mi> all </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> leaf </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> nodes </mi><mspace width="4pt"/></mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></munder><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0092.gif)

### 4.8.3 Growing Trees

A classification tree is trained (“grown”) by beginning with a single node, which is the root node and also a leaf, and iteratively splitting leaf nodes in the following way. Let *t* be a leaf node, let <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0094" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0093.gif"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0093.gif)

be the set of training data which enter *t*, and suppose that at least two distinct classes are represented in *R*, that is, |{*y[i]*: *x[i]* ∈ *t*}| ⩾ 2. Consider all partitions of *R* into two non-empty subsets, *R* = *R*[1]∪*R*[2], which arise by splitting the data according to the *j*th feature, for each *j* = 1, …, *m*, as follows. If the *j*th feature is continuous, splitting is performed by applying a threshold τ, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0095" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0094.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mi>&#x03c4;</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow><mspace width="2.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="2.em"/><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>&#x03c4;</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0094.gif)

There are infinitely many possible values of τ, but only finitely many such partitions to consider, since *R* is a finite set. If the *j*th feature is categorical, splitting is performed by partitioning the range of the categorical feature, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0096" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0095.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow><mspace width="2.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="2.em"/><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0095.gif)

where *S*[1]∪*S*[2] is a partition into two nonempty subsets of the finite set of values attainable by the *j*th feature. Each partition^([35](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0035)) of *R* corresponds to the addition of two new leaf nodes *t*[1] and *t*[2] to the tree extending from *t*, which is no longer a leaf node: *R*[1] is the set of training data which enter *t*[1] and *R*[2] is the set of training data which enter *t*[2]. The split which minimizes the impurity of the tree is retained, meaning that the new nodes *t*[1] and *t*[2] are added to the tree.^([36](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0036))

The splitting process is repeated, and splitting continues until each leaf node satisfies a stopping criterion, for example, leaf nodes may be split until each satisfies at least one of the following conditions: its training data are all of one class; its training data all have the same feature vector; it contains no more than some specified number of training data.

[Figure 4.23](#c04.xhtml#figure4-23) shows the first four steps of training of a classification tree on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). At each step, the partition of the data shown is that which minimizes the impurity of the tree with the empirical prior distribution <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0106.gif"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mn>48</mn><mn>150</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>49</mn><mn>150</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>53</mn><mn>150</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0106.gif)on the three classes.^([37](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0037)) The classification tree corresponding to the lower-right cell of [Figure 4.23](#c04.xhtml#figure4-23) is represented in [Figure 4.22](#c04.xhtml#figure4-22) as a decision tree algorithm. The predictions made by this tree are shown in the upper-right cell of [Figure 4.24](#c04.xhtml#figure4-24). Any tree with only two leaf nodes, such as that shown in the upper-left-hand cell of [Figure 4.23](#c04.xhtml#figure4-23), is called a *stump*.

![Figure 4.23 These four pictures show, from left to right and top to bottom, the first four steps of training a classification tree on the data of Figure 4.1. The lower-right cell corresponds to the tree shown in Figure 4.22, and to the predictions shown in the upper-right cell of Figure 4.24.](images/c04f023.jpg)

[**Figure 4.23**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-23) These four pictures show, from left to right and top to bottom, the first four steps of training a classification tree on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). The lower-right cell corresponds to the tree shown in [Figure 4.22](#c04.xhtml#figure4-22), and to the predictions shown in the upper-right cell of [Figure 4.24](#c04.xhtml#figure4-24).

![Figure 4.24 Classification decisions made using a classification tree trained on the data of Figure 4.1. The numbers 1, 5, 15, and 25 of leaf nodes correspond to cost-complexity parameter α values of about 2− 1, 2− 4, 2− 7, and 0, respectively, and produce respective estimated risks 0.665, 0.236, 0.243, and 0.259. The 15-leaf tree was selected as approximately optimal using leave-one-out cross-validation, described in Section 7.3, to estimate risk from the training data, though in this case the 5-node tree has significantly lower risk on test data.](images/c04f024.jpg)

The numbers 1, 5, 15, and 25 of leaf nodes correspond to cost-complexity parameter α values of about 2^(− 1), 2^(− 4), 2^(− 7), and 0, respectively, and produce respective estimated risks 0.665, 0.236, 0.243, and 0.259. ### 4.8.4 Pruning Trees

As explained so far, trees are trained until they have zero misclassification error on the training data (unless there are training data with identical feature vectors but different class labels) or some other stopping criterion is met. This suggests that they may be badly over-fit (see [Chapter 5](#c05.xhtml) and [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml)). There are two ways to avoid over-fit trees. The first is to stop growing the tree according to some criterion, such as if all nodes either pass a (non-zero) threshold on the measure of impurity or contain fewer than some number of training points. The second, recommended by Breiman et al. (1984), is to grow the tree completely and then to prune it back to a subtree of the full-grown tree.

Breiman et al. (1984) recommend pruning a full-grown tree in the following way. For a given value of a tuning parameter α > 0, find the subtree of the full tree which minimizes the *cost-complexity criterion*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0098" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0097.gif"><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>&#x03b1;</mi><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi> number </mi><mi> of </mi><mi> leaf </mi><mi> nodes </mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mspace width="2.em"/><mo>+</mo><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mrow><mi> all </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> leaf </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> nodes </mi><mspace width="4pt"/></mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></munder><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">min</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></munder><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

<span class="equationNumber"><a href="#c04-disp-0098-17">(4.17)</a></span>![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0097.gif)

The first term penalizes the size of the tree, the second penalizes the training estimate of the risk of the tree, and parameter α sets the relative importance of these two terms^([38](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0038)) (α = 0 puts no penalty on the size of the tree, in which case no nodes are pruned, and as α → ∞, the tree will be pruned back to the root node). [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml) of Breiman et al. (1984) shows how to compute efficiently the optimal subtree, in terms of cost-complexity criterion, for any given α. An approximately optimal value of α is chosen by cross-validation or some other method of risk estimation—see [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml).

**Exercise 4.16** *Show that under 0–1 loss, the cost-complexity criterion is* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0099" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0098.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03b1;</mi><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi> number </mi><mi> of </mi><mi> leaf </mi><mi> nodes </mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mrow><mi> all </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> leaf </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> nodes </mi><mspace width="4pt"/></mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></munder><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>-</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">max</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></munder><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>=</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0098.gif)

One of the strengths of trees is that they are very easy to interpret, and trees have even been designed for implementation by hand. For example, the pocket-sized book *Berry Finder: A Guide to Native Plants with Fleshy Fruits* by Dorcas S. Miller, illustrated by Cherie Hunter Day, contains a 54-page implementation of a classification tree consisting of approximately 120 leaf nodes and 150 internal nodes (some of which have more than two child nodes). Internal nodes are queries about features of a plant (leaves, stems, fruit, growing location, etc.) and leaf nodes predict a distinct species.^([39](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0039))

### 4.8.5 Regression Trees

Trees are also used for regression. Impurity measures used for regression trees are <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi> Var </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>Y</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>Y</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi mathvariant="italic">mean</mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi mathvariant="italic">absolute</mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi mathvariant="italic">deviation</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="italic">mean</mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi mathvariant="italic">absolute</mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi mathvariant="italic">deviation</mi></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mo>\[</mo><mo>|</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>-</mo><mi> median </mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>\[</mo><mi>Y</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>\]</mo><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0099.gif)

At a leaf node *t*, a regression tree predicts E\[*Y* | *X* ∈ *t*\] when squared-error loss is used, and median \[*Y* | *X* ∈ *t*\] when absolute-error loss is used.

## 4.9 Support Vector Machines

The last classification method covered in this chapter is the support vector machine. Support vector machines are somewhat different from all of the other methods in this chapter, in that they are not explicit approximations of the Bayes classifier. Support vector machines are motivated by a geometric idea of what makes a classifier “good” and we shall see that this results in a loss function which is different from the loss functions encountered in [Chapters 2](#c02.xhtml), [3](#c03.xhtml), and [4](#c04.xhtml) (indeed, which violates the definition of a loss function given in [Chapter 2](#c02.xhtml)). In particular, we shall encounter a loss function which takes into account *the location of a feature vector* relative to a class boundary, and *which may penalize correctly classified data* if their feature vectors are too close to this boundary.

### 4.9.1 Support Vector Machine Classifiers

Suppose there are *C* = 2 classes, that the feature space <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0109.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>![](images/c04_ILM0109.gif)is <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0110.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0110.gif)and that the two classes are *linearly separable* in the feature space, which means that there exists a hyperplane^([40](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0040)) <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0101" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0100.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>v</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="{" close="}"><mi>v</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>:</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>v</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mfenced></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0100.gif)

such that all data of one class lie on one side of H(θ[⋆], θ[0]) and all data of the other class lie on the other side. Data with two linearly separable classes are shown in [Figure 4.25](#c04.xhtml#figure4-25). Suppose also that our goal is to classify new data using a linear classification boundary: that is, we must choose a hyperplane in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0112.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0112.gif)and declare all points on one side to be class 1 and all points on the other side to be class 2. What is the best hyperplane to choose?

![Figure 4.25 Subsets of the orange and purple data of Figure 4.1, selected so that the two classes are linearly separable. Three distinct hyperplanes (lines) which separate the two classes are shown: there are, of course, infinitely many such lines. A geometric definition of what makes a line separating the two classes “good” motivates support vector machine (SVM) classifiers.](images/c04f025.jpg)

[**Figure 4.25**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-25) Subsets of the orange and purple data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1), selected so that the two classes are linearly separable. Three distinct hyperplanes (lines) which separate the two classes are shown: there are, of course, infinitely many such lines. A geometric definition of what makes a line separating the two classes “good” motivates support vector machine (SVM) classifiers.

One answer to this question is the following. First, restrict the choice to the set of hyperplanes which separate the training data. These and only these hyperplanes will produce a classifier with zero training error.^([41](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0041)) For any of these hyperplanes *H*, there is a minimum distance *d*[1] from *H* to the data in class 1 and a minimum distance *d*[2] from *H* to the data in class 2, and so *H* can be widened into a slab of width *d*[1] + *d*[2] which separates the two classes. The width *d*[1] + *d*[2] is called the *margin* of the classifier based on *H*. The basic assumption of a support vector machine classifier is that *under 0–1 loss and uniform prior distribution on class, the “best” two-class linear classifier is a separating hyperplane with maximum margin such that d*[1] = *d*[2].

Let the two class labels be encoded so that the response variables *Y[i]* are in { − 1, 1}. Data (*x*[1], *y*[1]), …, (*x[n]*, *y[n]*) are separated by a hyperplane if and only if there is a hyperplane H(θ[⋆], θ[0]) such that, for all *i*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0102" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0101.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> if </mi><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> if </mi><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></mrow></math></displayedItem>

(4.4)![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0101.gif)

which is written more compactly as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0103" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0102.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="1.em"/><mrow><mi> for </mi><mi> all </mi></mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

(4.5)\-->![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0102.gif)

The geometry of the situation, illustrated in [Figure 4.26](#c04.xhtml#figure4-26), is more apparent if the normal vector of the separating hyperplane is made to be a unit vector, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0104" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0103.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mfenced><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="2.em"/><mrow><mi> for </mi><mi> all </mi></mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

(4.6)\-->![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0103.gif)![Figure 4.26 The linearly separable data of Figure 4.25, with the maximum-margin separating hyperplane (solid line) and the two hyperplanes which define the margin (dashed lines). The unit vector  is shown at the lower right. The orange dots are class “1” and the purple dots are class “− 1,” and all data points (xi, yi) satisfy the inequality yi(θ⋆ xi + θ0) ⩾ 1. The three filled dots—two orange and one purple—are the support vectors, that is, the data points satisfying yi(θ⋆ xi + θ0) = 1.](images/c04f026.jpg)

[**Figure 4.26**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-26) The linearly separable data of [Figure 4.25](#c04.xhtml#figure4-25), with the maximum-margin separating hyperplane (solid line) and the two hyperplanes which define the margin (dashed lines). The unit vector <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0121.gif"><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></math>![](images/c04_ILM0121.gif)is shown at the lower right. The orange dots are class “1” and the purple dots are class “− 1,” and all data points (*x[i]*, *y[i]*) satisfy the inequality *y[i]*(θ[⋆] *x[i]* + θ[0]) ⩾ 1. The three filled dots—two orange and one purple—are the support vectors, that is, the data points satisfying *y[i]*(θ[⋆] *x[i]* + θ[0]) = 1.

Written this way, it is easy to see that the distance from feature vector *x[i]* to the separating hyperplane H(θ[⋆], θ[0]) is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0105" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0104.gif"><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="|" close="|"><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0104.gif)

and this is bounded below by <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0113.gif"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></math>![](images/c04_ILM0113.gif).

Maximizing the margin, then, means solving the optimization problem^([42](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0042)) <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0106" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0105.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>minimize</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>over</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mtext>:</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>subject</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>to,</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>all</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>i</mi><mtext>:</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

(4.7)![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0105.gif)

This is done (approximately) by quadratic programming techniques, resulting in trained parameter values <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0115.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub></math>![](images/c04_ILM0115.gif)and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0116.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![](images/c04_ILM0116.gif). A trained support vector machine consists of the trained parameters together with the classification rule “given a feature vector *X*, predict the class to be the sign of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0117.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mi>X</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0117.gif).” The margin of the trained support vector machine is <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0118.gif"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0118.gif). Any training data point (*x[i]*, *y[i]*) which satisfies (4.5) with equality, that is, satisfies *y[i]*(θ[⋆]*x[i]* + θ[0]) = 1, is a *support vector*.

While the details of quadratic programming are beyond the scope of this book, there are some points which are essential to mention here. The optimization problem (4.7) is solved by solving a dual problem in which the objective function depends on the data only through the set of inner products (*x[i]*^T*x[j]*)^(*n*)[*i*, *j* = 1]. Solving this dual problem results in estimation of an *n*\-long parameter vector ψ = (ψ[1], …, ψ[*n*]), with the property that <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0119.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#x2260;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0119.gif)only if the training data point (*x[i]*, *y[i]*) is a support vector. In terms of the dual parameter ψ, the predicted class of a new feature vector *X* is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0107" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0106.gif"><mrow><mi> sign </mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi> sign </mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo><mrow><mi> is </mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi> support </mi><mi> vector </mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></munder><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi> sign </mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0106.gif)

where <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0120.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo><mrow><mi> is </mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi> support </mi><mi> vector </mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></msub><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0120.gif).

If the classes are not linearly separable, as shown in [Figure 4.27](#c04.xhtml#figure4-27), then the inequality condition (4.5) cannot be satisfied. A weakened form of (4.5) can be satisfied, though, by introducing *slack variables*^([43](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0043)) <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0108" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0107.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">max</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0107.gif)

and changing (4.5) to <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0109" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0108.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="2.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="2.em"/><msub><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="2.em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>all</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>i</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

(4.8)![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0108.gif)![Figure 4.27 The data of Figures 4.25 and 4.26, modified so that the classes are not linearly separable. The data with positive slack variables are indicated by gray arrows. The purple dots above the solid line are data with slack variables ξi > 1 and are misclassified by the linear classifier. The purple dot below the solid line but above the dashed line, and the orange dot above the solid line but below the dashed line, are data with slack variables 0 < ξi < 1: they contribute to the penalty without being misclassified.](images/c04f027.jpg)

[**Figure 4.27**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-27) The data of [Figures 4.25](#c04.xhtml#figure4-25) and [4.26](#c04.xhtml#figure4-26), modified so that the classes are not linearly separable. The data with positive slack variables are indicated by gray arrows. The purple dots above the solid line are data with slack variables ξ[*i*] > 1 and are misclassified by the linear classifier. The purple dot below the solid line but above the dashed line, and the orange dot above the solid line but below the dashed line, are data with slack variables 0 < ξ[*i*] < 1: they contribute to the penalty without being misclassified.

Slack variable ξ[*i*] is the smallest amount which can be added to *y[i]*(θ[⋆] *x[i]* + θ[0]) so that the total is at least one: thus for each *i*, either *y[i]*(θ[⋆] *x[i]* + θ[0]) ⩾ 1 and ξ[*i*] = 0 or *y[i]*(θ[⋆] *x[i]* + θ[0]) + ξ[*i*] = 1, and ξ[*i*] > 0. A data point *exceeds the margin* if ξ[*i*] > 0. A data point is misclassified by the classification boundary H(θ[⋆], θ[0]) if and only if ξ[*i*] > 1. A support vector machine still seeks the maximum margin classifier, making allowance for some data points to exceed the margin and even to be misclassified. Optimization problem (4.7) becomes <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0110" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0109.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>minimize</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>over</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mtext>,</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mtext>:</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#x03b3;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>subject</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>to,</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>all</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>i</mi><mtext>:</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="1.em"/><msub><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

(4.23)![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0109.gif)

where γ ⩾ 0 is a tuning parameter. In this case, the support vectors are the training data points (*x[i]*, *y[i]*) which satisfy (4.7) with equality or for which ξ[*i*] > 0.

Optimization problem (4.9) has two goals: to maximize the margin (that is, to minimize ‖θ[⋆]‖) and to minimize a “risk” function of the training data, ∑^(*n*)[*i* = 1]ξ[*i*]. These goals are to be met simultaneously, and their relative importance is determined by γ. The “loss” function <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0111" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0110.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x21a6;</mo><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">max</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0110.gif)

assigns a zero penalty to correctly classified data which are on the correct side of the classification boundary by distance at least <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0122.gif"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></math>![](images/c04_ILM0122.gif). As the distance from a correctly classified datum to the boundary hyperplane goes from <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0123.gif"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></math>![](images/c04_ILM0123.gif)to 0, the “loss” goes from 0 to 1, and as this datum crosses the boundary hyperplane and becomes misclassified, the “loss” increases from 1 proportionately with the distance to the boundary.^([44](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0044)) This is made explicit by rewriting (4.9) as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0112" type="mathematics"><math display="block"
