width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

<span class="equationNumber"><a href="#c04-disp-0112-24">(4.24)</a></span>![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0111.gif)

The loss function max (0, 1 − *Y*(θ[⋆]*X* + θ[0])) is illustrated in [Figure 4.28](#c04.xhtml#figure4-28). In [Figure 4.28](#c04.xhtml#figure4-28), the left-hand dashed line drawn in the plane is {*v*: θ[⋆]*v* + θ[0] = 1}, the blue side of the margin: this line is where the blue surface representing the loss incurred by blue data changes from zero (to the left of the dashed line) to positive (to the right of the dashed line). The right-hand dashed line drawn in the plane is {*v*: θ[⋆]*v* + θ[0] = −1}, the purple side of the margin: this line is where the purple surface representing the loss incurred by purple data changes from positive (to the left of the dashed line) to zero (to the right of the dashed line). The solid line drawn in the plane is {*v*: θ[⋆]*v* + θ[0] = 0}, the separating hyperplane (class boundary): the trained support vector machine predicts the blue class to the left of this line, and predicts the purple class to the right of this line. On the solid line, both blue and purple data incur one unit of loss. Due to the shape looking somewhat like open hinge, the loss function max (0, 1 − *Y*(θ[⋆]*X* + θ[0])) is called *hinge loss*. Note that loss is incurred for any data point within the margin, that is, any point (*X*, *Y*) such that − 1 < θ[⋆]*X* + θ[0] < 1, whether or not it is correctly classified (though misclassified data are penalized more than correctly classified data).

![Figure 4.28 The loss functions max (0, 1 − Y(θ⋆X + θ0)) which are applied to the blue data (blue surface, class Y = 1) and the purple data (purple surface, class Y = −1) in the example of Figure 4.1. Training data which are support vectors are shown as solid dots, while the rest are shown as hollow dots, although this is partly obscured by the viewing angle—which dots are truly hollow and which are truly filled is more clearly seen in the lower-left-hand cell of Figure 4.29.](images/c04f028.jpg)

[**Figure 4.28**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-28) The loss functions max (0, 1 − *Y*(θ[⋆]*X* + θ[0])) which are applied to the blue data (blue surface, class *Y* = 1) and the purple data (purple surface, class *Y* = −1) in the example of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). Training data which are support vectors are shown as solid dots, while the rest are shown as hollow dots, although this is partly obscured by the viewing angle—which dots are truly hollow and which are truly filled is more clearly seen in the lower-left-hand cell of [Figure 4.29](#c04.xhtml#figure4-29).

An approximately optimal value of γ is chosen by cross-validation or some other method of risk estimation—see [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml). This is advisable even in the case of linearly separable classes. The effect of the penalty parameter γ is illustrated in [Figure 4.30](#c04.xhtml#figure4-30).

Support vector machines are applied to data of *C* > 2 classes by training multiple binary SVMs and combining their predictions. This is illustrated in [Figure 4.29](#c04.xhtml#figure4-29)—detailed discussion is deferred to [Section 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c6_1).

All three support vector machines were trained using error penalty value γ = 2.112.](images/c04f029.jpg)

### 4.9.2 Kernelization

One way to use a simple classifier on hard-to-separate data is to map the features into a higher-dimensional space in such a way that the classes become more easily separated than in the original feature space. For example, using a linear classifier in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0124.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0124.gif)to classify the data shown in [Figure 4.31](#c04.xhtml#figure4-31) seems like a bad idea. Consider, though, applying the map <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0125.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#x2192;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0125.gif), defined by <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0126.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0126.gif), to the data in [Figure 4.31](#c04.xhtml#figure4-31). The result is shown in [Figure 4.32](#c04.xhtml#figure4-32), where, by looking in the right direction, it can be seen that the classes have been made linearly separable in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0127.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0127.gif). The preimage in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0128.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0128.gif)of a linear classification boundary in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0129.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0129.gif)is an ellipse, shown in gray in [Figure 4.31](#c04.xhtml#figure4-31).

[**Figure 4.32**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-32) The data of [Figure 4.31](#c04.xhtml#figure4-31) have been mapped into a two-dimensional surface in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0131.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0131.gif)so that the classes are linearly separable: the right-hand cell shows that the two classes can be separated by a plane. The light gray ellipse of [Figure 4.31](#c04.xhtml#figure4-31) is the intersection of the surface containing the data with a class-separating plane in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0132.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0132.gif), projected back into <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0133.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0133.gif).

A disadvantage of mapping data from <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0134.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi> small </mi></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0134.gif)to <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0135.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi> big </mi></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0135.gif)is that training a classifier can become computationally expensive in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0136.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi> big </mi></msup></math>![](images/c04_ILM0136.gif). In some cases, though, there is a trick to avoid this computational cost. If, for example, all of the information in the features (*x[i]*)^(*n*)[*i* = 1] which is needed to train the classifier is contained in the *n* × *n* matrix of inner products <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0113" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0112.gif"><msubsup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mfenced><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0112.gif)

(as in the case of support vector machines), then one need not compute (φ(*x[i]*))^(*n*)[*i* = 1] but only the *n* × *n* matrix <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0114" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0113.gif"><mrow><msubsup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0113.gif)

Furthermore, *we don’t even need to know* φ, we merely need to construct a map <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0137.gif"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0137.gif)such that there exists some phi with <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0115" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0114.gif"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0114.gif)

Conditions under which a bivariate function *K*(*x*, *w*) has a decomposition as *K*(*x*, *w*) = φ(*x*)^Tφ(*w*) (where the dimension of the range of φ is perhaps countably infinite) are given by Mercer’s theorem^([45](#c04.xhtml#c04-note-0045)) (Ash, 1965). Typically one specifies *K* and replaces *x[i]*^T*x[j]* in (4.9) with *K*(*x[i]*, *x[j]*). Commonly used kernels are: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0116" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0115.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi> polynomial </mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b1;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi>w</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#x03b2;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>&#x03b4;</mi></msup></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi> sigmoid </mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">tanh</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b1;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi>w</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#x03b2;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> Gaussian </mi><mi> or </mi><mi> radial </mi></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mo>(</mo><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03b1;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>w</mi><msup><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0115.gif)

Parameter values of these kernels are chosen by cross-validation or some other risk estimation method.

In terms of the estimated intercept parameter <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0138.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![](images/c04_ILM0138.gif)and estimated dual parameter <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0139.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c04_ILM0139.gif), the predicted class of a new feature vector *X* is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0117" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0116.gif"><mrow><mi> sign </mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo><mrow><mi> is </mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi> support </mi><mi> vector </mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></munder><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0116.gif)

Predictions made by support vector machines using a polynomial kernel and Gaussian kernel, trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1), are shown in [Figure 4.33](#c04.xhtml#figure4-33).

![Figure 4.33 Classification decisions made using a radial kernel (left cell, with γ = 2.382 and α = 0.219) and a polynomial kernel (right cell, with γ = 1.073, α = 0.677, β = 0.492, and δ = 3.525) support vector machine trained on the data of Figure 4.1. All parameters of these two classifiers were set to approximately optimal values using leave-one-out cross-validation, described in Section 7.3, to estimate risk from the training data (with optimization performed by simulated annealing and the Nelder–Mead algorithm, described in Chapter 10). These classifiers have estimated risks 0.201 and 0.208, respectively.](images/c04f033.jpg)

[**Figure 4.33**](#c04.xhtml#figureanchor4-33) Classification decisions made using a radial kernel (left cell, with γ = 2.382 and α = 0.219) and a polynomial kernel (right cell, with γ = 1.073, α = 0.677, β = 0.492, and δ = 3.525) support vector machine trained on the data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). All parameters of these two classifiers were set to approximately optimal values using leave-one-out cross-validation, described in [Section 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c7_3), to estimate risk from the training data (with optimization performed by simulated annealing and the Nelder–Mead algorithm, described in [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml)). These classifiers have estimated risks 0.201 and 0.208, respectively.

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0119.gif)

### 4.9.3 Proximal Support Vector Machine Classifiers

It was observed empirically, some time in 1999 through 2001, that the minimization problem of SVMs (4.9) could be modified without changing classification performance, to <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0121" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0120.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>minimize</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>over</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mtext>:</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>&#x03b3;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msubsup><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> subject </mi><mi> to </mi><mo>,</mo><mi> for </mi><mi> all </mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mo>:</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="1.em"/><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

(4.11)![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0120.gif)

The objective function has been made into a homogeneous quadratic function by adding <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0142.gif"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0142.gif)and changing the measure of the error vector from the 1-norm to the 2-norm. This makes the function strongly convex, which makes the quadratic programming problem easier to solve. Note that the condition ξ ⩾ 0 has been made superfluous by changing to the 2-norm: any negative ξ[*i*] can be set to 0 while maintaining the inequalities and reducing the objective function.

A proximal support vector machine (PSVM) classifier, introduced by Fung and Mangasarian in 2001, is a further and more extreme modification of SVMs: the linear inequality constraints are changed to linear equations: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0122" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0121.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>minimize</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>over</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mtext>,</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mtext>:</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>&#x03b3;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msubsup><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>subject</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>to,</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>all</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>i</mi><mtext>:</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="1.em"/><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

(4.12)![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0121.gif)

It is very simple to fit a PSVM. After all, PSVM is solving a weighted least-squares regression problem, and the solution can be written down in closed form. Also, kernelization can be used with PSVMs just as in SVMs, as the dual problem still involves the data through inner products (Fung and Mangasarian, 2001).

Note that PSVMs differ from SVMs considerably in interpretation. The SVM constraint <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0123" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0122.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0122.gif)

means “data in class (+ 1 or − 1) lie *on or beyond* the hyperplane <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0143.gif"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>v</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> or </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0143.gif), except for some error.” The PSVM constraint <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0124" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0123.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03be;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0123.gif)

means “data in class (+ 1 or − 1) lie *on* the hyperplane <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c04\_ILM0144.gif"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>v</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> or </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c04_ILM0144.gif), except for some error.” That is, a trained PSVM is approximating the data in the two classes by a pair of parallel hyperplanes. Thus PSVM is essentially a prototype method, where the class prototypes are not points, but hyperplanes. If kernelization is used, then “hyperplane” becomes “manifold” in this statement, and the parallelism between the two class prototypes exists in some higher-dimensional space.

The interpretation of PSVMs is made more explicit by rewriting (4.12) as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c04-disp-0125" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c04\_M0124.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>minimize</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>over</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mtext>,</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mtext>:</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>&#x03b3;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

<span class="equationNumber"><a href="#c04-disp-0125-27">(4.27)</a></span>![numbered Display Equation](images/c04_M0124.gif)

The sum in (4.13) is the total squared-error loss incurred by simultaneously fitting the data in the two classes by the hyperplanes {*v*: θ[⋆] *v* − θ[0] = 1} and {*v*: θ[⋆] *v* − θ[0] = −1}, while the other two terms penalize the size of the parameter vector θ = (θ[0], θ[⋆]). Viewed this way, PSVMs are a rediscovery of ridge regression (see [Chapter 3](#c03.xhtml)).

## 4.10 Postscript: Example Problem Revisited

The result of fitting the models described in this Chapter (and also some models described in [Chapter 6](#c06.xhtml)) to the example data of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1) are summarized in [Table 4.2](#c04.xhtml#table4-2) and [Figure 4.34](#c04.xhtml#figure4-34). It is interesting to note that while the Gaussian mixture model with three components per class is the correct model, in the sense that the training data truly were generated by such a model, it produced relatively poor predictive performance. Many find this result counter-intuitive at first: this was addressed in [Section 4.4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_4_3) and will be addressed further in [Chapters 5](#c05.xhtml) and [8](#c08.xhtml).

*It is absolutely not the purpose of Table* [4.2](#c04.xhtml#table4-2) *and Figure* [4.34](#c04.xhtml#figure4-34) *to pass as evidence that any classification method is superior to any other on any dataset besides the one displayed in Figure* [4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1). Nor was the dataset of [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#figure4-1) designed to make any method appear favorably compared to any other. What [Table 4.2](#c04.xhtml#table4-2) and [Figure 4.34](#c04.xhtml#figure4-34) show is that a range of different risks can be expected among classifiers trained on a given set of data, and that the relative performance of the methods may give some clue to the nature of the data. In this example, the classifiers of [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml) fall naturally into two sets separated by a significant performance gap: those with risk 0.212 or below, and those with risk 0.220 or above. Seven of the eight classifiers with risk 0.220 or above produce class boundaries which are piecewise hyperplanes, and among these, performance tends to get worse when the hyperplanes are forced to be orthogonal to the coordinate axes. We might infer from this that whatever the class boundaries may be, they are not well approximated by hyperplanes and in particular are not well approximated by hyperplanes orthogonal to the coordinate axes. Practically, we might decide not to focus future classification effort in this example on classification trees or histograms, and focus instead on methods which can learn curved class boundaries. Fitting classifiers to data is an exploratory process!

## Notes

# 5  
Bias–Variance Trade-off

> A machine \[classifier\] with too much capacity \[ability to fit training data exactly\] is like a botanist with a photographic memory who, when presented with a new tree, concludes that it is not a tree because it has a different number of leaves from anything she has seen before; a machine with too little capacity is like the botanist’s lazy brother, who declares that if it’s green, then it’s a tree. Neither can generalize well.
> 
> —Christopher J. C. Burges, *Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery*, 1998

Recall from [Chapter 2](#c02.xhtml) that an approximation method is a function which maps a training dataset *S* to an approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0001.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub></math>![](images/c05_ILM0001.gif), and the risk of an approximation method is the expected loss with respect to the distribution of new data and of training datasets, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c05-disp-0001" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c05\_M0001.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c05_M0001.gif)

The risk of an approximation method decomposes in an informative way when squared-error loss is used. Specifically, under square-error loss, risk decomposes into a sum of three non-negative terms, one of which we can do nothing about and two of which we can affect. As we shall see in [Chapter 6](#c06.xhtml), viewing risk-minimization as minimization of the sum of two non-negative terms, and having useful interpretations of the two terms, strongly influences the design of approximation methods.

Various generalizations of this decomposition have been proposed for other loss functions in both regression and classification. While the author does not regard the issue of risk decomposition as definitively settled, intuitive understanding derived from what is known has been of unquestionable benefit to algorithm design.

## 5.1 Squared-Error Loss

In additive-noise regression problems, *Y* = *f*(*X*) + *E* with E\[*E*\] = 0, so E\[*Y*|*X*\] = *f*(*X*). In such settings, under squared-error loss, the risk decomposes as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c05-disp-0002" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c05\_M0002.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi> Var </mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

<a href="#c05-disp-0002-1">(5.1)</a>![numbered Display Equation](images/c05_M0002.gif)

(Geman et al., 1992).

The three terms in this decomposition are worth description in words. The first, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c05-disp-0003" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c05\_M0003.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c05_M0003.gif)

is the expected loss incurred when the predicted value at *X* is *f*(*X*). Under squared-error loss, this is the minimum-risk prediction, so *f*(*X*) is the *Bayes regressor* and the above term is the Bayes risk: in this context, it is called the *intrinsic risk* or the *irreducible risk*, indicating that this much risk is inherent in the problem. It is also E[*X*]\[Var[*Y*|*X*]\[*Y*\]\]. Note that it does not depend on any approximation of *f*.

The expression <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0002.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c05_ILM0002.gif)is called the *bias*^([1](#c05.xhtml#c05-note-0001)) of the approximation method (at *x*). The second term, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c05-disp-0004" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c05\_M0004.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c05_M0004.gif)

is the expected value (with respect to the distribution of *X*) of the squared bias. This measures how close the average approximation, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0005.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c05_ILM0005.gif), is to the true function, *f*, on average with respect to the distribution of *X*.

The variance, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0006.gif"><mrow><msub><mi> Var </mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c05_ILM0006.gif), measures the average squared distance between a particular approximation, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0007.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub></math>![](images/c05_ILM0007.gif), and the average approximation, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0008.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c05_ILM0008.gif). So the third term, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c05-disp-0005" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c05\_M0005.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi> Var </mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c05_M0005.gif)

measures the average squared distance (with respect to the distribution of *X*) between approximations <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0009.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub></math>![](images/c05_ILM0009.gif)produced by the method and the average approximation, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0010.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c05_ILM0010.gif).

**Exercise 5.1** *Prove (5.1), assuming that* E\[*Y*|*X*\] = *f*(*X*) *and that the training set S is independent of the point* (*X*, *Y*) *at which prediction is made.*

**Hint:** *Write* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0011.gif"><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c05_ILM0011.gif)*as* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c05-disp-0006" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c05\_M0006.gif"><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

*and use additivity of the integral.*

The bias and variance of three different methods of approximating function *f*(*x*) = 3/4 *x* + sin(*πx*) on the interval \[−1, 1\] are illustrated in [Figure 5.1](#c05.xhtml#figure5-1). In the examples illustrated, *n* one-dimensional feature vectors *X*[1], … *X*[*n*] are drawn uniformly from \[−1, 1\], and unioned with feature vectors *X*[*n* + 1] = −1 and *X*[*n* + 2] = 1. Then, for *i* = 1, …, *n*+2, response *Y[i]* | *X[i]* is drawn from a Gaussian distribution with mean *f*(*X[i]*) and unit variance (so the intrinsic risk with respect to squared-error loss is 1).

Each cell of [Figure 5.1](#c05.xhtml#figure5-1) shows four things: (1) the true function *f*, represented by a blue curve; (2) a specific 17-point dataset, represented by black dots; (3) the average approximation produced by one of the three methods, represented by a dashed orange curve^([2](#c05.xhtml#c05-note-0002)); (4) the specific approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0012.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c05_ILM0012.gif)obtained by applying one of the three methods to the specific 17-point dataset shown, represented by a thin gray curve. Three distinct datasets are shown, repeated across rows of cells.

The left-hand three cells of [Figure 5.1](#c05.xhtml#figure5-1) show a method which approximates *f* by the least-squares fit of a degree-6 polynomial, that is, by performing linear regression on the expanded vector (1, *x*, *x*², *x*³, *x*⁴, *x*⁵, *x*⁶). This method has high variance: each specific approximation (thin gray curve) is far from the average approximation (orange curve). It also has low bias: the average approximation (orange curve) is quite close to the true *f* (blue curve) in most places.

The center three cells of [Figure 5.1](#c05.xhtml#figure5-1) show a method which approximates *f* by the least-squares fit of a degree-3 polynomial, that is, by performing linear regression on the expanded (1, *x*, *x*², *x*³). This method has much lower variance and only slightly higher bias than a degree-6 polynomial, producing a much lower risk.

The right-hand three cells of [Figure 5.1](#c05.xhtml#figure5-1) show a method which approximates *f* by the least-squares fit of a degree-0 polynomial, that is, by performing linear regression on the constant vector (1). This produces a horizontal line intersecting the vertical axis at the mean response, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0013.gif"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c05_ILM0013.gif). This method has low variance: each specific approximation (thin gray line) is relatively close to the average approximation (orange line). It also has high bias: the average approximation (orange line) is far from the true *f* (blue curve) in most places.

The risk of most approximation methods generally decreases as the number of training data |*S*| increases, and therefore the bias and variance of such methods depend on the number of training data. This is illustrated in the examples just described by using training datasets of different sizes. For each data size |*S*| ∈ {15, 150, 1500, 15000, 150000}+2, the examples were replicated independently 10000 times so that estimates of bias and variance could be computed. The results are shown in [Table 5.1](#c05.xhtml#table5-1).

For squared-error loss, the *bias–variance trade-off* is the idea that minimizing risk requires minimizing the sum of the squared bias and the variance in (5.1), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c05-disp-0007" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c05\_M0007.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi> Var </mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

The importance of this has not always been recognized: in the early days of statistics, there was a great deal of emphasis on finding approximation methods with minimal variance, subject to having *zero* bias (that is, being *unbiased*). One can view ridge regression, described in [Section 3.10](#c03.xhtml#c3_10), as an early method which exploited the bias–variance trade-off, reducing variance while increasing bias in order to produce lower-risk predictions.

## 5.2 Arbitrary Loss

The bias and variance of an approximation method extend *intuitively* to learning in general (either regression or classification) with an arbitrary loss function:

*   *low bias* means 
    *   the average approximation is close to the truth^([3](#c05.xhtml#c05-note-0003));
*   *high bias* means 
    *   the average approximation is far from the truth,
    *   the approximation method is not sufficiently flexible,
    *   individual approximations are not adequately adapted to the data;
*   *low variance* means 
    *   each individual approximation is close to the average approximation,
    *   individual approximations tend to be similar to one another,
    *   the approximation method is “stable” with respect to which dataset (of all possible datasets) it is shown;
*   *high variance* means 
    *   individual approximations are often far from the average approximation,
    *   individual approximations are quite different from one another,
    *   the approximation method is very sensitive to which dataset it is shown.

For arbitrary loss, the *bias–variance trade-off* is the idea, motivated by (5.1), that finding a minimum-risk approximation method involves striking a balance between minimizing bias (and hence being right on average) and minimizing variance (and hence being stable with respect to variation in training datasets). An approximation method which performs poorly due to high variance is said to *over-fit* when presented with data. One which performs poorly due to high bias is said to *under-fit*.

[Figure 5.2](#c05.xhtml#figure5-2) illustrates bias and variance in the *k*\-nearest-neighbors classifier, trained on three different 150-point datasets drawn from the data source described in [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3) (the source of the running example of [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml)). Recall from [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml) that the Bayes risk for this problem, with respect to 0–1 loss, is 0.191705.

![Figure 5.2 Bias and variance in classification. The 1-NN, 9-NN and 100-NN classifiers trained on datasets drawn from the running example distribution of Section 4.3. See the text for explanation.](images/c05f002.jpg)

[**Figure 5.2**](#c05.xhtml#figureanchor5-2) Bias and variance in classification. The 1-NN, 9-NN and 100-NN classifiers trained on datasets drawn from the running example distribution of [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3). See the text for explanation.

[Figure 5.2](#c05.xhtml#figure5-2) shows 12 cells, arranged in four rows of three. The first three rows show three classifiers trained on three datasets. The first row shows the 1-NN, 9-NN, and 100-NN classifiers, each trained on one particular 150-point dataset drawn from the source described in [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3). The second row shows the 1-NN, 9-NN, and 100-NN classifiers, each trained on another 150-point dataset drawn from the source described in [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3). The third row shows the 1-NN, 9-NN, and 100-NN classifiers, each trained on yet another 150-point dataset drawn from the source described in [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3). The fourth row of [Figure 5.2](#c05.xhtml#figure5-2) shows the most common prediction made by the 1-NN, 9-NN, and 100-NN classifiers, taken over 1000 independent 150-point datasets drawn from the source described in [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3). These 1000 datasets were also used for risk estimation.

The left-most four cells of [Figure 5.2](#c05.xhtml#figure5-2) show the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier. This method has high variance: from cell to cell, the classifications made in the plane change considerably, particularly in the center of each cell. This method has low bias: the class boundary of the most common prediction is very close to the Bayes class boundary (white curve). The risk of this method is approximately 0.275 (standard deviation 0.017).

The center four cells of [Figure 5.2](#c05.xhtml#figure5-2) show the 9-nearest-neighbor classifier. This method has moderate variance: from cell to cell, the classifications made in the plane change, but not as much as those of the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier, particularly in the center of each cell. This method has moderate bias: the class boundary of the most common prediction is close to the Bayes class boundary (white curve) toward the center of the cell, but is not close toward the edges. The risk of this method is approximately 0.215 (standard deviation 0.010).

The right-most four cells of [Figure 5.2](#c05.xhtml#figure5-2) show the 100-nearest-neighbor classifier. This method has low variance: from cell to cell, the classifications made in the plane change hardly at all. This method has high bias: the class boundary of the most common prediction is quite far from the Bayes class boundary (white curve). In particular, the average class boundary is considerably less curved than the Bayes class boundary. The risk of this method is approximately 0.272 (standard deviation 0.047).^([4](#c05.xhtml#c05-note-0004))

Formal extension of the bias–variance trade-off to an arbitrary loss function, or just for classification with 0–1 loss, is an active area of research: see, for example, Kong and Dietterich (1995), Breiman (1996b), Kohavi and Wolpert (1996), Tibshirani (1996a), Friedman (1997b), James and Hastie (1997), Breiman (1998), Domingos (2000), James (2003), Efron (2004), and Le Borgne (2005). Most of these papers propose definitions of bias and variance for classification with 0–1 loss, though some also treat more general loss. Also, most of these papers decompose risk additively, into a sum of intrinsic risk plus bias plus variance (mirroring the form of (5.1)), although Domingos (1999) proposes a weighted additive decomposition, and Friedman (1997b) proposes a multiplicative decomposition composed with a Gaussian cumulative distribution function. It may be that formal extension of the bias–variance trade-off actually requires more terms than just intrinsic risk, bias, and variance: James considers this possibility in the case of symmetric loss functions.

The following extension of bias and variance to classification with 0–1 loss is from Breiman (1996b, 1998). Let <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0017.gif"><mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c05_ILM0017.gif)denote a classification method which takes as input a training dataset *S* and a point *X* in feature space, and returns a class label (the predicted class at *X*). Let *f[b]* denote the Bayes classifier, which in Exercise 4.2 was shown to be <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c05-disp-0008" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c05\_M0008.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi> argmax </mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>|</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c05_M0008.gif)

Let P[*S*] denote a probability distribution on training datasets of a given size, and let <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c05-disp-0009" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c05\_M0009.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>a</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi> argmax </mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c05_M0009.gif)

be the class label most likely to be predicted at *X* with respect to the distribution on sets of training data. Looking ahead slightly to [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml), one can think of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0018.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>a</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c05_ILM0018.gif)as arising from applying the classification method to many datasets drawn from P[*S*] and letting the trained classifiers “vote” on the predicted class label at *X*. Breiman calls <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0019.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>a</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c05_ILM0019.gif)the *aggregated classifier*.

Breiman defines a classification method to be *unbiased at* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0020.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c05_ILM0020.gif)if <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c05\_ILM0022.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>a</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c05_ILM0022.gif): that is, if the prediction made at *x* by the classification method is more likely to be the optimal (Bayes) prediction than it is to be any other single value. Breiman defines the *bias* and *variance* of a classification method under 0–1 loss as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c05-disp-0010" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c05\_M0010.gif"><mrow><mi> bias </mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>Y</mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2260;</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>a</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true">\[</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>Y</mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mspace width="4pt"/><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2260;</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>a</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true">\]</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c05_M0010.gif)

and <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c05-disp-0011" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c05\_M0011.gif"><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi> var </mi></mtd><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>Y</mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>a</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true">\[</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>Y</mi><mi> and </mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>a</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true">\]</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c05_M0011.gif)

and shows that, under 0–1 loss, the risk of a classification method can be decomposed as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c05-disp-0012" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c05\_M0012.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2260;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi> bias </mi><mo>+</mo><mi> variance </mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

<a href="#c05-disp-0012-3">(5.2)</a>![numbered Display Equation](images/c05_M0012.gif)

The first term on the right-hand side is the irreducible error, the Bayes error rate.

Approximating Breiman’s measures of bias and variance for the three *k*\-nearest-neighbor classifiers illustrated in [Figure 5.2](#c05.xhtml#figure5-2), using the 1000 independent 150-point datasets drawn from the source described in [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3), produces the following: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c05-disp-0013" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c05\_M0013.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi>k</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> Intrinsic </mi><mi> risk </mi></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mi> Bias </mi></mtd><mtd><mi> Variance </mi></mtd><mtd><mrow><mi> Total </mi><mi> risk </mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>191705</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>00002</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>082</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>275</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>9</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>191705</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>00049</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>021</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>215</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>100</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>191705</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>021</mn><mphantom><mpadded depth="0pt" height="0pt"><mn>00</mn></mpadded></mphantom></mrow></mtd><mtd><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>058</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>272</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

The point of the following exercise is that Breiman’s definitions of bias and variance have an odd property, which is that they can exhibit a discontinuity when a classifier goes from being slightly more like the Bayes classifier than guessing class labels uniformly at random to being slightly less like the Bayes classifier than guessing class labels uniformly at random.
