## Notes

# 6  
Combining Classifiers

> For each individual among the many has a share of virtue and prudence, and when they meet together, they become in a manner one man, who has many feet, and hands, and senses; that is a figure of their mind and disposition. Hence the many are better judges than a single man of music and poetry; for some understand one part, and some another, and among them they understand the whole.
> 
> —Aristotle, *Politics*, c. 350 BCE

The methods described in [Chapters 3](#c03.xhtml) and [4](#c04.xhtml) produce regressors or classifiers which are not naturally decomposable into collections of smaller regressors or classifiers. As such, these regressors and classifiers are called *base learners* or *primitive learners*—although perhaps a more descriptive term would be *atomic learners*. This chapter introduces classification methods which combine base learners in various ways. The design of specific methods is usually based on an understanding of the bias–variance trade-off described in [Chapter 5](#c05.xhtml).

## 6.1 Ensembles

If one is willing to do the work to train *L* classifiers, of any type or types, one can get a new classifier by having the *L* classifiers “vote” as a committee. That is, one can classify a new data point as the class most commonly assigned to it by the individual trained classifiers. The voting may be weighted to favor preferred classifiers, or the votes of the individual classifiers may be used as inputs to another classification algorithm. Such techniques are called *ensemble methods*, or *committee methods*.

An example of this type is illustrated in [Figure 6.1](#c06.xhtml#figure6-1). In [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml), 36 classifiers were trained on the data of [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3). The estimated risks of these classifiers, based on 50,000 test data, range from 0.195 (LVQ) to 0.665 (a one-leaf tree which always predicts the purple class). The author made an arbitrary choice to declare a classifier *bad* if its risk is at least 0.220. With this definition, there were 20 bad classifiers, representing every method in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml) except QDA and logistic regression. An ensemble composed of these 20 bad classifiers, all voting with equal weight, has risk 0.210, which is about 5.5 standard errors better than the risk of the best classifier in the ensemble.

![Figure 6.1 Predictions made by an ensemble of 20 bad classifiers (risk ⩾ 0.220) constructed on the data of Section 4.3. Each of the 20 base learners votes with equal weight. The ensemble has risk 0.210.](images/c06f001.jpg)

[**Figure 6.1**](#c06.xhtml#figureanchor6-1) Predictions made by an ensemble of 20 bad classifiers (risk ⩾ 0.220) constructed on the data of [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3). Each of the 20 base learners votes with equal weight. The ensemble has risk 0.210.

A binary classifier can be applied to an arbitrary number of classes *C* by committee. One way to do this is to train a binary classifier to distinguish class *c* from the union of all other classes, for each class *c* = 1, …, *C*, and to vote the resulting *C* binary classifiers in a committee. Another way to do this is to train a binary classifier to distinguish class *c* from class *d*, for all classes 1 ≤ *c* < *d* ≤ *C*, and to vote the resulting <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0001.gif"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></math>![](images/c06_ILM0001.gif)binary classifiers in a committee.^([1](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0001)) An example is shown in [Figure 6.2](#c06.xhtml#figure6-2).

![Figure 6.2 All trained support vector machines illustrated on the data of Section 4.3, which has C = 3 classes, were obtained by training  binary support vector machines. That is, support vector machines were trained to distinguish “orange vs. blue,” “orange vs. purple,” and “blue vs. purple,” and then voted in a committee to produce a three-class classifier. The case of linear support vector machines is illustrated here: the upper-left cell, which is identical to the right-hand cell of Figure 4.30, shows the majority vote while the other three cells show the three binary support vector machines (these are shown in Figure 4.29). As noted in Figure 4.30, the R function svm() has chosen (arbitrarily) to break ties by predicting orange.](images/c06f002.gif)

[**Figure 6.2**](#c06.xhtml#figureanchor6-2) All trained support vector machines illustrated on the data of [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3), which has *C* = 3 classes, were obtained by training <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0002.gif"><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0002.gif)binary support vector machines. That is, support vector machines were trained to distinguish “orange vs. blue,” “orange vs. purple,” and “blue vs. purple,” and then voted in a committee to produce a three-class classifier. The case of linear support vector machines is illustrated here: the upper-left cell, which is identical to the right-hand cell of [Figure 4.30](#c04.xhtml#figure4-30), shows the majority vote while the other three cells show the three binary support vector machines (these are shown in [Figure 4.29](#c04.xhtml#figure4-29)). As noted in [Figure 4.30](#c04.xhtml#figure4-30), the R function svm() has chosen (arbitrarily) to break ties by predicting orange.

Committees of regressors combine continuous-valued predictions (“votes”) of the base learners in some numerical way, such as computing the mean or using the individual votes as input to a linear function which is chosen to (approximately) minimize the risk of of the committee’s predictions. This can be applied to classification when some or all of the base learners compute approximate probabilities of class membership,

<displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0001" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0001.gif"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0001.gif)

by using a combined estimate of class probabilities to produce a single predicted class. If each of the classifiers under consideration compute approximate probabilities of class membership, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0002" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0002.gif"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0002.gif)

then one can get a new classifier by making the minimum risk prediction based on a combined estimate of the class probabilities (such as the mean of the estimated class probabilities).

The observation that a combination of many poor statistical predictions might form a good prediction is quite old. In 1907, Francis Galton reported an analysis of 787 guesses in a contest to guess the dressed weight of an ox, based on observation of the ox while alive (Galton, 1907). Galton found that the median guess, 1207 pounds, was very close to the actual dressed weight of the ox (1198 pounds) in spite of the fact that the set of guesses displayed considerable variation (the inter-quartile range was \[1162, 1236\] pounds, and the range between the 5th and 95th percentiles was \[1074, 1293\] pounds). Each person casting a vote presumably had access to the same data—visual observation of the live ox in question—but varied in experience and expertise.^([2](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0002))

## 6.2 Ensemble Design

An important part of the design of ensemble classifiers is the desire to control risk by controlling bias and variance. Because these concepts do not have widely agreed-upon formal definitions for classification and for general loss functions, as mentioned in [Section 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c5_2), ensemble design depends partly on intuition and analogy with the bias–variance trade-off for squared-error loss.

Some ensemble design approaches may be arrived at by considering the risk, under squared-error loss, incurred when estimating a real parameter vector. Suppose *Z*[1], …, *Z[L]* are estimators of an unknown real vector θ.^([3](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0003)) The *l*^(th) estimator of θ has a bias, Bias\[*Z[l]*\] = E\[*Z[l]*\] − θ, and a variance, Var\[*Z[l]*\].

Now consider combining the estimates *Z*[1], …, *Z[L]* into a single ensemble estimator of θ by forming the sample mean, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0003" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0003.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>L</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></munderover><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0003.gif)

The bias of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0003.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover></math>![](images/c06_ILM0003.gif)for θ and the variance of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0004.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover></math>![](images/c06_ILM0004.gif)are <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0004" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0004.gif"><mrow><mi> Bias </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>L</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></munderover><mi> Bias </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0004.gif)

and <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0005" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0005.gif"><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> Var </mi><mo>\[</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></munderover><mi> Var </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#x2260;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></munder><mi> Cov </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></munderover><mi> Var </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#x2260;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></munder><mi> Cor </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi> Var </mi><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow></msqrt><msqrt><mrow><mi> Var </mi><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow></msqrt><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

<span class="equationNumber"><a href="#c06-disp-0005-1">(6.1)</a></span>![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0005.gif)

**Ensemble Design Approach A.** The expressions for bias and variance show that if one can find a set of estimators *Z*[1], …, *Z[L]* which:

1.  all have the same bias, β,
2.  all have the same variance, σ² > 0, and
3.  are all uncorrelated,

then the estimator <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0005.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover></math>![](images/c06_ILM0005.gif)has bias β and variance <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0006.gif"><mfrac><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>L</mi></mfrac></math>![](images/c06_ILM0006.gif), and so has strictly smaller risk than any of the individual estimators. Thus one might produce a low-risk estimator <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0007.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover></math>![](images/c06_ILM0007.gif)of θ by constructing many high-risk estimators *Z*[1], …, *Z[L]*, provided that the individual high-risk estimators are uncorrelated and have low bias (but high variance).

**Ensemble Design Approach B.** The expressions for bias and variance also show that if one can find a set of estimators *Z*[1], …, *Z[L]* which:

1.  have non-zero biases β[1], …, β[*L*] which sum to zero, and
2.  all have the same variance, σ² > 0,

then the estimator <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0008.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover></math>![](images/c06_ILM0008.gif)has bias 0 and variance <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0006" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0006.gif"><mrow><mfrac><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#x2260;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></munder><mi> Cor </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#x2264;</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0006.gif)

and so has strictly smaller risk than any of the individual estimators. Thus one might produce a low-risk estimator <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0009.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover></math>![](images/c06_ILM0009.gif)of θ by constructing many high-risk estimators *Z*[1], …, *Z[L]*, provided that the individual high-risk estimators have low variance (but have high biases which cancel each other out). While it is possible that <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0010.gif"><mrow><mi> Var </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0010.gif), such cases are pathological^([4](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0004)) and typically, in addition to the bias being zero, we would expect that <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0012.gif"><mrow><mi> Var </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0012.gif).

**Exercise 6.1** *Consider a generalization of the sample average: Z* = ∑^(*L*)[*l* = 1]*c[l]Z[l]*, *where all the coefficients c[l] are non-negative and c*[1] + ⋅⋅⋅ + *c[L]* = 1. *Assuming that Z*[1], …, *Z[L] (1) all have the same bias, β, (2) have known, positive variances,* σ²[1], …, σ[*L*]², *and (3) are all uncorrelated, find values of the coefficients c*[1], …, *c[L] which minimize the risk of Z under squared-error loss.*

**Exercise 6.2** *For each of five ensemble methods (bagging, random forests, boosting, arcing, and stacking, described in [Sections 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c6_3), [6.5](#c06.xhtml#c6_5), [6.6](#c06.xhtml#c6_6), [6.7](#c06.xhtml#c6_7), and [6.8](#c06.xhtml#c6_8)), state whether it resembles design approach A or design approach B (or both, or neither). For each of these ensemble methods, can you find choices of base learners and parameters (of the ensemble method or of the base learners) which make the method resemble approach A, and other choices which make the method resemble approach B?*

## 6.3 Bootstrap Aggregation (Bagging)

The bootstrap is a technique, due to Efron (1979), for generating new datasets with approximately the same (unknown) sampling distribution as a given dataset. A *bootstrap sample* of a dataset of size *n* is obtained by sampling the set with replacement *n* times, independently and uniformly. Thus a bootstrap sample of the set <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0007" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0007.gif"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0007.gif)

might be <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0008" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0008.gif"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>}</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0008.gif)

Efron’s original motivation for the bootstrap was to estimate the variance of statistical estimators.

**Exercise 6.3** *Let ρ > 0. Show that if a dataset of size *n* is sampled independently and uniformly with replacement* ρ*n times, then the probability that any particular point in the dataset is excluded from the sample is* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0013.gif"><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#x03c1;</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></math>![](images/c06_ILM0013.gif). *Show that* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0009" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0009.gif"><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">lim</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi>&#x221e;</mi></mrow></munder><msup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mfenced><mrow><mi>&#x03c1;</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03c1;</mi></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0009.gif)

*Thus, the expected proportion of a dataset which is excluded from a given bootstrap sample (ρ = 1) is about e*^(− 1) ≈ 0.368, *and the expected proportion which is included is about* 1 − *e*^(− 1) ≈ 0.632.

*Bagging,* a portmanteau word meaning “bootstrap aggregation,” is an ensemble technique due to Breiman (1996a). Bagging is a simple idea: choose a classification algorithm, draw *L* independent bootstrap samples of the training data (that is, draw *L* sets of size *n* independently from the training data, with replacement), train a classifier on each of the *L* sets, and then combine them in a committee.

The size of the bootstrap samples used in bagging need not be *n*, the number of training data. Instead, bootstrap samples of size ρ*n*, for some real number ρ > 0, can be used (original bootstrapping corresponds to ρ = 1). In light of [Chapter 5](#c05.xhtml), one would expect that decreasing ρ would result in increasing both the variance and the bias of the base learners, while at the same time decreasing the correlation between any two base learners (because the expected proportion of training data common to two bootstrap samples of size ρ*n* is about (1 − *e*^(− ρ))²).

The effects of varying bootstrap sample size in bagged 1-nearest neighbor classifiers and bagged stumps,^([5](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0005)) trained on the data of [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3), are shown in Figures [6.3](#c06.xhtml#figure6-3) and [6.4](#c06.xhtml#figure6-4). The top two cells of [Figure 6.3](#c06.xhtml#figure6-3) show classification decisions made by a 1-nearest-neighbor classifier and a stump, trained on all of the data of [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3).

Bottom row: bagged 1-nearest neighbor classifiers trained on  bootstrap samples of size ρn with  (risk 0.199) and bagged stumps trained on  bootstrap samples of size ρn with  (risk 0.219). The bootstrap sample sizes in the bottom row were selected as approximately optimal using out-of-bag risk estimation, described in Section 7.3, to estimate risk from the training data.](images/c06f003.jpg)

![Figure 6.4 The risk of bagged 1-nearest-neighbor classifiers and bagged stumps trained on the data of Section 4.3, as a function of the size of the bootstrap samples. The horizontal axis is the ratio ρ of the bootstrap sample size to the total number of training data, n. For various values of ρ, a bagged classifier consisting of either 1-nearest-neighbor classifiers or stumps was constructed by drawing  bootstrap samples of size ρn (the variable number of bootstrap samples was chosen so that each bagged classifier was trained on about 100 n data replicates in total). The bootstrap sample size has a strong effect on the risk of the bagged classifier. In this example, since n = 150, choosing ρ much less than 2− 6, leads to bootstrap samples consisting of only one data point, and this results in an ensemble that predicts the same class at every point x.](images/c06f004.jpg)

[**Figure 6.4**](#c06.xhtml#figureanchor6-4) The risk of bagged 1-nearest-neighbor classifiers and bagged stumps trained on the data of [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3), as a function of the size of the bootstrap samples. The horizontal axis is the ratio ρ of the bootstrap sample size to the total number of training data, *n*. For various values of ρ, a bagged classifier consisting of either 1-nearest-neighbor classifiers or stumps was constructed by drawing <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0018.gif"><mfrac><mn>100</mn><mi>&#x03c1;</mi></mfrac></math>![](images/c06_ILM0018.gif)bootstrap samples of size ρ*n* (the variable number of bootstrap samples was chosen so that each bagged classifier was trained on about 100 *n* data replicates in total). The bootstrap sample size has a strong effect on the risk of the bagged classifier. In this example, since *n* = 150, choosing ρ much less than 2^(− 6), leads to bootstrap samples consisting of only one data point, and this results in an ensemble that predicts the same class at every point *x*.

The middle two cells show classification decisions made by bagged ensembles of 100 classifiers each, using bootstrap samples of size *n*. The bottom two cells show classification decisions made by bagged ensembles of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0019.gif"><mfrac><mn>100</mn><mi>&#x03c1;</mi></mfrac></math>![](images/c06_ILM0019.gif)classifiers each, using bootstrap samples of size ρ*n*, for values of ρ chosen to be approximately optimal based on out-of-bag risk estimation (described in [Section 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c7_3)).

Visual comparison of the top and middle rows of [Figure 6.3](#c06.xhtml#figure6-3) shows that the bagged classifiers with sample size *n* perform nearly identically to their corresponding single base learners trained on all of the data. [Figure 6.4](#c06.xhtml#figure6-4) shows the effect of ρ on the risk of bagged 1-nearest-neighbor classifiers and bagged stumps. When ρ = 1, the risk of each bagged classifier is essentially the same as the risk of its respective base learner trained on all of the training data, as one would expect from the classification decisions shown in [Figure 6.3](#c06.xhtml#figure6-3). As ρ decreases from 1, the risk decreases—the author interprets this to mean that the increased bias and variance in the base learners is more than offset by the decreased correlation between them. When ρ = 2^(− 5), each base classifier is trained on five data points, and when ρ = 2^(− 6), each base classifier is trained on two data points^([6](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0006)), and even for these small bootstrap sample sizes this example shows no evidence of the risk going back up. For sufficiently small ρ, each bootstrap sample contains only one data point and each base learner predicts the class of the datum it was trained on (regardless of the input feature vector), so the bagged classifier predicts whichever class was most represented in the set of size-1 bootstrap samples (again, regardless of the input feature vector). The author interprets this to mean that increased bias and variance in the base learners have overwhelmed the decreased correlation between them.

**Exercise 6.4** *Consider bagging the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier using L bootstrap samples, each of size* ρ*n for some positive number ρ. Let X be a feature vector to be classified by the bagged classifier, and let* (*x*, *y*) *be the nearest training data point to X*. *Assuming n is large enough that the approximation* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0020.gif"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#x03c1;</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#x2248;</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03c1;</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0020.gif)*of 6.3 can be used with negligible error, show that as L* → ∞, *the probability that at least half of the bootstrap samples contain the training point* (*x*, *y*) *approaches 1 if and only if ρ is greater than log 2 ≈ 0.693. Conclude that a bagged 1-nearest-neighbor classifier will perform similarly to a single 1-nearest-neighbor classifier unless ρ is less than about* log 2.

## 6.4 Bumping

Bumping, introduced in Tibshirani and Knight (1999), constructs bootstrap samples of the data, trains a classifier on each one, and then computes the training error of each classifier on the whole dataset. The classifier with the smallest overall training error is then used. This may be useful if a classifier is stuck at a sub-optimal fit due to a few misleading data points. Predictions made by a bumped 1-nearest-neighbor classifier trained on the data of [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3) are shown in the upper-left cell of [Figure 6.5](#c06.xhtml#figure6-5). This bumped classifier was selected from the set of all base classifiers trained in production of [Figure 6.4](#c06.xhtml#figure6-4).

![Figure 6.5 Classification decisions made by bumping a 1-nearest-neighbor classifier (upper left cell), applying a 1000-tree random forest (upper right cell), an ensemble of 1000 boosted stumps (lower left cell), and an ensemble of 1000 arced 1-nearest-neighbor classifiers (lower right cell), trained on the data of Section 4.3. The bumped classifier is a single 1-nearest-neighbor classifier chosen to have minimal out-of-bag risk from the set of all base classifiers trained in the bagging experiments illustrated in Figure 6.4. A stump is a classification tree constrained to have at most two leaf nodes. The estimated risks of these classifiers are 0.245 for bumped 1-nearest-neighbor, 0.220 for the random forest, 0.268 for boosted stumps, and 0.262 for arced stumps.](images/c06f005.jpg)

[**Figure 6.5**](#c06.xhtml#figureanchor6-5) Classification decisions made by bumping a 1-nearest-neighbor classifier (upper left cell), applying a 1000-tree random forest (upper right cell), an ensemble of 1000 boosted stumps (lower left cell), and an ensemble of 1000 arced 1-nearest-neighbor classifiers (lower right cell), trained on the data of [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3). The bumped classifier is a single 1-nearest-neighbor classifier chosen to have minimal out-of-bag risk from the set of all base classifiers trained in the bagging experiments illustrated in [Figure 6.4](#c06.xhtml#figure6-4). A *stump* is a classification tree constrained to have at most two leaf nodes. The estimated risks of these classifiers are 0.245 for bumped 1-nearest-neighbor, 0.220 for the random forest, 0.268 for boosted stumps, and 0.262 for arced stumps.

## 6.5 Random Forests

Random forest classifiers are due to Breiman (2001a) and are a combination of earlier techniques with which he is associated, classification trees and bagging.^([7](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0007)) Omitting one detail, a random forest classifier is simply bagged trees: on *L* bootstrap samples of the data, trees are trained (grown to be over-fit, with no pruning) and then the trees vote in a committee. The omitted detail is that at each step in growing the tree, a random training decision is made: a small random sample of the *m* features (typically about <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0021.gif"><msqrt><mi>m</mi></msqrt></math>![](images/c06_ILM0021.gif)of them) are considered for the split rather than all *m*. The purpose of this is to reduce the correlation between pairs of trees in the forest.^([8](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0008)) Predictions made by a 1000-tree random forest trained on the data of [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3) are shown in the upper-right cell of [Figure 6.5](#c06.xhtml#figure6-5).

Random forests are provably resistant to over-fitting in the sense that increasing the number of trees *L* without bound does not *cause* the random forest to be over-fit, in spite of the fact that the number of parameters needed to describe the forest goes to infinity.^([9](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0009)) Let P[(*X*, *Y*)] be the probability distribution from which data are drawn: it is assumed that the training data and all future data are drawn from this distribution. Let (*X*, *Y*) denote a random datum drawn from P[(*X*, *Y*)]. One can show that under 0–1 loss the risk of a random forest with trees *T*[1], …, *T[L]* is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0010" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0010.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msub><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mi> trees </mi><mi> voting </mi><mi> for </mi><mi> class </mi></mrow><mspace width="4pt"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>|</mo><mo>&lt;</mo></mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">max</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2260;</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mi> trees </mi><mi> voting </mi><mi> for </mi><mi> class </mi></mrow><mspace width="4pt"/><mi>c</mi><mo>|</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0010.gif)

Let P[*F*] be the probability distribution used for generating random decisions when training the trees for a random forest. Breiman (2001a) has shown that as *L* → ∞, the risk of a random forest with *L* trees approaches the probability that a new datum (*X*, *Y*) drawn from the data distribution P[(*X*, *Y*)] is misclassified by a random tree constructed on the training data using P[*F*] to make random training decisions, that is, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0011" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0011.gif"><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mspace width="1.em"/><mo>&#x2192;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msub><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi> tree </mi><mi> votes </mi><mi> for </mi><mi> class </mi></mrow><mspace width="4pt"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">max</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2260;</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi> tree </mi><mi> votes </mi><mi> for </mi><mi> class </mi></mrow><mspace width="4pt"/><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

<span class="equationNumber"><a href="#c06-disp-0011-2">(6.2)</a></span>![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0011.gif)

with probability 1. Thus in practice there is no reason to worry about making *L* too large, except computational cost.

Breiman defined the *random forest proximity* of two data points (*x*[*i*], *y*[*i*]) and (*x*[*j*], *y*[*j*]) to be the proportion of trees in a random forest with the property that (*x*[*i*], *y*[*i*]) and (*x*[*j*], *y*[*j*]) are in the same terminal node (leaf). Random forest proximity can be useful for discovering clusters in data, particularly clusters within a given class.

**Exercise 6.5** *Let* L(*d*, *c*) *be an arbitrary loss function with the (very minimal) property that* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0112" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0012.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1.em"/><mrow><mi> for </mi><mi> all </mi></mrow><mi>c</mi><mspace width="2.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="2.em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1.em"/><mrow><mi> for </mi><mi> all </mi></mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>&#x2260;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

*Show that if each tree in a random forest is grown until all leaf nodes have zero impurity (that is, contain training data of only one class), then the actual values taken by the loss function have no effect on predictions made by the forest. Does the marginal distribution on classes* (P(*Y* = 1), …, P(*Y* = *C*)) *have any effect, assuming* P(*Y* = *c*) > 0 *for all c*?

## 6.6 Boosting

Let real, non-negative *weights w*[1], …, *w[n]* be assigned to the training data, and let the loss incurred by misclassifying (*x[i]*, *y[i]*) as class *d* be *w[i]*L(*y[i]*, *d*). Weight *w[i]* reflects the relative importance of correctly classifying training datum (*x[i]*, *y[i]*).

**Exercise 6.6 Open-Ended Challenge.** *Modify each classification algorithm of [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml) so that it is applicable to weighted data.* **Hint:** *If all of the weights w*[1], …, *w[n] are integers, then treat this as equivalent to a situation where data are unweighted, but datum* (*x[i]*, *y[i]*) *occurs in the training set w[i] times. If all of the weights are rational, then the weights can be scaled up by an integer constant* ρ > 0 *such that* ρ*w*[1], …, ρ*w[n] are integers, and the loss function can be divided by* ρ. *A set of real weights can be handled as the limit of sets of rational weights.*

*Boosting* a classifier refers to an algorithm of the general type shown in [Figure 6.6](#c06.xhtml#figure6-6). A particular boosting algorithm is *AdaBoost* (short for “adaptive boosting”) (Freund and Schapire, 1997; Schapire and Freund, 2012). The original AdaBoost algorithm was defined for *C* = 2 classes. Using 0–1 loss, AdaBoost is shown in [Figure 6.7](#c06.xhtml#figure6-7) (Friedman et al., 2000).

![Figure 6.6 A generic boosting algorithm.](images/c06f006.jpg)

[**Figure 6.6**](#c06.xhtml#figureanchor6-6) A generic boosting algorithm.

![Figure 6.7 The AdaBoost algorithm for 0–1 loss and C = 2 classes. Modifications for the case C > 2 and a reason for the particular choice of weight  are described in the text and exercises.](images/c06f007.jpg)

[**Figure 6.7**](#c06.xhtml#figureanchor6-7) The AdaBoost algorithm for 0–1 loss and *C* = 2 classes. Modifications for the case *C* > 2 and a reason for the particular choice of weight <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0027.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0027.gif)are described in the text and exercises.

In Adaboost, if ever <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0023.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0023.gif)then no reweighting occurs (because no training data are misclassified), and if training in step (2A) is deterministic (that is, does not involve a source of randomness external to the data) then <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0024.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0024.gif). These apparently perfect classifiers have infinite weight assigned to their votes, so AdaBoost produces the same predictions as <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0025.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></math>![](images/c06_ILM0025.gif). If <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0026.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></math>![](images/c06_ILM0026.gif)is positive but very small, then <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0027.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0027.gif)is large and the relatively few misclassified points are greatly up-weighted, causing <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0028.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![](images/c06_ILM0028.gif)to focus on classifying these points correctly. Also, classifier <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0029.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></math>![](images/c06_ILM0029.gif)votes with relatively high weight. As long as <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0030.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0030.gif), the predictions made by <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0031.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></math>![](images/c06_ILM0031.gif)are taken to be better than predicting by tossing a fair coin, and so misclassified points are up-weighted and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0032.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></math>![](images/c06_ILM0032.gif)votes with positive weight.

If ever <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0033.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0033.gif)then predictions by <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0034.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></math>![](images/c06_ILM0034.gif)are taken to be equivalent to tossing a fair coin and weights are effectively not changed (raising again the possibility that <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0035.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0035.gif)). These perfectly useless classifiers have zero weight assigned to their votes.

If <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0036.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0036.gif), the predictions made by <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0037.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></math>![](images/c06_ILM0037.gif)are taken to be *worse* than predictions made by tossing a fair coin. This does not mean that the classifier is useless, it merely has confused the meaning of the two class labels (or equivalently, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0038.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></math>![](images/c06_ILM0038.gif)is experiencing *opposite day* (Watterson, 1988)). Thus its votes have negative weight, which is to say positive weight assigned to the opposite vote. Misclassified points are down-weighted, because from the perspective of AdaBoost, it is useful to make a worse-than-coin-toss classifier even worse, as long as we know to reverse the predictions of the classifier by giving its votes negative weight. If ever <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0039.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0039.gif)then the weights of all misclassified points are reduced to zero, and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0040.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></math>![](images/c06_ILM0040.gif)votes with infinite negative weight.

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0016.gif)

and the weight assigned to the vote of the *l*th classifier in step (3), which is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0014" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0017.gif"><mrow><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0017.gif)

As long as <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0048.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0048.gif), the interpretation and behavior of multiclass AdaBoost is the same as the original. If ever <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0049.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0049.gif), the predictions by <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0050.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></math>![](images/c06_ILM0050.gif)are taken to be equivalent to rolling a fair *C*\-sided die. Weights are effectively not changed in this case (raising the possibility that <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0051.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0051.gif)), and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0052.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></math>![](images/c06_ILM0052.gif)has zero weight assigned to its vote. If <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0053.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0053.gif)then generalized AdaBoost gives negative weight to votes by <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0054.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></math>![](images/c06_ILM0054.gif)since <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0055.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub></math>![](images/c06_ILM0055.gif)makes worse predictions than a fair die roll, but notice that with *C* > 2 classes being frequently wrong does not mean that a classifier’s predictions can be modified so that they are frequently right (as is the case when *C* = 2).

Predictions made by an ensemble consisting of 1000 stumps trained with three-class generalized AdaBoost on the data of [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3) are shown in the lower-left cell of [Figure 6.5](#c06.xhtml#figure6-5).

## 6.7 Arcing

*Arcing*, which stands for *adaptive resampling and combining*, is similar to boosting. Instead of applying weights to data within a classification algorithm, arcing draws a new dataset on which to train a classifier at each step by sampling from the training data with replacement according to a changing probability distribution.

A particular arcing algorithm,^([11](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0011)) modeled on AdaBoost with 0–1 loss, is shown in [Figure 6.8](#c06.xhtml#figure6-8). In the terminology of Breiman (1996b), AdaBoost is *non-random arcing*.

![Figure 6.8 An arcing algorithm based on the AdaBoost algorithm for 0–1 loss and C = 2 classes. Modifications for the case C > 2 are described in the text of Section 6.6.](images/c06f008.jpg)

[**Figure 6.8**](#c06.xhtml#figureanchor6-8) An arcing algorithm based on the AdaBoost algorithm for 0–1 loss and *C* = 2 classes. Modifications for the case *C* > 2 are described in the text of [Section 6.6](#c06.xhtml#c6_6).

Predictions made by an ensemble consisting of 1000 stumps trained with three-class generalized arcing on the data of [Section 4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_3) are shown in the lower-right cell of [Figure 6.5](#c06.xhtml#figure6-5).

## 6.8 Stacking and Mixture of Experts

Instead of casting votes as in a committee, the output of a set of trained classifiers (either predicted classes or estimated posterior distributions on the classes) can be used as input to another classifier. This is called *stacking* classifiers (Wolpert, 1992). When stacking, outputs of the trained classifiers are regarded as new features.

The left-hand cell of [Figure 6.9](#c06.xhtml#figure6-9) shows predictions made by a classification tree trained on the dataset <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0015" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0018.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>150</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>150</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0018.gif)

and the base learners <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0056.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0056.gif)are the bad classifiers described in [Section 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c6_1) (so *L* = 20). The vectors *z*[1], …, *z[n]* are regarded as categorical features for training the tree, since <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0057.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi> orange </mi><mo>,</mo><mi> blue </mi><mo>,</mo><mi> purple </mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0057.gif)for all *l* and *x[i]*.

The classification tree stacked on 20 bad classifiers was grown and pruned as described in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml), with the cost-complexity parameter chosen to minimize the leave-one-out cross-validation estimate of risk described in [Section 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c7_3). The tree has only three leaf nodes, and is shown in [Figure 6.10](#c06.xhtml#figure6-10). Two of the bad classifiers, the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier and the likelihood classifier based on kernel density estimation using bandwidth *h* = 0.1, are over-fit to the training data and have very low training risk, and as a result were identified by the classification tree as very good predictors of the class labels on the training data. The result is a stacked classifier which is very similar to its most over-fit base learners. The risk of the stacked classifier is 0.247, the risk of the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier is 0.248, and the risk of the likelihood classifier based on kernel density estimation using bandwidth *h* = 0.1 is 0.246. Visual comparison of predictions by these three classifiers (left-hand cell of [Figure 6.9](#c06.xhtml#figure6-9), upper-right cell of [Figure 4.7](#c04.xhtml#figure4-7), and upper-left cell of [Figure 4.12](#c04.xhtml#figure4-12)) show that they are very similar.

The predictions made by this tree are shown in the left-hand cell of [Figure 6.9](#c06.xhtml#figure6-9).

The right-hand cell of [Figure 6.9](#c06.xhtml#figure6-9) shows predictions made by a logistic regression classifier trained on the dataset <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0017" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0020.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>150</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>150</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>
