where <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0018" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0021.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0021.gif)

and the base learners <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0058.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0058.gif)are stumps trained on 100 full-size (size-150) bootstrap samples of the training data (so *L* = 100). As before, the vectors *z*[1], …, *z[n]* are regarded as categorical features for training the logistic regression classifier.

Stacking logistic regression required two minor modifications from logistic regression as described in [Section 4.6](#c04.xhtml#c4_6): dummy variables and parameter penalization. The predictions made by the *L* base learners are categorical features taking three possible values (orange, blue, or purple), and each of these categorical features was represented^([12](#c06.xhtml#c06-note-0012)) by two binary dummy variables, described in [Section 3.8](#c03.xhtml#c3_8). In terms of the dummy variables, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0019" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0022.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi> blue </mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi> purple </mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi> blue </mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi> purple </mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0022.gif)

is a 2*L*\-long binary vector: for *l* = 1, …, *L*, the coordinates (*z*[*i*, 2*l* − 1], *z*[*i*, 2*l*]) are (0, 0) if <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0059.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi> orange </mi></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0059.gif), (1, 0) if <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0060.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi> blue </mi></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0060.gif), and (0, 1) if <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c06\_ILM0061.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi> purple </mi></mrow></math>![](images/c06_ILM0061.gif). Since some of these dummy variables are highly correlated with one another, a quadratic penalty was placed on the non-intercept logistic regression parameters (compare this with ridge regression in [Section 3.10](#c03.xhtml#c3_10)). That is, the *C* × (*m* + 1) matrix of logistic regression model parameters <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0020" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0023.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0023.gif)

with *C* = 3 and *m* = 2*L* = 200 (the 100 base learners each have their class predictions represented by two binary dummy variables) is chosen to minimize <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0021" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0024.gif"><mrow><mo>-</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0024.gif)

(compare this with ridge regression in [Section 3.10](#c03.xhtml#c3_10), and note that the intercept parameters θ[*d*, 0] are not penalized). The weight parameter λ applied to the quadratic penalty was selected to be approximately optimal using leave-one-out cross-validation, described in [Section 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c7_3), to estimate the risk of the logistic regression classifier from the training data.

In stacking, the top-level classifier uses only the *L* base learner outputs: its input feature vectors are *z*[1], …, *z[n]*. If the top-level classifier uses both the *L* base learner outputs and also original features, so that its input feature vectors are (*x*[1], *z*[1]), …, (*x[n]*, *z[n]*), then the resulting classifier is called a *mixture of experts* (Jacobs et al., 1991). [Figure 6.11](#c06.xhtml#figure6-11) shows predictions made by a logistic regression classifier trained on the data set <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c06-disp-0021a" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c06\_M0025.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x2026;</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>150</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>150</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>150</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c06_M0025.gif)![Figure 6.11 Predictions made by using the predictions of 100 stumps trained on “full size” (size-150) bootstrap samples of the training data, and the original feature vectors, and training a logistic regression classifier. The risk of the logistic regression mixture of experts is 0.227.](images/c06f011.jpg)

[**Figure 6.11**](#c06.xhtml#figureanchor6-11) Predictions made by using the predictions of 100 stumps trained on “full size” (size-150) bootstrap samples of the training data, *and* the original feature vectors, and training a logistic regression classifier. The risk of the logistic regression mixture of experts is 0.227.

where each of *z*[1], …, *z*[150] is the concatenated output of stumps trained on 100 full size (size-150) bootstrap samples of the training data, as described above.

Neural networks can be regarded as a type of stacking or a mixture of experts, depending on the specific network architecture. The neurons in the hidden layer immediately below the output layer can be thought of as base learners which are soft versions of binary classifiers. The classes learned by each of these binary classifiers do not necessarily correspond to any of the classes 1, …, *C*. Rather, they are *latent classes* which are extracted from the data and which are in some way pertinent to solving the overall classification problem (if the neural network does a good job). The continuous-valued “votes” of the base learners are combined by using logistic regression in the top layer of the network. In a neural network, the base learners are trained at the same time the logistic-regression output layer is trained, and the base learners are all trained in parallel in an inter-dependent way, in contrast with bagging (where base learners are trained independently in parallel) and boosting (where base learners are inter-dependent but trained sequentially).

## Notes

# 7  
Risk Estimation and Model Selection

> Aesthetics and statistical accuracy might not be the same thing.
> 
> —Larry Wasserman, personal communication, 2001

> The very fact that the representation is of such generality that it can always be made to fit the data exactly is considered an argument against it, not for it.
> 
> —Harold Jeffreys, Scientific Inference, 1931

In [Chapter 2](#c02.xhtml), we stated our goal to be finding an approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0001.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0001.gif)of *f* with minimal risk <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0002.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0002.gif), the expected loss incurred when predicting values of response or class *Y* for new features *X*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0001" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0001.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0001.gif)

In general, there is no way to compute risk exactly because the joint distribution of (*X*, *Y*) is unknown. The risk <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0003.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0003.gif)must be estimated from data, just as *f* must be.

This chapter describes several methods of estimating the risk of an approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0004.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0004.gif)of *f*, and of selecting approximations with approximately minimal risk. [Sections 7.1](#c07.xhtml#c7_1) through [7.5](#c07.xhtml#c7_5) describe methods of estimating risk. All of these methods have drawbacks as well as advantages, and these are discussed. [Sections 7.6](#c07.xhtml#c7_6) through [7.9](#c07.xhtml#c7_9) describe model selection criteria which do not involve explicit risk estimation. [Sections 7.10](#c07.xhtml#c7_10) and [7.11](#c07.xhtml#c7_11) contain general remarks about model selection.

## 7.1 Risk Estimation via Training Data

Let (*x*[1], *y*[1]), …, (*x[n]*, *y[n]*) be the data used to train an approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0005.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0005.gif)of *f*. In [Chapter 2](#c02.xhtml), the training risk was defined as the average loss incurred by using <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0006.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0006.gif)to predict the value of *y[i]* on the training data, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0002" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0002.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> train </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0002.gif)

Training risk is cheap to compute, but it tends to underestimate risk (that is, to be an *optimistic risk estimate*) because the data used to evaluate <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0007.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0007.gif)are the same data used to compute <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0008.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0008.gif)in the first place. As a result, overly complex models with very high variance, which approximate *f* very well near the training data but poorly away from the training data, tend to be chosen when selecting models to minimize training risk (an example of this phenomenon was suggested in Exercise 2.4).

**Exercise 7.1** *Let x*[1], …, *x[n] be distinct real numbers and for each i* let *y[i]* = θ[1]*x[i]* + θ[0] + *e[i]*, *where e*[1], …, *e[n] are independent, identically distributed draws from a* N(0, σ²) *distribution. The pairs* (*x*[1], *y*[1]), …, (*x[n]*, *y[n]*) *are known. Unknown are* θ[0], θ[1], σ², *the e[i]’s and the fact that f*(*x*) = θ[1]*x* + θ[0] *is a linear function. Consider the sequence of approximations* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0009.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0009.gif)*to f where* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0010.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0010.gif)*is a degree-d real polynomial which minimizes training risk with respect to squared-error loss. Show that, with probability one,* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0011.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> train </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0011.gif)*is a decreasing function of the degree d*. *Show that* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0012.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> train </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0012.gif)*when d* ⩾ *n* − 1. *Explain these facts in terms of bias–variance trade-off.*

## 7.2 Risk Estimation via Validation or Test Data

The most accurate way to estimate the risk of an approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0013.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0013.gif)of *f* is by using data which have the same distribution as data to which <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0014.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0014.gif)is to be applied in the future, but which have not been used to train <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0015.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0015.gif). One way to obtain such *validation data* or *test data* is to remove it from the set of all available data before training any models.

### 7.2.1 Training, Validation, and Test Data

Let the set of all available data be partitioned randomly^([1](#c07.xhtml#c07-note-0001)) into either two or three sets: a *training dataset* on which models are trained, a *validation dataset* which is used to estimate the risk of trained models for the purpose of model selection, and perhaps also a *test dataset* which is used to estimate the risk of the best model found by the model selection process.

In some applications, an approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0016.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0016.gif)is considered worth implementing only if the risk, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0017.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0017.gif), can be shown to fall below a given threshold. Such applications require a test set in addition to a validation set. In other applications, the best approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0018.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0018.gif)will be used, at least on a trial basis, regardless of the risk, in which case only a validation set may be needed.

In what follows, let <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0019.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0019.gif)denote validation data. It is assumed to be drawn independently from the same distribution as the training data but *it is not used to train any models* and, to the greatest extent possible, *it is excluded from exploratory data analysis.*^([2](#c07.xhtml#c07-note-0002)) All remarks about validation data below also pertain to test data.

### 7.2.2 Risk Estimation

The *validation estimate* of the risk <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0020.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0020.gif)of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0021.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0021.gif)is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0003" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0003.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0003.gif)

The validation estimate of risk is unbiased, since <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0004" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0004.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></munderover><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0004.gif)

Consequently, by the strong law of large numbers, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0022.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0022.gif)with probability 1 as <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0023.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi>&#x221e;</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0023.gif). By the central limit theorem, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0024.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0024.gif)is approximately normal-distributed under weak assumptions. This enables convenient testing of hypotheses about risk, provided the variance of the risk estimate can be estimated.

**Exercise 7.2** *In the case of 0–1 loss, the risk (generalization error) of trained classifier* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0025.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0025.gif)*is* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0005" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0005.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi> probability </mi><mi> that </mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi> new </mi><mi> datum </mi><mi> is </mi><mi> misclassified </mi><mi> by </mi></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

**Exercise 7.4** *Use result of Exercise 7.3 to show that if the range of* L(*c*, *d*) *is* \[0, 1\] *(that is, the loss is never more than one) then* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0008" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0008.gif"><mrow><msub><mi> Var </mi><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

Exercises 7.3 and 7.4 lead to a simple plug-in estimator for the variance, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0010" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0010.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi> Var </mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></mfrac><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><msup><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0010.gif)

which in the case of 0–1 loss simplifies to <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0011" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0011.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi> Var </mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

### 7.2.3 Size of Training, Validation, and Test Sets

Given a dataset of a certain size, how large should the training, validation, and test sets be? The answer depends on balancing two (or three) competing demands. As more data are assigned to the validation set, the validation estimate of risk, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0029.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0029.gif), improves in the sense that the standard deviation of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0030.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0030.gif)goes to zero like <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0031.gif"><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup></math>![](images/c07_ILM0031.gif)by Exercise 7.3. The same is true of the test set and the test estimate of risk. But as more data are assigned to the validation and test sets, fewer data are assigned to the training set, and one naturally expects the risk of trained approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0032.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0032.gif)get worse as the number of training data decreases—though perhaps this effect is negligible if enough data remain in the training set.

**Exercise 7.5** *In a given application where 0–1 loss is used, it is desired that the validation estimate of risk have standard deviation no more than σ. Find the minimum number* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0033.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0033.gif)*of validation data needed to achieve this, assuming:*

1.  expert opinion or a pilot study suggests the risk of any “reasonable” classifier will be no more than ρ, for some given number <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0034.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c1;</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0034.gif);
2.  there is no knowledge of what the risk might be;
3.  *as in (A), with* ρ = 0.25 *and* σ = 0.01;
4.  Recommend a course of action in (C) if there are a total of 1800 data available.

One occasionally encounters heuristic rules on the size of training, validation, and test sets, such as *use 70% of the data for training, 20% for validation, and 10% for testing* (or 60-20-20, or 50-30-20). The author advises that decisions about data be made to suit the applied goal of the data analysis, rather than by heuristics which may be unrelated to the applied goal.

### 7.2.4 Testing Hypotheses About Risk

The approximate normal distribution of the risk estimate <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0035.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0035.gif)enables the construction of approximate confidence intervals for the true risk <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0036.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0036.gif)and hypothesis testing based upon such intervals. In addition to tests based on the asymptotic normality of the risk estimate, one can also use non-parametric tests.

**Exercise 7.6** *Assume that the number* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0037.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0037.gif)*of validation data is large enough that the validation estimate of risk,* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0038.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0038.gif), *can be thought of as normal-distributed with negligible error for any model* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0039.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0039.gif)*under consideration. Given an observation of a random variable (the test statistic) T* ∼ N(μ, σ²) *and a fixed value ρ, a level-α one-sided Z-test of the null hypothesis* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0012" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0012.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>:</mo><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mi>&#x03c1;</mi></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0012.gif)

*against the alternative hypothesis* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0013" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0013.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>&#x03c1;</mi></mrow></math></displayedItem>

*works as follows: (1) let threshold τ be such that* P(*U* ≤ τ) = α, *where U* ∼ N(ρ, σ²) (τ *is the αth quantile of the* N(ρ, σ²) *distribution); (2) reject H*[0] if *T* < τ *and otherwise retain H*[0].

1.  Show that if the null hypothesis is true, then the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis is no more than α (this is what it means for the test to have level α—see [Chapter 12](#c12.xhtml)).
2.  Suppose that in a given application, a trained classifier <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0040.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0040.gif)will not be implemented unless there is evidence that <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0041.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>&#x03c1;</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0041.gif), where ρ is a given threshold. ### 7.2.5 Example of Use of Training, Validation, and Test Sets

Say a classification dataset has been partitioned somehow into training, validation, and (perhaps) test sets and that, for concreteness of the example, we are determined to approximate *f* using a classification tree. We seek an approximately minimal-risk tree for making predictions and (perhaps) to estimate the risk of the optimal tree.

Recall from [Section 4.8](#c04.xhtml#c4_8) that training a classification tree is a two-stage process: the first stage is to grow the tree by successively splitting the data until a tree is obtained which has zero, or nearly zero, training risk; the second stage is to prune the tree by finding a subtree of the tree grown in the first stage which minimizes the cost-complexity criterion, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0014" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0014.gif"><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi>&#x03b1;</mi></mtd><mtd><mo>&#x00d7;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi> number </mi><mi> of </mi><mi> leaf </mi><mi> nodes </mi></mrow></mfenced></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mrow><mi> all </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> leaf </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> nodes </mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></munder><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">min</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></munder><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0014.gif)

Free, non-negative parameter α controls a penalty on the overall size of the tree: increasing α increases bias and decreases variance.

For simplicity, let us assume that all other aspects of tree-training described in [Section 4.8](#c04.xhtml#c4_8) are fixed. The set of trees obtainable from any given set of training data, then, is a one-parameter family indexed by α, and searching for an approximately optimal tree corresponds to searching for an approximately optimal value of α. Intuitively, setting α = 0 usually will result in a high-risk tree with very high variance and low bias. Increasing α from zero, we expect the risk of the tree which minimizes the cost-complexity criterion to decrease at first, then to reach some (not necessarily unique) minimum corresponding to the optimal bias–variance trade-off, and then to increase as the tree gets too much bias and too little variance. Eventually, for all α beyond some threshold, the tree which minimizes the cost-complexity criterion consists of only a single leaf node: this tree has high bias and low variance, and is usually high-risk.

An approximately optimal tree can be found in this way:^([3](#c07.xhtml#c07-note-0003))

1.  specify a finite set *A* of non-negative numbers to use as values of α;
2.  use the training data to compute, for each α ∈ *A*, the tree <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0051.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b1;</mi></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0051.gif)which minimizes the cost-complexity criterion;
3.  use the validation data to compute the validation estimate <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0052.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b1;</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0052.gif)of the risk of each tree <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0053.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b1;</mi></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0053.gif);
4.  choose the tree <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0054.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b1;</mi></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0054.gif)with minimal estimated risk <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0055.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b1;</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0055.gif).

The validation estimates of risk are *estimates*, so the criterion in step (4) is commonly replaced by

4.  choose the simplest tree <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0056.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b1;</mi></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0056.gif)such that one cannot reject the hypothesis that it has minimal risk, of all trees considered.

Having found^([4](#c07.xhtml#c07-note-0004)) an approximately optimal value <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0057.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b1;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0057.gif)of α, the trained tree returned by this selection process is that corresponding to <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0058.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b1;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0058.gif), trained either just on the training data or, so as not to waste data, on the training data and validation data combined. The test estimate of risk is then computed for this tree, if a test set has been created.

## 7.3 Cross-Validation

When data are not plentiful, an alternative to creating training and validation sets is *k-fold cross-validation*. In *k*\-fold cross-validation, the data are partitioned randomly into *k* subsets of approximately equal size, *S* = *S*[1]∪…∪*S[k]*. Specifically, the *k*\-fold cross-validation estimate of risk is the quantity <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0059.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> cv </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0059.gif)defined by the algorithm shown in [Figure 7.1](#c07.xhtml#figure7-1).

![Figure 7.1 An algorithm for k-fold cross-validation.](images/c07f001.jpg)

[**Figure 7.1**](#c07.xhtml#figureanchor7-1) An algorithm for *k*\-fold cross-validation.

The expected value of the cross-validated risk estimate (taken with respect to the random partition π of *S* into *k* subsets *and* the distribution of the training data) is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0015" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0015.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> cv </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>k</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></munderover><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2248;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

As shown above, the expected value of the cross-validated risk estimate, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0063.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> cv </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0063.gif), is (approximately) the risk of approximating *f* using <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0064.gif"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0064.gif)training data. When *k* is small, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0065.gif"><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></mfrac></math>![](images/c07_ILM0065.gif)is small and the expected value of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0066.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> cv </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0066.gif)is the risk of training the approximation method on substantially fewer training data than are actually available. Since decreasing the amount of training data available to a given approximation method tends to produce higher-risk approximations,^([5](#c07.xhtml#c07-note-0005)) <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0067.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> cv </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0067.gif)is generally biased toward overestimating the risk of training <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0068.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0068.gif)on *n* data (<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0069.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> cv </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0069.gif)is a *pessimistic risk estimate*). When *k* is large (the extreme case, *k* = *n*, is called *leave-one-out cross-validation*), <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0070.gif"><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></mfrac></math>![](images/c07_ILM0070.gif)is close to one and so <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0071.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> cv </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0071.gif)is nearly unbiased. The correlation between pairs of risk estimates, for example <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0072.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0072.gif)and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0073.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0073.gif), depends on *k*. When *k* is large, approximations <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0074.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0074.gif)and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0075.gif"><msub><mover mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0076.gif)and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0077.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0077.gif)will in general be highly correlated: in the extreme case of leave-one-out cross-validation, the (*n* − 1)-point datasets *S*∖*S*[1] and *S*∖*S*[2] used to train <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0078.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0078.gif)and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0079.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0079.gif)have *n* − 2 points in common. Thus when *k* is large, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0080.gif"><mrow><mi> Cor </mi><mo>\[</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0080.gif)is relatively large. When *k* is small, approximations <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0081.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0081.gif)and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0082.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0082.gif)are less correlated.

In computing the *k*\-fold cross-validation estimate of risk, there is a bias–variance trade-off problem in choosing *k*. When *k* is small, the estimate has relatively high bias and low variance, and when *k* is large, it has relatively low bias but high variance. Both the bias and variance get smaller as *n* increases, but this is of not much help since, for large datasets, we would generally choose to estimate risk using a separate validation set. It seems that *k* = 5, *k* = 10, and *k* = *n* are used most commonly in practice.^([6](#c07.xhtml#c07-note-0006))

## 7.4 Improvements on Cross-Validation

The inventor of the bootstrap proposed several ways to apply bootstrapping to risk estimation (Efron, 1983, 1986; Efron and Tibshirani, 1997). The general idea of these methods is to construct bootstrap samples of the training data, train a model on each bootstrap sample and apply the trained model to data not in the bootstrap sample on which it was trained, and average the resulting risk estimates (bootstrap samples are discussed in [Section 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c6_3)). In the words of Efron and Tibshirani (1997), “the bootstrap procedures are nothing more than smoothed versions of cross-validation, with some adjustments to correct for bias.” The best of these, as determined by simulation studies in Efron and Tibshirani (1997), is the *.632+ bootstrap risk estimate*, which is computed as follows (the notation follows Efron and Tibshirani (1997)).

First, construct *B* independent bootstrap samples from the training data: Efron and Tibshirani (1997) recommend *B* = 50 samples and also discusses criteria for choosing *B*. Train a model <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0083.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>b</mi></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0083.gif)on the *b*th bootstrap sample for *b* ∈ {1, …, *B*}. For *i* ∈ {1, …, *n*}, let <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0084.gif"><msub><mi mathvariant="script">B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0084.gif)be the set of indices of bootstrap samples which do not contain training datum (*x[i]*, *y[i]*), and let *E[i]* be the average (over <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0085.gif"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="script">B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0085.gif)) loss incurred when using <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0086.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>b</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0086.gif)in place of *y[i]*: <displayedItem Let the *leave-one-out bootstrap estimate of risk* be <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0019" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0019.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi> Err </mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0019.gif)

the average loss incurred by predicting the class or response of a datum using bootstrap samples not containing the datum. Denote the training risk by <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0087.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> train </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0087.gif)(<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0088.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0088.gif)with no subscript denotes a model trained on all of the training data, as usual). The *no-information risk* is the expected loss incurred, using <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0089.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0089.gif)to make predictions, when the input *X* and response or class label *Y* are independent, that is, when *X* is assumed to contain no information about *Y*, in the sense that the conditional distribution P(*Y* | *X*) is the same as the marginal distribution P(*Y*). The no-information risk is estimated by <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0020" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0020.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0020.gif)

and it is a very pessimistic risk estimate indeed! Efron and Tibshirani define <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0021" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0021.gif"><mrow><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi> Err </mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x0027;</mo></msup></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">min</mo><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi> Err </mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

which truncates the leave-one-out bootstrap risk estimate at the no-information risk estimate, and they define the *relative over-fitting rate* to be <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" If <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0093.gif"><mrow><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>&#x0027;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0093.gif), then <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0094.gif"><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi> Err </mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x0027;</mo></msup></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> train </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0094.gif), which means that the leave-one-out bootstrap estimate of risk is at least as pessimistic as the estimated no-information risk <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0095.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0095.gif). If <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0096.gif"><mrow><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>&#x0027;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0096.gif), then the training estimate of risk is at least as pessimistic as the leave-one-out bootstrap estimate.

accentunder="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>368</mn><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>632</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>&#x0027;</mo></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>368</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>&#x0027;</mo></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#x23df;</mo></munder><mrow><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>368</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></munder><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0023.gif)

Intuitively, the .632+ bootstrap risk estimate strikes a balance between an optimistic risk estimate (training risk) and one which tends to be pessimistic (the leave-one-out bootstrap estimate). The balance point is chosen based on how these two estimates disagree. The reader is directed to Efron (1983, 1986) and Efron and Tibshirani (1997) for discussion of bootstrap estimates of risk.

## 7.5 Out-of-Bag Risk Estimation

A classifier produced by bootstrap aggregation (bagging) of other base classifiers is called a *bagged classifier* (see [Section 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c6_3)). A random forest is a bagged classifier, for example. The risk of a bagged classifier can be estimated using the bootstrap samples already constructed in training.

Assuming that the bootstrap samples are of size *n*, each datum in a training set for a bagged classifier is used to train approximately proportion <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0097.gif"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>e</mi></mfrac><mo>&#x2248;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>632</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0097.gif)of the base classifiers. For these base classifiers, the datum is *in-bag* and for the remaining ones (which it is not used to train) it is *out-of-bag*: in the notation of [Section 7.4](#c07.xhtml#c7_4), <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0098.gif"><msub><mi mathvariant="script">B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0098.gif)indexes the bootstrap samples for which (*x[i]*, *y[i]*) is out-of-bag. The set of base classifiers for which a datum is out-of-bag, aggregated together into a committee classifier, is the *out-of-bag classifier* for that datum.

The *out-of-bag risk estimate* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0099.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> oob </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0099.gif)of a bagged classifier is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0024" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0024.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> oob </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi> most </mi><mi> common </mi><mi> class </mi><mi> among </mi></mrow><mrow><mo>{</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>b</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>:</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="script">B</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0024.gif)

The out-of-bag risk estimate is generally biased high (Bylander, 2002) that is, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0100.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> oob </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0100.gif)tends to over estimate the risk of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0101.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0101.gif). At least in the case of random forests, experiments by the author indicate that the bias becomes small as the number of trees increases. The author has observed empirically that a simple estimate of the variance of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0102.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> oob </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0102.gif), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0025" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0025.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi></mrow></munder><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><msub><mi>N</mi><mi> oob </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><msup><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> oob </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mstyle></mfenced></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0025.gif)
