where <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0025a" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0026.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi> oob </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mtext>number</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>of</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>training</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>data</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>such</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>that</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>the</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>out-of-bag</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>classifier</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>predicts</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0026.gif)

tends to be biased low.

## 7.6 Akaike’s Information Criterion

In the case of parametric models which are trained by computing maximum likelihood estimates of parameters (for example, likelihood methods, logistic regression, and neural networks), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0027" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0027.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msub><mi> argmax </mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0027.gif)

there is a computationally cheap method of choosing a model which has approximately minimal risk. This is by minimizing *Akaike’s information criterion (AIC)*, which is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0028" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0028.gif"><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0028.gif)

where *k* is the number of coordinates in the parameter vector θ. Here and elsewhere, log is the natural logarithm. AIC decreases the better the model fits the observed data, and increases the more complex the model is, where complexity is measured by the number of parameters, *k*. In literature and software, AIC is sometimes defined as the above expression multiplied by <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0103.gif"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>![](images/c07_ILM0103.gif), <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0104.gif"><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0104.gif)or − 1

Akaike’s criterion is an extension of the maximum likelihood principle. Suppose there are *L* models under consideration, *M*[1], … , *M*[*L*], that model *M*[*i*] has a vector parameter *θ*[*i*] of dimension *k*[*i*], and <math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![](images/pg138-1.gif)is an estimate of *θ*[*i*] derived somehow from a dataset *S* = {(*X*[1], *Y*[1]),  … , (*X*[*n*], *Y*[*n*])}. The *maximum likelihood principle* states that, given observed data (*x*[1], *y*[1]), … , (*x*[*n*], *y*[*n*]), the “best” choice of model *M*[*i*] and corresponding parameter *θ*[*i*] is the one that maximizes the likelihood of the observed responses or classes,

<displayedItem type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mtext>argmax</mtext><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=","><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=","><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mfenced separators="|" open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/pg138-2.gif)

Note that the maximization is taken over all models *M*[*i*] and all possible parameters *θ*[*i*] for each model *M*[*i*]. Exercise 7.1 indicates a potential problem with using the maximum likelihood principle for model selection. In contrast to the maximum likelihood principle, Akaike (1973) begins with the idea that the “best” choice of model *M*[*i*] is the one that maximizes the expected log‐likelihood of a future datum which has not yet been observed,

<displayedItem type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mtext>argmax</mtext><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mo>log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mfenced separators="|" open="(" close=")"><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/pg138-3.gif)

where the parameter estimate <math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![](images/pg138-1.gif)for model *M*[*i*] is estimated from the data set *S*. Akaike shows that, for large *n*, the model which maximizes the expected log‐likelihood is approximately the model which maximizes the formula for AIC given at the start of this section. In the case of regression with additive, Gaussian‐distributed noise, the expected log‐likelihood is

<displayedItem type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mo>log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mfenced separators="|" open="(" close=")"><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>log</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=","><mn>1</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi></mfenced><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/pg138-4.gif)

so selecting the model which maximizes the expected log‐likelihood is equivalent to selecting the model which minimizes risk with respect to squared‐error loss (see [Section 3.6](#c03.xhtml#c3_6)). In the case of classification by logistic regression and some neural networks, selecting the model which maximizes expected log‐likelihood is equivalent to selecting the model which minimizes risk with respect to cross‐entropy loss ([Sections 4.6](#c04.xhtml#c4_6) and [4.7](#c04.xhtml#c4_7), Exercise 4.11).

Shortly after cross-validation and AIC were both developed, Stone showed that in the case of parametric models which are trained by computing maximum likelihood estimates of parameters, cross-validation and AIC will choose the same model as the data size *n* → ∞ (Stone, 1977).

## 7.7 Schwartz’s Bayesian Information Criterion

The *Bayesian information criterion (BIC)* is applicable in the same setting as AIC, and has a similar form: choose a model to minimize <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0029" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0029.gif"><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0029.gif)

Like AIC, BIC decreases the better the model fits the observed data, and increases the more complex the model is, where complexity is measured by the number of parameters, *k*. In literature and software, BIC is sometimes defined as the above expression multiplied by <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0105.gif"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>![](images/c07_ILM0105.gif), <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0106.gif"><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0106.gif)or − 1.

The idea behind BIC is this. Suppose there are *L* models under consideration, *M*[1], …, *M[L]*, and that model *M[i]* has a vector parameter θ[*i*] of dimension *k[i]*, and let P(*M[i]*) and P(θ[*i*] | *M[i]*) denote prior distributions on the set of models and on the parameter space Θ[*i*] of the *i*th model, respectively. Given data, (*x*[1], *y*[1]), …, (*x[n]*, *y[n]*), the posterior probability of the *i*th model is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0030" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0030.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x221d;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><msub><mo>&#x222b;</mo><msub><mi>&#x0398;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0030.gif)

where the constant of proportionality, P(*y*[1], …, *y[n]*)^(− 1), is the same for all models. In Schwartz (1978), Schwartz proves that, under mild regularity conditions on the priors P(θ[*i*] | *M[i]*) and the likelihoods P(*y*[1], …, *y[n]* | *x*[1], …, *x[n]*, θ[*i*], *M[i]*), the logarithm of the expression above is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0031" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0031.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mtext>(a</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>term</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>bounded</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>in</mtext><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>n</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0031.gif)

where <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0107.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0107.gif)is the maximum likelihood estimate for θ[*i*]. Thus, as *n* → ∞, choosing the model with smallest BIC is equivalent to choosing the model with largest posterior probability.

Since selecting a model with maximal BIC is selecting a model with (approximately) maximal posterior probability, *BIC is a criterion for selecting a good explanatory model rather than a good predictive model*. BIC places a heavier penalty on the number of parameters than does AIC (provided models are trained on at least eight data points), so BIC chooses models no more complex, and usually simpler, than those chosen by AIC.

## 7.8 Rissanen’s Minimum Description Length Criterion

The *minimum description length (MDL) criterion* is applicable more generally than AIC or BIC. The MDL criterion is to choose the model which minimizes <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0032" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0032.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mo>-</mo><msub><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><msup><mrow/><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>H</mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mfrac><msup><mi>&#x03c0;</mi><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mrow><mi>&#x0393;</mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mstyle></mfenced></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0032.gif)

where log [2] is the base-2 logarithm and θ is a *k*\-long parameter vector. In the second term, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0033" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0033.gif"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><msup><mi>&#x2202;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mi>&#x2202;</mi><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>&#x2202;</mi><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>-</mo><msub><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mstyle></mfenced><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0033.gif)

is the Hessian of − log [2]P(*y*[1], …, *y[n]* | *x*[1], …, *x[n]*, θ) as a function of θ, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0108.gif"><mrow><msup><mi>&#x03c0;</mi><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mo>/</mo><mi>&#x0393;</mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mstyle></mfenced></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0108.gif)is the volume of a *k*\-dimensional Euclidean unit ball, and for any positive number *z*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0034" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0034.gif"><mrow><msubsup><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0034.gif)

is a finite sum of all of the positive terms of the form log [2]⋅⋅⋅log [2](*z*). Note that the MDL criterion applies to selection of a value of parameter θ as well as model complexity *k*, unlike AIC and BIC, where θ is estimated by maximum likelihood.

The idea behind the MDL criterion is that the best model is one which simultaneously encodes the data efficiently while being itself efficient to encode. The first term in the MDL criterion, − log [2](P(*y*[1], …, *y[n]* | *x*[1], …, *x[n]*, θ)), is the number of bits required to represent the observed responses *y*[1], …, *y[n]*, given the model, parameter θ, and observed feature vectors *x*[1], …, *x[n]*. The second term in the MDL criterion, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0109.gif"><mrow><msubsup><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><msup><mrow/><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>H</mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><msup><mi>&#x03c0;</mi><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mo>/</mo><mi>&#x0393;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0109.gif), is the number of bits required to represent the model in an approximately optimal encoding of models constructed in Rissanen (1978). Like AIC and BIC, the MDL criterion decreases the better the model fits the observed data, and increases the more complex the model is, although in MDL, the complexity of a model is measured in the information-theoretic sense just described.

The MDL criterion is a practical criterion which builds on the idea of *Kolmogorov complexity*, which defines the complexity of a dataset to be the length of the shortest program which would cause a universal Turing machine to produce the dataset as output^([7](#c07.xhtml#c07-note-0007)) (Cover and Thomas, 2006; Kolmogorov, 1968; Rissanen, 1978, 1983; Solomonoff, 1964a, 1964b). Since selecting a model with optimal MDL criterion is selecting a model which (approximately) provides the simplest representation of the data in an information-theoretic sense, *the MDL criterion is, like BIC, a criterion for selecting a good explanatory model rather than a good predictive model.*

## 7.9 *R*² and Adjusted *R*²

In the standard regression setting with squared-error loss, training error times *n* is called the *residual sum of squares* (RSS) of a model, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0035" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0035.gif"><mrow><mi> RSS </mi><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> train </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0035.gif)

See [Section 3.4](#c03.xhtml#c3_4). RSS is interpreted as the variability in the observed response *not* explained by the trained model <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0110.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c07_ILM0110.gif). The *total sum of squares* (TSS) is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0036" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0036.gif"><mrow><mi> TSS </mi><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> train </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi> constant </mi><mi> model </mi></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0036.gif)

where <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0111.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0111.gif)is the mean response in the data: it measures the overall variability in the observed response. RSS can be no more than TSS (under very mild model assumptions) and the trained model predicts the observed response perfectly if and only if <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0112.gif"><mrow><mi> RSS </mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0112.gif). The *model sum of squares* is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0037" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0037.gif"><mrow><mi> MSS </mi><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="true">&c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mspace width="0.25em"/><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0037.gif)

The model sum of squares measures the overall variability of the fitted values about the mean observed response.

A commonly used measure of fit in regression is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0038" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0038.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mi> RSS </mi><mi> TSS </mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi> MSS </mi><mi> TSS </mi></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0038.gif)

It is interpreted as *the proportion of the variation in the response which is explained by the model.* When *R*² is close to 1, the model explains most of the variation in the data, and when *R*² is close to 0, the model explains very little. As stated in Exercise 3.6, *R*² is the square of the sample correlation between the vector of observed responses (*y*[1], …, *y[n]*) and the vector of fitted responses <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0113.gif"><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c07_ILM0113.gif).

As models become more complex, *R*² tends to increase (in fact, cannot decrease if the models are nested—see Exercise 7.1). After all, RSS is ![](images/pg141-1.gif). This is compensated for in *adjusted R*², <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0039" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0039.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi> adj </mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mi> RSS </mi><mi> TSS </mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0039.gif)

which penalizes model complexity (the number of parameters, *k*).^([8](#c07.xhtml#c07-note-0008)) Note that when *k* = *m* + 1, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c07-disp-0040" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c07\_M0040.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi> adj </mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mfrac><mi> RSS </mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mi> TSS </mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mfrac></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c07_M0040.gif)

and, as seen in [Chapter 3](#c03.xhtml), <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0114.gif"><mfrac><mi> TSS </mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![](images/c07_ILM0114.gif)is an unbiased estimate of Var\[*Y*\] while <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0115.gif"><mfrac><mi> RSS </mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![](images/c07_ILM0115.gif)is an unbiased estimate of Var\[*E*\]. The goal is to choose a model for which <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0116.gif"><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi> adj </mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math>![](images/c07_ILM0116.gif)is relatively large, ideally close to 1.

## 7.10 Stepwise Model Selection

Let {1, …, *m*} index the set of all available features, let *I* denote a subset of this index set, and let <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0117.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>I</mi></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0117.gif)denote a classifier trained on the training data using exactly the features indexed by *I* (note that if *I* is empty then <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0118.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>I</mi></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0118.gif)predicts all data to be of the same class). *Stepwise model selection*, generically, refers to any kind of discrete optimization algorithm used to search the subsets of {1, …, *m*} to find a subset *I* for which the estimated risk of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c07\_ILM0119.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>I</mi></msub></math>![](images/c07_ILM0119.gif)is minimal.^([9](#c07.xhtml#c07-note-0009)) It also refers to the specific algorithm shown in [Figure 7.2](#c07.xhtml#figure7-2), which is a discrete form of gradient descent (see [Section 10.1](#c10.xhtml#c10_1)).

![Figure 7.2 An algorithm for stepwise model selection.](images/c07f002.jpg)

[**Figure 7.2**](#c07.xhtml#figureanchor7-2) An algorithm for stepwise model selection.

## 7.11 Occam’s Razor

*Occam’s Razor* is a principle which says (in the context of statistical models) that, given a set of statistical models, we ought to choose the simplest one which has sufficiently low risk, or the simplest one for which there is no more complex model with significantly lower risk. This principle is followed when simplicity of a model is considered a virtue. Reasons for preferring a simple model include:

*   a simple model is easier to understand than a complex one and therefore is more likely to lead to insights about the data and to be understood—hence believed (Jeffreys, 1931) and applied—by those not involved with its construction;
*   a simple model may be computationally less burdensome than a complex one, particularly when the complex model requires expensive-to-acquire features which are not used by the simple model.

However, *simple models do not necessarily make better predictions than complex ones.* To return to the quote at the start of the chapter, “aesthetics and statistical accuracy might not be the same thing.”

## Notes

# 8  
Consistency

> When you have data, you analyze the data. When you don’t have data, you prove theorems.

By this point, the mathematically sophisticated reader may, upon consideration of all of the classification and regression methods presented in [Chapters 3](#c03.xhtml), [4](#c04.xhtml), and [6](#c06.xhtml), throw up his or her hands in frustration due to the feeling that such a wide array of different methods is a sign not of knowledge and understanding, but of ignorance. “Surely,” such a reader might say, “there ought to be *one* method that solves all classification problems optimally, at least as the number of data, *n*, increases without bound?”

This short chapter answers that question in the affirmative, introducing the reader to a property of classification methods known as consistency. A classification method is *consistent* for a given classification problem if the risk of the trained classifier(s) it produces converges to the risk of the Bayes classifier for that problem as *n* → ∞ (for some appropriate definition of convergence). A classification method is *universally consistent* if it is consistent with respect to all joint distributions P(*X*, *Y*) on a given domain and range, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0001.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0001.gif).

The main results presented in this chapter are: there are classification methods which are known to be universally consistent; there is at least one classification method (random forests) which is widely used in practice and which is known to be not universally consistent; and (in the author’s opinion) the behavior of a classification method on an arbitrary problem as *n* → ∞ does not provide much useful insight about how to solve any particular applied problem. That said, the application-minded reader may skip this chapter without harm. The theory-minded reader can find proofs and other details, omitted in what follows, in Devroye et al. (1996), Biau et al. (2008), and Biau and Devroye (2010).

## 8.1 Convergence of Sequences of Random Variables

Let *Z*[1], *Z*[2], … denote an infinite sequence of real-valued random vectors, and let *Z* denote another real-valued random vector. The sequence *Z*[1], *Z*[2], … *converges in probability* to *Z* if, for any ε > 0, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0001" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0001.gif"><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">lim</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi>&#x221e;</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>&#x03f5;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_M0001.gif)

Convergence in probability is denoted <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0002.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo></mfrac><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0002.gif). The sequence *Z*[1], *Z*[2], … *converges almost surely* to *Z* (or *converges strongly* to *Z*, or *converges with probability 1* to *Z*) if <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0002" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0002.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">lim</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi>&#x221e;</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>Z</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_M0002.gif)

Almost sure convergence is denoted <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0003.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mo>.</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2192;</mo></mfrac><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0003.gif).^([1](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0001))

## 8.2 Consistency for Parameter Estimation

Let *z* be a fixed but unknown quantity, and let *Z*[1], *Z*[2], … be a sequence of random variables which serve as estimates of *z*. The sequence of estimates *Z*[1], *Z*[2], … is *consistent for z* (respectively *strongly consistent for z*) if *Z*[1], *Z*[2], … converges in probability to *z* (respectively converges strongly to *z*).^([2](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0002))

For example, consider the case that *z* is the mean of some distribution, that an unlimited sequence of data *W*[1], *W*[2], … are drawn independently from this distribution, and that, for each *n*, *Z[n]* is the sample mean of the first *n* data, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0007.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0007.gif). In this case, the sequence *Z*[1], *Z*[2], … is both consistent and strongly consistent for *z*—these two facts are respectively known as the *weak law of large numbers* and the *strong law of large numbers*.^([3](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0003))

Under certain regularity conditions (see Ferguson (1996) or van der Vaart (2000)) maximum likelihood estimators of model parameters are both consistent and strongly consistent. In particular, in linear regression with independent, identically distributed Gaussian noise, the regression parameter estimate <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0004" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0004.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_M0004.gif)

obtained in Exercise 3.2 and Exercise 3.7 is strongly consistent for the true parameter θ when the data (*X*[1], *Y*[1]), (*X*[2], *Y*[2]), … are in fact generated by the linear model, that is, when *Y[i]* = (1, *X[i]*)θ + *E[i]* where *E*[1], *E*[2], … are independent, identically distributed N(0, σ²).

## 8.3 Consistency for Prediction

Recall from [Chapter 2](#c02.xhtml) that an approximation method is a function which takes an observed dataset (of size *n*, say) as input and outputs an approximation of the true unknown function *f* which has produced class labels or continuous responses. The risk of an approximation method (trained on datasets of size *n*) is the expected loss incurred by drawing a random training set *S* of size *n*, constructing an approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0008.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub></math>![](images/c08_ILM0008.gif)of *f* from it and using <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0009.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0009.gif)in place of *Y* for new data (*X*, *Y*), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0005" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0005.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_M0005.jpg)

where ![](images/c08_145_001.jpg)is the risk of approximation ![](images/c08_145_002.jpg). Recall from [Section 4.1](#c04.xhtml#c4_1) that the Bayes risk is the minimum possible risk for any approximation method for data with a given joint distribution on (*X*, *Y*), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0006" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0006.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi> Bayes </mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">min</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></munder><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>|</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_M0006.gif)

The Bayes risk is the risk of the Bayes classifier.

*With respect to a given joint distribution* P(<i>X</i>, <i>Y</i>) <i>on</i> <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0010.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0010.gif)*,* a prediction method is a *consistent prediction method* (or a *weakly consistent prediction method*) if <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0007" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0007.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo></mfrac><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi> Bayes </mi></msub></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_M0007.jpg)

![](images/c08_143_001.jpg)and is a *strongly consistent prediction method* if <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0008" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0008.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mo>.</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2192;</mo></mfrac><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi> Bayes </mi></msub><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_143_002.jpg)

A prediction method is a *universally consistent prediction method* (respectively a *universally strongly consistent prediction method*) if it is consistent (respectively strongly consistent) with respect to all joint distributions on <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0011.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0011.gif).

## 8.4 There Are Consistent and Universally Consistent Classifiers

Much is known about consistency and universal consistency in general and for various specific classification methods. We summarize it here for *binary* classifiers, following closely the book Devroye et al. (1996) and also the papers Biau et al. (2008) and Biau and Devroye (2010).

The *diameter of a set* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0012.gif"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0012.gif)is the supremum of the Euclidean distance between any two points in *R*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0009" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0009.gif"><mrow><mi> diam </mi><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">sup</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_M0009.gif)

**Theorem 8.1 Consistency of Partitioning Classifiers.** *Let features <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0013.gif"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0013.gif). Let a binary classification method operate by partitioning <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0014.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c08_ILM0014.gif)into disjoint regions and, given any point <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0015.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0015.gif), under 0–1 loss, predicting the majority class of the training data in the region *R*(*x*) containing *x* (with ties broken in a fixed but arbitrary way). The classification method is consistent for P(*X*, *Y*) if, as *n* → ∞,* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0010" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0010.gif"><mrow><mi> diam </mi><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo></mfrac><mn>0</mn></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_M0010.gif)

and <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0011" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0011.gif"><mrow><mrow><mi> the </mi><mi> number </mi><mi> of </mi><mi> training </mi><mi> data </mi><mi> in </mi></mrow><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo></mfrac><mi>&#x221e;</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_M0011.gif)

Histogram classifiers ([Section 4.4.5](#c04.xhtml#c4_4_5)) and classification trees ([Section 4.8](#c04.xhtml#c4_8)) are examples of classifiers to which this theorem applies.

A *cubic histogram* classifier is one which partitions <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0016.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c08_ILM0016.gif)into cubes of side length *h* and, given any point <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0017.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0017.gif), predicts the majority class of the training data in cube *R*(*x*) containing *x*, breaking ties in a fixed but arbitrary way. In the next theorem, which follows from Theorem 8.1, the bandwidth (side length) *h* = *h*(*n*) is a function of the number *n* of training data.

**Theorem 8.2 Universal Consistency of the Cubic Histogram Classifier.** *The cubic histogram classifier is universally consistent if, as *n* → ∞, *h*(*n*) → 0 and *n* *h*(*n*)^(*m*) → ∞.*

A *weighted average classifier* assigns a weight *w*(*x*, *x[i]*) to any point <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0018.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0018.gif)and any training point *x[i]*, *i* = 1, …, *n*. At a point <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0019.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0019.gif), it predicts the class *c* such that the sum of the weights of that class is maximal, that is, it predicts <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0012" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0012.gif"><mrow><msub><mi> argmax </mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></msub><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi>w</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_M0012.gif)

For example, the *k*\-nearest-neighbor classifier is a weighted average classifier where <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0013" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0013.gif"><mrow><mi>w</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>is</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>one</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>of</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>the</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>k</mi><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>nearest</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>training</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>points</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>to</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>x</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>e</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_M0013.gif)

**Theorem 8.3 Consistency of the Weighted-Average Classifier (Stone).** *Under the following three conditions on the distribution of *X* and weights *w*(*X*, *x[i]*), *i* = 1, …, *n*, the weighted-average classifier is consistent:*

1.  there is a constant α such that for every measurable^([4](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0004)) function *g*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0014" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0014.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>&#x221e;</mi><mspace width="2.em"/><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> implies </mi><mspace width="2.em"/><mspace width="1.em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi>w</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>&#x03b1;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_M0014.gif)
2.  for all ε > 0, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0015" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0015.gif"><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">lim</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi>&#x221e;</mi></mrow></munder><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi>w</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>&#x03f5;</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_M0015.gif)
3.  <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c08-disp-0016" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c08\_M0016.gif"><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">lim</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi>&#x221e;</mi></mrow></munder><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">max</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></munder><mi>w</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/c08_M0016.gif)

Theorem 8.3 implies universal consistency of the *k*\-nearest-neighbor classifier under certain conditions.

**Theorem 8.4 Universal Consistency of the *k*\-Nearest-Neighbor Classifier (Stone).** *The *k*\-nearest-neighbor classifier is universally consistent if, as *n* → ∞, *k* → ∞ and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0020.gif"><mrow><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0020.gif).*

Likelihood methods based on parametric models are consistent, provided that the model assumption is correct and a consistent estimator of the model parameters is used.

**Theorem 8.5 Consistency of Parametric Likelihood Classifiers with Plug-in Parameter Estimates.** *Let P(*Y* | *X*) = P(*Y* | *X*, θ) be a continuous function of a feature vector *X* and a parameter vector θ. If P(*Y* | *X*, θ) is a continuous function of *X* and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0021.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo></mfrac><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0021.gif), then the likelihood classifier constructed from <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0022.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0022.gif)is consistent.*

Some classifiers are known to be *not* universally consistent. For example, if *k* remains bounded away from ∞ or if <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0023.gif"><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></mfrac></math>![](images/c08_ILM0023.gif)remains bounded away from 0 as *n* → ∞ then the *k*\-nearest-neighbor classifier is not universally consistent (Devroye et al., 1996, Exercise 11.1). Random forests are also known to be not universally consistent, although there are bagged classifiers which are universally consistent Biau et al. (2008).

## 8.5 Convergence to Asymptopia Is Not Uniform and May Be Slow

The following two theorems should modulate any sense of euphoria caused by the preceding section. The first says that for every classification method and every data size, there is some joint distribution such that we are still arbitrarily far from Asymptopia. The second says that there is some joint distribution such that the approach to Asymptopia is arbitrarily slow.

**Theorem 8.6 Every Method Fails Badly on Some Easy Problem (Devroye).** *Under 0–1 loss, for any ε > 0, any integer *n* and any binary classification method, there is a joint distribution on (*X*, *Y*) with Bayes risk 0 such that the risk of the method satisfies <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0024.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03f5;</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0024.gif).*

**Theorem 8.7 Convergence to Bayes Risk Can Be Arbitrarily Slow (Devroye).** *Let <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c08\_ILM0025.gif"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>16</mn></mfrac><mo>&#x2265;</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#x2265;</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c08_ILM0025.gif)be any sequence of positive numbers converging to zero. Under 0–1 loss, for any sequence of binary classification methods applied to *n* training data, there is a joint distribution on (*X*, *Y*) with Bayes risk 0 such that the risk of the *n*th method satisfies R[*n*] > *a[n]*.*

Selecting a consistent classification method may not lead to a good classifier trained on limited data. [Figure 8.1](#c08.xhtml#figure8-1) shows QDA and LDA classifiers for a binary classification problem where QDA is the correct model (that is, the data of each class are drawn from a Gaussian, and the Gaussians have different covariance matrices). QDA is a consistent classifier in this case (Devroye et al., 1996, Theorem 16.1) and LDA is not, but LDA has the lower risk when the two are trained on fewer than 10,000 points. What is happening in [Figure 8.1](#c08.xhtml#figure8-1) is that QDA has higher variance and lower bias than LDA. The variance of QDA is reduced as the number of training data increase, but LDA wins the bias–variance trade-off for small data sizes.^([5](#c08.xhtml#c08-note-0005))

![Figure 8.1 The risk of QDA and LDA binary classifiers, as functions of the size of the training data. The data were generated by drawing data of class 1 from one 100-dimensional Gaussian distribution and the data of class 2 from another with different mean and covariance. QDA is consistent for this problem and LDA is not.](images/c08f001.jpg)

[**Figure 8.1**](#c08.xhtml#figureanchor8-1) The risk of QDA and LDA binary classifiers, as functions of the size of the training data. The data were generated by drawing data of class 1 from one 100-dimensional Gaussian distribution and the data of class 2 from another with different mean and covariance. QDA is consistent for this problem and LDA is not.

## Notes

# 9  
Clustering

> Do not assume that “clustering” methods are the best way to discover interesting groupings in the data; in our experience the visualization methods are often far more effective. There are many different clustering methods, often giving different answers, and so the danger of over-interpretation is high.
> 
> —W. N. Venables and B. D. Ripley, *Modern Applied Statistics with S-PLUS, Third Edition*, 2001

As described in [Chapter 2](#c02.xhtml), the goal of clustering is to learn an unknown, discrete-valued function *f* without observing its outputs. Since no observed outputs of *f* are available, no loss function which compares a predicted output to an observed output can be computed. As a result, clustering tends to be driven by algorithms and heuristics rather than by trying to minimize a meaningful measure of risk as is done in classification.

The clustering algorithms presented in this chapter naturally fall into two groups. Algorithms which are applicable when the observed data *x*[1], …, *x[n]* are in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0001.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c09_ILM0001.gif)(for example, Gaussian mixture models, *k*\-means, and mode-hunting in a density estimate) are presented first, and algorithms which are applicable more generally (for example, *k*\-medoids and hierarchical methods) are presented later. Some clustering algorithms partition the data *x*[1], …, *x[n]* into *k* distinct clusters—that is, they perform a *k-clustering* of the data—where *k* is a user-specified parameter of the algorithm. Other clustering algorithms perform *k*\-clusterings for a range of *k*’s, or for all *k* = 1, …, *n*. [Section 9.9](#c09.xhtml#c9_9) discusses methods for determining how many clusters are in a given dataset.

## 9.1 Gaussian Mixture Models

Suppose that the data *x*[1], …, *x[n]* are drawn from a Gaussian mixture model. That is, suppose the data are drawn from a distribution which has a density function P(*x*) of the form <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c09-disp-0001" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c09\_M0001.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>J</mi></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c09_M0001.gif)

where φ(*x* | μ, Σ) denotes a Gaussian density function with mean μ and covariance matrix Σ, *w*[1], …*w[J]* are non-negative weights with *w*[1] + ⋅⋅⋅ + *w[J]* = 1, and *J* > 0 is the number of clusters presumed to be in the data. Gaussian mixture models are discussed in [Section 4.4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_4_3) in the context of likelihood-based classifiers. Fitting Gaussian mixture models (that is, estimating parameters μ[1], …, μ[*J*], Σ[1], …, Σ[*J*], *w*[1], …, *w[J]* for a given value of *J*) is done by the expectation-maximization algorithm described in [Section 10.7](#c10.xhtml#c10_7). Methods for selecting such models (that is, selecting *J*) are described in several sections of [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml): see in particular the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) in [Section 7.7](#c07.xhtml#c7_7).

A fitted Gaussian mixture model provides a “soft” or “fuzzy” clustering rule, expressed in terms of the *responsibility* γ[*ij*] of mixture component *j* for datum *x[i]*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c09-disp-0002" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c09\_M0002.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03b3;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>J</mi></msubsup><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c09_M0002.gif)

The fitted means <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0002.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>J</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c09_ILM0002.gif)are the *cluster centers*. Two advantages of clustering with a Gaussian mixture model are that it provides a measure of certainty regarding which data points are assigned to clusters, and it is an interpretable, statistical model. A disadvantage is that the expectation-maximization algorithm tends to converge slowly, particularly when *m* is large and the covariance matrices Σ[*j*] are unconstrained. Using other distributions in place of the Gaussian distribution may be useful in some situations: for example, using Student’s *t* can provide robustness to outliers.

## 9.2 *k*\-Means

The *k-means algorithm* begins with an initial set of putative cluster centers, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0003.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c09_ILM0003.gif)(obtained, for example, by randomly sampling the data *x*[1], …, *x[n]* without replacement *k* times). The *k*\-means algorithm then iterates the two steps shown in [Figure 9.1](#c09.xhtml#figure9-1). The algorithm terminates when the cluster assignments do not change between iterations.

![Figure 9.1 The k-means clustering algorithm iterates two steps.](images/c09f001.jpg)

[**Figure 9.1**](#c09.xhtml#figureanchor9-1) The *k*\-means clustering algorithm iterates two steps.

The *k*\-means algorithm approximates fitting a Gaussian mixture model, giving up the flexibility of the mixture model (soft cluster assignment and variable covariance matrices) in exchange for speed. Step (1) shown in [Figure 9.1](#c09.xhtml#figure9-1) is an approximation of the expectation-step in the expectation-maximization algorithm, and step (2) is an approximation of the maximization-step (see [Section 10.7](#c10.xhtml#c10_7)). Geometrically, using the mean in step (2) implicitly ties the *k*\-means algorithm to (squared) Euclidean distance. This is because the sample mean of a set of data *S* in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0004.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c09_ILM0004.gif)is the point *z* which minimizes the sum of squared deviations between *z* and every point in *S*. Thus step (2) is equivalent to <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c09-disp-0003" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c09\_M0003.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi> argmin </mi><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>cluster</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>j</mi></mrow></munder><msup><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c09_M0003.gif)

## 9.3 Clustering by Mode-Hunting in a Density Estimate

Clustering data *x*[1], …, *x[n]* can be identified with the problem of finding modes (local maxima) in the density function P(*x*) of the unknown probability distribution on <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0005.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>![](images/c09_ILM0005.gif)from which the data were drawn (when taking this approach, the density function is assumed to exist). The density function P(*x*) can be estimated in a variety of ways, either through parametric methods, such as Gaussian mixture models, or non-parametric methods, such as kernel density estimation: a variety of methods are described in [Section 4.4](#c04.xhtml#c4_4) in the context of likelihood methods for classification. Modes in a density estimate <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0006.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c09_ILM0006.gif)can be found by applying a numerical optimization algorithm from many different starting points, and keeping track of the local maxima at which the algorithm terminates. An algorithm for clustering by mode-hunting in a density estimate is shown in [Figure 9.2](#c09.xhtml#figure9-2).

![Figure 9.2 A generic mode-hunting clustering algorithm.](images/c09f002.jpg)

[**Figure 9.2**](#c09.xhtml#figureanchor9-2) A generic mode-hunting clustering algorithm.

Clustering by mode-hunting can be sensitive to parameters of the optimization algorithm used, and it can also be expensive. Note that for the purpose of clustering, the propensity of an optimization algorithm to terminate in a local, rather than a global, optimum is a desirable feature: this affects the choice of optimizer and its parameters. Computational cost can be reduced by terminating the optimization algorithm early, combined with relaxing the criterion “distinct” in step (3).

## 9.4 Using Classifiers to Cluster

“If you can classify, you can cluster”—or so one hears, occasionally. One way to interpret this statement is the following trick for using a binary classifier to construct a density estimate, which can then be used for clustering as in [Section 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c9_3). Let data *x*[1], …, *x[n]* be given, and let this unlabeled data all be labeled as class 1. Our goal is to estimate the density function for the distribution from which the data were drawn: we write this density function as P(*x* | *Y* = 1).
