The trick is to synthesize data <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0007.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c09_ILM0007.gif), which will all be labeled class 2, by drawing it randomly from a probability distribution with *known* density function P(*x* | *Y* = 2). A binary classification algorithm is trained on the marked data <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c09-disp-0004" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c09\_M0004.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msup></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c09_M0004.gif)

to produce an estimate of the posterior distribution of each class,^([1](#c09.xhtml#c09-note-0001)) <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c09-disp-0005" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c09\_M0005.gif"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c09_M0005.gif)

which can be evaluated at any point <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0008.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c09_ILM0008.gif). Since <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c09-disp-0006" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c09\_M0006.gif"><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow></mstyle></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

<a href="#c09-disp-0006-1">(9.1)</a>![numbered Display Equation](images/c09_M0006.gif)

solving for P(*x* | *Y* = 1) yields <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c09-disp-0007" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c09\_M0007.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

The density for data of class 2 is known, the conditional probabilities of the class labels are estimated by the trained classifier, and the ratio of marginal probabilities of the class labels is <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0009.gif"><mfrac><msup><mi>n</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msup><mi>n</mi></mfrac></math>![](images/c09_ILM0009.gif)by construction. This produces the density estimate <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c09-disp-0008" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c09\_M0008.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfrac><msup><mi>n</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msup><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

## 9.5 Dissimilarity

Clustering requires an idea of something like distance between data. This often takes the form of a *dissimilarity measure*, which is a function <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0010.gif"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c09_ILM0010.gif)such that *d*(*x*, *x*) = 0 for all <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0011.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c09_ILM0011.gif)and *d*(*w*, *x*) = *d*(*x*, *w*) for all <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0012.gif"><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c09_ILM0012.gif). For a particular dataset, the *dissimilarity matrix* is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c09-disp-0009" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c09\_M0009.gif"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c09_M0009.gif)

an *n* × *n* symmetric matrix with zeros on the diagonal. Ideally the dissimilarity function will reflect something meaningful about the data, but it is often chosen for convenience. Common convenience choices of dissimilarity when <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0013.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c09_ILM0013.gif)are Euclidean and Manhattan distance on suitably scaled and transformed data—see Exercise 11.8.

Dissimilarity of data can be extended to dissimilarity of sets of data in a variety of ways. Three popular ways of measuring the dissimilarity of two subsets, *S*[1] and *S*[2], are: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c09-disp-0010" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c09\_M0010.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi mathvariant="italic">single</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">linkage</mi></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">min</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></munder><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi mathvariant="italic">complete</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">linkage</mi></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">max</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></munder><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi mathvariant="italic">average</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">linkage</mi></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>|</mo><mo>|</mo></mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></munder><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mstyle></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c09_M0010.gif)

Some clustering algorithms, such as the hierarchical algorithms in [Sections 9.7](#c09.xhtml#c9_7) and [9.8](#c09.xhtml#c9_8), make use of dissimilarity of clusters.

## 9.6 *k*\-Medoids

The *k-medoids algorithm* is a generalization of *k*\-means to an arbitrary dissimilarity function. It requires that the cluster centers be observed data. As in *k*\-means, the *k*\-medoids algorithm begins with an initial set of putative cluster centers, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0014.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c09_ILM0014.gif)(obtained, for example, by randomly sampling the data *x*[1], …, *x[n]* without replacement *k* times). It then iterates the two steps shown in [Figure 9.3](#c09.xhtml#figure9-3). The algorithm terminates when the cluster assignments do not change between iterations.

The cluster centers found in step (2) are the *medoids* of the clusters. Generally, clustering by *k*\-medoids is more expensive than clustering by *k*\-means because finding the argmin in step (2) is computationally more intensive than computing a sample mean.

![Figure 9.3 The k-medoids clustering algorithm iterates two steps.](images/c09f003.jpg)

[**Figure 9.3**](#c09.xhtml#figureanchor9-3) The *k*\-medoids clustering algorithm iterates two steps.

## 9.7 Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering

*Agglomerative hierarchical clustering* constructs a *k*\-clustering of the data for all *k* = 1, …, *n*. It produces a *hierarchical clustering* in the sense that, for any *k* < *k*′, every cluster in the *k*′-clustering is contained in a unique cluster in the *k*\-clustering. Agglomerative hierarchical clustering begins by considering all *n* data to be clusters of size one. It iteratively computes the dissimilarity of all pairs of clusters and merges two minimally dissimilar clusters, terminating when there is only one cluster, as shown in [Figure 9.4](#c09.xhtml#figure9-4).

![Figure 9.4 A generic agglomerative clustering algorithm.](images/c09f004.jpg)

[**Figure 9.4**](#c09.xhtml#figureanchor9-4) A generic agglomerative clustering algorithm.

It is sometimes useful to think of clustering algorithms in terms of graph algorithms. Suppose the dissimilarity function is bounded by some maximum value, which by re-scaling we can assume to be 1. Let the *similarity function s*(*w*, *x*) be defined by *s*(*w*, *x*) = 1 − *d*(*w*, *x*) and define the *similarity graph* of the data *x*[1], …, *x[n]* as follows: each datum is a vertex; an edge joins vertices *x[i]* and *x[j]* if and only if *s*(*x[i]*, *x[j]*) > 0; and an edge joining *x[i]* and *x[j]* has weight *s*(*x[i]*, *x[j]*). Thinking of data-clustering in terms of operations in the similarity graph can suggest computational methods which are very efficient when the graph is sparse, that is, when the number of edges, *e*, is much less than the maximum possible number of edges, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0015.gif"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></math>![](images/c09_ILM0015.gif). For example, most of the work in agglomerative hierarchical clustering, when using the single-linkage criterion to measure the dissimilarity between clusters, can be done by finding a minimal spanning tree of the similarity graph. Efficient algorithms^([2](#c09.xhtml#c09-note-0002)) can find a minimal spanning tree in *O*(*e*log (*e*)) time, which can be much less than the *O*(*n*²) time required by a naive approach to single-linkage agglomerative hierarchical clustering when the graph is sparse.

## 9.8 Divisive Hierarchical Clustering

Similar to agglomerative hierarchical clustering, *divisive hierarchical clustering* constructs a *k*\-clustering of the data for all *k* = 1, …, *n* such that, for any *k* < *k*′, every cluster in the *k*′-clustering is contained in a unique cluster in the *k*\-clustering. Divisive hierarchical clustering begins by considering all data to belong to a single cluster and then iteratively splits clusters until all clusters have size one. A specific divisive hierarchical clustering algorithm, the DIANA algorithm of Kaufman and Rousseeuw (1990), is shown in [Figure 9.5](#c09.xhtml#figure9-5).

![Figure 9.5 The DIANA divisive clustering algorithm.](images/c09f005.jpg)

[**Figure 9.5**](#c09.xhtml#figureanchor9-5) The DIANA divisive clustering algorithm.

## 9.9 How Many Clusters Are There? Interpretation of Clustering

Determination of how many clusters are “really” in a dataset is a statistical inference, so it should be addressed using statistical models for the data. One way to approach this is by fitting Gaussian mixture models with different numbers of mixture components and selecting a model with maximal probability in an appropriate sense, either using an asymptotic approximation such as selecting a model with maximal Bayesian Information Criterion as described in [Section 7.7](#c07.xhtml#c7_7), or using an explicit, fully Bayesian procedure and sampling from a posterior distribution on the number of clusters via reversible-jump Markov chain Monte Carlo (Green, 1995).^([3](#c09.xhtml#c09-note-0003))

An extension of a statistical inferential method to a heuristic applicable to clustering, due to Sugar and James (2003), estimates the number of clusters in data as follows. For *k* ∈ {*k*[1], *k*[1] + 1, …, *k*[2]}, the data *x*[1], …, *x[n]* are clustered with the *k*\-means algorithm and the *distortion* is computed, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c09-disp-0011" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c09\_M0011.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mrow><mi> center </mi><mi> of </mi><mi> cluster </mi><mi> which </mi><mi> contains </mi></mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c09_M0011.gif)

The Sugar–James estimate of the number of clusters in the data is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c09-disp-0012" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c09\_M0012.gif"><mrow><msub><mi> argmax </mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>{</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi><mi>c</mi></msubsup><mo>-</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>c</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c09_M0012.gif)

where *c* is a positive constant (Sugar and James (2003) recommend <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c09\_ILM0016.gif"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c09_ILM0016.gif)).

Selecting a reasonable clustering from among a hierarchical set of clusterings is a well studied problem: see Gan et al. (2007), Chapter 17 for a survey. One method, based on a non-parametric statistical test, is as follows. A clustering of the data *x*[1], …, *x[n]* partitions the set of all pairwise dissimilarities <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c09-disp-0013" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c09\_M0013.gif"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>:</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mn>1</mn><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c09_M0013.gif)

into two sets: dissimilarities between two items which are in the same cluster, and dissimilarities between two items which are in different clusters. Clusterings look meaningful to the (author’s) eye when the inter-cluster pairwise item dissimilarities are generally lower than the intra-cluster pairwise item dissimilarities.

The Mann–Whitney test (Conover, 1999, [Section 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c5_1)), also known as the Wilcoxon test, is a non-parametric statistical test of the null hypothesis that two sets of numbers are drawn from the same one-dimensional probability distribution.^([4](#c09.xhtml#c09-note-0004)) It is powerful against alternatives in which the distributions have different medians. One way to measure the quality of a clustering is the strength of evidence which the Mann–Whitney test statistic gives against the null hypothesis that the inter-cluster similarities and the intra-cluster similarities have the same distribution. More generally, a clustering of a set into *k* clusters partitions the set of pairwise item similarities into *k* + 1 sets: similarities between items in cluster 1, similarities between items in cluster 2, ..., similarities between items in cluster *k* and finally similarities between items which are in different clusters. The Kruskal–Wallis test^([5](#c09.xhtml#c09-note-0005)) (Conover, 1999, [Section 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c5_2)) is a generalization of the Mann–Whitney test to the case of more than two sets. It tests the null hypothesis that the *k* + 1 sets of pairwise item similarities have the same distribution, and it is powerful against alternatives in which some of the *k* + 1 distributions have different medians.

## 9.10 An Impossibility Theorem

Clustering is sometimes perceived as a “squishy” subject due to the lack of an explicit, rigorous statement of a goal (compared to predictive modeling, where the goal of risk-minimization is relatively clear). Clustering can be the subject of rigorous, general statements: we close with a remarkable theorem due to Kleinberg (2002).

Kleinberg defines three properties of clustering algorithms, all of which seem desirable:

*   *Scale-invariance*: The output of the algorithm does not change when the dissimilarity matrix is scaled by a positive constant;
*   *Richness*: Given any partition of *n* data points, there is some *n* × *n* dissimilarity matrix which will cause the algorithm to produce that partition;
*   *Consistency*: Given a clustering of data produced by the algorithm, decreasing the dissimilarity between points in the same cluster and increasing the dissimilarity between points in different clusters and running the algorithm again will *not* cause the clusters to change.

He then proves three theorems:

**Theorem 9.1 Kleinberg’s Impossibility Theorem.** *For *n* ⩾ 2, no clustering algorithm satisfies all three of these properties.*

**Theorem 9.2** *For any two of these three properties, a stopping condition (which Kleinberg explicitly states) can be defined for single-linkage agglomerative clustering so that the resulting algorithm satisfies the two properties.*

**Theorem 9.3** *A general class of centroid-based clustering algorithms, which includes both k-means and k-medoids and which trivially does not satisfy the richness property, also does not satisfy the consistency property.*

Critics have pointed out that Kleinberg’s consistency property is not necessarily desirable, as [Figure 9.6](#c09.xhtml#figure9-6) shows.

![Figure 9.6 A two-dimensional dataset is shown in the left-hand cell. The center cell shows a function applied to the dataset, with the property that the distance between any two points in the image of the dataset (shown in red) is less than the distance between the corresponding two points in the original dataset (shown in black). The image of the dataset is shown in the right-hand cell. The function has transformed data apparently in one cluster to data apparently in two clusters, but no clustering algorithm which can detect this change is consistent in Kleinberg’s sense.](images/c09f006.jpg)

[**Figure 9.6**](#c09.xhtml#figureanchor9-6) A two-dimensional dataset is shown in the left-hand cell. The center cell shows a function applied to the dataset, with the property that the distance between any two points in the image of the dataset (shown in red) is less than the distance between the corresponding two points in the original dataset (shown in black). The image of the dataset is shown in the right-hand cell. The function has transformed data apparently in one cluster to data apparently in two clusters, but no clustering algorithm which can detect this change is *consistent* in Kleinberg’s sense.

## Notes

# 10  
Optimization

> I envy you your self-confidence and assurance, but I mistrust exceedingly the soundness of your judgment.
> 
> —Alcon of Thrale in Edward E. Smith, *Second Stage Lensmen*, 1943

Many predictive modeling techniques of [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml), and clustering methods of [Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml), require that certain numerical optimization problems be solved (at least approximately). This chapter presents several classes of optimization techniques.

The problem of optimization is, given a known^([1](#c10.xhtml#c10-note-0001)) *objective function* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0005.gif"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0005.gif), find a *minimizer*^([2](#c10.xhtml#c10-note-0002))ω^⋆ of *g*, defined by <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0006.gif"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">min</mo><mrow><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0006.gif). The minimizer may be unique, or it may not. In some cases, the minimum value *g*(ω^⋆) is of interest, but in the context of [Chapters 3](#c03.xhtml),[4](#c04.xhtml),[6](#c06.xhtml), and [9](#c09.xhtml) we are usually more interested in the minimizer, ω^⋆.

All of the methods of this chapter are iterative: that is, they begin with an initial guess of the minimizer, ω¹, and for each iteration *t* = 1, 2, 3, …, they construct a new approximation ω^(*t* + 1). The new approximation may or may not be better than the previous one. Typically, the methods are run until some upper bound on iterations is reached, or convergence in both the domain and range of *g* is detected, for example by both <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0001" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0001.gif"><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">max</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></munder><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>-</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mrow><msubsup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced><mspace width="2.em"/><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="2.em"/><mspace width="1.em"/><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0001.gif)

falling below some preassigned thresholds. When the objective function is differentiable, there may also be a convergence criterion applied to a norm of the gradient, ∇*g*(ω^(*t*)): for example, to the maximum absolute value of any coordinate, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0002" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0002.gif"><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">max</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></munder><mfenced separators="" open="|" close="|"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mi>&#x2202;</mi><mrow><mi>&#x2202;</mi><msub><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mstyle></mfenced><msub><mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup></mrow></msub><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0002.gif)

The domain of *g* is a continuum in this chapter, but many of the methods presented here have discrete-domain analogues.

## 10.1 Quasi-Newton Methods

### 10.1.1 Newton’s Method for Finding Zeros

![Figure 10.1 The geometry of Newton’s method for finding zeros. From estimate ωt on the ω-axis, move vertically to the point (ωt, g(ωt)) on the curve (ω, g(ω)), then leave (ωt, g(ωt)) on the ray tangent to the curve and toward the real line. The point at which the ray hits the ω-axis is the new estimate ωt + 1.](images/c10f001.jpg)

[**Figure 10.1**](#c10.xhtml#figureanchor10-1) The geometry of Newton’s method for finding zeros. From estimate ω^(*t*) on the ω-axis, move vertically to the point (ω^(*t*), *g*(ω^(*t*))) on the curve (ω, *g*(ω)), then leave (ω^(*t*), *g*(ω^(*t*))) on the ray tangent to the curve and toward the real line. The point at which the ray hits the ω-axis is the new estimate ω^(*t* + 1).

We begin with Newton’s method for approximately finding zeros of a differentiable function <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0007.gif"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0007.gif). The goal is to find an <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0008.gif"><mrow><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi></msup><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0008.gif)such that *g*(ω^⋆) = 0, starting from an initial and presumably incorrect guess ω¹ of such a point. From a current estimate, ω^(*t*), Newton’s method produces a new estimate, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0003" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0003.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mo>&#x0027;</mo></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0003.gif)

The geometric motivation for updating the estimate this way is shown in [Figure 10.1](#c10.xhtml#figure10-1).

Newton’s method does not always converge. Depending on the function *g* and the starting point ω[1], it may diverge to ± ∞ or get stuck revisiting a finite set of points over and over in an infinite cycle.

### 10.1.2 Newton’s Method for Optimization

Newton’s method for optimizing a differentiable function *g* is to find a zero of the gradient of *g*. Let ∇*g* denote the gradient of *g* and let H*g* denote the Hessian of *g*, and let a starting point <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0009.gif"><mrow><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0009.gif)be given. From a current estimate, ω^(*t*), Newton’s method produces a new estimate, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0004" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0004.gif"><mrow><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03c1;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x2207;</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0004.gif)

where ρ ∈ (0, 1\] is a parameter (called the *learning rate*) which can be used to limit the step size.

Computation of the inverse Hessian, (H*g*(ω^(*t*)))^(− 1), can be expensive and can also be numerically unstable. Furthermore, away from a local minimum of *g* the Hessian H*g*(ω^(*t*)) may not be positive definite, which means that there may be no point on the ray leaving ω^(*t*) in the direction of − (H*g*(ω^(*t*)))^(− 1) ∇*g*(ω^(*t*)) which has a value of *g* as small as *g*(ω^(*t*)). Heuristically, it is faster to perform more iterations of an approximate version of Newton’s algorithm. Such methods are called *quasi-Newton methods*.

**Exercise 10.1** *A matrix *M* is a *positive definite matrix* if *M* is symmetric and *x*^T*Mx* > 0 for all <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0010.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0010.gif), *x* ≠ 0. Show that if *M* is positive definite and ∇*g*(ω^(*t*)) ≠ 0, then taking a sufficiently small step from ω^(*t*) in the direction of − *M*^(− 1) ∇*g*(ω^(*t*)) results in a reduction of the value of *g*. ***Hints:*** (1) a sufficiently small step from ω^(*t*) in the direction of a vector *v* results in a reduction of the value of *g* if and only if the directional derivative of *g* at ω^(*t*) in the direction of *v*, ∇*g*(ω^(*t*)) · *v*, is negative; (2) all positive definite matrices are invertible, and the inverse of a positive definite matrix is positive definite.*

### 10.1.3 Gradient Descent

The *gradient descent* algorithm is the result of approximating the Hessian H*g*(*x*) in Newton’s method by the *m* × *m* identity matrix, so the update rule is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0005" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0005.gif"><mrow><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03c1;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x2207;</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0005.gif)

Gradient descent tends to be slow to converge when the starting point ω¹ is not near a zero of the gradient ∇*g* and when it encounters regions in the domain of *g* where ‖∇*g*‖ is small but no zero of ∇*g* is nearby. Gradient descent (in its stochastic form— see [Section 10.6.2](#c10.xhtml#c10_6_2)) seems to be the *de facto* standard algorithm for training neural networks.

### 10.1.4 The BFGS Algorithm

The *Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) algorithm* keeps a running approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0011.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0011.gif)of (H*g*(ω^(*t*)))^(− 1), the inverse Hessian of *g* at ω^(*t*). The initial value, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0012.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0012.gif), is the *m* × *m* identity matrix. At each iteration, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0013.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0013.gif)is updated by addition of three rank-1 matrices.^([3](#c10.xhtml#c10-note-0003)) Specifically, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0006" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0006.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>u</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></mrow><mi>t</mi></mfrac><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>w</mi><mi>w</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></mrow><mi>s</mi></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>s</mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></mfrac><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mi>w</mi><mi>s</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></mfrac><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mi>w</mi><mi>s</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0006.gif)

where vectors *u*, *v*, and *w*, and scalars *s* and *t* are defined by <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0007" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0007.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi>u</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>-</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup></mrow></mtd><mtd><mi>s</mi></mtd><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd><mrow><mi>v</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>v</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup><mi>v</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi>v</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>&#x2207;</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x2207;</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd><mi>t</mi></mtd><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd><mrow><mi>u</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi>v</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi>w</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup><mi>v</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0007.gif)

Instead of moving ρ units in the direction of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0016.gif"><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup><mi>&#x2207;</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0016.gif), the BFGS algorithm performs a one-dimensional numerical minimization of *g* on the ray leaving ω^(*t*) in the direction of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0017.gif"><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup><mi>&#x2207;</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0017.gif). Furthermore, the update formula for <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0018.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0018.gif)is such that <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0019.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0019.gif)always remains positive definite,^([4](#c10.xhtml#c10-note-0004)) so unless the algorithm has converged there is always a point on this ray with a lower value of *g* than ω^(*t*).

BFGS is sometimes used for maximum-likelihood estimation (as in logistic regression in [Section 4.6](#c04.xhtml#c4_6), for example). Upon convergence, it is tempting to use the last BFGS estimate of the inverse Hessian, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0021.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0021.gif), to construct Gaussian confidence intervals for the true parameters, but BFGS may converge to an approximate local minimum *without* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0022.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0022.gif)converging to a good estimate of the inverse Hessian evaluated at that minimum.

### 10.1.5 Modifications to Quasi-Newton Methods

Quasi-Newton methods are widely used, and through experimentation some modifications have been found to be generally useful. One of these modifications is to add *momentum*, which in gradient descent changes the update rule to <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0008" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0008.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03c1;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>t</mi></munderover><msup><mi>&#x03b7;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x2207;</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>s</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0008.gif)

where η ∈ \[0, 1\] is the *momentum parameter*. This is implemented by initializing a *momentum term* ν¹ = 0 and iteratively updating <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0009" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0009.gif"><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msup><mi>&#x03bd;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mtd><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>&#x03b7;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mi>&#x03bd;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#x2207;</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mtd><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><msup><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03c1;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mi>&#x03bd;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

<span class="equationNumber"><a href="#c10-disp-0009-1">(10.1)</a></span>![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0009.gif)

A second modification is to use an *adaptive learning rate*, that is, to allow parameter ρ = ρ[*i*] to change over time. One way to do this in gradient descent is the *bold driver* method,^([5](#c10.xhtml#c10-note-0005)) which uses the update rule

![](images/c10uf001.jpg)

Here, *c*[1] and *c*[2] are *adaptation parameters*, with *c*[1] > 1 and *c*[2] < 1. Typically *c*[1] ∈ \[1.01, 1.10\] and *c*[2] ≈ 0.5.

A third modification will be seen in [Section 10.6.2](#c10.xhtml#c10_6_2).

### 10.1.6 Gradients for Logistic Regression and Neural Networks

The cost of computing the gradient ∇*g* of the objective function *g* can depend on multiple factors, such as dimension of the input space (<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0023.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0023.gif), in this chapter), and whether computation of *g* involves accumulation of some quantity over a set of observed data. This is illustrated in the next two exercises by cases which arise when fitting a logistic regression model or single-hidden-layer neural network described in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml), where the objective function is the training estimate of risk with respect to cross-entropy loss.
