## 10.2 The Nelder–Mead Algorithm

The *Nelder–Mead algorithm* is useful for optimizing functions which are not differentiable (or where the derivative is too expensive or troublesome to compute).^([6](#c10.xhtml#c10-note-0006)) It begins with the *m* + 1 vertices of a simplex in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0027.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0027.gif), with function *g* evaluated at each vertex.^([7](#c10.xhtml#c10-note-0007))

Each iteration of the algorithm is as illustrated in [Figure 10.2](#c10.xhtml#figure10-2). Moving along the ray from *A* to the midpoint of the opposite simplex facet can be interpreted as an approximation, given the available information, of a move in the direction of steepest descent.

The Nelder–Mead algorithm is sometimes called the “amoeba method” because the simplex oozes around <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0030.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0030.gif), adapting its shape and size to the contours of the surface defined by *g*. Convergence is declared when <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0031.gif"><mfrac><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>-</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>|</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>|</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>|</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>|</mo></mrow></mfrac></math>![](images/c10_ILM0031.gif)falls below a given threshold.

![Figure 10.2 The points evaluated and the operations performed on a simplex by one iteration of the Nelder–Mead algorithm.](images/c10f002.jpg)

[**Figure 10.2**](#c10.xhtml#figureanchor10-2) The points evaluated and the operations performed on a simplex by one iteration of the Nelder–Mead algorithm.

## 10.3 Simulated Annealing

*Simulated annealing* is a random search strategy. Given the current state, ω^(*t*), a new point *w* is drawn randomly from some probability distribution P, called the *proposal distribution*, which is part of the definition of the algorithm and usually depends on the current state. The decision whether to accept the proposed point *w* as the new state ω^(*t* + 1) is also made randomly: the probability depends on *g*(*w*), *g*(ω^(*t*)) and a positive parameter *T*, the *annealing temperature*, which decreases as the algorithm proceeds. Specifically, one step of a simulated annealing algorithm is

![](images/c10uf002.jpg)

Usually, *T* is reduced by multiplication by a constant close to but less than one (for example, 0.999) at each step.

Note that if *g*(*w*) ⩽ *g*(ω^(*t*)) then the proposed move is always accepted, meaning ω^(*t* + 1) = *w*. If, on the other hand, *g*(*w*) > *g*(ω^(*t*)) then the proposed move from ω^(*t*) to *w* is accepted with some positive probability, which depends on how much worse *g*(*w*) is than *g*(ω^(*t*)). As the annealing temperature *T* > 0 decreases, the probability of accepting any given proposal *w* with *g*(*w*) > *g*(ω^(*t*)) decreases. Toward the beginning, simulated annealing is willing to move from a “good” point to a “bad” one, while later on it is reluctant to move to a “bad” point, essentially becoming a greedy random search. This makes simulated annealing a good search strategy when *g* has many local minima.

## 10.4 Genetic Algorithms

In a *genetic algorithm*, a point ω in the domain of *g* is called a *gene*. The algorithm acts iteratively on a set of genes, known as the *population*. Each gene ω has a property called *fitness*, which is a non-negative number that increases as *g*(ω) decreases: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0026" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0026.gif"><mrow><mi> fitness </mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0026.gif)

is a typical example. The algorithm requires two randomized functions: a *crossover map C* which takes a pair of genes and returns a new gene, and a *mutation map M* which takes a single gene and returns a new gene.

At the *t*th iteration, the current population *S^t* is used to produce a new population *S*^(*t* + 1) as follows:

![](images/c10uf003.jpg)

Typically, the population size remains constant from one iteration (also known as a *generation*) to the next.

In some genetic algorithms, *S*^(*t* + 1) may include unmutated crossovers of genes in *S^t* and *S*^(*t* + 1) may include mutations of single genes drawn from *S^t*. Also, *S*^(*t* + 1) may include genes directly copied from *S^t*, for example, by replacing *S*^(*t* + 1) with the fittest elements of *S^t*∪*S*^(*t* + 1).

The mutation map *M* is similar to a simulated annealing proposal distribution: given a gene ω, it draws a random gene from some distribution, typically with probability mass centered at ω in some sense. The defining characteristic of a genetic algorithm is the crossover map *C*, which creates a new gene by combining parts of the two other genes. For example, when the domain of *g* is <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0032.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0032.gif), a crossover map applied to genes *u* and *v* could be defined as *C*(*u*, *v*) = (*w*[1], …, *w[m]*), where each *w[i]* is an independent, uniform random draw from the set {*u[i]*, *v[i]*}.

Genetic algorithms are most useful for minimizing functions which have a known (or suspected) structural relationship among the inputs which can be exploited by a well chosen crossover map. To give an unrealistically simple example, suppose the domain of *g* is <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0033.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>6</mn></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0033.gif)and <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0028" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0027.gif"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">max</mo><mo>(</mo><mo>|</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo>|</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>|</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>|</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>|</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mrow><mo>|</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mrow><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">max</mo><mo>(</mo><mo>|</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mrow><mo>|</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>|</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mrow><mo>|</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>|</mo></mrow><msub><mi>&#x03c9;</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mrow><mo>|</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0027.gif)

Here, if *g* is small then the first three coordinates or the last three coordinates are all small. A crossover map which exploits this property to propose new members of the population with potentially small values of *g* is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0029" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0028.gif"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>a</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>fair</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>coin</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>toss</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>comes</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>up</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>\`\`heads""</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mi> otherwise </mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0028.gif)

## 10.5 Particle Swarm Optimization

*Particle swarm optimization algorithms* are an outgrowth proposed in Kennedy and Eberhart (1995) of computer models for simulating the behavior of bird flocks, fish schools, and other group behavior. A *particle swarm* is a set of objects, each of which has the following properties:

1.  a *position p*, point in the domain of *g*;
2.  a *velocity v*, a vector in the domain of *g*;
3.  a *personal best point*, the minimizer of *g* among all positions which the particle has occupied in the past;
4.  the *global best point*, the minimizer of *g* among all positions which *any* particle has occupied in the past.

Particles’ positions and velocities are initialized randomly (often in such a way that they are well dispersed in the domain of *g*).

At each iteration, each particle in the swarm is updated according to the rules: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0030" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0029.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi> new </mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi> current </mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi> current </mi></msub></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0029.gif)

and <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0031" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0030.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi> new </mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi> current </mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mtext>personal</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>best</mtext></mrow><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi> current </mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mtext>global</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>best</mtext></mrow><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi> current </mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0030.gif)

In the velocity update formula, *k*, *c*[1] and *c*[2] are universal positive constants and *U*[1] and *U*[2] are draws from a Uniform (0, 1) distribution (drawn independently for each particle at each iteration). Particles’ personal best points and the global best point are updated at each iteration.

The purpose of constants *k*, *c*[1] and *c*[2] are to control how “attracted” each particle is to its own personal best point and to the global best point. Constants *c*[1] and *c*[2] are respectively called the *cognitive parameter* and the *social parameter*, and constant *k* is the *constriction rate*. Based on simulation studies, Carlisle and Dozier (2000) recommend *c*[1] = 2.8, *c*[2] = 1.3, and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0034.gif"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mrow><mrow><mo>|</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>-</mo></mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>-</mo><msqrt><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>-</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt><mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#x2248;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>7298</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0034.gif).

There are many variations of particle swarm optimizers. One common variation imposes a neighborhood structure on the particles, replacing the “global best” with a “neighborhood best.” This means that information about the global best point found so far propagates slowly through the swarm, as it is passed from neighbor to neighbor in each iteration, which has the effect of making the swarm less aggressive and more robust. Other variations include multiple swarms which avoid each other and multiple types of particles in a swarm (“settlers” which refine estimates of local minima and “explorers” which search for new local minima). How to identify when a particle swarm has converged is an open question.

## 10.6 General Remarks on Optimization

### 10.6.1 Imperfectly Known Objective Functions

In machine learning it is usually the case that the objective function *g* we truly wish to optimize is not computable, and therefore we are reduced to optimizing an approximation or estimate, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0035.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c10_ILM0035.gif), of the ideal objective function *g*. Uncertainty in the estimate <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0036.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c10_ILM0036.gif)of *g* can lead to a new halting criterion for iterative optimization algorithms: *halt if the algorithm can’t tell whether it is really improving.*

Let a training dataset be given, let a classification method be specified, and let θ be a vector of both model parameters and tuning parameters which control the method’s behavior: in classification trees, for example, θ could include the cost-complexity parameter, while in a neural network θ could encode the number of hidden layers and the number of neurons in each hidden layer as well as the parameters of the neurons.^([8](#c10.xhtml#c10-note-0008)) Training the classifier defines a function <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0037.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x21a6;</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0037.gif), and the optimal value of θ is that which minimizes the risk of the trained classifier. That is, the objective function *g* is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0032" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0031.gif"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0031.gif)

The true risk of the trained classifier is not computable (because it depends on the unknown probability distribution P(*X*, *Y*)), so an estimate must be used instead. For example, if a validation dataset is available (see [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml)), parameter θ can be sought to minimize the validation estimate of risk. This provides a surrogate objective function <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0038.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c10_ILM0038.gif), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0033" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0032.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0032.gif)

The surrogate objective function <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0039.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c10_ILM0039.gif)is derived from data, and hence is random with mean and variance (and variance estimators) as described in [Section 7.2.2](#c07.xhtml#c7_2_2).

**Exercise 10.4** *Assume that the number <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0040.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></math>![](images/c10_ILM0040.gif)of validation data is large enough that <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0041.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> valid </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0041.gif), can be thought of as normal-distributed with negligible error for any value of θ under consideration. Describe a halting criterion for an iterative optimization algorithm θ[1], θ[2], … based on a level-α statistical test of the null hypothesis that *g*(θ[*i* + 1]) ⩾ *g*(θ[*i*]) using the validation estimate <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0042.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c10_ILM0042.gif)for *g*. If a maximum number *I* of iterations is fixed in advance, explain how Bonferroni correction, described in [Chapter 12](#c12.xhtml), can be used so that the probability of any false rejection of the null is bounded by α. **Hint:** See part (C) of Exercise 7.5 for the test, and see Exercise 12.7 for the development of Bonferroni’s method.*

### 10.6.2 Objective Functions Which Are Sums

In some cases, the objective function *g* to be optimized (or a surrogate, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0043.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c10_ILM0043.gif)) is naturally expressed as a sum. For example, some classifiers are trained by explicitly minimizing a training or validation estimate of risk, in which case <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0034" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0033.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0033.gif)

or <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0035" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0034.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0034.gif)

Some classifiers are trained by maximizing a log-likelihood function^([9](#c10.xhtml#c10-note-0009)) for independent data, in which case <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0036" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0035.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo>-</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0035.gif)

Ignoring the distinction between whether the objective function is the ideal one or a surrogate, in both of the above cases the objective function is a sum over data, with the *i*th summand depending only on the parameter θ and the *i*th datum. The same is also true of the gradient, thus: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0037" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0036.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="2.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="2.em"/><mi>&#x2207;</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi>&#x2207;</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0036.gif)

When the number of data *n* is large, *g* and ∇*g* can be expensive to compute, and even more so if the number of parameters *k* is large. One response to this situation, when using quasi-Newton optimization methods, is to approximate ∇*g* by computing it only on a random sample of the data, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0038" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0037.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mi>&#x2207;</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2248;</mo><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></munder><mi>&#x2207;</mi><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0037.gif)

where *S* is a small sample drawn randomly from {1, …, *n*}. In the most extreme case, the random sample is a single data point: *stochastic gradient descent* is the gradient descent algorithm with ∇*g*(θ) approximated by ∇*g*(*x[i]*, *y[i]*, θ) computed for a single point (*x[i]*, *y[i]*), which is drawn uniformly at random from the data at each iteration of the algorithm.^([10](#c10.xhtml#c10-note-0010))

### 10.6.3 Optimization from Multiple Starting Points

Heuristically, it is good practice to start optimization algorithms from multiple points. Indeed for a given total amount of work, many applications of a simple optimization algorithm from different starting points may (in the aggregate) find a better optimum than a sophisticated algorithm starting from only one point. Some algorithms incorporate this heuristic explicitly: there are particle swarms with “explorer” and “settler” particles, and genetic algorithms with the population divided into “islands” which interbreed only when a fluctuating “sea level” is sufficiently low.

It is also good practice, when an optimization algorithm converges to an approximate minimizer *ω*\*, to restart the algorithm at *ω*\*. Either the algorithm does not find a better minimizer than *ω*\*, in which case it typically declares convergence at *ω*\* after little work, relative to the work performed to find *ω*\* in the first place; or it does find a better minimizer than *ω*\*.

## 10.7 The Expectation-Maximization Algorithm

### 10.7.1 The General Algorithm

In some applications, important data are missing. One example of this, which we shall examine in detail, is the fitting of a Gaussian mixture model when the available data are points <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0044.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0044.gif)*without* any accompanying information about which points were drawn from which mixture component of the distribution. In this section we will denote observed (or observable) data by *X*, and unobserved (or hidden, or latent) data by *Z*.

Let a statistical model be given for observable data *X* and hidden data *Z*, parametrized by θ. The likelihood is P(*X*, *Z* | θ), and a maximum likelihood estimate <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0045.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c10_ILM0045.gif)for θ is desired. Ideally, this would be obtained by marginalizing out—that is, averaging over—the distribution of the hidden data *Z* (which presumably depends on θ), selecting a value of θ which maximizes the marginal distribution of the observed data, P(*X* | θ): <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0039" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0038.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msub><mi> argmax </mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi> argmax </mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>&#x222b;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

<a href="#c10-disp-0039-8"></a>(10.1)![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0038.gif)

In the language of optimization, we seek θ to minimize the objective function *g*(θ) = −P(*x*[1], …, *x[n]* | θ) for some observed data *x*[1], …, *x[n]*. The integral in (10.1) is often too hard to deal with, leading to an objective function which is not computable.

In response to this situation, Dempster et al. (1977) developed the *expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm*, an iterative algorithm for approximating <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0046.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c10_ILM0046.gif). Given observed data *x*[1], …, *x[n]* and an initial value <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0047.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0047.gif), the EM algorithm repeats the following two steps until convergence is declared:

![](images/c10uf004.jpg)

The expectation step looks daunting, but it really involves computing parameters which describe a state of knowledge or belief at the *t*th iteration about the hidden data *Z*.

### 10.7.2 EM Climbs the Marginal Likelihood of the Observations

It is remarkable (so we make this remark) that at any iteration of the EM algorithm, the marginal likelihood of the observed data satisfies <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0040" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0039.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0039.gif)

The reason for this is as follows. For any value of θ, *x*, and *z*, the joint density for the observed and unobserved data can be factored as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0041" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0040.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0040.gif)

Taking logs, this becomes <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0042" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0041.gif"><mrow><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>-</mo><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

<a href="#c10-disp-0042-9"></a>(10.2)![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0041.gif)

Since equation (10.2) holds for all values *z* of the hidden variables, both sides can be integrated with respect to *any* distribution on the hidden variables and still have equality. In particular, we can pick some value <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0048.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></math>![](images/c10_ILM0048.gif)of θ and integrate both sides of (10.2) with respect to the distribution it induces on the hidden data, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0049.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0049.gif). This yields <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0043" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0042.gif"><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mspace mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

<a href="#c10-disp-0043-10"></a>(10.3)![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0042.gif)

Consider the second term on the right-hand side of (10.3). The following sequence of exercises shows that, as a function of θ, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0044" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0043.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

<a href="#c10-disp-0044-11"></a>(10.4)![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0043.gif)

is maximal when <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0050.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0050.gif).

**Exercise 10.5 Jensen’s Inequality.** *A function <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0051.gif"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0051.gif)is a *concave function* if for any <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0052.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0052.gif)and any *t* ∈ \[0, 1\], *g*(*tx* + (1 − *t*)*y*) ⩾ *tg*(*x*) + (1 − *t*)*g*(*y*), and is a *strictly concave function* if *g*(*tx* + (1 − *t*)*y*) > *tg*(*x*) + (1 − *t*)*g*(*y*). Equivalently, *g* is concave if, at each point *x*, there is a line through the point (*x*, *g*(*x*)) such that the curve parametrized by (*y*, *g*(*y*)) is always on or below the line. This is called a *supporting line* of the curve at *x*. Put this way, *g* is strictly concave if, at each point *x*, there is a line through the point (*x*, *g*(*x*)) such that the curve parametrized by (*y*, *g*(*y*)) is below the line, touching the line only at the point (*x*, *g*(*x*)). These definitions are illustrated in [Figure 10.3](#c10.xhtml#figure10-3). Show that for a real random variable *X*, and a concave function *g*,* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0045" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0044.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mo>\[</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>\]</mo><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mo>\[</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>\]</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0044.gif)

Show that if *g* is strictly concave, then E\[*g*(*X*)\] = *g*(E\[*X*\]) if and only if P(*X* = *c*) = 1 for some constant *c*. **Hint:** Let α = E\[*X*\], consider a line with equation *g*(α) + *s*(*y* − α) which lies above the curve (*y*, *g*(*y*)), and integrate both sides of an inequality.

![Figure 10.3 A concave function (left) and a strictly concave function (right). For each curve, a dashed supporting line is shown at a point (x, g(x)). For the strictly concave function, the supporting line intersects the curve at only this point, while for the concave function, the line may intersect the curve elsewhere (shown in bold).](images/c10f003.jpg)

[**Figure 10.3**](#c10.xhtml#figureanchor10-3) A concave function (left) and a strictly concave function (right). For each curve, a dashed supporting line is shown at a point (*x*, *g*(*x*)). For the strictly concave function, the supporting line intersects the curve at only this point, while for the concave function, the line may intersect the curve elsewhere (shown in bold).

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0045.gif)

*with equality if and only if P(*P*[0](*X*) = *P*[1](*X*)) = 1. **Hint:** Use Jensen’s inequality, the fact that log is strictly concave on the positive real line, and the fact that densities integrate to 1.*

If θ and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0054.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></math>![](images/c10_ILM0054.gif)are any two values such that <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0048" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0047.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2264;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

<a href="#c10-disp-0048-13"></a>(10.6)![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0047.gif)

(for example, if θ is a maximizer of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0055.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0055.gif)), then inserting (10.5) and (10.6) into (10.3) makes the positive term no smaller (generally bigger) and the negative no bigger (generally smaller), yielding <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0049" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0048.gif"><mrow><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0048.gif)

In actual implementation, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0056.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0056.gif)and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0057.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0057.gif)is set to the maximizer of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0058.gif"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0058.gif).

Thus the EM algorithm results in a sequence of parameter estimates <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0059.gif"><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0059.gif)for which <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0060.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c10_ILM0060.gif)is non-decreasing (and in fact is increasing unless equality holds in both (10.4) and (10.6)). Furthermore, we need not actually maximize the expected log-likelihood in step (2) of EM (the M-step): it is sufficient to merely find a new parameter <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0061.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0061.gif)which produces a greater expected log-likelihood than the current parameter, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0062.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0062.gif). Algorithms which improve but do not maximize the log-likelihood in step (2) are called *generalized EM algorithms*.

### 10.7.3 Example—Fitting a Gaussian Mixture Model Via EM

The EM algorithm is illustrated by providing technical details omitted in [Section 4.4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_4_3) and [Section 9.2](#c09.xhtml#c9_2). Let *x*[1], …, *x[n]* be independent draws from a Gaussian mixture with *J* components. For each *i*, the density at *x[i]* is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0050" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0049.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>J</mi></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0049.gif)

where φ(*x* | μ, Σ) denotes a Gaussian density function with mean μ and covariance matrix Σ, *w*[1], …, *w[J]* are non-negative weights which sum to 1 and <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0051" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0050.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>J</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mi>J</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mi>J</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0050.gif)

is a shorthand for all of the parameters. For *i* = 1, …, *n*, define *z[i]* ∈ {1, …, *J*} to be the label of the mixture component from which *x[i]* was drawn. One can think of the data as generated this way:

![](images/c10uf005.jpg)

If *z*[1], …, *z[n]* are known then it is easy to compute the maximum likelihood estimate of θ. The log-likelihood can be written as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" stretchy="true">(</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace stretchy="true">)</mo><mo stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mstyle></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd columnalign="left"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" form="prefix">log</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace and each term in the right-hand sum over *j* can be maximized separately.

**Exercise 10.8** *Show that the maximum likelihood estimates of the parameters are:*

<displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0053" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0052.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>|</mo><mo>{</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>}</mo><mo>|</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="2.em"/><mspace width="2.em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>|</mo><mo>{</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>}</mo><mo>|</mo></mrow></mfrac><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0052.gif)

*and*

<displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0054" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0053.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>|</mo><mo>{</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>}</mo><mo>|</mo></mrow></mfrac><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0053.gif)

***Hint:** Don’t forget to put in a Lagrange multiplier term to capture the constraint *w*[1] + ⋅⋅⋅ + *w[J]* = 1.*

*If *z*[1], …, *z[n]* are unknown, an approximate maximizer of the marginal log-likelihood,* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0055" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0054.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>J</mi></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mstyle></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c10_M0054.gif)

*can be found by the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm.*

### 10.7.4 Example—The Expectation Step

Theoretically, the point of the expectation step is to obtain the expected value of the joint log-likelihood of *X* and *Z* with respect to the distribution on *Z*[1], …, *Z[n]* induced by the current estimate <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0063.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0063.gif)for θ. Specifically, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0056" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0055.gif"><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd/><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><msub><mi Probability γ^(*t*)[*ij*] is called the *responsibility* of mixture component *j* for data *x[i]* at iteration *t*, and it expresses “what is known so far” about the hidden states *Z*[1], …, *Z[n]*. The responsibilities can be computed using Bayes’ theorem, since <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c10-disp-0058" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c10\_M0057.gif"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#x03b3;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>&#x221d;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>j</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

From a computational or algorithmic point of view, the purpose of the expectation step is to compute all of the γ^(*t*)[*ij*]’s from <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0067.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0067.gif), while the purpose of the maximization step is to compute <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c10\_ILM0068.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![](images/c10_ILM0068.gif)from the γ^(*t*)[*ij*]’s.

## Notes

1.  of all distributions on *S* = ( − ∞, ∞) with mean μ and variance σ², the Gaussian distribution has maximum entropy;
2.  of all distributions on *S* = (0, ∞) with mean μ, the exponential distribution has maximum entropy;
3.  of all distributions on *S* = \[*a*, *b*\], the uniform distribution has maximum entropy;
4.  of all distributions on *S* = {1, 2, 3, …} with mean μ, the geometric distribution has maximum entropy.

# 11  
High-Dimensional Data

> By lumping all these choices together, we “reduce” the problem to a classical problem of determining the maximum of a given function. ...
> 
> There are, however, some details to consider. In the first place, the effective analytic solution of a large number of even simple equations as, for example, linear equations, is a difficult affair. Lowering our sights, even a computational solution usually has a number of difficulties of both gross and subtle nature. Consequently, the determination of this maximum is quite definitely not routine when the number of variables is large.
> 
> All this may be subsumed under the heading “the curse of dimensionality.” Since this is a curse which has hung over the head of the physicist and astronomer for many a year, there is no need to feel discouraged about the possibility of obtaining significant results despite it.
> 
> —Richard E. Bellman, *Dynamic Programming,* 1957

Although it was originally defined in the context of numerical equation-solving and optimization (in the quote above), the *curse of dimensionality* now serves as a catch-all term describing difficulties which arise when the number of features, *m*, is large. This chapter focuses on a major source of difficulty for the design and application of machine learning algorithms: the fact that high-dimensional Euclidean space has properties which conflict with intuition obtained from two- and three-dimensional Euclidean space. In particular, three-dimensional intuition about the set of points approximately a given distance away from a given point can be quite misleading because of the changing relationship between distance and volume as the dimension of Euclidean space increases.

Approaches to dealing with the curse of dimensionality fall roughly into two categories. First, there is searching for explicit or implicit mappings of a high-dimensional feature space into a lower dimensional space such that useful information for solving a given learning problem is preserved. Methods for this approach may be as simple as linear projection, or as complex as deep autoencoders. Second, there are methods which view high-dimensional data as a bias–variance problem, and introduce bias into estimates of model parameters (typically by forcing them to be smaller in absolute value than they would be otherwise) in order to reduce variance and produce a lower-risk approximation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0001.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c11_ILM0001.gif). Such methods, encountered in specific instances in [Chapters 3](#c03.xhtml) and [4](#c04.xhtml), are discussed in more detail and generality in this chapter.

## 11.1 The Curse of Dimensionality

This section illustrates the curse of dimensionality with some examples, leaving theoretical results to the exercises. A *ball* in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0002.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0002.gif)is the set of points no more than some given distance from a given point, that is, a ball is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0001" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0001.gif"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>:</mo><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0001.gif)

for some center <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0003.gif"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0003.gif)and positive radius *r*. For future reference, volume and surface area of an *m*\-dimensional ball of radius *r* are respectively <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0002" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0002.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>&#x03c0;</mi><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>&#x0393;</mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="1.em"/><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>&#x03c0;</mi><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mi>m</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>&#x0393;</mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mfenced></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mi>&#x03c0;</mi><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>&#x0393;</mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0002.gif)

where Γ(*z*) = ∫^∞[0]*t*^(*z* − 1)*e*^(− *t*) *dt* is the gamma function, the usual generalization of factorial: Γ(*z* + 1) = *z*! for integer *z* ⩾ 0. For our purposes, there is nothing special about a sphere: it is merely an analytically tractable stand-in for an *m*\-dimensional “blob” in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0004.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0004.gif).

Consider a *spherical shell S* consisting of all points in a ball which are within a given distance δ < 1 from the boundary (equivalently, *S* is a unit ball with a concentric radius-(1 − δ) ball removed): <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0003" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0003.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi>S</mi></mtd><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>:</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03b4;</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>}</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd><mo>=</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mo>{</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mrow><mo>:</mo><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>}</mo><mo>&#x2216;</mo><mo>{</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mrow><mo>:</mo><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03b4;</mi><mo>}</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0003.gif)

How big does the distance δ need to be so that the volume of the spherical shell is a given proportion of the volume of the sphere—for specificity, say, 90% of the volume? The answer is whatever value of δ satisfies <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0004" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0004.gif"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>-</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03b4;</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0004.gif)

which is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0005" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0005.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03b4;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi></mfrac></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0005.gif)

This value of δ is shown for various dimensions *m* in [Figures 11.1](#c11.xhtml#figure11-1) and [11.2](#c11.xhtml#figure11-2). As the dimension becomes large, the radius of the “smaller” concentric ball removed grows to be nearly that of the original ball, as shown in [Figure 11.2](#c11.xhtml#figure11-2). What this means is that *nearly all the points in a high-dimensional ball are nearly on the boundary.*^([1](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0001))

In <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0007.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0007.gif), 90% of the volume of a unit sphere lies within a distance of about 0.54 units of its boundary (right).
