The distribution of the distance between pairs of points chosen uniformly at random from a unit ball is shown in [Figure 11.3](#c11.xhtml#figure11-3) (each cell is a histogram derived from 20,000 randomly drawn pairs). Note that as the dimension increases, the distribution becomes quite concentrated around a single value (<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0010.gif"><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt></math>![](images/c11_ILM0010.gif)). What this means is that *nearly all pairs of points in a high-dimensional ball are nearly equidistant from each other.*

![Figure 11.3 The distribution of distance between pairs of points drawn uniformly from a unit ball, in various dimensions. Each histogram was obtained from a sample of 20,000 pairs of points.](images/c11f003.jpg)

**Figure 11.3** The distribution of distance between pairs of points drawn uniformly from a unit ball, in various dimensions. Each histogram was obtained from a sample of 20,000 pairs of points.

The curse of dimensionality can negatively affect machine learning techniques which depend on distance. For example, consider the following binary classification problem. Feature vectors are points drawn uniformly from the *m*\-dimensional unit sphere centered at the origin, and a hyperplane *H* is given, passing through the center of the sphere. Data falling on one side of *H* are defined to be class 1, while data falling in or on the other side of *H* are defined to be class 2. The Bayes error rate is zero.

[Figure 11.4](#c11.xhtml#figure11-4) shows how the curse of dimensionality wrecks the performance of the 1-nearest-neighbor classification method on this problem relative to the performance of logistic regression and a linear support vector machine. Each point in the figure corresponds to training one of these classifiers on 10,000 training data and reporting the test error, estimated by using 10,000 test data.^([2](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0002)) As the dimension increases, the risk of the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier rapidly increases toward one-half (shown as a gray horizontal line), the maximum possible risk under 0–1 loss.^([3](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0003)) This is not surprising: since nearly all pairs of points are nearly equidistant, the distance between any pair of points provides little information about the points. The two linear classifiers are less affected by increasing dimension.

![Figure 11.4 The effect of dimension on the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier using Euclidean distance, compared to logistic regression and a linear support vector machine, on a binary classification problem with zero Bayes risk and a linear class boundary. The risk of the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier rapidly increases with dimension, because the information contained in the distance between points decreases. The horizontal gray line shows the maximum possible risk under 0–1 loss.](images/c11f004.jpg)

**Figure 11.4** The effect of dimension on the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier using Euclidean distance, compared to logistic regression and a linear support vector machine, on a binary classification problem with zero Bayes risk and a linear class boundary. The risk of the 1-nearest-neighbor classifier rapidly increases with dimension, because the information contained in the distance between points decreases. The horizontal gray line shows the maximum possible risk under 0–1 loss.

By symmetry, if *X* and *Y* are independent, uniformly distributed points in the unit ball or sphere then the distribution of *X*^T*Y* is the same as the distribution of ‖*Y*‖ *X*[1], the length of *Y* times the first coordinate of *X* (the dot product of *X* with the first standard basis vector). Thus by Exercises 11.2, 11.3, and 11.4 below, if *X* and *Y* are independent and uniform in the ball then <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0006" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0006.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x00b7;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> Var </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x00b7;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mo stretchy="true">\[</mo><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true">\]</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mo>\[</mo><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mo>\]</mo><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0006.gif)

and if *X* and *Y* are independent and uniform in the sphere then <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0007" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0007.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x00b7;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> Var </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x00b7;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0007.gif)

In this sense, *nearly all vectors in a high-dimensional ball or sphere centered at the origin are nearly orthogonal to any given vector.*

*Show that *X*[1] has the distribution of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0016.gif"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0016.gif), where the sign *N* is uniformly distributed on the set { − 1, 1},* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0013" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0013.gif"><mrow><mi>W</mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mo>&#x223c;</mo><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> Beta </mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0013.gif)

*and *N* and *W* are independent.*

***Hint:** See the hint for Exercise 11.2. Note that *X*[1] is both the dot product of *X* with the first standard basis vector and also the cosine of the angle between these vectors.*

Note that by symmetry, Exercise 11.2 gives the distribution of the dot product of a uniformly distributed random point in the unit ball <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0017.gif"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>:</mo><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>}</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0017.gif)and any given unit vector (in the exercise, the ball was rotated so that the given unit vector is (1, 0, …, 0)). Similarly, Exercise 11.3 gives the distribution of the dot product of a uniformly distributed random point in the unit sphere <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0018.gif"><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>:</mo><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>}</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0018.gif)and any given unit vector. Both of these distributions are symmetric about zero (and therefore have expected value zero) and have variances which approach zero as *m* → ∞. Thus for large *m*, for any vector *v*, the vector from the origin to a uniform random point in the ball or sphere is likely to be nearly orthogonal to *v*.

## 11.2 Two Running Examples

In what follows it will be useful to have examples for illustrative purposes. As in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml), we introduce the examples here and then refer to them in the rest of the chapter.

### 11.2.1 Example 1: Equilateral Simplex

The *simplex dataset* consists of 650 points *x*[1], …, *x*[650] in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0031.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>64</mn></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0031.gif), and was constructed as follows. An equilateral, 64-dimensional simplex with side length 1 was specified, and its 65 vertices labeled *v*[1], …, *v*[65]. Then for each *i* ∈ {1, …, 650}, an index *j* was drawn uniformly at random from the set {1, …, 65}, and *x[i]* was drawn from a Gaussian distribution with mean *v[j]* and covariance matrix equal to the identity matrix scaled by 10^(− 5). This dataset contains 65 tight clusters, all approximately equidistant from one another and approximately the same size (the clusters vary in size from 4 to 19 data points). In plots, data points will be colored according to membership in one of the 65 clusters, which is known due to the way the data are generated.

The methods of [Section 11.3](#c11.xhtml#c11_3) will be applied to either the 64-dimensional vectors of this dataset, or to the dissimilarity between vectors, as measured by Euclidean distance. This dataset is a difficult case for dimension-reduction because, while it has identifiable structure in the form of tight clusters, the structure is not low-dimensional.

### 11.2.2 Example 2: Text

The *text dataset* is obtained from this book itself.^([6](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0006)) This book can be decomposed into 130 small documents: 110 numbered chapter sections, 13 chapter introductions (considered as “Section 0” of each chapter), plus [Chapter 1](#c01.xhtml) (which has no sections), four appendices (labeled A through D), a preface (labeled P, and including the organization and acknowledgements), and a list of references (labeled R). Each of these is contained in a computer file written in the <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0032.gif"><mrow/></math>![](images/c11_ILM0032.gif)typesetting language.^([7](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0007)) In plots, sections will be colored by chapter.

A feature vector was constructed for each of the 130 files by counting the occurrences of the terms in each file. A *character N-gram* is any sequence of *N* consecutive characters, including whitespace characters. For example, the first ten five-grams of this sentence, allowing overlaps, are <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0001a" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0021.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mtext>\`\`</mtext><mtext>Fore</mtext><mtext>""</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>\`\`</mtext><mtext>orex</mtext><mtext>""</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>\`\`</mtext><mtext>rexa</mtext><mtext>""</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>\`\`</mtext><mtext>exam</mtext><mtext>""</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>\`\`examp""</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>\`\`xampl""</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>\`\`ample""</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>\`\`mple,""</mtext><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mspace width="1.em"/><mtext>\`\`</mtext><mtext>ple,</mtext><mtext>""</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>\`\`</mtext><mtext>le,t</mtext><mtext>""</mtext><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0021.gif)

where the symbol “<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0035.gif"><mrow/></math>![](images/c11_ILM0035.gif)” stands for a single space character. In this example, a *term* is any five-gram, allowing overlaps as above, which occurs in this book. This book contains 61,190 distinct terms, the six most common being, in order, “<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0036.gif"><mrow/></math>![](images/c11_ILM0036.gif)the<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0037.gif"><mrow/></math>![](images/c11_ILM0037.gif)” (which occurs 6429 times), “tion<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0038.gif"><mrow/></math>![](images/c11_ILM0038.gif)” (2876), “<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0039.gif"><mrow/></math>![](images/c11_ILM0039.gif)and<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0040.gif"><mrow/></math>![](images/c11_ILM0040.gif)” (2145), “param” (1784), “regre” (1706), and “class” (1573)—the high frequency of the terms “param” and “regre” is due, in part, to the author’s use of the <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0041.gif"><mrow/></math>![](images/c11_ILM0041.gif)macro \\regreparam to typeset the symbol θ.

The occurrences of each term in each file are counted, producing a 61,190-long *term-frequency (TF)* vector. The term-frequency vector can be treated as a numeric feature vector describing each file. It is generally useful to weight the coordinates of this vector so that terms which occur in most files (for example, “<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0042.gif"><mrow/></math>![](images/c11_ILM0042.gif)the<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0043.gif"><mrow/></math>![](images/c11_ILM0043.gif)” occurs in all 130 sections of this book, “<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0044.gif"><mrow/></math>![](images/c11_ILM0044.gif)and<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0045.gif"><mrow/></math>![](images/c11_ILM0045.gif)” occurs in 126, and “<math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0046.gif"><mrow/></math>![](images/c11_ILM0046.gif)data” occurs in 110) are suppressed and terms which occur in relatively few files (for example, “eigen” occurs in only five sections of this book) are enhanced. One way to accomplish this is to count the number of sections in which each term occurs (since the terms are precisely those *N*\-grams which occur in the book, each term occurs in at least one section) and weight each term inversely to the number of sections. This is typically done on a logarithmic scale, so that the feature vector associated with each section *S* of the book is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0021" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0022.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfenced open="(" close=""><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mtext>number</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>of</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>times</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>term</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>t</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mtext>occurs</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>in</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>document</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>S</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></mfenced></mstyle></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><msub><mfenced separators="" open="" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mspace width="1.em"/><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><mtext>total</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>number</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>of</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>documents</mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext>number</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>of</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>documents</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>in</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>which</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>term</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">t</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>occurs</mtext></mrow></mfrac></mfenced></mstyle></mfenced><mrow><mi> all </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> terms </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi mathvariant="italic">t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0022.gif)

This is called the *term-frequency inverse-document-frequency (TF-IDF)* vector associated with section *S*. TF-IDF vectors are usually scaled so that they are unit vectors. In many applications, the set of terms is much larger than the set of terms occurring in any particular document, in which case most coordinates of the resulting TF-IDF vectors are equal to zero.

Let *x*[1], …, *x[n]* denote the TF-IDF vectors for the *n* = 130 sections of the book. One commonly used way to measure the similarity between these vectors is *cosine similarity*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0022" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0023.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">cos</mo><mi>&#x2220;</mi><mi>w</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>w</mi><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#x00b7;</mo><mfrac><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0023.gif)

When vectors *w* and *x* have all non-negative coordinates, as is the case for TF-IDF vectors, *s*(*w*, *x*) ∈ \[0, 1\]. When the cosine similarity of two TF-IDF vectors is large, it generally means that some relatively rare terms occur relatively frequently in both documents.

The methods of [Section 11.3](#c11.xhtml#c11_3) will be applied to either the 61,190-dimensional TF-IDF vectors of this dataset (normalized to be unit vectors), or to the dissimilarity between vectors, as measured by cosine dissimilarity (that is, one minus the cosine similarity). The dissimilarity between sections of this book are shown in [Figure 11.5](#c11.xhtml#figure11-5).

![Figure 11.5 The matrix of pairwise dissimilarities between the 130 sections of this book, as measured by the cosine similarity between the corresponding TF-IDF vectors computed from 5-grams. The dissimilarity is shown in grayscale, and ranges from zero (black) to one (white).](images/c11f005.jpg)

**Figure 11.5** The matrix of pairwise dissimilarities between the 130 sections of this book, as measured by the cosine similarity between the corresponding TF-IDF vectors computed from 5-grams. The dissimilarity is shown in grayscale, and ranges from zero (black) to one (white).

## 11.3 Reducing Dimension While Preserving Information

This section presents various approaches to finding a *k*\-dimensional, approximate representation <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0047.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0047.gif)of an observed set of *m*\-dimensional feature vectors <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0048.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0048.gif), where *k* < *m*. There are several reasons one might wish to do this: because not all *m* features carry information relevant to a given problem, and a smaller, more informative feature space is desired; because certain algorithms are perceived to offer better performance (lower-risk predictions, lower computational cost, or both) working in a lower-dimensional space; or for exploratory plots of the data (in which case the values *k* = 1, *k* = 2, and *k* = 3 are of particular interest).

Each approach is distinguished by a set of criteria defining a “good” low-dimensional representation of *x*[1], …, *x[n]*, and a method of finding an optimal (or approximately optimal) representation with respect to its criteria. Some approaches (principal component analysis, linear multidimensional scaling, projection pursuit, autoencoders) construct explicit maps <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0049.gif"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#x2192;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0049.gif)which can be applied to as-yet-unobserved data, while others (stress-minimizing multidimensional scaling, manifold learning, clustering) work only on the data given. Some approaches (multidimensional scaling, manifold learning) depend only on a matrix of dissimilarities between feature vectors, and thus generalize to the case where only these dissimilarities are given, in which case the goal is to find a set of *n* points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0050.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0050.gif)whose interpoint Euclidean distances approximate the given dissimilarities.

### 11.3.1 The Geometry of Means and Covariances of Real Features

When all features are real, the observed feature vectors can be expressed in the rows of a *n* × *m* matrix^([8](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0008)) <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0024" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0025.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>11</mn></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>12</mn></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>21</mn></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>22</mn></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd/><mtd><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0025.gif)

We follow the convention of treating all vectors—including the feature vectors *x*[1], …, *x[n]*—as column vectors, although *x*[1], …, *x[n]* are represented as the rows of **X**. Sometimes it is convenient to have the data translated so that the mean feature vector is at the origin, and sometimes it is convenient to have the data rotated so that the features are uncorrelated. This can be done by matrix operations on **X** as follows.

Let the sample mean and the sample covariance matrix of feature vectors *x*[1], …, *x[n]* (the rows of **X**) be denoted respectively by <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0025" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0026.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="1.em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0026.gif)

Translating the data so that the mean feature vector is at the origin is equivalent to subtracting <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0051.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover></math>![](images/c11_ILM0051.gif)from each row of **X**, and data which have been so translated are said to be *centered*. One way to center data is by multiplying **X** on the left^([9](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0009)) by the *n* × *n centering matrix* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" The following exercise says that if a dataset is represented by the rows of **X**, then the centered dataset is represented by the rows of **HX**.

**Exercise 11.10** *Show that matrix **HX** is equal to matrix **X** with <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0054.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover></math>![](images/c11_ILM0054.gif)subtracted from each row. Show that **H**² = **H**. Show that the sample covariance matrix of **X** and of **HX** is* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0027" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0028.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0028.gif)

The sample covariance matrix **S** is non-negative definite, so it can be represented as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0028" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0029.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x039b;</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0029.gif)

where <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0055.gif"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x039b;</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi> diag </mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0055.gif)and λ[1] ⩾ λ[2] ⩾ ⋅⋅⋅ ⩾ λ[*m*] ⩾ 0 are the eigenvalues of **S** written in non-increasing order,^([10](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0010)) and where **Q** is an *m* × *m* orthogonal matrix^([11](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0011)) whose columns are the corresponding eigenvectors. Rotating the centered data so that the features are uncorrelated is accomplished by multiplying **HX** on the right by **Q**. Feature vectors which have been translated so that the mean feature vector is at the origin and rotated so that the features are uncorrelated are said to be *centered and decorrelated*.

**Exercise 11.11** *Show that the sample covariance matrix of **HXQ** is the diagonal matrix <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0056.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x039b;</mi></mrow></math>*![](images/c11_ILM0056.gif).

This process can be taken one step further: the rows of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0057.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x039b;</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0057.gif)have sample mean zero and sample covariance matrix equal to the identity matrix. Feature vectors which have been translated, rotated, and scaled this way are said to be *sphered*.

### 11.3.2 Principal Component Analysis

The goal of *principal component analysis (PCA)* is to find a linear projection of *n* centered data points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0058.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0058.gif)into <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0059.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0059.gif), *k* < *m*, which preserves as much information as possible, where information is measured in terms of variance. Given a centered dataset represented by the rows of **HX**, a linear map <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0060.gif"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#x2192;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0060.gif), represented by an *m* × *k* matrix **W** = \[*W*[1], …, *W[k]*\], is sought such that:

1.  the columns *W*[1], …, *W[k]* are mutually orthogonal unit vectors;
2.  <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0061.gif"><mrow><mi> SVar </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mi> SVar </mi><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>z</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0061.gif)for all unit vectors <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0062.gif"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0062.gif), that is, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0029" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0030.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><munder><mi> argmax </mi><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>:</mo><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></munder><mi> SVar </mi><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>z</mi></mfenced><mspace width="4pt"/><mo>;</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0030.gif)
3.  for *j* = 2, …, *k*, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0063.gif"><mrow><mi> SVar </mi><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mi> SVar </mi><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>z</mi></mfenced></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0063.gif)for all unit vectors <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0064.gif"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0064.gif)such that **HX***z* is uncorrelated with all of **HX***W*[1], …, **HX***W*[*j* − 1], that is, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0030" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0031.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munder><mi> argmax </mi><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>:</mo><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi> SCor </mi><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>z</mi><mo>\]</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi> SCor </mi><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>z</mi><mo>\]</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></munder><mi> SVar </mi><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>z</mi></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0031.gif)

where <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0065.gif"><mrow><mi> SVar </mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mo>&#x00b7;</mo></mfenced></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0065.gif)and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0066.gif"><mrow><mi> SCor </mi><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mo>&#x00b7;</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>&#x00b7;</mo></mfenced></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0066.gif)represent the sample variance and correlation, respectively. In words, the *first principal component W*[1] is a unit vector in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0067.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0067.gif)pointing in the direction in which the data have maximal variance. The *second principal component* *W*[2] is a unit vector in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0068.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0068.gif), constrained to be orthogonal to the first principal component, pointing in the direction in which the data have maximal variance. And so on: the *jth principal component W[j]* is a unit vector in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0069.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0069.gif), constrained to be orthogonal to all of the first *j* − 1 principal components, pointing in the direction in which the data have maximal variance. The rows of the *n* × *k* matrix **HXW** are the *n* feature vectors (data points) projected onto their first *k* principal components.

**Exercise 11.12** *Show that the *m* × *k* matrix \[*Q*[1], …, *Q[k]*\] formed by taking the first *k* columns of **Q** satisfies properties (1), (2), and (3), so the first *k* columns of **HXQ** are *x*[1], …, *x[n]* projected onto their first *k* principal components.*

Exercise 11.12 states that principle component analysis is the same as translating a dataset to the origin, rotating it to decorrelate the features, and taking the first *k* decorrelated features. This means that computationally, the projection of the data onto the first *k* principal components is the same as finding the *k* largest eigenvalues of the covariance matrix **S** and their corresponding eigenvectors. It also means that the variance of the data projected onto the *i*th principal component is λ[*i*], the *i*th largest eigenvalue of **S**. The results of applying PCA to the simplex dataset to produce a two-dimensional representation is shown in the left-hand cell of [Figure 11.6](#c11.xhtml#figure11-6).

The choice of *k* is usually made heuristically, balancing the need in any given application for *k* to be small against the need to preserve information in the data. The *proportion of total variation* preserved in projecting data onto its first *k* principal components is defined as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0031" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0032.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi> tr </mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="4pt"/><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mspace width="4pt"/><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

<a href="#c11-disp-0031-1"></a>(11.1)![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0032.gif)

In the context of PCA, the columns *Q*[1], …, *Q[k]* of **Q** are called *loading vectors*. The loading vectors can sometimes be interpreted to gain insight into the sources of variance in the data. For example, one might find that most of the coordinates of the first loading vector *Q*[1] are negligibly small relative to a few of the coordinates. Ignoring what is negligibly small, the first principal component can be viewed as a linear combination of a few of the original features, with weights given according to the non-negligible coordinates of *Q*[1]. Depending on the application, this particular combination of the features may be found to be meaningful. Similarly for *Q*[2], and so on.

### 11.3.3 Working in “Dissimilarity Space”

A *dissimilarity measure* on feature space <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0070.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>![](images/c11_ILM0070.gif)is a function <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0071.gif"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0071.gif)such that *d*(*x*, *x*) = 0 for all <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0072.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0072.gif)and *d*(*w*, *x*) = *d*(*x*, *w*) for all <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0073.gif"><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0073.gif). The value *d*(*w*, *x*) is interpreted as the dissimilarity of two feature vectors *w* and *x*. In general, *d*(*w*, *x*) need not satisfy a triangle inequality, although commonly used dissimilarity measures on <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0074.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0074.gif)often do, such as the family of metrics defined in Exercise 11.8. Construction of a good dissimilarity measure for any particular application is something of an art: some specific measures and their motivation will be discussed later in this chapter.^([12](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0012))

A dissimilarity measure allows one to apply certain techniques without further regard for the structure of the feature space <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0075.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>![](images/c11_ILM0075.gif).^([13](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0013)) For example, the hierarchical and *k*\-medoid clustering algorithms described in [Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml), and the *k*\-nearest-neighbor and nearest-cluster classifiers described in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml), can be applied given only the matrix of dissimilarity values <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0032" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0033.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0033.gif)

### 11.3.4 Linear Multidimensional Scaling

*Multidimensional scaling (MDS)* is a family of techniques for moving from dissimilarity space to real feature space <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0077.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0077.gif). Suppose there are objects *o*[1], …, *o[n]* (which may or may not be represented by vectors in some feature space) and a matrix of pairwise dissimilarities between the objects is given, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0033" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0034.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0034.gif)

Given a value of *k*, multidimensional scaling attempts to construct a set of *n* points, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0078.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0078.gif), with the property that the matrix of Euclidean distances between the points, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0034" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0035.gif"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0035.gif)

is close to the dissimilarity matrix **D** in some user-specified sense. The points <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0079.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0079.gif)are then used as surrogates for the objects *o*[1], …, *o[n]*, and the coordinates of the <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0080.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![](images/c11_ILM0080.gif)’s are interpreted as *latent features* of the objects.^([14](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0014)) This section presents the original, linear multidimensional scaling algorithm. A different approach is presented in [Section 11.3.6](#c11.xhtml#c11_3_6).

We begin with the geometric motivation for a definition. Suppose that dissimilarity matrix **D** actually arose as the matrix of pairwise Euclidean distances between points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0081.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0081.gif): that is, suppose the objects *o*[1], …, *o[n]* correspond to points <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0082.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0082.gif)and that **D**[*i*, *j*] = *d*(*o[i]*, *o[j]*) = *d*[2](*x[i]*, *x[j]*) for all *i* and *j*. Then for all *i* and *j*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0035" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0036.gif"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0036.gif)

which means that the matrix of distances **D** can be obtained from the matrix of inner products \[*x*^T[*i*]*x[j]*\]^(*n*)[*i*, *j* = 1]. Since the distances between points *x*[1], …, *x[n]* are translation invariant, **D** can also be obtained from the matrix of inner products of the *x[i]*’s after they have been centered. Thus **D** can be obtained from the matrix <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0036" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0037.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0037.gif)

Furthermore, the matrix **B** of inner products can be obtained directly from the matrix of distances.

**Exercise 11.13** *Show that in the above, **B** = **HAH**, where* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0037" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0038.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mstyle></mfenced><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0038.gif)

*and **H** is the centering matrix.*

This observation motivates a general definition. Given *any* dissimilarity matrix **D** = \[*d*(*o[i]*, *o[j]*)\]^(*n*)[*i*, *j* = 1] (not just a Euclidean distance matrix), define matrices **A** and **B** by <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0038" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0039.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>d</mi><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mstyle></mfenced><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0039.gif)

**Theorem 11.1 A Property of Euclidean Distance (Young and Householder).** *A necessary and sufficient condition for **D** to be the pairwise distances of a set of points in Euclidean space is that the matrix **B** be non-negative definite, and in this case the set of points is unique apart from a rigid motion.*

Linear multidimensional scaling is the result of treating the matrix **B** as if it is a matrix of inner products of *n* points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0083.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0083.gif), for some value of *k*. Since **B** is real and symmetric, it has an eigendecomposition <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0039" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0040.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x039b;</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0040.gif)

where <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0084.gif"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x039b;</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi> diag </mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0084.gif)and λ[1] ⩾ λ[2] ⩾ ⋅⋅⋅ ⩾ λ[*m*] are the eigenvalues of **B** written in non-increasing order. It is possible that some of the eigenvalues are negative: in fact, at least one of the eigenvalues must be negative unless **D** is Euclidean by Theorem 11.1. If fewer than *k* of the eigenvalues are positive, linear MDS cannot construct a *k*\-dimensional realization. If at least *k* of the eigenvalues are positive, linear MDS can construct a *k*\-dimensional realization: it consists of the rows of the *n* × *k* matrix <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0040" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0041.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi> diag </mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mn>1</mn><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mi>k</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msubsup><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0041.gif)

Two generalizations of the proportion of total variation (11.1), both interpreted as “the proportion of the dissimilarity matrix explained” by a *k*\-dimensional representation, are (Mardia et al., 1979): <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0041" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0042.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

<a href="#c11-disp-0041-2"></a>(11.2)![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0042.gif)

and <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0042" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0043.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0043.gif)

We shall use (11.2) in the examples which follow.

When it exists, the *k*\-dimensional dataset returned by linear MDS is optimal with respect to two criteria, expressed in terms of the matrix of pairwise Euclidean distances between rows of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0085.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c11_ILM0085.gif), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0043" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0044.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0044.gif)

and the corresponding matrix of inner products, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0044" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0045.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><msubsup><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mstyle></mfenced><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0045.gif)

The optimality criteria are stated in terms of distance with respect to the Frobenius norm. The *Frobenius norm* of an *n* × *m* real matrix **M** is its Euclidean length, considered as an *nm*\-long vector: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0045" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0046.gif"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0046.gif)

Constrained Optimality Criterion of Linear MDS.

**Theorem 11.2 Constrained Optimality Criterion of Linear MDS.** *If dissimilarity matrix **D** is the matrix of Euclidean distances between the rows of **X**, then the linear MDS realization minimizes <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0086.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo>-</mo></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0086.gif)over all configurations of *n* points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0087.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0087.gif)obtained by a projection of **X** into <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0088.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math>*![](images/c11_ILM0088.gif).

**Theorem 11.3 Global Optimality Criterion of Linear MDS.** *The linear MDS realization minimizes* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0089.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mo>-</mo></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0089.gif)*over all configurations of *n* points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0090.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math>*![](images/c11_ILM0090.gif).

Note that in Theorem 11.3, the matrix <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0091.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c11_ILM0091.gif)is a matrix of inner products, but the matrix **B** need not be (because the matrix **D** need not be a matrix of Euclidean distances among some set of points).

![Figure 11.6 Linear MDS applied to the simplex dataset (left cell) and the text dataset with TF-IDF (right cell) of Section 11.2. In the simplex dataset, linear MDS (which in this case is equivalent to PCA) has separated the single largest cluster, of size 19, from the rest of the data on the first principal axis (horizontal). It has separated the two second-largest clusters, each of size 16, from each other and the rest of the data on the second principal axis (vertical). Linear MDS has preserved the fact that these three clusters are approximately equidistant from each other, at the cost of collapsing the other 62 clusters together. The two-dimensional linear MDS representation of the simplex data has preserved 5.4% of the total variation (11.1). In the text dataset, linear MDS has separated most of Chapter 3 (regression) and parts of Chapters 4 (logistic regression, neural networks, and support vector machines), 10 (quasi-Newton methods, general remarks, and EM), and 11 (model regularization) from the rest of the book on the first principal axis (horizontal). It has separated most of Chapter 14 (R code) from the rest of the book on the second principal axis (vertical). The two-dimensional linear MDS representation of the text data has preserved 10.3% of the dissimilarity matrix (11.2).](images/c11f006.jpg)

**Figure 11.6** Linear MDS applied to the simplex dataset (left cell) and the text dataset with TF-IDF (right cell) of [Section 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11_2). In the simplex dataset, linear MDS (which in this case is equivalent to PCA) has separated the single largest cluster, of size 19, from the rest of the data on the first principal axis (horizontal). It has separated the two second-largest clusters, each of size 16, from each other and the rest of the data on the second principal axis (vertical). Linear MDS has preserved the fact that these three clusters are approximately equidistant from each other, at the cost of collapsing the other 62 clusters together. The two-dimensional linear MDS representation of the simplex data has preserved 5.4% of the total variation (11.1). In the text dataset, linear MDS has separated most of [Chapter 3](#c03.xhtml) (regression) and parts of [Chapters 4](#c04.xhtml) (logistic regression, neural networks, and support vector machines), [10](#c10.xhtml) (quasi-Newton methods, general remarks, and EM), and [11](#c11.xhtml) (model regularization) from the rest of the book on the first principal axis (horizontal). It has separated most of [Chapter 14](#c14.xhtml) (R code) from the rest of the book on the second principal axis (vertical). The two-dimensional linear MDS representation of the text data has preserved 10.3% of the dissimilarity matrix (11.2).

### 11.3.5 The Singular Value Decomposition and Low-Rank Approximation

When the dissimilarity matrix **D** arises as the Euclidean distances between points <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0092.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0092.gif), PCA and linear MDS are exactly the same thing. This can be shown by using a low-rank (as opposed to low-dimension) approximation of the centered data matrix **HX** obtained from its singular value decomposition.

The *singular value decomposition (SVD)* of an *n* × *m* matrix **M** is defined as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0046" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0047.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x03a3;</mi></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0047.gif)

where **U** is an *n* × *n* orthogonal matrix, **V** is an *m* × *m* orthogonal matrix, and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0093.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x03a3;</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0093.gif)is an *n* × *m* diagonal matrix with diagonal entries σ[1] ⩾ σ[2] ⩾ ⋅⋅⋅ ⩾ σ[min (*n*, *m*)] ⩾ 0. The diagonal entries of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0094.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x03a3;</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0094.gif)are the *singular values* of the matrix **M**, the columns of **U** are the *left singular vectors* of **M**, and the columns of **V** (the rows of **V**^T) are the *right singular vectors* of **M**.

**Theorem 11.4 Existence of the SVD.** *Every real matrix has a singular value decomposition.*

The SVD can be used to construct low-rank approximations of a matrix which are optimal with in the sense of distance with respect to the Frobenius norm.

Optimality Criterion of the SVD (Eckhart-Young).

**Theorem 11.5 Optimality Criterion of the SVD (Eckhart-Young).** *Let **M** be an *n* × *m* matrix with SVD <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0095.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x03a3;</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0095.gif)and let <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0096.gif"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mi> rank </mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0096.gif). Among all *n* × *m* matrices **Z** of rank *k*, ‖**M** − **Z**‖[*F*] is minimized by the matrix* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0047" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0048.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mtd><mtd/><mtd/><mtd/></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mtd><mtd/><mtd/></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22f1;</mo></mtd><mtd/></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd/><mtd><msub><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0048.gif)

*where *U*[1], …, *U[k]* are the first *k* columns of **U**, *V*[1], …, *V[k]* are the first *k* columns of **V**, and the matrix in the middle is <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0097.gif"><mrow><mi> diag </mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0097.gif). The optimal matrix **Z** is uniquely defined if σ[*k*] > σ[*k* + 1].*
