For an arbitrary matrix **M**, the eigendecomposition of both **MM**^T and **M**^T**M** can be obtained from the singular value decomposition of **M**: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0048" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0049.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x03a3;</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x03a3;</mi></mrow></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mspace width="4pt"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x03a3;</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x03a3;</mi></mrow></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0049.gif)

are the eigendecompositions of the respective matrices. In particular, the eigenvalues of **MM**^T are σ²[1] ⩾ σ[2]² ⩾ ⋅⋅⋅ ⩾ σ²[min (*n*, *m*)] ⩾ 0, plus *n* − *m* additional zero eigenvalues if *n* > *m*, and the eigenvalues of **M**^T**M** are σ²[1] ⩾ σ[2]² ⩾ ⋅⋅⋅ ⩾ σ²[min (*n*, *m*)] ⩾ 0, plus *m* − *n* additional zero eigenvalues if *m* > *n*.

**Exercise 11.14** *Let **X** be an *n* × *m* matrix whose rows represent *n* feature vectors in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0098.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0098.gif). Let **HX** be the matrix of centered feature vectors and let <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0099.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x03a3;</mi></mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0099.gif)be the singular value decomposition of **HX**.*

1.  *Show that projection of **HX** onto its first *k* principal components is the first *k* columns of **HXV**.*
2.  *Show that linear multidimensional scaling constructs the first *k* columns of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0100.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#x03a3;</mi></mrow></mrow></math>*![](images/c11_ILM0100.gif).
3.  *Show that these are the same.*

Exercise 11.14 shows that when principal component analysis is applicable, linear multidimensional scaling on the matrix of Euclidean distances is also applicable and produces the same *k*\-dimensional realization as PCA. Multidimensional scaling, however, is applicable more generally than PCA since MDS only requires a dissimilarity matrix, and the dissimilarity matrix can be non-Euclidean. The results of applying linear MDS to find two-dimensional realizations of the simplex and text datasets are shown in [Figure 11.6](#c11.xhtml#figure11-6).

### 11.3.6 Stress-Minimizing Multidimensional Scaling

Another way to approach multidimensional scaling is by approximate numerical solution of an optimization problem. Given a configuration of points <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0101.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0101.gif), let <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0049" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0050.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0050.gif)

be the matrix of interpoint Euclidean distances. Given a target dissimilarity matrix **D**, the closeness of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0102.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c11_ILM0102.gif)to **D** is measured by an objective function, which in this context is called a *stress function*: for example, the Frobenius distance from <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0103.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c11_ILM0103.gif)to **D**, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0104.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo>-</mo></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow><mo>&#x2225;</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0104.gif). Starting from an initial configuration of points, an optimization algorithm from [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml) can be used to find an approximately optimal configuration in the sense of minimizing the stress between <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0105.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/c11_ILM0105.gif)and **D**. There are many variations of stress-minimizing MDS: interpoint distances need not be Euclidean and the stress function need not be Frobenius distance.

![Figure 11.7 Stress-minimizing MDS applied to the simplex dataset (left cell) and the text dataset (right cell) of Section 11.2. In the simplex dataset, stress-minimizing MDS has separated all 65 clusters from one another, and has fragmented eight clusters (cluster fragments are connected by gray line segments). In the text dataset, stress-minimizing MDS has kept most of the chapters mostly together, exceptions being Chapter 4 (classification), Chapter 6 (ensembles), Chapter 8 (consistency), and Chapter 12 (communications), which are relatively diffuse.](images/c11f007.jpg)

**Figure 11.7** Stress-minimizing MDS applied to the simplex dataset (left cell) and the text dataset (right cell) of [Section 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11_2). In the simplex dataset, stress-minimizing MDS has separated all 65 clusters from one another, and has fragmented eight clusters (cluster fragments are connected by gray line segments). In the text dataset, stress-minimizing MDS has kept most of the chapters mostly together, exceptions being [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml) (classification), [Chapter 6](#c06.xhtml) (ensembles), [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml) (consistency), and [Chapter 12](#c12.xhtml) (communications), which are relatively diffuse.

Given a high-dimensional dataset <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0106.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0106.gif), configurations of points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0107.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0107.gif)whose interpoint distances are close to the interpoint distances between *x*[1], …, *x[n]* are found by both stress-minimizing MDS and PCA (or linear MDS, which is the same thing in this case). One difference between the methods is that PCA constructs a function from <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0108.gif"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#x2192;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0108.gif)while stress-minimizing MDS does not. A consequence of this is that new data *x*[*n* + 1], … can be mapped into a *k*\-dimensional realization by the function found by PCA, while this cannot be done with stress-minimizing MDS. Thus one criterion for choosing between the two methods is whether an application requires that as-yet-unobserved data be mapped onto an existing low-dimensional realization of observed data. The results of applying stress-minimizing MDS to find two-dimensional realizations of the simplex and text datasets are shown in [Figure 11.7](#c11.xhtml#figure11-7).

### 11.3.7 Projection Pursuit

Principal component analysis finds a linear projection of *n* data points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0109.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0109.gif)into <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0110.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0110.gif), *k* < *m*, which is optimal with respect to the criteria listed in (1), (2), and (3) of [Section 11.3.2](#c11.xhtml#c11_3_2), and computation of this optimum is achieved by computation of the singular value decomposition of the centered data matrix **HX**. As an alternative, one could retain the idea of linear projection, but replace (1), (2), and (3) with any set of criteria and use the methods of [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml) to search for the best representation of a dataset with respect to the given criteria. Such approaches are called *projection pursuit*.

![Figure 11.8 Projection pursuit applied to the simplex dataset (left cell, with tuning parameters p = 0.1, R = 10, and ) and the text dataset (right cell, with tuning parameters p = 0.1, R = 0.1, and ) of Section 11.2. In the simplex dataset, projection pursuit has separated some of the clusters and achieved a fairly uniform spread of the data in both the horizontal and vertical directions. In the text dataset, projection pursuit has put Chapters 6 and 9 mostly in the upper-right corner, Chapter 14 mostly along the bottom side, and Chapters 2, 10, 12, and 13 in the upper-left corner.](images/c11f008.jpg)

**Figure 11.8** Projection pursuit applied to the simplex dataset (left cell, with tuning parameters *p* = 0.1, *R* = 10, and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0111.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>R</mi></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0111.gif)) and the text dataset (right cell, with tuning parameters *p* = 0.1, *R* = 0.1, and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0112.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>R</mi></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0112.gif)) of [Section 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11_2). In the simplex dataset, projection pursuit has separated some of the clusters and achieved a fairly uniform spread of the data in both the horizontal and vertical directions. In the text dataset, projection pursuit has put [Chapters 6](#c06.xhtml) and [9](#c09.xhtml) mostly in the upper-right corner, [Chapter 14](#c14.xhtml) mostly along the bottom side, and [Chapters 2](#c02.xhtml), [10](#c10.xhtml), [12](#c12.xhtml), and [13](#c13.xhtml) in the upper-left corner.

This section describes one of the earliest approaches to projection pursuit. Based on observation of human interaction with high-dimensional datasets, Friedman and Tukey (1974, p. 882) proposed a criterion which rewards projections that “produce many very small interpoint distances while, at the same time, maintaining the overall spread of the data.” Let **M** = \[*M*[1], …, *M[k]*\] be an *m* × *k* matrix whose columns are constrained to be unit vectors and mutually orthogonal, so that multiplication on the right by **M** performs a linear projection of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0113.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0113.gif)into <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0114.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0114.gif). The projection pursuit realization <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0115.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0115.gif)will be the rows of the matrix <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0116.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0116.gif). Let three tuning parameters be given: <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0117.gif"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0117.gif), *R* > 0, and a function ψ: \[0, ∞) → \[0, ∞) which decreases monotonically to zero on \[0, *R*\] and is identically zero on \[*R*, ∞). Friedman and Tukey proposed the objective function <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0050" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0051.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03b4;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x220f;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></munderover><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0051.gif)

where δ(**M**) measures “local density” of projected data <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0118.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0118.gif), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0051" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0052.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03b4;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0052.gif)

and σ(**M**[*j*]) measures the “spread” of the one-dimensional projected data <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0119.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0119.gif)by a trimmed standard deviation: σ(**M**[*j*]) is the standard deviation of the set of numbers formed by sorting the coordinates of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0120.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub></math>![](images/c11_ILM0120.gif)and deleting the *pn* smallest and *pn* largest. The factor δ(**M**) is large when data are concentrated locally, while the factor σ(**M**[*j*]) is large when the data are spread out in the *j*th direction. The results of applying Friedman–Tukey projection pursuit to the simplex and text datasets is shown in [Figure 11.8](#c11.xhtml#figure11-8).

### 11.3.8 Feature Selection

*Feature selection* is a projection of feature space onto a subspace consisting certain coordinates, and the process of searching for a set of features which produce a low-risk model can be viewed as a particular form of projection pursuit. Given a risk estimate or model selection criterion from [Chapter 7](#c07.xhtml)–or any other model selection criterion—feature selection seeks a subset of the features {*i*[1], *i*[2], …, *i[k]*}⊆{1, …, *m*} such that a model trained on that subset of features, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0052" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0053.gif"><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd/><mtd><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0053.gif)

optimizes the criterion. This can be done by discrete optimization, using a discrete analogue of methods described in [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml) or stepwise feature selection described in [Section 7.10](#c07.xhtml#c7_10).

### 11.3.9 Clustering

Application of a clustering algorithm to any dataset can viewed as a “projection” of *m*\-dimensional features onto a single categorical variable (the cluster labels assigned to the feature vectors). Different clusterings—obtained by changing the algorithms, parameters, or raw features used—give different categorical variables.

### 11.3.10 Manifold Learning

Sometimes multidimensional scaling is preceded by a step in which a given dissimilarity matrix <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0053" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0054.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0054.gif)

is replaced by another dissimilarity matrix <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0054" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0055.gif"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi></mrow><mo>&#x0027;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>&#x0027;</mo></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0055.gif)

where dissimilarity measure *d*′ is constructed from measure *d*, but *d*′ is thought to represent information about the objects *o*[1], …, *o[n]* better than *d*. This situation arises when data in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0121.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0121.gif)lie in (or approximately in) a manifold^([15](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0015)) of lower dimension than *m*, and dissimilarity measure *d* is Euclidean distance in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0122.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0122.gif). In this case, a dissimilarity measure *d*′ which respects the geometry of the manifold might be preferred to *d*, since curvature of the manifold in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0123.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0123.gif)might lead points which are far apart with respect to *d*′ to be close to one another with respect to *d*. The problem of recovering the manifold distance *d*′ is called *manifold learning*.

Several manifold methods approach the problem by constructing a weighted *nearest neighbors graph* from the data and producing a new distance *d*′ from path weights in the graph. These will be illustrated by a particular method, due to Tenenbaum et al. (2000), known as *isomap* (short for “isometric feature mapping”). Two data objects *o[i]* and *o[j]* are said to be neighbors if the distance *d*(*o[i]*, *o[j]*) < ε for some given threshold ε > 0, or, in an alternative approach, *o[i]* and *o[j]* are neighbors if *o[i]* is one of the *k* closest data to *o[j]*—or vice versa—for a given parameter *k* ⩾ 1. Each datum corresponds to a *vertex* of the graph, and the pair of vertices corresponding (*o[i]*, *o[j]*) is connected by an *edge* of the graph if and only if *o[i]* and *o[j]* are neighbors. If an edge corresponding to the pair (*o[i]*, *o[j]*) is in the graph, it is assigned an *edge weight* of *d*(*o[i]*, *o[j]*). The distance between *o[i]* and *o[j]* within the (presumed) manifold is approximated by the lowest-weight path (sequence of edges) in the graph which connects the vertex corresponding to *o[i]* to the vertex corresponding to *o[j]*.^([16](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0016))

![Figure 11.9 The isomap manifold learning algorithm applied to the simplex-edges dataset. The top three cells show distances between all pairs of points in the dataset, with the points in order along the one-dimensional manifold (points are colored to make a rainbow along the manifold). The center two cells show the result of applying one-dimensional linear MDS to the Euclidean (left) and approximate geodesic (right) distance matrices, with vertical jitter added for clarity. The bottom two cells show the result of applying two-dimensional linear MDS the Euclidean (left) and approximate geodesic (right) distance matrices. Further analysis is given in the text.](images/c11f009.jpg)

**Figure 11.9** The isomap manifold learning algorithm applied to the simplex-edges dataset. The top three cells show distances between all pairs of points in the dataset, with the points in order along the one-dimensional manifold (points are colored to make a rainbow along the manifold). The center two cells show the result of applying one-dimensional linear MDS to the Euclidean (left) and approximate geodesic (right) distance matrices, with vertical jitter added for clarity. The bottom two cells show the result of applying two-dimensional linear MDS the Euclidean (left) and approximate geodesic (right) distance matrices. Further analysis is given in the text.

This is illustrated in [Figure 11.9](#c11.xhtml#figure11-9) using a variation of the simplex dataset of [Section 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11_2). The *simplex-edges dataset* consists of 1000 points *x*[1], …, *x*[1000] in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0124.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>64</mn></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0124.gif), and was constructed as follows. An equilateral, 64-dimensional simplex with side length 1 was specified, and its 65 vertices labeled *v*[1], …, *v*[65]. For each *i* ∈ {1, …, 1000}, an index *j* was drawn uniformly at random from the set {1, …, 64}, and *x[i]* was drawn uniformly at random from the edge of the simplex \[*v[j]*, *v*[*j* + 1]\]. This dataset lies within a simple polygonal path through the edges of the simplex, which we will think of as a one-dimensional manifold (perhaps imagining that the corners of the path have been slightly rounded). In [Figure 11.9](#c11.xhtml#figure11-9), data points are colored so that data on each edge is the same color, and the colors corresponding to the edges form a rainbow as the polygonal arc is traced from *v*[1] to *v*[65].

The top three cells of [Figure 11.9](#c11.xhtml#figure11-9) illustrate the matrix of Euclidean distances between all pairs of points in the simplex-edges dataset, the matrix of true geodesic distance within the manifold, and the matrix of approximate geodesic distances obtained from the isomap algorithm (using the *k*\-nearest-neighbors graph with *k* = 13, the smallest value which resulted in a connected graph). The center two cells show the result of applying one-dimensional linear MDS the Euclidean (left) and approximate geodesic (right) distance matrices, with vertical jitter added for clarity: one-dimensional linear MDS has preserved 3.0% of the Euclidean distance matrix and 99.3% of the approximate geodesic distance matrix, as measured by (11.2). The bottom two cells show the result of applying two-dimensional linear MDS the Euclidean (left) and approximate geodesic (right) distance matrices: two-dimensional linear MDS has preserved 5.9% of the Euclidean distance matrix and 99.5% of the approximate geodesic distance matrix. Working from the Euclidean distance matrix, the first MDS dimension separates a set of edges with a relatively large number of data (colored purple) from a set of edges with a relatively small number of data (colored orange through yellow-green). Working from the approximate geodesic distance matrix, the first MDS dimension has essentially recovered the order of the points along the manifold (isomap plus linear MDS has correctly recovered the fact that the data approximately lie on a one-dimensional manifold in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0125.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mn>64</mn></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0125.gif)).

The strand to the left of the central ring contains sections of Chapter 6 (ensemble design, boosting, and arcing) together with corresponding sections of Chapter 14 (R code for bagging, boosting, and arcing). The “fuzz” at the top of the ring also contains sections of Chapter 4 (classification) near corresponding sections of Chapter 14 (R code). The strand below the central ring shows Chapter 10 (optimization) separated from the rest of the book.](images/c11f010.jpg)

**Figure 11.10** A two-dimensional linear MDS representation of the approximate geodesic distances recovered by the isomap manifold learning algorithm applied to the text dataset. The strand to the left of the central ring contains sections of [Chapter 6](#c06.xhtml) (ensemble design, boosting, and arcing) together with corresponding sections of [Chapter 14](#c14.xhtml) (R code for bagging, boosting, and arcing). The “fuzz” at the top of the ring also contains sections of [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml) (classification) near corresponding sections of [Chapter 14](#c14.xhtml) (R code). The strand below the central ring shows [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml) (optimization) separated from the rest of the book.

The isomap algorithm was applied to the matrix of TF-IDF cosine dissimilarities between all points in the text dataset (using the *k*\-nearest-neighbors graph with *k* = 2, the smallest value which resulted in a connected graph), and a two-dimensional linear MDS representation of the resulting approximate geodesic distance matrix is shown

in [Figure 11.10](#c11.xhtml#figure11-10). In this case, two-dimensional linear MDS has preserved 34.8% of the approximate geodesic distance matrix, as measured by (11.2).

### 11.3.11 Autoencoders

This section describes a rather clever idea for training deep neural networks which has led to a way of finding useful lower-dimensional representations of high-dimensional data. Originating with the work of Hinton and Salakhutdinov (2006), it has led to the dramatic increase in research and application of neural networks since about 2007.

Suppose that feature space <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0126.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0126.gif). This may occur naturally, or it may occur by transforming real feature space in some way.^([17](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0017)) Consider a single-hidden-layer neural network, where the output layer *T* consists of *m* nodes, and both the output layer *T* and the *N*\-node hidden layer *Z* consist of neurons (this is slightly different from the networks in [Section 4.7](#c04.xhtml#c4_7), where the output layer consisted of linear functions). In the notation of [Section 4.7](#c04.xhtml#c4_7), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0055" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0056.gif"><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mspace width="4pt"/><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mspace width="4pt"/><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0056.gif)

and <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0056" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0057.gif"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mspace width="4pt"/><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mspace width="4pt"/><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0057.gif)

The neural network is a map <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0127.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>&#x2192;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0127.gif).

Observing that first layer’s matrix of parameters θ^((1))[⋆] is *N* × *m* and the second layer’s matrix of parameters θ^((2))[⋆] is *m* × *N*, the following constraint can be placed on the parameters: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0057" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0058.gif"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>&#x2605;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0058.gif)

The other parameters, θ^((1))[0] and θ^((2))[0], are unconstrained. Thus the free parameters of this neural network are the full matrix θ^((1)) and the *m*\-long vector θ^((2))[0].

Let *d* be any dissimilarity measure on elements of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0128.gif"><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></math>![](images/c11_ILM0128.gif).^([18](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0018)) A *single-hidden-layer autoencoder* is a neural network of the type just described, with the parameters chosen to make the outputs match the inputs as closely as possible, with respect to the dissimilarity measure *d*, on a given dataset. That is, the free parameters θ^((1)) and θ^((2))[0] are chosen to minimize <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0058" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0059.gif"><mrow><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0059.gif)

In other words, the network is trained to approximate the identity function at the training data *x*[1], …, *x[n]* (and presumably also nearby the training data). A single-hidden-layer autoencoder is illustrated in [Figure 11.11](#c11.xhtml#figure11-11).

Using the estimated parameters <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0129.gif"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></math>![](images/c11_ILM0129.gif), a set of intermediate vectors *z*[1], …, *z[n]* ∈ \[0, 1\]^(*N*) is computed from the set of input vectors *x*[1], …, *x[n]* ∈ \[0, 1\]^(*m*), <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0059" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0060.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x2605;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mspace width="1.em"/><mi> for </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0060.gif)

The *N*\-long vectors *z*[1], …, *z[n]* represent the state of the hidden layer *Z* when the *m*\-long observed feature vectors *x*[1], …, *x[n]* are fed through the network. A new single-hidden-layer autoencoder can be trained on the intermediate vectors *z*[1], …, *z[n]*.

![Figure 11.11 A single-hidden-layer autoencoder. The N-long hidden layer is Z = σ(θ(1)0 + θ(1)⋆X) and the m-long top layer is T = σ(θ(2)0 + θ(2)⋆Z). Values for parameter matrices θ(1) and θ(2) are sought which minimize ∑ni = 1d(xi, T(xi)) subject to the constraint θ(2)⋆ = (θ(1)⋆)T, where d is some dissimilarity measure on feature space.](images/c11f011.jpg)

**Figure 11.11** A single-hidden-layer autoencoder. The *N*\-long hidden layer is *Z* = σ(θ^((1))[0] + θ^((1))[⋆]*X*) and the *m*\-long top layer is *T* = σ(θ^((2))[0] + θ^((2))[⋆]*Z*). Values for parameter matrices θ^((1)) and θ^((2)) are sought which minimize ∑^(*n*)[*i* = 1]*d*(*x[i]*, *T*(*x[i]*)) subject to the constraint θ^((2))[⋆] = (θ^((1))[⋆])^T, where *d* is some dissimilarity measure on feature space.

This process can be iterated *k* times, according to the steps shown in [Figure 11.12](#c11.xhtml#figure11-12). The result, when *k* > 1, is called a *deep autoencoder* and is illustrated in [Figure 11.13](#c11.xhtml#figure11-13). The deep autoencoder has hidden layers *Z*^((1)), *Z*^((2)), …, *Z*^((*k* − 1)), *Z*^((*k*)), *Z*^((*k* + 1)), …, *Z*^((2*k* − 1)) of respective lengths *N*^((1)), *N*^((2)), …, *N*^((*k* − 1)), *N*^((*k*)), *N*^((*k* − 1)), …, *N*^((2)), *N*^((1))—the symmetry is a natural result of the iterative process, due to hidden layers *Z*^((*j*)) and *Z*^((2*k* − *j*)) being constructed at the *j*th iteration. Typically *N*^((1)) > *m* (*N*^((1)) ≈ 2*m* is a popular choice) and *N*^((1)) ⩾ *N*^((2)) ⩾ … ⩾ *N*^((*k*)), with *N*^((*k*)) ≪ *m*.

![Figure 11.12 Iteration of a single-hidden-layer autoencoder to train a deep autoencoder.](images/c11f012.jpg)

**Figure 11.12** Iteration of a single-hidden-layer autoencoder to train a deep autoencoder.

![Figure 11.13 A (2k − 1)-hidden-layer “deep” autoencoder. First, parameter matrices θ(j) and θ(2k − j) are obtained sequentially for j = 1, …, k, by training a single-hidden-layer autoencoder on Z(j − 1) (where Z(0) = X). Using the resulting parameters as an initial state, values for parameter matrices θ(1), …, θ(2k) are sought which minimize ∑ni = 1d(xi, T(xi)), without constraints, where d is a given dissimilarity measure on feature space. The resulting function  given by X↦Z(k) yields a lower-dimensional representation of feature space when N(k) < m.](images/c11f013.jpg)

**Figure 11.13** A (2*k* − 1)-hidden-layer “deep” autoencoder. First, parameter matrices θ^((*j*)) and θ^((2*k* − *j*)) are obtained sequentially for *j* = 1, …, *k*, by training a single-hidden-layer autoencoder on *Z*^((*j* − 1)) (where *Z*^((0)) = *X*). Using the resulting parameters as an initial state, values for parameter matrices θ^((1)), …, θ^((2*k*)) are sought which minimize ∑^(*n*)[*i* = 1]*d*(*x[i]*, *T*(*x[i]*)), without constraints, where *d* is a given dissimilarity measure on feature space. The resulting function <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0130.gif"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#x2192;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0130.gif)given by *X*↦*Z*^((*k*)) yields a lower-dimensional representation of feature space when *N*^((*k*)) < *m*.

Having trained a deep autoencoder, the map <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0131.gif"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#x2192;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0131.gif)given by *X*↦*Z*^((*k*)) can be viewed as a lower-dimensional representation of feature space <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0132.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0132.gif). If, overall, the deep autoencoder does a good job at minimizing its objective function, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0060" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0061.gif"><mrow><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0061.gif)

then the set of intermediate states <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0133.gif"><mrow><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0133.gif), which constitutes an *N*^((*k*))\-dimensional representation of the data *x*[1], …, *x[n]*, must contain sufficient information about these original feature vectors to nearly reconstruct them (at least, as far as dissimilarity measure *d* can tell) via the map <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0134.gif"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></msup><mo>&#x2192;</mo><msup><mrow><mo>\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0134.gif)given by *Z*^((*k*))↦*T*. Approximate reconstruction of the original feature vectors in this sense (essentially, compression) is the criterion which can be viewed as motivating deep autoencoders.

Deep autoencoders were originally developed to enable the training of *deep neural networks* (networks with many hidden layers) as follows. To construct a neural network with *k* hidden layers, first a (2*k* − 1)-hidden-layer autoencoder is constructed. The top *k* − 1 hidden layers, *Z*^((*k* + 1)), …, *Z*^((2*k*)), are discarded and the bottom *k* hidden layers, *Z*^((1)), …, *Z*^((*k*)), are retained. A new, linear output layer *T* with *C* nodes is added above the hidden layer *Z*^((*k*)) and, using the trained autoencoder parameters <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0135.gif"><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0135.gif)as an initial state, the entire network is trained as in [Section 4.7](#c04.xhtml#c4_7).^([19](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0019)) A deep neural network is illustrated in [Figure 11.14](#c11.xhtml#figure11-14). Of course, one can use marked training data (*x*[1], *y*[1]), …, (*x[n]*, *y[n]*) to train any classifier on the (marked) transformed feature vectors (*z*^((*k*))[1], *y*[1]), …, (*z*^((*k*))[*n*], *y[n]*), and one can iteratively adapt parameters <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0136.gif"><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0136.gif)to optimize the performance of any classifier.

![Figure 11.14 A k-hidden-layer neural network, constructed by discarding the top (k − 1) hidden layers from the autoencoder of Figure 11.13 and adding a C-node linear output layer. Using the parameter values from the autoencoder as an initial state, the network is trained as described in Section 4.7.](images/c11f014.jpg)

**Figure 11.14** A *k*\-hidden-layer neural network, constructed by discarding the top (*k* − 1) hidden layers from the autoencoder of [Figure 11.13](#c11.xhtml#figure11-13) and adding a *C*\-node linear output layer. Using the parameter values from the autoencoder as an initial state, the network is trained as described in [Section 4.7](#c04.xhtml#c4_7).

## 11.4 Model Regularization

In the context of fitting predictive models to high-dimensional data, one can first find a low-dimensional representation of the data using one of the methods described in [Section 11.3](#c11.xhtml#c11_3) and then fit a predictive model to the low-dimensional representation of the data. Alternatively, one can design methods of predictive modeling which are biased toward producing models which use a small subset of the features. This is done by simultaneously maximizing a measure of model quality (usually maximizing a likelihood function or minimizing some estimate of risk) and minimizing a measure of model complexity, where the measure of model complexity is associated with the number of features actually used by the model.^([20](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0020)) This is known variously as *model regularization*, *parameter penalization*, or *shrinkage*.

The principal tool in model regularization is the addition of a penalty function of the model parameters θ to the objective function describing what makes a modeling technique “good.” In the most general case, a *penalty function* of θ is a function which takes a minimum on some set Ω, and increases as θ moves away from Ω. Intuitively, Ω represents a set of “default” values of θ, and the penalty function describes one’s willingness (or unwillingness) to accept values of θ outside of Ω in the face of evidence derived from data. Explicit connection between penalty functions and prior belief about θ will be made in [Section 11.4.2](#c11.xhtml#c11_4_2).

Consider the case of least-squares linear regression, described in [Chapter 3](#c03.xhtml). Using the squared-error loss function, parameters are chosen to minimize a training estimate of risk, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0061" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0062.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msub><mi> argmin </mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mspace width="4pt"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0062.gif)

In Exercise 3.7 the goal was to show that, in the case of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0137.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mi>&#x03c3;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfenced></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0137.gif)\-distributed residuals, choosing θ to minimize the sum of squared errors is the same as choosing θ to maximize the likelihood of the data. A penalty function commonly applied to a parameter vector θ = (θ[0], θ[1], …, θ[*m*]) is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0062" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0063.gif"><mrow><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0063.gif)

for some constant *p* > 0. In this penalty function, no penalty is applied to the intercept term θ[0], while all other parameters are penalized increasingly as they grow large in absolute value: the penalty function is minimal on the set <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0138.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03a9;</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>{</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>:</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0138.gif). Using this penalty function, *penalized least-squares regression* chooses parameters which minimize a weighted sum of the training risk and the penalty function, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0063" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0064.gif"><mrow><mspace width="-18.0pt"/><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msub><mi> argmin </mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

<a href="#c11-disp-0063-3"></a>(11.3)![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0064.gif)

where weight parameter λ is chosen to minimize the estimated risk of the penalized model.

In logistic regression, parameters are chosen to maximize the log-likelihood of the data <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0064" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0065.gif"><mrow><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>T</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0065.gif)

which corresponds to the case where, for each *i*, *Y[i]* is drawn from the multinomial distribution on {1, …, *C*} with probabilities <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c11\_ILM0139.gif"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c11_ILM0139.gif). In Exercise 4.11 the goal was to show that choosing θ to maximize this likelihood function is the same as choosing θ to minimize the training estimate of risk with respect to cross-entropy loss. Using the same penalty function as above, *penalized logistic regression* chooses parameters which minimize a weighted sum of the training risk and the penalty function, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0065" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0066.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msub><mi> argmin </mi><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mo>-</mo><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

<a href="#c11-disp-0065-4"></a>(11.4)![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0066.gif)

where weight parameter λ is chosen to minimize the estimated risk of the penalized model.

### 11.4.1 Duality and the Geometry of Parameter Penalization

In some cases there is a useful duality between optimization of a penalized function with no constraints and optimization of an unpenalized function with inequality constraints. For example, for any given *p* ⩾ 1 and λ ⩾ 0, parameter estimation in penalized least-squares regression is performed by solving the unconstrained optimization problem <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0066" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0067.gif"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="monospace">minimize</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext mathvariant="monospace">over</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mtext>:</mtext><mspace width="1.em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><msup><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#x03bb;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0067.gif)

which is equivalent to the constrained optimization problem <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c11-disp-0067" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c11\_M0068.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="monospace">minimize</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext mathvariant="monospace">over</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mtext>:</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mspace width="1.em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>-</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mtext mathvariant="monospace">subject</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext mathvariant="monospace">to:</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mspace width="1.em"/><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup><mo>&#x2264;</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c11_M0068.gif)

The upper bound *c* in the constrained problem depends on the penalty parameter λ in the unconstrained problem. A similar example appears in [Section 4.9](#c04.xhtml#c4_9), in the context of support vector machines.
