accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></msub></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi mathvariant="monospace">edatDF</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mrow><mi> test </mi><mi> feature </mi><mi> vectors </mi><mo>(</mo></mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="4pt"/><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi> data </mi><mi> frame </mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></msub></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">edat</mi><mo>\[</mo><mo>,</mo><mn mathvariant="monospace">3</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> test </mi><mi> class </mi><mi> labels </mi></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></msub></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi mathvariant="monospace">nc</mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> number </mi><mi> of </mi><mi> classes </mi></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mi>C</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0003.gif)

In the R code which follows, each method will be applied to test data, producing an R vector pred.class of predicted class labels. The following function compares a vector of predicted class labels for the test data to the true labels, and reports the test estimate of risk, plus or minus one standard deviation.

```

risk.test = function(pred.class) {
 err = sum(as.numeric(pred.class)!=edat[,3]);
 p = err/ne; sd = round(sqrt(p*(1-p)/ne),4); p = round(p,4);
 print(paste(“test estimate of risk:”,p,“+/-”,sd));
}
```

## 14.4 The Bayes Classifier ([Section 4.1](#c04.xhtml#c4_1))

Under 0–1 loss, with a uniform prior probability distribution on class labels, the Bayes classifier predicts that a feature vector *X* has the class which maximizes the conditional likelihood <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0011.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0011.gif), that is, the Bayes classifier predicts <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0003" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0004.gif"><mrow><msub><mi> argmax </mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mfenced></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0004.gif)

(this statement is Exercise 4.2). The Bayes classifier is implemented by three R functions. Function bayes.lik.one() inputs a feature vector *x* and a mean μ, and returns the likelihood function of the Gaussian distribution with mean μ and unit covariance matrix, evaluated at *x*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0004" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0005.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0005.gif)

```

bayes.lik.one = function(x,mu) { return(exp(-0.5*(x-mu)%*%
(x-mu))/(2*pi)); }
```

Function bayes.lik.mix() inputs a feature vector *x*, a matrix of means <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0005" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0006.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mi>J</mi></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0006.gif)

and vector of non-negative weights *w* = (*w*[1], …, *w[J]*), and returns the likelihood function of the Gaussian mixture distribution with means given by the rows of μ, unit covariance matrices, and weights *w*, evaluated at *x*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0006" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0007.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>J</mi></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0007.gif)

```

bayes.lik.mix = function(x,mu,w) {
 liks.one = apply(mu,1,bayes.lik.one,x=x);
 return(sum(w*liks.one));
}
```

The first line of bayes.lik.mix() applies the function bayes.lik.one() to each row of the input matrix mu, producing the *J*\-long vector <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0007" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0008.gif"><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mi>J</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mi>J</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mstyle></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0008.gif)

The second line multiplies this vector coordinatewise by the vector of weights (*w*[1], …, *w[J]*) and returns the sum of the resulting *J* numbers. The number of mixture components *J* is not explicitly specified in the R code because it is carried by the dimension of the input matrix mu and the length of the input vector w.

The Bayes classifier applies function bayes.lik.mix() at a given point *x*, using each set of three means corresponding to each of the three classes, with equal mixture weights in each case. Function bayes.predict() outputs the class^([4](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0003)) corresponding to a Gaussian mixture model which produces maximal likelihood at *x*.

```

bayes.predict.one = function(x) {
 liks.mix = c( bayes.lik.mix(x,mus[1:3,],rep(1/3,3)),
  bayes.lik.mix(x,mus[4:6,],rep(1/3,3)),
  bayes.lik.mix(x,mus[7:9,],rep(1/3,3)) );
 return(max.col(t(liks.mix)));
}
bayes.predict.many = function(x) { return(apply(x,1,
bayes.predict.one)); }
```

Note that the constant <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0012.gif"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![](images/c14_ILM0012.gif)in bayes.lik.one() has no effect on the Bayes classifier, and can be omitted to save work, as can the value <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0013.gif"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></math>![](images/c14_ILM0013.gif)for the equal weights of the mixture components in each Gaussian mixture in bayes.lik.mix(). The Bayes risk can be estimated by applying the Bayes classifier to the test data:

```

pred.class = bayes.predict.many(edat[,1:2]);
risk.test(pred.class);
```

## 14.5 Quadratic Discriminant Analysis ([Section 4.4.1](#c04.xhtml#c4_4_1))

A quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA) model is fit using the function qda() in the MASS library:

```

library(MASS);
m = qda(as.factor(tdat[,3])˜.,data=tdatDF,method=“mle”);
```

Fitting the model is equivalent to computing the mean and covariance of the training data for each class separately. The estimated mean for each class is saved as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0010" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0011.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>bad hbox</mtext></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0011.gif)

for *c* = 1, …, *C*. Instead of saving the estimated covariance matrices for each class, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0014.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>C</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0014.gif), the qda() function saves the Cholesky factors^([5](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0004)) of the inverse covariance matrices. That is, qda() computes and saves triangular matrices <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0011" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0012.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>bad hbox</mtext><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0012.gif)

where <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0015.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0015.gif), for *c* = 1, …, *C*. This is done for computation of the likelihood function at any point *x* under the fitted model: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0012" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0013.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c6;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0013.gif)

Predictions using the fitted model m are made on the test data using the function predict(), and the predictions can be compared to the true class labels of the test data to produce the test estimate of risk.

```

pred.class = predict(m,edatDF)$class;
risk.test(pred.class);
```

## 14.6 Linear Discriminant Analysis ([Section 4.4.2](#c04.xhtml#c4_4_2))

A linear discriminant analysis (LDA) model is fit using the function lda() in the MASS library:

```

library(MASS);
m = lda(as.factor(tdat[,3])˜.,data=tdatDF,method=“mle”);
```

As with qda(), the estimated mean for each class is saved in m$means. The function returns a not-necessarily-triangular matrix <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0013" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0014.gif"><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">scaling</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0014.gif)

with the property that <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0016.gif"><mrow><mi>W</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>W</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0016.gif). Predictions using the fitted model m are made on the test data using the function predict(), exactly as for QDA,

```

pred.class = predict(m,edatDF)$class;
risk.test(pred.class);
```

## 14.7 Gaussian Mixture Models ([Section 4.4.3](#c04.xhtml#c4_4_3))

A Gaussian mixture model is fit using the function MclustDA() in the mclust library.

```

library(mclust);
```

The number of mixture components used for each class is represented by a vector (*J*[1], …, *J[C]*), which is user-specified. In [Section 4.4](#c04.xhtml#c4_4), we considered using either two mixture components for each class or three mixture components for each class,

```

J = c(2,2,2);
```

or

```

J = c(3,3,3);
```

Given J, the model is fit by calling

```

m = MclustDA(tdat[,1:2],tdat[,3],G=as.integer(J),
modelNames=“VVV”);
```

Fitting the model is equivalent to, for each class *c* = 1, …, *C*, finding weights <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0017.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0017.gif), means <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0018.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0018.gif), and covariance matrices <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0019.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mrow><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0019.gif)which approximately maximize the likelihood <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0014" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0015.gif"><mrow><munderover><mo>&#x220f;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>J</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi><msub><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msub><msup><mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><msubsup><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0015.gif)

This is done using the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm, as described^([6](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0005)) in [Section 10.7](#c10.xhtml#c10_7). The string argument modelNames=”VVV” indicates that no constraints are placed on the covariance matrices in the search for optimal parameters.

The estimated weights, means, and covariances for each class *c* = 1, …, *C* and each mixture component *j* = 1, …, *J[c]*, are saved as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0015" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0016.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mo>"</mo></mrow><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>"</mo><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">parameters</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">pro</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mo>"</mo></mrow><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>"</mo><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">parameters</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">mean</mi><mo>\[</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03a3;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mo>"</mo></mrow><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>"</mo><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">parameters</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">variance</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">sigma</mi><mo>\[</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>\]</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0016.gif)

Cholesky factors of the estimated covariance matrices are also saved, with cholsigma in place of sigma in the last line above. Predictions using the fitted model m are made on the test data using the function predict(),

```

pred.class = as.numeric(predict(m,edat[,1:2])$class);
risk.test(pred.class);
```

## 14.8 Kernel Density Estimation ([Section 4.4.4](#c04.xhtml#c4_4_4))

Kernel density estimation begins with a kernel function. In [Section 4.4](#c04.xhtml#c4_4), the Gaussian kernel was defined as

```

K = function(x) { return(exp(-0.5*x%*%x)); }
```

and the Epanechnikov kernel was defined as

```

K = function(x) { return(max(0,length(x)+4-x%*%x)); }
```

In the code above, the normalization constant <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0020.gif"><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup></math>![](images/c14_ILM0020.gif)has been omitted from the Gaussian kernel and the normalization constant <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0021.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x0393;</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>&#x03c0;</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0021.gif)has been omitted from the Epanechnikov kernel because these constants do not affect predictions made by the KDE classifier.

Function kde.liks() inputs a point <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0022.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0022.gif), a set of *k* points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0023.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c14_ILM0023.gif)stored as the rows of a *k* × *m* matrix <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0016" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0017.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">dat</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0017.gif)

and a bandwidth parameter *h*, and computes the kernel density estimate of a likelihood function at *x*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0017" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0018.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>k</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></munderover><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>h</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>K</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0018.gif)

```

kde.liks = function(x,dat,h) {
 v = t(x-t(dat))/h;
 liks = apply(v,1,K);
 return(mean(h∧-dim(dat)[2]*liks));
}
```

The first line of kde.liks() computes the vector <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0018" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0019.gif"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">dat</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">dat</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0019.gif)

and the second line applies the kernel function *K* to this vector coordinatewise, computing <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0019" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0020.gif"><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi>K</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">dat</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">dat</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0020.gif)

The third line scales each coordinate of this vector by *h*^(− *m*), sums the entries of the resulting *k*\-long vector, and divides by *k*.

Function kde.predict.one() inputs a point <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0024.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0024.gif), a set of *n* points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0025.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c14_ILM0025.gif)stored as the rows of a *n* × *m* matrix datx, an *n*\-long vector of class labels <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0026.gif"><mi mathvariant="monospace">daty</mi></math>![](images/c14_ILM0026.gif)in the range 1, …, *C*, and an *C*\-long vector of bandwidths *h* = (*h*[1], …, *h[C]*). In the first line, it estimates the prior (marginal) distribution of class labels based on the counts of vector daty, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0020" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0021.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>&#x221d;</mo><mo>|</mo><mo>{</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>:</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">daty</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>\]</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>}</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0021.gif)

for *c* = 1, …, *C*. In the second and third lines, it computes kernel density estimates of the likelihood function of data for each class, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0021" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0022.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msubsup></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>K</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0022.gif)

for *c* = 1, …, *C*. In the fourth line it predicts a class with maximal posterior probability, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0022" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0023.gif"><mrow><msub><mi> argmax </mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mi> argmax </mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mfenced><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0023.gif)

```

kde.predict.one = function(x,datx,daty,h) {
 t = table(daty); priors = t/sum(t);
 liks = vector(“numeric”,nc);
 for(cc in 1:nc) {
  liks[cc] = kde.liks(x,datx[daty==cc,],h[cc]); }
 return(max.col(t(priors*liks)));
}
```

Selecting a KDE classifier means selecting a vector of bandwidths *h* = (*h*[1], …, *h[C]*) to optimize some estimate of risk. Function kde.loo.one() inputs a *n* × *m* matrix of feature vectors datx, an *n*\-long vector of class labels daty, a *C*\-long vector of bandwidths *h*, and an index *o* in the set {1, …, *n*}. It predicts the class of the *o*th datum using the KDE classifier with the bandwidth vector *h* and all data except the *o*th. It then compares the prediction to the true class, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0027.gif"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">daty</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>o</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0027.gif). It returns the R Boolean value TRUE (numeric value 1) if the KDE classifier made an incorrect prediction, and returns the R Boolean value FALSE (numeric value 0) if the KDE classifier made the correct prediction.

```

kde.loo.one = function(datx,daty,h,o) {
 pred = kde.predict.one(datx[o,],datx[-o,],daty[-o],h);
 return(pred!=daty[o]);
}
```

Function kde.loo.all() applies the function kde.loo.one() with each datum held out in turn, and returns the average number of times the KDE classifier made an incorrect prediction: that is, kde.loo.all() computes the leave-one-out cross-validation estimate of risk under 0–1 loss for a KDE classifier using a given vector of bandwidths *h* and given training data datx and daty.

```

kde.loo.all = function(datx,daty,h) {
 errs = sapply(1:dim(datx)[1],kde.loo.one,datx=datx,
  daty=daty,h=h);
 return(mean(errs));
}
```

Introducing the constraint that all bandwidths be equal, *h*[1] = ⋅⋅⋅ = *h[C]*, which seems reasonable in the running example of [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml), bandwidth selection is reduced to a one-dimensional optimization. [Figure 14.2](#c14.xhtml#figure14-2) shows leave-one-out risk estimates for various bandwidths, for both the Gaussian and Epanechnikov kernel. The plots in [Figure 14.2](#c14.xhtml#figure14-2) suggest that any bandwidth roughly in the range \[0.3, 1.2\] might be equally good, and that from a risk perspective there is not much reason to choose the Gaussian kernel over the Epanechnikov kernel.

```

hcol = c(0.01,0.05,seq(0.1,1.5,0.05),2:5);
hmat = cbind(hcol,hcol,hcol);
errs = apply(hmat,1,kde.loo.all,datx=tdat[,1:2],
 daty=tdat[,3]);
plot(hcol,errs,xlab=“Bandwidth”,ylab=“Estimated Risk”,
 type=“l”,ylim=c(0,0.4*1.05));
```

![Figure 14.2 Leave-one-out cross-validated estimates of the risk of the kernel density estimate classifier as a function of the bandwidth h = h1 = h2 = h3 used for each class.](images/c14f002.jpg)

[**Figure 14.2**](#c14.xhtml#figureanchor14-2) Leave-one-out cross-validated estimates of the risk of the kernel density estimate classifier as a function of the bandwidth *h* = *h*[1] = *h*[2] = *h*[3] used for each class.

One need not accept the constraint *h*[1] = ⋅⋅⋅ = *h[C]*, and could instead search for a vector of bandwidths (*h*[1], …, *h[C]*) which minimizes the leave-one-out cross-validated estimate of risk, using an optimization method such as the Nelder–Mead algorithm (described in [Section 10.2](#c10.xhtml#c10_2)). This is done by the R function optim(), starting from a user-specified point (starting from *h* = (0.8, 0.8, 0.8) in the code below).

```
library(stats);
optim(rep(0.8,3),kde.loo.all,method=“Nelder-Mead”,
datx=tdat[,1:2],daty=tdat[,3]);
```

In this example, over many starts, Nelder–Mead tends to reach optima roughly in the region *h* ∈ \[0.3, 1.2\]³, and if Nelder–Mead is started at a value in this box then it quickly becomes stuck in a local optimum close to its starting point. This suggests that the objective function (the leave-one-out cross-validation estimate of risk) is sufficiently noisy that there is little or no information to allow us to choose among bandwidth vectors in this region.

Classifiers are often applied to predict the class of more than one point at a time. Function kde.predict.many() is an efficient way to apply kde.predict.one() to many input points at once. The feature vectors to be classified are stored as the rows of the input matrix x.

```

kde.predict.many = function(x,datx,daty,h) {
 return(apply(x,1,kde.predict.one,datx=datx,daty=daty,h=h));
}
```

For example, kde.predict.many() could be used to compute the test estimate of the KDE classifier’s risk:

```

pred.class = kde.predict.many(edat[,1:2],tdat[,1:2],tdat[,3],
rep(0.5,3));
risk.test(pred.class);
```

## 14.9 Histograms ([Section 4.4.5](#c04.xhtml#c4_4_5))

Given a feature vector *x* = (*x*[1], …, *x[m]*), and a *C* × *m* matrix of bandwidth parameters <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0023" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0024.gif"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd/><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0024.gif)

the rectangle <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0028.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2282;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0028.gif)which contains *x*, for each class *c* = 1, …, *C*, can be found by setting ^([7](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0001aa)) <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0024" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0025.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="&#x230a;" close="&#x230b;"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0025.gif)

for all *j* = 1, …, *m* (here, ⌊*r*⌋ represents the integer floor of a real number *r*). The key to implementing a histogram classifier is constructing an efficient function which inputs a feature vector *x* and outputs the number of training data in the class-*c* rectangle *R[c]*(*i*[1], …, *i[m]*) which contains *x*, for each class *c* = 1, …, *C*. One way to do this, which in many cases is efficient, is by constructing a hash table.

For the present purpose, a *hash table* can be thought of as an array where the index, instead of being a non-negative (or positive) integer, is an element of an arbitrary discrete set.^([8](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0006)) The indices of a hash table are called the *keys* of the hash table, and the entries indexed by the keys are the *values* of the hash table.^([9](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0007)) Hash tables are implemented in the R library hash.

```

library(hash);
```

Selecting a histogram classifier is done by three functions: hist.key(), hist.insert(), and hist.train(). These functions create and operate on an R data structure (specifically, an R list) which has the following components:

1.  HT\[\[1\]\], … , HT\[\[*C*\]\]—a list of *C* hash tables, one for each class;
2.  HT$h—the *C* × *m* matrix of bandwidth parameters, *h*;
3.  HT$iv—a vector (*V*(*R*[1])^(–1),…,*V*(*R*[*C*])^(–1)) of reciprocals of cell volumes;
4.  HT$prior—the marginal distribution of class labels which occur in the training data.

The data structure HT will be a global variable and will not be explicitly passed in and out of the R functions which operate on it.

Function hist.key() inputs a feature vector *x* and a class label *c*, and outputs the index (*i*[1], …, *i[m]*) of the class-*c* rectangle *R[c]*(*i*[1], …, *i[m]*) which contains *x*. In the output of hist.key(), the index (*i*[1], …, *i[m]*) is represented as a string (class “character” in R): this string of characters will be used as a key in a hash table which will be constructed in the function hist.train().

```

hist.key = function(datx,cc) {
 bins = floor(as.numeric(datx)/HT$h[cc,]);
 return(deparse(bins));
}
```

Function hist.insert() inputs a feature vector and class label pair (*x*, *y*). In the second line, it calls hist.key() to find the index (*i*[1], …, *i[m]*) of the class-*y* rectangle *R[y]*(*i*[1], …, *i[m]*) which contains *x*. In the third and fourth lines, if no previous feature vector of class *y* has landed in *R[y]*(*i*[1], …, *i[m]*), then hist.insert() creates an entry in the class-*y* hash table recording that one feature vector has landed in *R[y]*(*i*[1], …, *i[m]*), and otherwise it increments the count of the class-*y* feature vectors landing in *R[y]*(*i*[1], …, *i[m]*) by one.

```

hist.insert = function(dat) {
 datx = dat[1:(length(dat)-1)]; daty = dat[length(dat)];
 key = hist.key(datx,daty);
 if(has.key(key,HT[[daty]])==FALSE) { HT[[daty]][key]=HT$iv[daty]; }
 else { HT[[daty]][key]=values(HT[[daty]][key])+HT$iv[daty]; }
}
```

Function hist.train() inputs a set of *n* points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0030.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c14_ILM0030.gif)stored as the rows of a *n* × *m* matrix datx, an *n*\-long vector of class labels daty in the range 1, …, *C*, and a *C* × *m* matrix of bandwidths *h*, and produces a trained histogram classifier by first creating the necessary hash tables, then processing every training point (*x*, *y*) in the appropriate hash table using hist.insert(), and finally computing the empirical distribution of class labels and storing it in HT$prior.

```

hist.train = function(datx,daty,h) {
 HT <<- vector(“list”,nc); HT$h <<- h;
 for(cc in 1:nc) { HT[[cc]] <<-hash(); };
 HT$iv <<– 1/apply(HT$h,1,prod);
 apply(cbind(datx,daty),1,hist.insert);
 HT$prior <<- as.numeric(table(daty)/length(daty));
}
```

The trained histogram classifier is HT, the structure which contains *C* hash tables, the bandwidth matrix, and the marginal distribution of classes.

Making predictions with a trained histogram classifier is done with four functions: hist.lookup(), hist.post(), hist.predict.one(), and hist.predict.many(). Function hist.lookup() inputs a feature vector *x* and a class label *y*, and returns the number of training data of class *y* which fall in the class-*y* rectangle which contains *x*. It does this by computing the index (*i*[1], …, *i[m]*) of the class-*y* rectangle which contains *x* in the first line. If this index does not occur as a key in the class-*y* hash table, hist.lookup() returns the value 0 because the absence of this index as a key in the hash table indicates that no class-*y* training data fall in *R[y]*(*i*[1], …, *i[m]*). Otherwise, (*i*[1], …, *i[m]*) occurs as a key in the class-*y* hash table, and hist.lookup() returns the value associated with the key, which is the number of class-*y* training data in the rectangle, |{*j*: *y[j]* = *y* and *x[j]* ∈ *R[y]*(*i*[1], …, *i[m]*)}|.

```

hist.lookup = function(datx,daty) {
 key = hist.key(datx,daty);
 if(has.key(key,HT[[daty]])==FALSE) { return(0); }
 return(as.numeric(values(HT[[daty]][key])));
}
```

Function hist.post() inputs a feature vector *x* and returns the number of training data which occur in the class-*c* rectangle containing *x* for each class *c* = 1, …, *C*. This is proportional to the histogram classifier’s estimate of the posterior distribution <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0031.gif"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0031.gif)by Exercise 4.8. If there is a tie among classes with maximal posterior probability (which happens if no training data fall in any rectangle containing *x*), it is broken by the prior distribution on classes.

```

hist.post = function(datx) {
 posterior = sapply(1:nc,hist.lookup,datx=datx);
 idx = which(posterior==max(posterior));
 if(length(idx)>1) { posterior=rep(0,nc);
  posterior[idx]=HT$prior[idx]; }
 return(posterior);
}
```

Selecting a histogram classifier means selecting a matrix of bandwidths *h* to optimize some estimate of risk. Function hist.loo.one() inputs a *n* × *m* matrix of feature vectors datx, an *n*\-long vector of class labels daty, a *C* × *m* matrix of bandwidths *h*, and an index *o* in the set {1, …, *n*}. It predicts the class of the *o*th datum using the histogram classifier with the bandwidth matrix *h* and all data except the *o*th. It then compares the prediction to the true class, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0032.gif"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">daty</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>o</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0032.gif). It returns the R Boolean value TRUE (numeric value 1) if the histogram classifier made an incorrect prediction, and returns the R Boolean value FALSE (numeric value 0) if the histogram classifier made the correct prediction.

```

hist.loo.one = function(datx,daty,o) {
 posterior = hist.post(datx[o,]);
 posterior[daty[o]] = posterior[daty[o]]-1;
 pred = max.col(t(posterior));
 return(pred!=daty[o]);
}
```

Function hist.loo.all() applies the function hist.loo.one() with each datum held out in turn, and returns the average number of times the histogram classifier made an incorrect prediction: that is, hist.loo.all() computes the leave-one-out cross-validation estimate of risk under 0–1 loss for a histogram classifier using a given vector of bandwidths *h* and given training data datx and daty.

```

hist.loo.all = function(datx,daty,h) {
 hist.train(datx,daty,h);
 errs = sapply(1:dim(datx)[1],hist.loo.one,datx=datx,
  daty=daty);
 return(mean(errs));
}
```

Introducing the constraint that all bandwidths be equal, *h*[1, 1] = ⋅⋅⋅ = *h*[*C*, *m*], which seems reasonable in the running example of [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml), bandwidth selection is reduced to a one-dimensional optimization. [Figure 14.3](#c14.xhtml#figure14-3) shows leave-one-out risk estimates for various bandwidths. The plot in [Figure 14.3](#c14.xhtml#figure14-3) suggests that any bandwidth roughly in the range \[1.5, 2\] might be equally good.

![Figure 14.3 Leave-one-out cross-validated estimates of the risk of the histogram classifier, as a function of the common bandwidth used for each feature and each class. Bandwidth is an m × C matrix h, but we have added the constraint that its entries are all equal to each other.](images/c14f003.jpg)

[**Figure 14.3**](#c14.xhtml#figureanchor14-3) Leave-one-out cross-validated estimates of the risk of the histogram classifier, as a function of the common bandwidth used for each feature and each class. Bandwidth is an *m* × *C* matrix *h*, but we have added the constraint that its entries are all equal to each other.

Function hist.predict.one inputs a feature vector *x* and predicts a class with maximal posterior probability based on the trained histogram classifier. Function hist.predict.many inputs a *k* × *m* matrix of feature vectors and predicts a class for each.

```

hist.predict.one = function(datx) {
 return(max.col(t(hist.post(datx)))); }
hist.predict.many = function(datx) {
 return(apply(datx,1,hist.predict.one)); }
```

Now a histogram classifier with bandwidths *h*[1, 1] = ⋅⋅⋅ = *h*[*C*, *m*] = 2 can be trained, and a test estimate of its risk can be computed:

```

hist.train(tdat[,1:2],tdat[,3],matrix(2.0,3,2));
pred.class = hist.predict.many(edat[,1:2]);
risk.test(pred.class);
```

## 14.10 The Naive Bayes Classifier ([Section 4.4.6](#c04.xhtml#c4_4_6))

Applying the naive Bayes classifier using kernel density estimation for each feature begins with a kernel function. We could use either the Gaussian or Epanechnikov kernel functions as defined in [Section 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14_8), but since the naive Bayes classifier will apply these kernels with scalar rather than vector input x, it is slightly more efficient to use R’s scalar multiplication x\*x rather than R’s vector inner product x%\*%x. Thus we define one-dimensional versions of the Gaussian and Epanechnikov kernel functions,

```

K = function(x) { return(exp(-0.5*x*x));}
```

and

```

K = function(x) { return(max(0,length(x)+4-x*x)); }
```

As in [Section 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14_8), the normalization constant <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0033.gif"><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow></msqrt></math>![](images/c14_ILM0033.gif)has been omitted from the Gaussian kernel and the normalization constant <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0034.gif"><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>20</mn><msqrt><mn>5</mn></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></math>![](images/c14_ILM0034.gif)has been omitted from the Epanechnikov kernel because they do not affect predictions.

Function kde.liks.one() is a one-dimensional specialization of the function kde.liks() in [Section 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14_8): it inputs a point <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0035.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0035.gif), a set of *k* points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0036.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0036.gif)stored in a *k*\-long vector dat, and a bandwidth *h*, and computes the one-dimensional kernel density estimate of a likelihood function at *x*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0025" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0026.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>k</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></munderover><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>h</mi></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>K</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0026.gif)

```

kde.liks.one = function(x,dat,h) {
 v = (x-dat)/h;
 liks = K(v);
 return(mean(h∧-1*liks));
}
```

The first line of kde.liks.one() computes the vector <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0026" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0027.gif"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">dat</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">dat</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0027.gif)

and the second line applies the kernel function *K* to this vector coordinatewise, computing <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0027" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0028.gif"><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi>K</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">dat</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">dat</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0028.gif)

The third line scales each coordinate of this vector by *h*^(− 1), sums the entries of the resulting *k*\-long vector, and divides by *k*.

Function kde.liks.dim() applies kde.liks.one() to one dimension of a multi-dimensional input. Specifically, kde.liks.dim() inputs a point <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0037.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0037.gif), a set of *k* points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0038.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c14_ILM0038.gif)stored as the rows of a *k* × *m* matrix dat, an *m*\-long vector of bandwidths *h* = (*h*[1], …, *h[m]*), and an index *i* ∈ {1, …, *m*}, and outputs the value of kde.liks.one() applied to the *i*th dimension of the inputs (that is, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0039.gif"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">kde</mi><mo>.</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">liks</mi><mo>.</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">dim</mi><mo>(</mo></mrow><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">dat</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">kde</mi><mo>.</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">liks</mi><mo>.</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">one</mi><mo>(</mo></mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">dat</mi><mo>\[</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo>\]</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0039.gif)).

```

kde.liks.dim = function(x,dat,h,i) {
 return(kde.liks.one(x[i],dat[,i],h[i])); }
```

Function nb.kde.liks() inputs a point <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0040.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0040.gif), a set of *k* points in <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0041.gif"><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></math>![](images/c14_ILM0041.gif)stored as the rows of a *k* × *m* matrix dat, and an *m*\-long vector of bandwidths *h* = (*h*[1], …, *h[m]*), and outputs the naive Bayes estimate of a density function, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0028" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0029.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>x</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#x220f;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0029.gif)

by applying kde.liks.dim() to each dimension of the input and multiplying the results.

```

nb.kde.liks = function(x,dat,h) {
 marginal.liks = sapply(1:dim(dat)[2],kde.liks.dim,x=x,
  dat=dat,h=h);
 return(prod(marginal.liks));
}
```

The application of the density estimate to a classifier works exactly as in the KDE classifier of [Section 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14_8), with one exception: where the KDE classifier used a *C*\-long vector of bandwidth parameters *h* = (*h*[1], …, *h[C]*), with bandwidth *h[c]* used to form the density estimate for data of class *c*, the naive Bayes classifier based on one-dimensional KDE uses a *C* × *m* matrix of bandwidth parameters <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0029" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0030.gif"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd/><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0030.gif)

with bandwidth *h*[*c*, *j*] used to form the density estimate of feature *j* for data of class *c* (as for the Histogram classifier of [Section 14.9](#c14.xhtml#c14_9)).

Functions for applying the naive Bayes classifier are essentially the same as functions for applying the KDE classifier in [Section 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14_8). Function nb.kde.predict.one() is identical to function kde.predict.one(), except that the former calls function nb.kde.liks() where the latter calls kde.liks() and a vector of bandwidths (*h*[*c*, 1], …, *h*[*c*, *m*]) is used instead of a scalar bandwidth *h[c]*.

```

nb.kde.predict.one = function(x,datx,daty,h) {
 t = table(daty); priors = t/sum(t);
 liks = vector(“numeric”,nc);
 for(cc in 1:nc) {
  liks[cc] = nb.kde.liks(x,datx[daty==cc,],h[cc,]); }
 return(max.col(t(priors*liks)));
}
```

Functions kde.loo.one(), kde.loo.all(), and kde.predict.many() from [Section 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14_8) can be reused simply by replacing the string “kde” with “nb.kde” everywhere it occurs.

```

nb.kde.loo.one = function(datx,daty,h,o) {
 pred = nb.kde.predict.one(datx[o,],datx[-o,],daty[-o],h);
 return(pred!=daty[o]);
}
 
nb.kde.loo.all = function(datx,daty,h) {
 errs = sapply(1:dim(datx)[1],nb.kde.loo.one,datx=datx,daty=
  daty,h=h);
 return(mean(errs));
}
 
nb.kde.predict.many = function(x,datx,daty,h) {
 return(apply(x,1,nb.kde.predict.one,datx=datx,
  daty=daty,h=h));
}
```

Once a matrix of bandwidths is chosen, nb.kde.predict.many() could be used to compute the test estimate of the naive Bayes classifier’s error rate as follows:

```

pred.class = nb.kde.predict.many(edat[,1:2],tdat[,1:2],
tdat[,3],matrix(0.7,3,2)); risk.test(pred.class);
```

## 14.11 *k*\-Nearest-Neighbor ([Section 4.5.1](#c04.xhtml#c4_5_1))

A *k*\-nearest-neighbor (KNN) classifier is trained using the function knn() in the class library.

```

library(class);
```

Given the training feature vectors tdat\[,1:2\] with associated class labels tdat\[,3\], and given a value of *k*, say

```

k = 9;
```

the *k*\-nearest-neighbor classifier predicts class labels for test feature vectors edat\[,1:2\] in via the function call

```

pred.class = knn(tdat[,1:2],edat[,1:2],tdat[,3],k);
risk.test(pred.class);
```

Selecting a KNN classifier means selecting a number of prototypes *k* to optimize some estimate of risk. Function knn.loo.one() inputs a *n* × *m* matrix of feature vectors datx, an *n*\-long vector of class labels daty, a number of prototypes *k*, and an index *o* in the set {1, …, *n*}. It predicts the class of the *o*th datum using the KNN classifier with *k* prototypes and all data except the *o*th. It then compares the prediction to the true class, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0042.gif"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">daty</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>o</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0042.gif). It returns the R Boolean value TRUE (numeric value 1) if the KNN classifier made an incorrect prediction, and returns the R Boolean value FALSE (numeric value 0) if the KNN classifier made the correct prediction.

```

knn.loo.one = function(datx,daty,k,o) {
 pred = knn(datx[-o,],datx[o,],daty[-o],k);
 return(pred!=daty[o]);
}
```

Function knn.loo.all() applies the function knn.loo.one() with each datum held out in turn, and returns the average number of times the KNN classifier made an incorrect prediction: that is, knn.loo.all() computes the leave-one-out cross-validation estimate of risk under 0–1 loss for a KNN classifier using a given number of prototypes *k* and given training data datx and daty.

```

knn.loo.all = function(datx,daty,k) {
 errs = sapply(1:dim(datx)[1],knn.loo.one,datx=datx,
  daty=daty,k=k);
 return(mean(errs));
}
```

Selecting the number of prototypes is a one-dimensional optimization. The left-hand cell of [Figure 14.4](#c14.xhtml#figure14-4) shows leave-one-out cross-validated risk estimates for various numbers of prototypes. This graph suggests that the number of prototypes should be small (about *k* = 9).

```

ks = 1:100; errs = vector(“numeric”,length(ks));
errs = sapply(ks,knn.loo.all,datx=tdat[,1:2],daty=tdat[,3]);
plot(ks,errs,xlab=“Number of Nearest Neighbors”,
ylab=“Estimated Risk”,type=“l”,ylim=c(0,0.3*1.05));
```

![Figure 14.4 Leave-one-out cross-validated estimates of the risk of the k-nearest-neighbor classifier (left) and the learning vector quantization classifier (right), as functions of the number of nearest neighbors or the number of prototypes per class.](images/c14f004.jpg)

[**Figure 14.4**](#c14.xhtml#figureanchor14-4) Leave-one-out cross-validated estimates of the risk of the *k*\-nearest-neighbor classifier (left) and the learning vector quantization classifier (right), as functions of the number of nearest neighbors or the number of prototypes per class.

## 14.12 Learning Vector Quantization ([Section 4.5.4](#c04.xhtml#c4_5_4))

A learning vector quantization (LVQ) classifier is trained using the functions lvqinit() and olvq1() in the class library.

```

library(class);
```

Given the training feature vectors tdat\[,1:2\] with associated class labels tdat\[,3\], and given a value of the total number of prototypes *k*, say

```

k = 6;
```

the LVQ classifier is initialized by the function call

```

cd1 = lvqinit(tdat[,1:2],tdat[,3],size=k);
```

This function selects a uniform random sample of training points, without replacement, as the initial set of prototypes of each class. The number of prototypes of the *c*th class is <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0043.gif"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0043.gif), rounded to the nearest integer. Since the training data consists of 49, 48, and 53 points of the three classes respectively, setting *k* = 6 results in two prototypes per class. The LVQ classifier is trained, starting from the initial state cd1, by the function call

```

cd2 = olvq1(tdat[,1:2],tdat[,3],cd1,niter=3000*k);
```

It is applied to test data edat using the function lvqtest(),

```

pred.class = lvqtest(cd2,edat[,1:2]);
risk.test(pred.class);
```

The trained LVQ classifier consists of a list of prototypes for each class. For *i* = 1, …, *k*, the feature vector and class label of the *i*th prototype are given by the pair <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0030" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0031.gif"><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">cd</mi><mn mathvariant="monospace">2</mn><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">x</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">cd</mi><mn mathvariant="monospace">2</mn><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">cl</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>\]</mo></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0031.gif)

Training an LVQ classifier means selecting a number of prototypes *k* to optimize some estimate of risk. Function lvq.loo.one() inputs a *n* × *m* matrix of feature vectors datx, an *n*\-long vector of class labels daty, a number of prototypes *k*, and an index *o* in the set {1, …, *n*}. It predicts the class of the *o*th datum using the LVQ classifier with *k* prototypes and all data except the *o*th. It then compares the prediction to the true class, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0044.gif"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">daty</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>o</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0044.gif). It returns the R Boolean value TRUE (numeric value 1) if the LVQ classifier made an incorrect prediction, and returns the R Boolean value FALSE (numeric value 0) if the LVQ classifier made the correct prediction.

```

lvq.loo.one = function(datx,daty,k,o) {
 cd1 = lvqinit(datx[-o,],daty[-o],size=k);
 cd2 = olvq1(datx[-o,],daty[-o],cd1,niter=3000*k);
 pred = lvqtest(cd2,datx[o,]);
 return(pred!=daty[o]);
}
```

Function lvq.loo.all() applies the function lvq.loo.one() with each datum held out in turn, and returns the average number of times the LVQ classifier made an incorrect prediction: that is, lvq.loo.all() computes the leave-one-out cross-validation estimate of risk under 0–1 loss for a LVQ classifier using a given number of prototypes *k* and given training data datx and daty.

```

lvq.loo.all = function(datx,daty,k) {
 errs = sapply(1:dim(datx)[1],lvq.loo.one,datx=datx,
  daty=daty,k=k);
 return(mean(errs));
}
```

Selecting the number of prototypes is a one-dimensional optimization. The right-hand cell of [Figure 14.4](#c14.xhtml#figure14-4) shows leave-one-out risk estimates for various numbers of prototypes. This graph suggests that the number of prototypes should be small (about *k* = 6).

```

ks = 3:20; errs = vector(“numeric”,length(ks));
for(i in 1:length(ks)) {
 errs[i] = lvq.loo.all(tdat[,1:2],tdat[,3],ks[i]);
}
plot(ks,errs,xlab=“Number of Prototypes”,
 ylab=“Estimated Risk”,type=“l”,ylim=c(0,0.3*1.05));
```

<p><math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0045.gif"/><img src="images/c14\_ILM0045.gif" alt=""/></p> 

## 14.13 Logistic Regression ([Section 4.6](#c04.xhtml#c4_6))

For polytimous (*C* > 2) classification, a logistic regression classifier is trained using the function multinom() in the nnet library.^([10](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0008))

```

library(nnet);
```

The logistic regression model is trained by the function call

```

m = multinom(as.factor(tdat[,3])˜.,maxit=10000,data=tdatDF,
MaxNWts=3000);
```

It is applied to test data using the function predict(),

```

pred.class = predict(m,edatDF,type=“class”);
risk.test(pred.class);
```

The logistic regression model assumes that the log-odds in favor of each class *c* relative to a particular reference class (which might as well be class 1) is a linear function of the feature vectors, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley"
