close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0032.gif)

Fitting a logistic regression model means finding a *C* × (*m* + 1) matrix θ of real parameters (*m* + 1 of which are constrained to be zero) which approximately maximizes the likelihood of the training data. The fitted matrix of parameters, in the format above, can be obtained from the fitted model m as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0032" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0033.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">rbind</mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">rep</mi><mo>(</mo><mn mathvariant="monospace">0</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">summary</mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mo>)</mo><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">coefficients</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0033.gif)

More explicitly, for *i* = 2, …, *C* and *j* = 0, …, *m*, <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0033" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0034.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">summary</mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mo>)</mo><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">coefficients</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\]</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0034.gif)

Selection among multiple competing logistic regression models (say, ones which included different features or combinations of features) could be done by writing functions for cross-validated risk estimation, but since the parameter estimates are found by maximizing the likelihood of the training data, selection could also be done by choosing a model for which Akaike’s information criterion (AIC) is minimal. AIC is computed by the function AIC() in the stats library,

```

library(stats);
AIC(m);
```

## 14.14 Neural Networks ([Section 4.7](#c04.xhtml#c4_7))

A single-hidden-layer neural network classifier is trained using the function nnet() in the nnet library.^([11](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0009))

```

library(nnet);
```

Given a number *k* of neurons in the hidden layer, say

```

k = 2;
```

the neural network classifier is trained by the function call

```

m = nnet(as.factor(tdat[,3])˜.,size=k,maxit=10000,data=
tdatDF,MaxNWts=3000);
```

It is applied to test data edatDF using the function predict(),

```

pred.class = predict(m,edatDF,type=“class”);
risk.test(pred.class);
```

An equivalent way to do this, using R matrix and vector input instead of the R data frame and formula above, is

```

m = nnet(tdat[,1:2],class.ind(tdat[,3]),size=k,maxit=10000,
MaxNWts=3000);
pred.class = max.col(predict(m,edat));
risk.test(pred.class);
```

The number of neurons in the hidden layer, *k*, was selected to minimize the leave-one-out cross-validated estimate of risk. The functions nnet.onestart() and nnet.multistart() train multiple neural networks on a given set of data, and returns the network which maximizes the likelihood of the data (equivalently, minimizes the training risk with respect to cross-entropy loss). This is done to add some robustness to the gradient descent optimization which trains networks in nnet(), as it can get stuck in local optima.

```

nnet.onestart = function(i,datx,daty,k) {
 m = nnet(datx,class.ind(daty),size=k,maxit=10000,
MaxNWts=3000,trace=FALSE);
return(m);
}
 
nnet.multistart = function(datx,daty,k,nstart) {
 ms = lapply(1:nstart,nnet.onestart,datx=datx,daty=daty,
k=k);
 best.idx = which.min(unlist(lapply(ms,getElement,“value”)));
 return(ms[[best.idx]]);
}
```

Function nnet.loo.one() inputs a *n* × *m* matrix of feature vectors datx, an *n*\-long vector of class labels daty, number *k* of neurons in the hidden layer, and an index *o* in the set {1, …, *n*}. It predicts the class of the *o*th datum using a neural network with *k* nodes in the hidden layer and all data except the *o*th. It then compares the prediction to the true class, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0046.gif"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">daty</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>o</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0046.gif). It returns the R Boolean value TRUE (numeric value 1) if the neural network made an incorrect prediction, and returns the R Boolean value FALSE (numeric value 0) if the neural network made the correct prediction.

```

nnet.loo.one = function(datx,daty,k,o) {
 m = nnet.multistart(datx[-o,],daty[-o],k,20);
 pred = max.col(t(predict(m,datx[o,])));
 return(pred!=daty[o]);
}
```

Function nnet.loo.all() applies the function nnet.loo.one() with each datum held out in turn, and returns the average number of times the neural network made an incorrect prediction: that is, nnet.loo.all() computes the leave-one-out cross-validation estimate of risk under 0–1 loss for a neural network with *k* neurons in the hidden layer and given training data datx and daty.

```

nnet.loo.all = function(datx,daty,k) {
 if(require(parallel)) {
  errs = unlist(mclapply(1:dim(datx)[1],nnet.loo.one,
datx=datx,daty=daty,k=k,mc.cores=256));
 } else {
 errs = sapply(1:dim(datx)[1],nnet.loo.one,datx=datx,
daty=daty,k=k);
}
 return(mean(errs));
}
```

The plot shown in [Figure 14.5](#c14.xhtml#figure14-5) suggests that any number of hidden neurons in the range from two to five might be equally good.

```

ks = 1:16; errs = sapply(ks,nnet.loo.all,datx=tdat[,1:2],
daty=tdat[,3]);
plot(ks,errs,xlab=“Number of Hidden Neurons”,
ylab=“Estimated Risk”,type=“l”,ylim=c(0,max(errs)*1.05));
```

![Figure 14.5 Leave-one-out cross-validated estimates of the risk of a single-hidden-layer neural network classifier with various numbers of neurons in the hidden layer.](images/c14f005.jpg)

[**Figure 14.5**](#c14.xhtml#figureanchor14-5) Leave-one-out cross-validated estimates of the risk of a single-hidden-layer neural network classifier with various numbers of neurons in the hidden layer.

Because there are 150 training data in the example problem, and we are using leave-one-out cross-validation, and each neural network is trained from 20 random starting points (values of *θ*), and 16 different numbers of hidden neurons are considered (*k* ranging from 1 up to 16), the process described above requires training 150 × 20 × 16 = 48, 000 small neural networks. Since none of these networks depends on any of the others, they can all be trained in parallel if that is supported by the available computing environment. Function nnet.loo.all() performs its loop over the training datum left out in parallel using the mclapply() function from the parallel library if it is available, and otherwise performs the loop serially using the sapply() function.

As described in [Section 4.7](#c04.xhtml#c4_7), the parameters of a single-hidden-layer neural network can be written as two matrices, an *N* × (*m* + 1) matrix *θ*^((1)) which governs how the hidden-layer neurons respond to a feature vector, and a *C* × (*N* + 1) matrix *θ*^((2)) which governs how the output functions respond to the vector of hidden-layer neuron outputs. ## 14.15 Classification Trees ([Section 4.8](#c04.xhtml#c4_8))

A classification tree is trained using the function rpart() in the rpart library.

```

library(rpart);
```

A tree is trained by the function call

```

m = rpart(as.factor(tdat[,3])˜.,method=“class”,data=tdatDF,
cp=0.006,minsplit=2,minbucket=1);
```

It is applied to test data using the function predict(),

```

pred.class = predict(m,edatDF,type=“class”);
risk.test(pred.class);
```

As described in [Section 4.8](#c04.xhtml#c4_8), the function rpart() grows and prunes a tree to optimize the cost-complexity criterion <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0038" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0039.gif"><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>&#x03b1;</mi><mo>&#x00d7;</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi> number </mi><mi> of </mi><mi> leaf </mi><mi> nodes </mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd/><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mspace width="1.em"/><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>all</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>leaf</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>nodes</mtext></mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></munder><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><munder><mo movablelimits="true" form="prefix">min</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></munder><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0039.gif)

and this depends on a tuning parameter α which must be selected. In function rpart(), one does not specify α directly, but instead specifies a parameter cp which is related to α: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0039" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0040.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">cp</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>&#x03b1;</mi><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0040.gif)

where <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0049.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![](images/c14_ILM0049.gif)is the training estimate of risk of a tree consisting of a single leaf node. The value of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0050.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![](images/c14_ILM0050.gif)depends only on the loss function and the prior distribution of classes, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0051.gif"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0051.gif), and it can be extracted from the output of rpart() as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0040" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0041.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">frame</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">dev</mi><mo>/</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">frame</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">n</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>\[</mo><mn mathvariant="monospace">1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0041.gif)

The estimated risk <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0052.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![](images/c14_ILM0052.gif)of the one-leaf tree can be computed by setting the complexity parameter to infinity and applying the resulting tree to the training data:

```

m = rpart(as.factor(tdat[,3])˜.,method=“class”,data=tdatDF,
cp=Inf);
pred.class = predict(m,tdatDF,type=“class”);
rhat0 = mean(pred.class!=tdat[,3]);
```

In [Section 4.8](#c04.xhtml#c4_8), it was shown that in the running example, under 0–1 loss and estimating class priors from the training data, a tree consisting of a single leaf node predicts the purple class and thus has training error <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0053.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>48</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>49</mn></mrow><mn>150</mn></mfrac><mo>&#x2248;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>647</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0053.gif). If left unspecified by the user, cp defaults to the value 0.01, which in the running example corresponds to a default value of α ≈ 0.00647.

The value of α, or equivalently of cp, can be selected to minimize a cross-validated estimate of risk. An efficient method to do this, which takes advantage of the fact that a sequence of trees trained on a given dataset with increasing values of α are nested one within the other, is known and implemented in the function rpart() (see Breiman et al., 1984, [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml)). The function rpart() computes a *k*\-fold cross-validated estimate of risk, where *k* is specified by the optional rpart() argument xval (the default value of *k* is 10, and the user can turn off cross-validation by setting *k* = 0). The leave-one-out cross-validation estimate of risk is computed by setting xval=nt (recall that nt is the number of training data) in the function call

```

m = rpart(as.factor(tdat[,3])˜.,method=“class”,data=tdatDF,
cp=0,minsplit=2,minbucket=1,xval=nt);
```

Here, the complexity parameter cp=0 is set to allow the tree to maximally overfit, and the optional arguments minsplit=2 and minbucket=1 are set to prevent the tree-growing process from halting before overfitting has occurred. The cross-validated estimates of risk, and the minimum corresponding values of cp, are stored in the R matrix m$cptable. Specifically, the first column of m$cptable is a set of values of cp, the second column of m$cptable is one less than the number of leaf nodes in the trees corresponding to the values in the first column, and the fourth column of m$cptable is the cross-validated risk estimate of the trees corresponding to the values in the first column. These are displayed graphically by the following code, and shown in the left-hand cell of [Figure 14.6](#c14.xhtml#figure14-6).

```

cps = m$cptable[,1]; cps=c(cps[1]*1.1,cps);
cps[cps==0]=min(cps[cps>0]/2);
errs = m$cptable[,4]*rhat0; errs=c(errs[1],errs);
leaves=1+m$cptable[,2];
plot(cps,errs,xlab=“Complexity Parameter cp”,ylab=“Estimated
Risk“,type=”S“,ylim=c(0,max(errs)*1.05),log=”x“);
err = errs[1]; lines(c(max(cps),max(cps)*2),c(err,err),lty=2);
err = errs[length(errs)]; lines(c(min(cps),min(cps)/2),
c(err,err),lty=2);
text((cps[-length(cps)]+cps[-1])/2,errs[-1]+0.025,leaves);
```

![Figure 14.6 Leave-one-out cross-validated estimates of the risk of a classification tree, as a function of the complexity parameter cp (left), and a linear support vector machine, as a function of the penalty parameter γ (right). Both horizontal axes are plotted on a logarithmic scale. The curve plotted in the left-hand cell is drawn as a step function to emphasize that while the complexity parameter cp is real-valued, there are only a finite number of classification tree which can be produced from a given dataset. The number above each line segment of the curve in the left-hand cell is the number of leaf nodes in the tree corresponding to a given range of cp values.](images/c14f006.jpg)

[**Figure 14.6**](#c14.xhtml#figureanchor14-6) Leave-one-out cross-validated estimates of the risk of a classification tree, as a function of the complexity parameter cp (left), and a linear support vector machine, as a function of the penalty parameter γ (right). Both horizontal axes are plotted on a logarithmic scale. The curve plotted in the left-hand cell is drawn as a step function to emphasize that while the complexity parameter cp is real-valued, there are only a finite number of classification tree which can be produced from a given dataset. The number above each line segment of the curve in the left-hand cell is the number of leaf nodes in the tree corresponding to a given range of cp values.

As noted in [Section 4.8](#c04.xhtml#c4_8), in this case, selecting a classification tree which minimizes the leave-one-out risk estimate results in selecting a sub-optimal tree (it selects a 15-leaf-node tree, while a 5-leaf-node tree trained on the same data has significantly lower risk).

Classification trees can be represented by a variety of data structures. This section describes the representation used by the R library rpart: the representation used by the R library randomForest is presented in [Section 14.20](#c14.xhtml#c14_20). The function rpart() returns an R object of the class rpart, which contains the trained tree and information about how it was constructed. The trained tree can be recovered from two components of the object m: m$frame and m$splits. Component m$frame is an R data frame which has one row for each node in the tree. The *j*th node of the tree is a leaf if m$frame$var\[*j*\]=<leaf> and otherwise it is internal, in which case m$frame$var\[*j*\] is the name of the feature used for the split. Component m$splits is an R matrix which has a variable number of rows: the rows of interest here are those corresponding to internal nodes, which are indexed by the variable internal defined as follows (Therneau et al., 2017, source code for labels.rpart.R).

```
notleaf = (m$frame$var!=“<leaf>“);
idx<?hsp -1pt?> =<?hsp -1pt?> cumsum(c(1,m$frame$ncompete+m$frame$nsurrogate+notleaf))<?hsp -1pt?>;
internal = idx[c(notleaf,FALSE)];
```

Suppose that the *j*th row of m$frame happens to be the *i*th internal node of the tree, counting 1-up from the top of m$frame. Assuming that R's names for the *m* features (stored in m$frame$var) are simply the integers 1, …, *m*, let <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" numbered="no" id="c14-disp-0001a" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0042.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>bad hbox</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>&#x03c4;</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>bad hbox</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>bad hbox</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>bad hbox</mtext><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0042.gif)

A feature vector *X* which reaches this internal node is sent to the “left” child of the node—that is, the unique node corresponding to the index value 2*b* in row.names(m$frame)—if *X[k]*, τ, and *s* satisfy <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" numbered="no" id="c14-disp-0101" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0043.gif"><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.277778em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="0.277778em"/><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>&#x03c4;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.277778em"/><mi> or </mi><mspace width="0.277778em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.277778em"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="0.277778em"/><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mi>&#x03c4;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0043.gif)

and otherwise feature vector *X* is sent to the “right” child of the node—that is, the unique node corresponding to the index value 2*b* + 1 in row.names(m$frame). If, on the other hand, the *j*th row of m$frame corresponds to a leaf node, then any feature vector *X* which reaches this node is predicted to belong to the class m$frame$yval\[*j*\]. Thus, for example, the tree illustrated^([12](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0010)) in [Figure 4.22](#c04.xhtml#figure4-22) is represented by <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" ## 14.16 Support Vector Machines ([Section 4.9](#c04.xhtml#c4_9))

A support vector machine is trained using the function svm() in the e1071 library.

```

library(e1071);
```

A linear support vector machine is trained by the function call

```

m = svm(as.factor(tdat[,3])˜.,data=tdatDF,kernel=“linear”,
cost=2.112);
```

and it is applied to test data using the function predict(),

```

pred.class = predict(m,edatDF);
risk.test(pred.class);
```

The value of the penalty parameter γ (represented by the argument cost in the function svm()) was selected to minimize the leave-one-out cross-validated estimate of risk. Function svm() provides the capability to perform *k*\-fold cross-validation by calling it with the option <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0054.gif"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">cross</mi><mo>=</mo></mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0054.gif), in which case the cross-validated risk estimate can be obtained from the function’s output as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0045" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0046.gif"><mstyle scriptlevel="0" displaystyle="true"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> cv </mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">tot</mi><mo>.</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">accuracy</mi></mrow><mn>100</mn></mfrac><mo>.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0046.gif)

Thus leave-one-out cross-validation can be performed by

```

svmlin.loo.all = function(datx,daty,gamma) {
 m = svm(as.factor(daty)˜.,data=datx,kernel=“linear”,
cost=gamma,cross=dim(datx)[1]);
 return(1-m$tot.accuracy/100);
}
 
gammas = 2∧seq(-12,12);
errs = sapply(gammas,svmlin.loo.all,datx=tdatDF,
daty=tdat[,3]);
plot(log2(gammas),errs,xlab=expression(paste(“Penalty
Parameter “,log[2],”(“, gamma,”)“)),ylab=”Estimated Risk“,
type=“l”,ylim=c(0,max(errs)*1.05));
```

Given a value of γ, function svmlin.loo.all() returns the leave-one-out cross-validated estimate of the risk of a linear support vector machine with penalty parameter γ. The leave-one-out risk estimate is computed for many values of γ, and a value of γ which approximately minimizes this is found by looking at the numbers or plotting a graph, such as that shown in the right-hand cell of [Figure 14.6](#c14.xhtml#figure14-6).

Fitting a support vector machine with one of the commonly used kernels introduces one, two, or three additional parameters to be optimized in addition to the penalty parameter γ: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0046" type="mathematics"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0047.gif"><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi> polynomial </mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b1;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi>w</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#x03b2;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>&#x03b4;</mi></msup></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mi> sigmoid </mi></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">tanh</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03b1;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi>w</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#x03b2;</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> Gaussian </mi><mi> or </mi><mi> radial </mi></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">exp</mo><mo>(</mo><mo>-</mo><mi>&#x03b1;</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>w</mi><msup><mo>&#x2225;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0047.gif)

These parameters are all selected to minimize the leave-one-out cross-validated estimate of risk. For example,

```

svmpoly.loo.all = function(datx,daty,theta) {
 m = svm(as.factor(daty)˜.,data=datx,kernel=“polynomial”,
cost=theta[1],gamma=theta[2],coef0=theta[3],
degree=theta[4],cross=dim(datx)[1]);
 return(1-m$tot.accuracy/100);
}
library(stats);
opt = optim(c(1,1/nt,0,3),svmpoly.loo.all,method=
“Nelder-Mead”,datx=tdatDF,daty=tdat[,3]);
```

Given a value of *θ* (now a four-long vector), function svmpoly.loo.all() returns the leave-one-out cross-validated estimate of the risk of a support vector machine with a polynomial kernel, with penalty parameter γ = *θ*[1] and kernel parameters α = *θ*[2], β = *θ*[3], and δ = *θ*[4]. Approximately optimal values of these parameters are found using the general-purpose, multi-variate optimization function optim() from the stats library. Function optim() implements versions of several optimization algorithms: Nelder–Mead ([Section 10.2](#c10.xhtml#c10_2)), BFGS ([Section 10.1.4](#c10.xhtml#c10_1_4)), conjugate gradient (a quasi-Newton method similar in spirit to BFGS, not covered in [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml)), and simulated annealing ([Section 10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10_3)). In this application, the Nelder–Mead algorithm is a convenient choice which quickly finds a (local) minimizer of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0055.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> cv </mi></msub></math>![](images/c14_ILM0055.gif). The author was unable to find a better minimizer than the one found by Nelder–Mead, despite some effort. The approximate minimizer of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0056.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> cv </mi></msub></math>![](images/c14_ILM0056.gif)is recovered from the output of optim() as <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0047" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0048.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03b3;</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">opt</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">par</mi><mo>\[</mo><mn mathvariant="monospace">1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="4.0pt"/><mi>&#x03b1;</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">opt</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">par</mi><mo>\[</mo><mn mathvariant="monospace">2</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="6.0pt"/><mi>&#x03b2;</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">opt</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">par</mi><mo>\[</mo><mn mathvariant="monospace">3</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="4.0pt"/><mi> and </mi><mspace width="6.0pt"/><mi>&#x03b4;</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">opt</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">par</mi><mo>\[</mo><mn mathvariant="monospace">4</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0048.gif)

and the approximate minimum value is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0048" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0049.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> cv </mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">opt</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">value</mi></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0049.gif)

The optimal polynomial svm can then be fit on the training data and applied to test data by

```

theta = opt$par;
m = svm(as.factor(tdat[,3])˜.,data=tdatDF,kernel=“polynomial”,
cost=theta[1],gamma=theta[2],coef0=theta[3],
degree=theta[4]);
pred.class = predict(m,edatDF);
risk.test(pred.class);
```

As described in [Section 4.9](#c04.xhtml#c4_9), a support vector machine is a binary classifier with class labels in the set { − 1, 1}, and the class label predicted for a new feature vector *X* by a trained support vector machine is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0049" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0050.gif"><mrow><mi> sign </mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mi> is </mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi> support </mi><mi> vector </mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></munder><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0050.gif)

where <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0057.gif"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![](images/c14_ILM0057.gif)is the estimated intercept parameter and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0058.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0058.gif)are parameters of a dual optimization problem, where <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0059.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#x2260;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0059.gif)only if (*x[i]*, *y[i]*) is a support vector. As described in [Section 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c6_1), when faced with data of *C* > 2 classes, the function svm() trains a binary support vector machine to distinguish class *c* from class *d*, for all classes 1 ⩽ *c* < *d* ⩽ *C*, and the resulting <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0060.gif"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></math>![](images/c14_ILM0060.gif)classifiers vote in a committee. Thus the classifier output by svm() is determined by <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0061.gif"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></math>![](images/c14_ILM0061.gif)intercept parameters, *θ*^((*c*, *d*))[0], <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0062.gif"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></math>![](images/c14_ILM0062.gif)sets of support vectors, and <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0063.gif"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></math>![](images/c14_ILM0063.gif)sets of values <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0050" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0051.gif"><mrow><mo>{</mo><msubsup><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>:</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mtext>is</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>a</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>support</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>vector</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>the</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mtext>th</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>classifier</mtext><mo>}</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0051.gif)

where 1 ⩽ *c* < *d* ⩽ *C*. Note that a given training datum (*x[i]*, *y[i]*) may be a support vector for one, several, or none of the <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0064.gif"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></math>![](images/c14_ILM0064.gif)binary support vector machines. Within the function svm(), when the *C* class labels are the integers 1, 2, …, *C*, the binary classifier trained to distinguish class *c* from class *d* encodes class *c* as class “1” and class *d* as class “− 1” if and only if *c* < *d*.

The output of the function svm() contains all the estimated parameters of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0065.gif"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></math>![](images/c14_ILM0065.gif)models concatenated together. For 1 ⩽ *c* < *d* ⩽ *C*, let the paired indices (*c*, *d*) be written in the order <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0051" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0052.gif"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0052.gif)

and let this ordered set of paired indices be identified with the ordered set <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0066.gif"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0066.gif): explicitly, the map from a paired index (*c*, *d*) to a single index *i* is <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0052" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0053.gif"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>-</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0053.gif)

The negative of the intercept parameter of the (*c*, *d*)th classifier, − *θ*^((*c*, *d*))[0], is stored in a <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0067.gif"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></math>![](images/c14_ILM0067.gif)\-long vector m2$rho: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0053" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0054.gif"><mrow><mo>-</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mn mathvariant="monospace">2</mn><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">rho</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>\]</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0054.gif)

The support vectors used by all <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0068.gif"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced></math>![](images/c14_ILM0068.gif)classifiers are stored as the rows of a single matrix m$SV with *m* columns. The support vectors are grouped by class in the rows of m$SV: first the support vectors of class 1, then those of class 2, etc. The number of support vectors of each class is stored in the *C*\-long vector m$nSV. Thus the support vectors, as rows of m$SV, are <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" For future reference, we introduce a convenient way of indexing the support vectors of each class. Let <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0055" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0057.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">idx</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">c</mi><mo>(</mo><mn mathvariant="monospace">0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">cumsum</mi><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">nSV</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0057.gif)

so that the support vectors of class *c* are the rows <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0056" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0058.gif"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">SV</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">nSV</mi><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">idx</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo>\]</mo><mo>+</mo><mn mathvariant="monospace">1</mn><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">SV</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">m</mi><mi>&#x0024;</mi><mi mathvariant="monospace">nSV</mi><mo>\[</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">idx</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>\]</mo><mo>\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>\]</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0058.gif)

The binary support vector machine trained to distinguish class *c* from class *d* (with *c* < *d*) makes decisions for new feature vectors *X* according to <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0057" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0059.gif"><mrow><mi> sign </mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mtable><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>:</mo><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>)</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mi> is </mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi> support </mi><mi> vector </mi></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>the</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>\`\`</mtext><mi>c</mi><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>vs.</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mi>d</mi><mtext>""</mtext><mspace width="4.pt"/><mtext>classifier</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></munder><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>K</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0059.gif)

where the superscripts (*c*, *d*) indicate that the trained dual parameters <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0069.gif"><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03c8;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup></math>![](images/c14_ILM0069.gif)and the assignment of class labels to the set { − 1, 1} depends on the classes *c* and *d*: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0058" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0060.gif"><mrow><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> if </mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> if </mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0060.gif)

In the above expression, the sum can be taken over a larger set of vectors (because ψ^((*c*, *d*))[*i*] = 0 unless *x[i]* is a support vector for the “*c* vs. *d*” classifier), so the binary support ## 14.17 Bootstrap Aggregation ([Section 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c6_3))

The following two functions enable implementation of any committee classification method by predicting the class which wins a weighted plurality vote. Function weighted.count() inputs class label *c*, a vector *v* of class labels, and a vector *w* of weights (which may be positive or negative, and may or may not all be equal to each other), and outputs the sum of the weights in *w* corresponding to the occurrences of class *c* in *v*: <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0063" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0065.gif"><mrow><munder><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0065.gif)

```

weighted.count = function(c,v,w) {
 return(sum(w[which(v==c)])); }
```

Function vote() combines weighted.count() and max.col() to input a vector *v* of class labels and a vector *w* of weights and output a class label which receives a maximal sum of weighted votes, with ties decided uniformly at random among all classes which received the same sum of weighted votes.

```

vote = function(v,w) {
 votes = sapply(1:nc,weighted.count,v=v,w=w);
 return(max.col(t(votes)));
}
```

Thus *L* trained classifiers can be combined into a committee by collecting their votes into a vector (*v*[1], …, *v[L]*), and the weights of their votes into a vector (*w*[1], …, *w[L]*), and applying the function vote().

The committee methods of bagging, boosting, and arcing will all be illustrated using trees as the base learners, specifically stumps. A *stump* is a tree which is constrained to have at most two leaves. The following function applies the tree-training function rpart() from the rpart library to construct a stump.^([14](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0012))

```

library(rpart);
train.stump = function(y,x,wt=NULL) {
 if(length(wt)==0) { wt=rep(1,length(y)); }
 m = rpart(as.factor(y)˜.,data=x,method=“class”,maxdepth=1,
cp=0,minsplit=2,weights=wt);
 return(m);
}
```

A committee of *L* (or in code, nbase) bagged stumps is trained by the following code. Although it would be more efficient to use the R function lapply() (or mclapply(), since bagged classifiers can be trained in parallel), we have used a for loop to simplify comparison of the code for bagging with later code for boosting and arcing. This block of code outputs an *L*\-long R list of trained stumps, called committee, and an *L* × *n* matrix oob. If the training datum (*x[i]*, *y[i]*) is out-of-bag for the *l*th classifier, then <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0084.gif"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">oob</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0084.gif)is the class predicted by the *l*th classifier for feature vector *x[i]*. Otherwise, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0085.gif"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="monospace">oob</mi><mo>\[</mo></mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>\]</mo></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0085.gif)is the special R value NA to show that (*x[i]*, *y[i]*) is in-bag for the *l*th classifier (the function votes() ignores values of NA, so using NA as the in-bag indicator simplifies implementation of out-of-bag risk estimation).

```

nbase = 1000; bagsize = nt;
committee = vector(“list”,nbase); oob = matrix(NA,nbase,nt);
for(i in 1:nbase) {
 idx = sample(1:nt,bagsize,replace=TRUE);
 m = train.stump(tdat[idx,3],tdatDF[idx,]);
 committee[[i]] = m;
 oob[i,setdiff(1:nt,idx)] = predict(m,newdata=tdatDF[-idx,],
type=“class”);
}
```

The parameters of a bagged classifier are the number *L* of classifiers used and the size of the bootstrap sample on which each classifier is trained (and, of course, the choice of classifier and any parameters it may use). As noted in Section 6, the size of the bootstrap sample can be quite important, and can be selected by minimizing the out-of-bag estimate of risk, which is computed by the following code.

```

pred.oob = apply(oob,2,vote,w=rep(1,nbase));
errs = pred.oob!=tdat[,3]; risk.oob = mean(errs);
```

Once <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0086.gif"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">nbase</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0086.gif)and bagsize are chosen, the trained bagged classifier can be applied to new data,

```

pred.stumps = do.call(rbind,lapply(committee,predict,
newdata=edatDF,type=“class”));
pred.class = apply(pred.stumps,2,vote,w=rep(1,nbase));
risk.test(pred.class);
```

## 14.18 Boosting ([Section 6.6](#c06.xhtml#c6_6))

The following code implements a classifier consisting of <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0087.gif"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">nbase</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0087.gif)boosted stumps. It uses the same R structures as the code for bagging, and otherwise is a translation of the Adaboost pseudocode shown in [Figure 6.7](#c06.xhtml#figure6-7), using the multi-class generalization of Zhu et al. (2009) described in [Section 6.6](#c06.xhtml#c6_6).

```

nbase = 1000; committee = vector(“list”,nbase);
committee.risk = rep(NA,nbase); data.weights = rep(1/nt,nt);
for(i in 1:nbase) {
m = train.stump(tdat[,3],tdatDF,data.weights);
committee[[i]] = m;
pred.class = predict(m,tdatDF,type=“class”);
idx = which(pred.class!=tdat[,3]);
committee.risk[i] = risk = sum(data.weights[idx]);
data.weights[idx] = data.weights[idx] * (1-risk)/risk *
(nc-1);
data.weights = data.weights/sum(data.weights);
}
```

Applying a trained, boosted classifier is similar to applying the bagged classifier, except that the individual stumps vote with different weights,

```

pred.stumps = do.call(rbind,lapply(committee,predict,
newdata=edatDF,type=“class”));
committee.weights = log((1-committee.risk)/committee.risk*
(nc-1));
pred.class = apply(pred.stumps,2,vote,w=committee.weights);
risk.test(pred.class);
```

## 14.19 Arcing ([Section 6.7](#c06.xhtml#c6_7))

There is only a small difference between boosting and arcing, in terms of the code needed to implement them. An implementation of arcing is exactly the same boosting above, except that the first line of the boosting loop, which is deterministic,

```

m = train.stump(tdat[,3],tdatDF,data.weights);
```

is replaced by a randomized process,

```

idx = sample(1:nt,nt,replace=TRUE,prob=data.weights);
m = train.stump(tdat[idx,3],tdatDF[idx,]);
```

## 14.20 Random Forests ([Section 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c6_5))

A random forest is trained using the function randomForest() in the randomForest library:

```

library(randomForest);
m = randomForest(as.factor(tdat[,3])˜.,data=tdat[,1:2],
ntree=1000);
```

Selecting a random forest is equivalent to training some number (ntree) of generally over-fit trees. The *i*th tree in the forest can be viewed by using the function getTree,

```
getTree(m,<y><i> i</i></y>)
```

for <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/c14\_ILM0088.gif"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="monospace">ntree</mi></mrow></math>![](images/c14_ILM0088.gif). When all features are real-valued, a random forest tree reported by getTree() is represented as a *k* × 6 matrix <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="c14-disp-0064" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/c14\_M0066.gif"><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd><mtd/><mtd><mo>&#x22ee;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mo>&#x22ef;</mo></mtd><mtd><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>

![numbered Display Equation](images/c14_M0068.gif)

Since random forests are based on bagging, the out-of-bag estimate of risk can be used. The out-of-bag confusion matrix is stored in m$confusion, and the confusion matrix and the out-of-bag risk estimate with respect to 0–1 loss^([15](#c14.xhtml#c14-note-0013)) can be obtained from

```

print(m);
```

Predictions using the trained random forest m are made on the test data using the function predict(),

```

pred.class = predict(m,edat);
risk.test(pred.class);
```

4.  *Differentiating the result of part C with respect to τ,* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="bapp02-disp-0010" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/bapp02\_M0007.gif"><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>&#x03c4;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03c4;</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03c4;</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msup><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>p</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#x03c0;</mi></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>&#x03c4;</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>
    
    ![numbered Display Equation](images/bapp02_M0007.gif)
    
    *Setting this equal to zero and solving for τ yields a unique critical point,*
    
    <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="bapp02-disp-0011" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/bapp02\_M0008.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c4;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfrac><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mfrac></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>
    
    ![numbered Display Equation](images/bapp02_M0008.gif)
    
    *The derivative* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0001.gif"><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>&#x03c4;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03c4;</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0001.gif)*approaches zero from below as τ → −∞ and approaches zero from above as τ → ∞, so* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0002.gif"><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>&#x03c4;</mi></mrow></mfrac><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03c4;</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0002.gif)*is negative to the left and positive to the right of the unique critical point, which is therefore a minimum. Note that as μ*[1] *→ μ*[2] *from the left, the critical point goes to ± ∞ according to the sign of the log term.*
    
5.  *If* L(1, 2) = L(2, 1), *the critical point is* <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="bapp02-disp-0012" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/bapp02\_M0009.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c4;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo form="prefix">log</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mfrac></mfenced></mrow></math></displayedItem>
    
    ![numbered Display Equation](images/bapp02_M0009.gif)
    
    *and if, furthermore*, <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0003.gif"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0003.gif), *the critical point is*
    
    <displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="bapp02-disp-0013" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/bapp02\_M0010.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03c4;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem>
    
    ![numbered Display Equation](images/bapp02_M0010.gif)
    
    *which is the midpoint between* μ[1] *and* μ[2].
    

**Exercise 2.4** *Consider the following algorithm: given a training data set* {(*x*[1], *y*[1]), …, (*x[n]*, *y[n]*)} *and a feature vector x to classify, if* *x* = *x[i] for any i*, *predict y[i]*, *and otherwise draw the prediction uniformly at random from the set of class labels* {1, …, *C*}. *The training risk for this algorithm is zero, and the actual risk is* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0004.gif"><mfrac><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></mfrac></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0004.gif).

*The last line is recognizable as the risk of approximation* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0005.gif"><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0005.gif), <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0006.gif"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0006.gif), when for each class *c the loss incurred by misclassifying *c* as any other class is <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0007.gif"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0007.gif)(and zero loss is incurred by correctly classifying class *c*). There are certainly classification problems in which some classes are rare (have small marginal probability) and important (incur high loss for misclassification). But the class-averaged inaccuracy criterion seems to say that *a class is important because it is rare*, or at any rate that the importance of a class is proportional to how rare it is.*

*Setting the gradient equal to zero and solving for θ yields a unique critical point,*

<displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="bapp02-disp-0023" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/bapp02\_M0013.gif"><mrow><mi>&#x03b8;</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/bapp02_M0013.gif)

*provided that* **x**^T**x** *is invertible. Since* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0009.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi> train </mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>&#x03b8;</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>&#x2265;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0009.gif)*and is quadratic, this critical point is the unique global minimum.*

**Exercise 3.5** *Let* **1** *denote the n*\-*long vector* (1, 1, …, 1), *and let v[T]*, *v[R]*, *and v[M]* be *n*\-*long vectors defined by*

*Observe that*

<displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="bapp02-disp-0028" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/bapp02\_M0015.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/bapp02_M0015.gif)

*Also*, *v[M] and v[R] are orthogonal because*

<displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="bapp02-disp-0029" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/bapp02\_M0016.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">i</mi><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">i</mi><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>-</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#x203e;</mo></mover><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><msup><mrow/><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">i</mi><mo>-</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/bapp02_M0016.gif)

*and Exercise 3.3 established that* **hh** = **h** *(so the first term on the right-hand side is zero) and that* **h1** = **i1** *since* **1** *is in the column space of* **x** *(so the second term on the right-hand side is zero). Since the squared Euclidean lengths of v[R]*, *v[M]*, *and v[T] are respectively RSS, MSS, and TSS, the Pythagorean theorem establishes that*

<displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="bapp02-disp-0030" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/bapp02\_M0017.gif"><mrow><mi> TSS </mi><mo>=</mo><mi> MSS </mi><mo>+</mo><mi> RSS </mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/bapp02_M0017.gif)

**Exercise 3.9** *Here, the values* 1 *and* − 1 *are stand-ins for any positive and negative numbers, respectively. They need not be equal.*

1.  *θ[*a*] =* −1 and *θ*[*c*] = 1.
2.  *θ*[*c*] = 1 and *θ*[2*c*] = −1.
3.  *θ*[*a*] = 1, *θ*[*c*] = 1, *and θ*[(*a*, *c*)] = −1.
4.  *θ*[*a*] = 1, *θ*[*c*] = 1, *and θ*[(*a*, *c*)] = 1.
5.  *The intercept parameter θ*[0] *is a measure of how much the person likes food, on average.*
6.  *Replace the continuous feature* *x[b] with the binary feature* \[*x[b]* > 0\]. *Make θ*[*b*] *large and negative.*

**Exercise 4.1** *Let* P(*Y* | *X*) *be some conditional distribution with the property that*

<displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="bapp02-disp-0049" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/bapp02\_M0018.gif"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&lt;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/bapp02_M0018.gif)

*for at least one value of (*X*, *Y*). The Bayes classifier with respect to this conditional distribution is*

<displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="bapp02-disp-0050" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/bapp02\_M0019.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi> Bayes </mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>=</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi> argmin </mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>c</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>=</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>=</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><msub><mi> argmin </mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mo>{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#x22ef;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>}</mo></mrow></msub><munderover><mo>&#x2211;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>=</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/bapp02_M0019.gif)

*where the notation emphasizes the dependence on* P. *Let* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0010.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0010.gif)*be the probability distribution which puts probability* 1 *on* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0011.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi> Bayes </mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0011.gif), *that is*,

<displayedItem xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" xmlns="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley" xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" id="bapp02-disp-0051" type="mathematics" numbered="no"><math display="block" location="image\_n/bapp02\_M0020.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mrow><mi> if </mi><mspace width="4pt"/><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi> Bayes </mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mi> else </mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/bapp02_M0020.gif)

*Then* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0012.gif"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi> Bayes </mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi> Bayes </mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0012.gif)for all <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0013.gif"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#x2208;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">X</mi></mrow></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0013.gif)but <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0014.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mo>&#x2260;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0014.gif)(because <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0015.gif"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo>&#x02dc;</mo></mover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mo>|</mo><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mi>X</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0015.gif)*is always* 0 *or* 1, *and* P(*Y* | *X*) is not).

mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.166667em"/><mfrac><mi>p</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mfenced></mrow></mstyle></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="right"><mi> else </mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math></displayedItem> ![numbered Display Equation](images/bapp02_M0022.gif)

*Therefore the answer is yes, the Bayes classifier has the form “predict class 1 if the feature falls below a threshold, and otherwise predict class 2.” The solution of part D of Exercise 2.2 is the Bayes classifier.*

*and using the value* <math xmlns:wiley="http://www.wiley.com/namespaces/wiley/wiley" xmlns:cms="http://cms.wiley.com" xmlns:dctm="http://www.documentum.com" display="inline" location="image\_n/bapp02\_ILM0016.gif"><mrow><msub><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#x03bc;</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></math>![](images/bapp02_ILM0016.gif)*in the above solution causes the derivatives of the log-likelihood with respect to both μ[*c*] and Σ[*c*] to be zero simultaneously.*
